papers.abstract: Video generation models can now depict remarkably realistic motion. Yet it is unclear how to use this motion beyond pixels: to animate a specific 3D asset and replay the animation in its 3D scene. For instance, a video model can show a monkey jumping over a crossbar, but it cannot return that jump as replayable 3D motion placed in the 3D scene. Here we present a model that directly co-generates the video and 3D motion for any supplied rig, along with a camera that registers this motion to the scene. Prior video-motion models either handle only human skeletons, often adding billions of parameters, or triangulate 3D motion from generated 2D pose maps. We instead keep 3D motion in a separate model that supports arbitrary skeletons, and connect it to a pretrained video model through a small set of cross-attention layers. This separation lets the motion model first learn how skeletons move from motion-only data, which is easier to obtain and augment than paired video. Additionally, our model learns to locate each joint in the video frames, which lets us recover the camera and place the 3D motion in the scene. To train across many skeletons, we use a generative video editor to place animated 3D assets in scenes suited to their actions, curating the edits so their known motion remains valid. Together with human and robot video, this yields nearly 200K training pairs. Our evaluations demonstrate that our model animates diverse rigs from text more faithfully than video-first pipelines, and its motion responds to the surrounding scene. It also turns video into rig motion, rig motion into video, and enables keyframe-based control of the 3D motion. Videos and additional results are available on our project page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/par/projects/jca/.
authors: Noam Rotstein, Yoad Tewel, Chen Tessler, Haggai Maron, Gal Chechik, Or Litany, Yoni Kasten, Yuval Atzmon
bullets: Addresses the gap between realistic video generation and usable 3D animation for specific assets.
Separates an arbitrary-skeleton 3D motion model from a pretrained video model, linking them with lightweight cross-attention.
Predicts joint locations in video to recover the camera and register 3D motion in the scene.
Uses curated synthetic edits plus human and robot video to create nearly 200K training pairs.
Supports text-to-motion/video, video-to-rig motion, rig-motion-to-video, and keyframe control; evaluations report more faithful, scene-responsive animation than video-first pipelines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture overview. Given a text prompt, a rig, and an optional reference image, the model jointly denoises video latents Zv and motion tokens Zm. A graph network encodes the rig into per-joint descriptors D, using the joints’ 2D locations in the reference image, and these condition the motion branch; a graph-attention layer inside each Motion DiT block propagates features along the rig edges. Zero-initialized cross-attention bridges exchange features in both directions at paired blocks, each branch querying the other’s intermediate features, so joint training begins from the two pretrained branches acting as they did in isolation. An auxiliary joint-localization head (right) attends from joint features to video patches and returns each joint’s image position as a weighted combination of patch coordinates, giving 2D–3D correspondences used to fit a camera.

Figure 3: Text-driven rig animation across diverse assets. Each row shows a text prompt, an input mesh, and sampled poses from animations generated by competing methods and JCA (ours). Our method more faithfully captures the requested actions while preserving the asset’s geometry.

Figure 5: Scene-aware rig animation and motion localization. Given a penguin rig, a rendered initial frame of a snowy 3D scene, and a text prompt, our model jointly generates video and 3D rig motion. Top: frames from the generated video, where the penguin moves forward and slides down the snowy slope. Middle: the raw 3D motion produced by the motion branch, rendered in the input scene before localization. The penguin’s motion is not aligned with the depicted scene geometry and, in later frames, appears beneath the snow surface. Bottom: the same generated motion after applying our joint-localization and camera-alignment scheme described in section 3.3. The estimated alignment correctly places the motion on the visible penguin and registers it with the generated video and scene.

Figure 6: Prompt-adherence evaluation of one animation with GPT-6 Astra. In the first turn, the judge is given the asset’s short description and 48 frames of the animation, 16 from each of the front, right, and left views, each frame labeled with its view; the figure shows two frames per view. It is asked to describe the motion it observes in chronological order. In the second turn, it scores the motion against the action prompt. The complete prompts and responses are given in section B.3.

papers.abstract: Current world models for explicit world simulation typically follow two distinct pathways: (1) video generative models (e.g., Sora), which simulate realistic appearances but fail to preserve 3D consistency; and (2) 3D generative models (e.g., Marble), which generate geometrically consistent scenes but often yield static, less realistic observations. We present AEON, a unified framework that bridges video-based and 3D-based world models and combines the benefits of both. The key insight of AEON lies in a generative model that operates within the text- or image-conditioned video latent space while producing renderable 4D graphics primitives---specifically, 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS)---as the explicit world representation. We train a 4D reconstruction model to predict both 4DGS and camera poses from monocular videos, serving as our initialized 4D decoder. Furthermore, we design a domain adapter that translates generative video latents into reconstructive 4D latents through a distillation process on the video VAE. AEON naturally supports video-based world modeling by rendering 4DGS at predicted camera trajectories, and constructs a persistent 4D environment with scene dynamics for realistic world simulation. Consequently, AEON empowers a diverse range of world modeling applications and achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks. Project Page: https://weiqi-zhang.github.io/AEON
authors: Weiqi Zhang, Wenyuan Zhang, Yu-Shen Liu, Junsheng Zhou
bullets: Addresses the gap between video models’ visual realism and 3D models’ geometric consistency and persistence.
Operates in text- or image-conditioned video latent space while producing explicit, renderable 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS).
Trains a monocular-video 4D reconstruction model to predict 4DGS and camera poses, then adapts generative video latents through VAE distillation.
Supports video-based simulation by rendering 4DGS along predicted camera trajectories and enables persistent dynamic environments.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of AEON. Top (1). The 4D Reconstruction Model (4DRM) decodes a monocular video into a 4DGS world through four task-specific heads that respectively predict depth, Gaussian appearance, dynamic evolution, and camera poses. The resulting primitives are rasterized into RGB, depth, and normal maps for end-to-end supervision. Bottom (2). We train AEON for generative world modeling by distilling the world generative capability of a frozen video diffusion model (e.g., Wan 2.2 [38]) and the 4D reconstructive capability of a teacher 4DRM via a Domain Adapter and a learnable student 4DRM. The generated explicit 4DGS world enables versatile world modeling applications.

papers.abstract: Game engines and coding agents can specify the layout, motion, and camera of a scene, yet turning such coarse structure into realistic video requires a renderer that follows the structure and completes the appearance it leaves open. Existing renderers are tied to the representation of one engine, need tens of denoising steps or a costly distillation of their own, and learn from conditions that are not aligned with their target videos. We present SolarRenderer, a structure-conditioned video renderer that adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B backbone with two lightweight LoRAs. Structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone at the positions of the frames they describe, without a type identifier and described only in plain text, so that a single control LoRA follows arbitrary structural representations. Starting from a pretrained four-step LoRA, structure-guided distribution matching renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling, while preserving the learned control. A block-causal variant extends the same design to streaming and renders 768p video in real time. To train the model, we build a frame-aligned corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos. Experiments on an in-distribution test set and a generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations show that SolarRenderer achieves state-of-the-art results across both, and generalizes to 11 unseen representations, including pose skeletons, drawings, and point clouds.
authors: Guian Fang, Shengju Qian, Dongyue Lu, Junchao Huang, Lutao Jiang, Xin Wang, Yiren Song, Li Jiang, Mike Zheng Shou

papers.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.
authors: Yazhuo Liu, Kunqing Ding, Xiaoguo Gong, Zifeng Wang, Yichen Yang, Yifeng Che, Wen Chen, Josh Kacher, Olivier Pierron, Shigenobu Ogata, Ting Zhu
bullets: Targets general asymmetric grain boundaries, which are common in polycrystalline materials but difficult to study because of structural complexity and interfacial mismatch.

Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt grain boundaries in nickel to characterize interfacial defects and diverse deformation modes.
Shows that secondary grain-boundary misfit dislocations substantially affect sliding resistance, while metastable structures can cause anomalously high shear resistance.
Demonstrates a workflow connecting systematic computational screening with targeted, mechanistic materials analysis.

papers.abstract: Dexterous multi-finger hands hold promise to unlock diverse skills like functional grasps, in-hand reorientation, and dynamic handover that the human-designed world assumes, yet existing learning recipes force a trade-off. Goal-reaching reinforcement learning generalizes to arbitrary object poses but, lacking any human prior, converges to unnatural and unreliable finger strategies; motion tracking reproduces human-like behavior from a single clip but cannot deviate from it. We present AdaDex, a goal-conditioned RL framework that turns a single hand-object trajectory of a few seconds---from mocap data or HOI reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video---into an adaptable dexterous skill. At the core of AdaDex is Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking: a shared policy is trained on two populations of massively parallel environments: motion tracking environments trained with dense motion tracking objective, which instill the human prior from human motion; and generalization environments with noised initial states and goals and a sparse object-success reward, which force the skill to work far off the reference. From seconds of human motion per skill, the resulting policies can learn diverse adaptable dexterous skills, such as functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch. Our method outperforms baselines in terms of generalization and functionality, and we demonstrate transfer across simulators and to the real world. Project page: https://yuxuank.com/AdaDex/.
authors: Yuxuan Kuang, Jiashun Wang, Yixuan Sun, Yufei Ye, Sungjae Park, Umar Iqbal, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Shubham Tulsiani
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between natural human-like behavior and robustness to varied object poses and goals.

Supports demonstrations from mocap or hand–object reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video.
Learns skills including functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and throw-and-catch.
Reports improved generalization and functionality over baselines, with transfer across simulators and to the real world.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Overview of our RGB-D hand-object reconstruction pipeline. A table plane is estimated from depth points using RANSAC. We align hand translations to the observed depth, then apply GeoCalibbased gravity alignment and table-height alignment to express the hand, object, and table in a shared world coordinate frame.

papers.abstract: Motivated by the human ability to integrate experience across language, perception, and action, we introduce UniWALM, a unified world-action-language model that learns video, action, and language in a single shared representation, where each modality is both a conditioning signal and a supervision target. We ask: can jointly generating language enrich this shared representation, improving manipulation and supporting memory-dependent behavior? Unlike prior approaches that attach a reasoning or vision-language model to a video-action backbone and run them as distinct stages, UniWALM unifies all three modalities inside a single mixture-of-transformers backbone whose per-modality diffusion heads co-denoise synchronously, decoding subtask and textual memory in the same pass as action with no separate planning stage; the generated language is re-consumed on the next step, closing a language-as-memory loop without an external planner or memory bank. To keep the action stream reliable under this richer objective, we further introduce Flow Matching with Correction (FMC), a training objective that teaches recovery from perturbed action trajectories at no inference-time cost. UniWALM consistently improves over same-backbone baselines (e.g., FastWAM) on compositional pick-and-place (MolmoSpaces) and across the memory-dependent subset of RMBench, where it reaches 34.5% without any pretrained language or reasoning model and exceeds Mem-0's keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using only a single anchor frame. On a real-world Find-the-Item task, generating textual memory lifts success from 11.1% to 61.1%, while state-of-the-art VLAs stay at or below chance (<=33.3%).
authors: Rahul Sajnani, Diego Romeres, Mingyuan Zhang, Kai Gao, Carl Qi, Baichuan Huang, Srinath Sridhar, Dylan Randle, Lillian J. Ratliff, Jose Barreiros, Manikantan Nambi, Jeroen Vanbaar
bullets: Learns shared representations across video, actions, and language, with each modality serving as both input and training target.
Uses a mixture-of-transformers backbone with synchronized modality-specific diffusion heads to generate actions and textual memory in one pass.
Re-consumes generated language on subsequent steps, creating a language-as-memory loop without an external memory bank or planner.
Introduces Flow Matching with Correction to improve recovery from perturbed action trajectories without inference-time overhead.
Reports gains on compositional manipulation, memory-dependent benchmarks, and a real-world Find-the-Item task; scope is demonstrated on these tasks and settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of UniWALM. UniWALM is a unified mixture-of-transformers (MoT) world-action-language model that co-denoises video, language, and action in a single shared representation. Given the current observation, task instruction, proprioception, an optional visual memory F (one or more frames; in our experiments a single anchor at episode start), and the previously generated textual memory, UniWALM processes inputs through a (a) video, (b) language, and (c) action DiT that share features via unified self-attention. The language stream emits a subtask together with a textual memory string, which is re-consumed as the prompt on the next control step, closing a language-as-memory loop across time. Video generation is disabled at inference, so the language and action DiTs run without producing future frames.

Figure 5: Qualitative Results of UniWALM. Our work can perform various tasks including: (a) pick and place tasks, (b) find the item memory task, (c) simple high-dexterous task, and (d) complex dexterous bi-manual task involving difficult items to grasp. For each demonstration, the top row displays the subtasks and memory predicted by the model, and the task instruction is shown below the images. Note, in (b) we make the task difficult by shifting items mid way during roll out for the policy to update its memory. In (d) UniWALM reasons about both the hands and retries to remove objects with varying geometries.

Figure 3: Flow Matching with Correction (FMC). A clean action x0 (green path) and its perturbed counterpart x0 + ϵ1 (red path) are noised to the same time t. The model is trained to transport the perturbed sample back onto the clean trajectory within ∆t (yellow arrow), while the clean branch follows standard flow matching. This requires no extra conditioning or model capacity and leaves inference unchanged.

Figure 11: FMC vs vanilla flow matching on 2D robot trajectories (overlay view). Blue curves are ground-truth demonstrations; red are model-generated trajectories, overlaid for direct comparison. Top row: vanilla flow matching frequently drifts off the demonstration manifold, truncates the shape, or collapses mode coverage. Bottom row: FMC tracks the ground-truth distribution more faithfully across all three shape classes, consistent with the quantitative Chamfer improvements in Tab. 6.

Figure 6: RMBench M(n) qualitative rollouts. Each row is a successful UniWALM rollout on one M(n) task; we display a subsampled sequence of inference steps for clarity. papers.abstract: Understanding human needs and selecting responses require distinct judgments that aggregate accuracy can obscure. We introduce PsycheMME, a video benchmark informed by psychology, with eight capabilities spanning grounding, states, needs, interaction decisions, memory, and risk. Drawing on Social Information Processing and the Perception-Action Cycle, this organization separates human understanding from response selection. We construct 1,000 questions from 630 episodes through independent answering with proposed references withheld and expert review. Our Reasoning-Verified protocol weights answer credit by the support and logical consistency of explicit rationales against annotated cues. Across 17 models, Timing has the lowest Verified scores and credit retention, with weaker support judgments for correct Timing answers. Models with similar Need scores still differ in answer completeness on open questions. Input controls and SFT/GRPO examine context dependence and adaptation. Evaluating answers alongside rationales locates where models fail across understanding, response selection, and justification.
authors: Heran Hu, Yuhang Dong, Zhucun Xue, Kaiwei Chen, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
bullets: Covers eight capabilities, including grounding, mental states, needs, interaction decisions, memory, and risk.
Uses 1,000 questions from 630 video episodes, with expert-reviewed references and withheld-answer construction.
Its Reasoning-Verified protocol credits answers based on rationale support and logical consistency with annotated cues.
Across 17 models, Timing is the weakest capability, while models with similar Need scores vary in open-ended answer completeness.
The benchmark helps identify failures in understanding, response selection, and justification; its scope centers on the evaluated video episodes and capabilities.

papers.abstract: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster.
authors: Michael Chen, Hong Chul Nam, Xi Deng, Anima Anandkumar
bullets: Uses reflecting obstacle boundaries and a goal Dirichlet condition to preserve navigation signals along long routes.
Extends the Walk on Stars Monte Carlo solver to higher-dimensional, mesh-free PDE computation.
Amortizes noisy, partially converged field estimation by learning geometry-to-field mappings.
Combines predicted global fields with bounded local search at inference time.
Across four noise levels, achieves 95–100% success on a 4D replanning benchmark with the lowest runtime; at the highest noise, it is 3.29–32.15× faster than alternatives.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence has recently been assessed through generative tasks such as spatially grounded image editing, yet language-guided generation of spatially consistent views from partial multi-view observations remains underexplored. We introduce MindView, a benchmark for generative multi-view spatial intelligence with 1,500 samples from 513 scenes across three indoor datasets. Its seven tasks form two families: geometry-dominant tasks specify changes in camera position and orientation, while semantics-dominant tasks require inferring target viewpoints by grounding referred objects and interpreting spatial relations and reference-frame cues. Evaluation of eleven generators reveals substantial room for improvement on MindView. A paired context analysis further shows that all eleven generators obtain lower overall scores under the expanded context setting. These findings motivate us to investigate whether task-specific supervision can improve target-view generation and whether models can use additional multi-view evidence effectively. We therefore fine-tune BAGEL on the MindView training dataset, improving its overall score by 24.3 points and yielding gains across all seven MindView tasks. Beyond these generation gains, the fine-tuned model also yields higher scores on three spatial-understanding benchmarks without training on their annotations, suggesting that learning to generate spatially grounded views may benefit spatial understanding. To improve evidence utilization under expanded context, we propose MindCue, a training-free spatial evidence selector guided by a target-view hypothesis. MindCue reverses the drop in overall score under expanded context and outperforms the standard-context baseline. Overall, MindView provides a concrete testbed for generative multi-view spatial intelligence.
authors: Yanbo Wang, Siqi Luo, Siyu Zhang, Chenming Zhu, Wenzhao Zheng, Qian Yu, Juncheng Yan, Bin Fu, Tai Wang, Yu Qiao, Yihao Liu, Jiwen Lu

Evaluates 11 generators and finds substantial room for improvement, with performance declining when more context is provided.
Fine-tuning BAGEL on MindView improves its overall score by 24.3 points and benefits all seven tasks.
The fine-tuned model also improves three spatial-understanding benchmarks without using their annotations.
MindCue, a training-free target-view-guided evidence selector, reverses the expanded-context performance drop and surpasses the standard-context baseline.

papers.abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) can accelerate language-model decoding by drafting several tokens and verifying them in a single target-model pass. However, the best speculation horizon changes with context: longer drafts offer greater amortization when reliable, but can waste compute on suffixes discarded after a rejection. Unlike autoregressive drafting, where a stopping rule can decide token by token, MTP must fix the horizon before drafting, as all heads fire in the same forward pass. We therefore formulate horizon selection as an online control problem, using verification feedback to learn how far the draft can be trusted in each context, and introduce Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP): a lightweight controller that requires no retraining and leaves the exact verifier unchanged. To guide horizon selection, we characterize the expected number of tokens committed at each horizon via acceptance survival, the probability that a draft prefix is fully accepted. Before each round, AMTP predicts how far the draft is likely to survive and picks the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second, learning freely from every verification pass. Theoretically, we show that any online learner's prediction error translates into throughput regret against the best horizon for each context, and in turn into a bound on wall-clock completion time. With online gradient descent, this regret is sublinear. Across five draft-target pairings built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with Medusa heads, Meta's MTP models, and Qwen3-4B-Inst-2507-MTP, evaluated on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, AMTP decodes up to 4.1x faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings, with throughput gains of up to 10%.
authors: Emile Anand, Mohammed Rehan Parwani, Xinyuan Cao
bullets: MTP faces a context-dependent trade-off: longer drafts can improve amortization but waste compute when rejected.
AMTP treats horizon selection as online control and predicts draft-prefix survival before each decoding round.
It chooses the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second using feedback from every verification pass.
Theoretical analysis links horizon-prediction error to throughput regret and wall-clock completion time; online gradient descent gives sublinear regret.
Across 10 draft-target settings on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, AMTP reaches up to 4.1× faster decoding and matches or exceeds fixed-window MTP in 8 settings, with up to 10% throughput gains.

papers.abstract: Evaluating and post-training robot policies through physical interaction is costly and difficult to scale, motivating action-conditioned world models as interactive simulators. However, visually plausible predictions can misrepresent contact dynamics, providing unreliable feedback for policy evaluation and learning. We introduce PhysCanvas, a state-consistent visuo-tactile world model for contact-rich robot manipulation. PhysCanvas unifies multi-view RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, task state, and actions within a unified vision space. All modalities share a video VAE and pretrained generative backbone, allowing optical touch to reuse visual and temporal priors. Motion images derived through forward kinematics and camera projection provide spatially aligned action conditioning, while an initial RGB anchor and updated reference observations guide sequential generation. Our consistency-aware post-training uses the frozen Scene Reward Model, Modality Reward Model, and State Reward Model to supervise scene preservation, visual-tactile compatibility, and agreement with real task outcomes. The resulting world model supports closed-loop policy rollouts for evaluation and provides imagined interactions and rewards for GRPO policy updates. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, when policies are rolled out in the world model, State Reward Model supervision increases the arithmetic mean of task-wise Pearson correlations between world-model and real-world success rates from 0.602 to 0.885. Policy post-training in the reward-guided world model further increases $\pi_{0.5}$'s mean real-world success rate from a 59.1% SFT baseline to 70.8%. These results demonstrate the value of unified multimodal modeling and consistency-aware post-training for robot policy evaluation and learning. Project page: https://zebinx.github.io/PhysCanvas_HomePage/.

papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning remains underexplored for low-resource languages, including Dialectal Arabic. To bridge this gap, we introduce the DAR-MGSM (Dialectal Arabic Multilingual Grade School Math) Benchmark, the first manually curated benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning in Dialectal Arabic. DAR-MGSM consists of math word problems (MWPs) requiring multi-step reasoning and covers five major Arabic dialects alongside Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). The benchmark comprises two parallel versions: translated-only and translated & culturally localized. The latter version adapts entities and references to regional varieties. We evaluate eleven Arabic-centric and multilingual large language models on DAR-MGSM. The results show that the performance generally declines on the localized version, highlighting the challenges introduced by culturally grounded adaptations. However, the magnitude of this effect varies across models, with Arabic-centric models exhibiting different levels of sensitivity to localization. A mechanistic interpretability analysis shows that translated and localized variants of the same MWPs often induce distinct internal reasoning trajectories, even when aggregate accuracy remains similar. Overall, our results show that mathematical reasoning performance depends on both linguistic variety and cultural context.

papers.abstract: TS2Vec is one of the strongest self-supervised methods for time series classification, introduced in 2022. It is designed to be trained anew on every dataset: self-supervised pre-training followed by linear probing. Since then, the field has shifted towards foundation models that reuse one encoder across datasets. Yet TS2Vec offers a compact convolutional architecture that operates directly on temporal samples and accepts variable-length inputs without resampling. We ask whether these properties can be retained when the encoder is pre-trained only once, and show that they can: TS2Vec can essentially be turned into a foundation model. Three changes suffice: pre-train on a synthetic corpus, feed the encoder a raw amplitude view and an instance-normalized shape view of the input through two small stems, and distill one specialist encoder per view into a single encoder. The result, TS2Vec-FM, is a 1.6M-parameter dilated convolutional network that, kept frozen, reaches 83.3% on UCR-128 and 75.3% on UEA-27 under linear probing, within 0.3 pp of MantisV2, the current state of the art, and above TS2Vec trained separately on each target dataset. What we find most interesting is how different TS2Vec-FM is from other foundation models in design: near-parity is reached without attention, without a patch tokenizer, and without intermediate-layer extraction, using an "old-school" convolutional encoder and a two-layer MLP stem.
authors: Vasilii Feofanov, Zhenghan Tai, Andrei Ermakov, Irina Rish

papers.abstract: Reliable multi-view forecasting requires videos from different cameras to describe the same evolving 3D scene. To this end, we introduce Video-Point Model (VPM), a world model that conditions on multi-view video histories and a language instruction to jointly forecast future videos from arbitrary viewpoints and the 3D trajectories of persistent scene points. We extend a pretrained world model with camera-conditioned multi-view processing that integrates complementary observations across cameras, and add a trajectory head that predicts how physical points move through time. Each trajectory tracks a single point across all views, and supervising these trajectories alongside video generation therefore anchors appearance changes in every camera to a shared description of 3D motion. To support training and evaluation, we build VPM-Data, a simulation corpus pairing synchronized multi-view videos with persistent point trajectories, and VP-WorldBench, a forecasting benchmark spanning simulated and real environments. We further extend VPM to robot control by adding robot actions as a token modality in the generator. Action tokens share the point-supervised backbone and are denoised jointly with future videos, thereby grounding the policy in the same 3D-aware representation. On VP-WorldBench and existing 4D generation benchmarks, point supervision improves both video fidelity and 3D motion accuracy over a video-only counterpart, and in simulated and real-robot experiments, it also raises the manipulation success of the action-enabled model.

papers.abstract: Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners' own capabilities. In contrast, coding agents have improved substantially by post-training the model itself. We therefore investigate whether post-training can also improve robot planners. However, applying it across robot harnesses requires accommodating different execution mechanisms, including VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. To this end, we introduce AgenticRoboRL, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses. The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning. To accommodate different execution mechanisms, harness-specific adapters connect recorded planner interactions with task outcomes, enabling a common RL training pipeline while keeping execution components fixed. On LIBERO-PRO, AgenticRoboRL raises the success rate of a 9B-parameter planner from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory, approaching the 72.1% achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory. These results demonstrate post-training as an effective approach for improving robot planners. We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints.
authors: Xinxin Liu, Bingxin Xu, Wenrui Bao, Ming Li, Wentao Bao, Chen Chen, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: Addresses reliance on powerful closed-source planners by improving the planner model itself.

On LIBERO-PRO, raises a 9B planner’s success rate from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory.
Framework and trained planner checkpoints are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Agentic on-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student agent on its own trajectories while a teacher scores every token. A natural explanation of where it goes wrong is compounding error: the student's mistakes carry its trajectories beyond the region where the teacher is reliable, so recent methods keep training inside that region, through episode-length curricula, teacher-guided turns, prefix replay, or teacher intervention where the two disagree. We show this explanation is incomplete. From the states where the student departs most from the teacher, the teacher's own takeovers still finish the task, yet the student trained on its token scores keeps running out of turns. We attribute this to the myopia of next-token scoring. The teacher rates each token without seeing where the episode ends, so its scores let through the safe, delaying moves that outcome-based RL would punish with zero reward, a penalty agentic OPD lacks. We call this difference between what the teacher does and what it scores the rollout-scorer gap. We propose Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation (R2S), which repairs the scorer before distillation by mining high-disagreement states from the untrained student, running teacher takeovers from them, keeping the states where enough takeovers pass a reward-free check such as consensus or an LLM judge, and fine-tuning the teacher to give its takeover-informed scores on every assistant token from the divergence turn onward, without the takeover in context. The repaired teacher is frozen as the sole scorer for standard OPD, requiring no task reward during repair or training. Across three environments, two teachers and four students, R2S outperforms three state-of-the-art agentic-OPD methods in all twelve teacher-student-environment cells, by 12.8 success points on average over the best of them in each cell. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/r2s/.
authors: Shu Zhao, Tan Yu
bullets: Problem: Token-level teacher scores can reward safe but delaying actions, creating a rollout–scorer gap that causes students to run out of turns even when the teacher can complete the task.
Method: Mine high-disagreement student states, run teacher takeovers, retain states passing consensus or an LLM-based reward-free check, and fine-tune the teacher on takeover-informed token scores.
Training then uses the repaired teacher as the frozen sole scorer in standard agentic OPD, without task rewards or takeover context.
Across three environments, two teachers, and four students, R2S beats three prior agentic-OPD methods in all 12 evaluated cells.
It gains an average of 12.8 success points over the strongest prior method per cell.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses a specific failure mode in agentic distillation (rollout-scorer gap) and proposes a repair mechanism, relevant to test-time adaptation and agent learning.

papers.tldr: R2S repairs a teacher’s myopic token scorer using reward-free teacher takeovers before on-policy distillation, improving agent success across all tested settings.

papers.abstract: Simulation is a powerful tool for robotics, but building diverse, simulation-ready scenes at scale remains difficult. Reconstructing scenes from single images is a promising alternative, but visual similarity alone is insufficient: objects must also be recovered, accurately placed, and physically grounded. Existing methods that rely on post-hoc physics settling often misplace objects, producing scenes that look correct but behave poorly under manipulation. We present SceneRig, an agentic system that turns a single image into an editable, simulation-ready scene. SceneRig combines geometric, visual, and physical tools to reconstruct a faithful 3D scene. An agent then performs edit-and-validate loops inside a physics simulator to achieve physical stability. Across diverse inputs, SceneRig improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement while keeping the reconstructed scenes physically stable. Furthermore, SceneRig is effective for downstream robotics: its scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline method and more reliably support replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.
authors: Rundong Luo, Yunong Liu, Di Cao, Matthew Tancik, Shyamal Buch, Colton Stearns, Wenqi Xian
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually plausible reconstruction and physically correct object placement.
Combines geometric, visual, and physical tools with agent-driven edit-and-validate loops in a physics simulator.
Improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement across diverse inputs.
Produces physically stable scenes that better predict real-robot policy outcomes than the baseline.
Supports more reliable replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive models (ARMs) face a "Sequentiality Bottleneck" in reasoning, while diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallelism but lack semantic coherence. To addresses both limitations, we propose Collaborative Reasoning Asymmetric Learning (CoRAL), a hybrid framework via an Asymmetric Planner-Executor (APE) architecture: a DLM Planner generates K diverse reasoning trajectories in parallel, while a large ARM Executor selects the optimal plan and synthesizes the final answer. To train the Planner effectively, we introduce Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT (RDC), which integrates outcome-based rewards into the diffusion process to steer it toward goal-directed reasoning. Experiments on vision-language benchmarks show that CoRAL significantly outperforms prior diffusion-based methods and achieves competitive performance against strong ARMs, achieving both superior efficiency and quality.
authors: Wei Cai, Jian Zhao, Yuchen Yuan, Xuelong Li
bullets: Targets the sequentiality bottleneck of autoregressive reasoning and the semantic-coherence limitations of diffusion language models.
Uses an Asymmetric Planner-Executor architecture: a diffusion planner generates K diverse reasoning trajectories in parallel, while an autoregressive executor selects and completes the best plan.
Introduces Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT to steer diffusion-generated reasoning toward goal-directed solutions using outcome-based rewards.
On vision-language benchmarks, CoRAL outperforms prior diffusion-based methods and is competitive with strong autoregressive models in both efficiency and quality.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image personalization aims to equip pretrained diffusion models with the ability to learn user-specific concepts from only a few reference images. Existing methods, however, typically train each concept independently or assume that all concepts are available simultaneously. In practical applications, concepts often arrive sequentially, requiring models to continually learn new subjects, objects, or styles while minimizing interference with previously acquired concepts. We address this continual concept personalization setting by extending residual-space adaptation to the stochastic adaptation process of pretrained diffusion models. Our work achieves the highest concept fidelity among competing continual personalization methods while maintaining near-zero forgetting. Beyond these empirical gains, the learned residual-space dynamics reveal where adaptation capacity is concentrated within the diffusion model. Restricting adaptation to the identified layers by our method preserves nearly the same performance while reducing the number of trainable parameters by up to 72\%, demonstrating that residual-space dynamics can identify the layers that contribute most to continual concept personalization and directly guide more parameter-efficient adaptation.
authors: Yuzhi Liu, Enis Simsar, Giulia Lanzillotta, Thomas Hofmann
bullets: Addresses continual personalization, where user-specific concepts arrive sequentially rather than all at once.
Extends residual-space adaptation to the stochastic adaptation process of pretrained diffusion models.
Reports the highest concept fidelity among competing continual personalization methods while maintaining near-zero forgetting.
Uses residual-space dynamics to identify layers most important for adaptation.
Restricting training to those layers preserves nearly the same performance and reduces trainable parameters by up to 72%.

papers.abstract: Robots exploring unknown indoor environments must decide where to move while much of the environment remains unseen. Predicting the occupancy of unseen space beyond the current sensor range can improve these decisions, but recent approaches commonly rely on learned models that require offline training and repeated inference during exploration. We introduce the Mondrian-Anchored Prior for Learning-free Indoor Exploration (MAPLE), a training-free predictive approach that adapts the Mondrian process into an online generative prior conditioned on observed geometric cues in the current partial map. MAPLE generates multiple plausible map hypotheses and evaluates visibility separately within each to estimate frontier gain, preserving differences in predicted visibility across hypotheses. Across KTH floor-plans and real-SLAM environments at multiple sensor ranges, MAPLE consistently improves over non-predictive exploration and remains competitive with learned predictive approaches. Its lightweight procedural construction enables predictive exploration with limited computational resources. Experimental results further show that more accurate map prediction does not necessarily produce better exploration, highlighting the importance of how predictions are represented and used in exploration decisions.
authors: Kelvin Aladum, Nisar Ahmed
bullets: Addresses exploration decisions when large parts of an indoor environment are beyond the sensor range.
Adapts the Mondrian process into an online generative prior conditioned on geometric cues from the partial map.
Evaluates visibility separately for each map hypothesis, preserving uncertainty in predicted frontier gains.
Improves over non-predictive exploration and remains competitive with learned predictive methods across floor-plan and real-SLAM settings.
Shows that better map prediction alone does not guarantee better exploration; prediction representation and decision use are crucial.

papers.abstract: Continuous flow language models offer a path to parallel generation with tools for control and acceleration unavailable to discrete diffusion, yet effective techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. We present Lafa (Large flow language model), a fast, high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in a data-efficient manner. Lafa is a blockwise flow model with causal attention on the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design enables efficient training by adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) models and fast inference via prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding. We train Lafa at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, more efficient than previous diffusion models, and evaluate it on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, where the learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and can be distilled into flow maps for one- and few-step generation. Notably, flow training preserves or even improves pretrained AR capabilities via a multi-token prediction effect, which we leverage in a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within a single model. This yields 2.54x the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality, outperforming multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion methods. Our findings show that continuous flows can serve as a scalable foundation for language modeling.
authors: Arnav Chavan, Chanhyuk Lee, Udbhav Bamba, Jaehoon Yoo, Seunghoon Hong, Aditi Raghunathan, Jinwoo Kim
bullets: Addresses the limited scalability of continuous flow language models compared with established autoregressive approaches.
Uses causal attention over prefixes and bidirectional asynchronous flow within blocks, supporting prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding.
Adapts pretrained autoregressive models and trains models up to 8B parameters using fewer than 30B tokens.
Matches or surpasses autoregressive quality on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, while supporting one- and few-step distilled generation.
A self-speculative decoding scheme verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within the same model, achieving 2.54× AR throughput at comparable quality.

papers.abstract: Statistical learning in high dimensions suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Fortunately, many functions of practical interest are compositionally sparse, meaning they admit a composition of local functions, each depending on only a few variables, allowing sample complexity to depend on local arity rather than ambient dimension. Yet realizing this benefit requires exploiting hidden compositional structure, which theory does not establish for practical gradient-based training. We study this gap with CSFRBench, a controlled benchmark that hides the target's compositional computation during training but retains it for diagnosis, and find that dense networks and sparsity-based baselines leave much of that benefit unrealized. Inspired by the spatial organization of biological neural circuits, we introduce Learned Wiring (LeWi): each neuron has a learned low-dimensional embedding, only nearby neurons connect, and embeddings and weights are trained jointly. LeWi improves sample efficiency on targets with hierarchical structure, intermediate reuse, or independent modules. Across 32 additional targets generated by independently sampled computation graphs, LeWi is the most sample-efficient method not given the target graph, with 27% lower mean learning-curve area than dense networks. Dense networks perform better on targets with a single high-arity function. LeWi's representations and connectivity align with the target computation. On 17 world-model prediction tasks spanning control, navigation, and manipulation, LeWi beats the dense baseline on 16 and wins 99/119 baseline comparisons. These results show that jointly learning connectivity and weights can exploit computational structure to improve sample efficiency.
authors: Hangyu Zhou, Constantine Dovrolis, Stephen Mussmann
bullets: High-dimensional learning is sample-inefficient when models fail to exploit compositionally sparse functions.
CSFRBench evaluates whether methods can discover hidden computational structure without access to the target graph.
LeWi embeds neurons in a low-dimensional space and connects nearby neurons while jointly training embeddings and weights.
LeWi is strongest on hierarchical, reusable, or modular targets; dense networks do better for single high-arity functions.
Across benchmarks, LeWi reduces mean learning-curve area by 27% versus dense networks and wins 99 of 119 comparisons on world-model tasks.

papers.title: Learning Computational Structure for Sample-Efficient Prediction

papers.abstract: Despite the success of video world models, extending them to multiple agents is difficult because it requires generating several agent-specific video streams that are consistent in time and between agents. To address this gap, we introduce OverSeer, a multi-agent world model that augments egocentric agent views with auxiliary camera views. We suggest that, by fixing the auxiliary views in space, they act as a proxy for a world-centric representation: Unlike the agents' views, which can change entirely due to a simple change in agent position, changes in the auxiliary views directly map to localized changes in the world state. We show that these fixed views substantially help the model to maintain consistency. We also show that, due to their redundant and semi-static nature, the auxiliary views can be efficiently compressed with a delta-VAE that encodes only the changes relative to a static reference image, reducing the number of tokens required to process them. Experiments in Minecraft and Doom demonstrate improved world and agent consistency, with qualitative results on real-world multi-camera captures indicating that the approach is not tied to game engines. Our compression analysis further shows that delta-VAE substantially reduces the computational overhead of auxiliary-view generation. We conclude that these fixed views provide a simple and efficient way to improve multi-agent world models.
authors: Runjia Li, Kam Woh Ng, Minghao Chen, Junlin Han, Jianyuan Wang, Zhaochong An, Juan-Manuel Perez-Rua, Andrea Vedaldi, Shikun Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of generating multiple temporally and cross-agent-consistent video streams.
Augments egocentric agent views with spatially fixed auxiliary cameras as a proxy for world-centric state.
Uses a delta-VAE to encode only changes from static reference images, reducing auxiliary-view token and computation costs.
Experiments in Minecraft and Doom show improved world and agent consistency; qualitative real-world multi-camera results suggest broader applicability.
Scope: demonstrated primarily in game environments, with real-world evidence limited to qualitative results.

Figure 1 OverSeer sees beyondwhat agents see. Two agents interact in a shared Minecraft environment (Left). These auxiliary streams establish a persistent shared reference, enforcing world consistency over time and agent consistency across views.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive language models are trained by next-token cross-entropy, yet several recent systems also iterate a hidden state without emitting a token: continuous thoughts, pause steps, and recurrent depth. This note separates three risks on one latent process. The token risk $R_{\mathrm{tok}}$ scores a readout. The teacher-forced latent risk $R_1$ scores a one-step map that sees the true hidden state. The open-loop risk $R_H$ scores the same map after it has been iterated on its own outputs. If the Bayes next-token posterior is a function of a $k$-dimensional statistic with full-rank covariance, a width-$k$ latent, a linear least-squares transition, and a refit unembedding match the Bayes token predictor. The statistic is identified only up to an invertible gauge: whitening the residual stream does not change the token law once the unembedding is refit. The matching obstructions are sharp. A constant latent drives $R_1$ to zero while token cross-entropy falls back to the marginal entropy. A perfect token predictor can still hide a null-space walk whose open-loop error grows linearly in the horizon. A small next-latent loss does not certificate next-token prediction, and a small next-token loss does not certificate free latent rollout, unless a rank or injectivity condition is stated with the number.
authors: Yuzhou Hong
bullets: Separates token risk, teacher-forced one-step latent risk, and open-loop rollout risk.
Shows that a full-rank k-dimensional sufficient statistic can support Bayes-optimal token prediction with a width-k latent, linear transition, and refit unembedding.
Establishes gauge freedom: invertible latent transformations, including whitening, preserve token predictions when the unembedding is refit.
Provides obstructions: constant latents can minimize one-step latent risk without predicting tokens, while perfect token prediction can conceal latent drift whose open-loop error grows with horizon.
Concludes that small latent-transition loss or token loss alone does not certify the other objective without stated rank or injectivity conditions.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses the weights of a trained model with limited compute and data. Down to 4 bits it is near-lossless, but at 2 bits scalar PTQ configurations fall to chance-level accuracy. We study three choices usually treated as implementation details that matter little at 4 bits but decide 2-bit quality: the quantization representation, the calibration data, and the recovery fine-tuning data, across six dense and mixture-of experts models (ranging from $3.8$ to $32$B parameters). Representation is the largest factor and vector codebooks restore usable models where scalar PTQ pipelines collapse. Most of the remaining loss in accuracy is on \emph{generative} tasks, and the amount of performance drop is model-dependent. Furthermore, at a short recovery budget, calibration and recovery data are coupled. The best recovery data depends on the calibration data, so the two must be chosen jointly. The resulting recipe involves a vector codebook representation, a small task-aligned calibration mixture, and an inexpensive codebook-only recovery stage. Including codebooks, it uses about $2.3$ effective bits per weight and retains $89$ to $97\%$ of full-precision question-answering (QA) accuracy where scalar PTQ is at chance, and, including recovery, uses $1.4$ to $30\times$ less compute than the strongest quantization-aware-training (QAT) baseline.
authors: Rhea Sanjay Sukthanker, Riccardo Grazzi, James Hensman, Pashmina Cameron
bullets: At 2 bits, scalar PTQ can collapse to chance-level accuracy, making representation, calibration data, and recovery data critical.
Vector codebook representations are the most important factor for restoring usable low-bit models.
Calibration and recovery data interact under limited recovery budgets and should be selected jointly, with task alignment.
Across six 3.8B–32B dense and mixture-of-experts models, the method retains 89–97% of full-precision QA accuracy using about 2.3 effective bits per weight.
Including recovery, it requires 1.4–30× less compute than the strongest QAT baseline; generative-task degradation remains model-dependent.

papers.abstract: Collaborative perception enables agents to retrieve the scene semantics and geometry beyond the field of view of any individual agent. This broader scene understanding enhances transportation safety and improves efficiency in multi-robot systems. However, existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods rely on dense 3D voxel annotations and are limited to recognizing objects within a predefined set of semantic classes. To overcome these limitations, we present CoGaussian, an open-vocabulary Gaussian-based collaborative semantic occupancy prediction framework. CoGaussian represents a scene as a set of foundation model-aligned sparse 3D Gaussians, which serve as a compact representation for communicating and fusing geometric and semantic information across multiple agents. On the Semantic-OPV2V benchmark, our method outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of open-vocabulary collaborative scene understanding.
authors: Om Shivam Verma, Shaya Farahmand, Lingjun Zhao, Lu Gan
bullets: Addresses the limits of existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods, which require dense 3D voxel annotations and fixed semantic classes.
Represents scenes with sparse 3D Gaussians aligned to foundation models.
Uses Gaussians to communicate and fuse geometric and semantic information across agents.
Evaluated on Semantic-OPV2V, where it outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent methods.
Targets broader scene understanding for transportation safety and multi-robot efficiency.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview. CoGaussian starts with randomly initialized embeddings. A transformer layer uses multiscale features of images to update the embeddings, followed by a Head Layer that predicts Gaussians. During Joint Training, all agents predict ego Gaussians which are communicated with each other and aggregated. This set of Gaussians is used for training. In the Fusion pipeline, the neighbors predict and send Gaussian embeddings to the ego agent. Radius-gated Attention uses these neighbor Gaussian embeddings to update ego embeddings. The Fusion Head predicts ego Gaussians, and pre-trained Head from Joint Training predicts neighbor Gaussians. These are aggregated to form the final prediction used for both training and inference.

Fig. 1. Qualitative comparison of three variants of CoGaussian with ground truth. The ego vehicle is marked as E. Another agent is in the front-right (not visible here), partially completing the front-right of the ego vehicle in collaborative predictions. Class legends are shown in Table I.

papers.tldr: CoGaussian enables multiple agents to collaboratively understand 3D scenes with open-vocabulary semantics using compact, foundation-model-aligned Gaussian representations.

papers.abstract: Humanoid-human interaction requires robots to operate under severe partial observability: during close physical contact, the human partner is occluded, truncated, or outside the robot's field of view, causing pose estimation to fail and often necessitating external tracking or privileged human state. At the same time, heavy mutual occlusions introduce errors into the human-human motion-capture data used for learning. We present REACT, a framework for learning deployable humanoid-human interaction policies from human-human demonstrations. REACT treats semantic contact structure as the key supervisory signal connecting demonstration processing, interaction learning, and onboard control. First, a VLM-guided contact modeling and retargeting pipeline identifies semantically meaningful contacts and transfers them onto humanoid-human geometry while preserving interaction structure. Using these annotations, privileged interaction policies learn physically grounded behaviors through interaction-aware contact rewards and are then distilled into deployable egocentric depth policies trained entirely from onboard sensing using photorealistic human depth rendering. To address severe partial observability, we introduce generative partner-state modeling objectives that predict partner motion from occluded egocentric views. We evaluate REACT in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid across five contact-rich interactions. Semantic contact modeling substantially improves preservation of demonstrated interactions, while generative partner-state modeling improves contact recall on four of five interactions, most under heavy occlusion. On real hardware, REACT performs all five interactions using onboard sensing alone.
authors: Yuto Shibata, Kotaro Amaya, Kashu Yamazaki, Lalit Jayanti, Yoshimitsu Aoki, Mariko Isogawa, Katerina Fragkiadaki
bullets: Addresses partial observability and occlusion that make human pose estimation unreliable during close contact.
Uses semantic contact annotations to retarget human-human demonstrations onto humanoid-human geometry while preserving interaction structure.
Learns privileged interaction policies with contact-aware rewards, then distills them into egocentric depth policies using onboard sensing.
Generative partner-state modeling improves contact recall in four of five evaluated interactions, especially under heavy occlusion.
Demonstrated all five contact-rich interactions in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 using onboard sensing alone.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of REACT. REACT first annotates semantic contacts in human–human demonstrations with a VLM and retargets them onto the humanoid while preserving them. A privileged teacher then learns the interaction with contact rewards and is finally distilled into an egocentric depth student that predicts the partner’s motion and runs on the real robot.

After each embrace the robot releases the partner, re-approaches, and re-establishes contact, so the three hug cycles appear as three separate close-contact phases across the panels. The policy sustains repeated contact-rich interaction over a long horizon rather than a single one-shot contact.

Right three: hug; at the instant of embrace the partner’s torso occludes the camera, and the reconstruction collapses into a large error behind the true mesh. The estimator degrades precisely in the close-contact, self-occluded regime that REACT’s end-to-end student handles directly from depth.

D.2 establishes a dense body correspondence that maps every SMPL-X body vertex to a (link, plocal) pair, so the same mesh can be projected onto either target surface, the Unitree G1 robot or the partner’s SMPL-X collision capsules. The three columns show one identical set of colour-coded SMPL-X vertices in three configurations, from left to right: projected onto the G1 robot surface, in their SMPL-X template positions, and projected onto the partner capsule surface. Each colour denotes the G1 link a vertex is registered to, and the connecting lines join the same representative vertices across the three configurations, so that any contact vertex can be carried onto the corresponding robot or capsule surface by forward kinematics. The columns are drawn at true relative scale, exposing the proportion mismatch between the human template and the shorter G1 that the registration must bridge. The dense map covers the full template at a mean vertex-to-surface residual of 0.89mm, well below the ϵ = 10 cm contact threshold.

papers.abstract: Video generation and feed-forward 3D reconstruction typically use separate representations, requiring RGB decoding and visual re-encoding to recover geometry from generated latents. We propose Latent Bridge, which connects video generative latent spaces with geometric feature spaces to directly predict 3D geometry from video latents. We develop representation-specific bridges for Wan2.1 and V-RAE, enabling feed-forward prediction of cameras, depth, and 3D point clouds without the intermediate RGB pathway. Each bridge is trained on RGB videos through feature distillation, while the video encoder and geometry model remain frozen. Training requires neither ground-truth geometry nor execution of the downstream geometric aggregator or prediction heads. At inference, the same video latents support both RGB decoding and geometry prediction. The same trained bridge can be reused for image-to-video and text-to-video generation within the same video latent space, without bridge retraining. Experiments on Co3Dv2 and WildRGB-D demonstrate competitive geometric reconstruction quality, efficient end-to-end generation and reconstruction, and faster latent-to-geometry decoding, highlighting latent alignment as a practical and reusable interface between video generation and 3D reconstruction. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hustvl/Latent-Bridge.
authors: Shuai Zhang, Zhanpeng Ouyang, Zhengqing Chen, Ruohong Mei, Shaoyu Chen, Weiqiang Ren, Hui Sun, Qian Zhang, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of recovering geometry from generated video latents through an intermediate RGB pathway.
Learns representation-specific bridges for Wan2.1 and V-RAE to predict cameras, depth, and 3D point clouds.
Uses feature distillation on RGB videos while freezing the video encoder and geometry model; no ground-truth geometry is required.
The same bridge supports image-to-video and text-to-video generation within a latent space without retraining.
Experiments on Co3Dv2 and WildRGB-D show competitive reconstruction, efficient generation–reconstruction, and faster latent-to-geometry decoding.

papers.abstract: Understanding contact and tactile magnitude in hand-object interaction is a key step toward physically intelligent systems, yet learning such representations is limited by the cost and restricted coverage of tactile measurements. We present Touch-JEPA, a framework for learning tactile representations from hand-object videos with limited tactile supervision. We first introduce a self-supervised pretraining objective that learns from video alone without tactile supervision. Using video-derived hand geometry, Touch-JEPA predicts masked visual features at corresponding hand-surface locations from spatial and temporal context, encouraging the representation to capture latent contact dynamics. We then extend this formulation to joint representation learning, where masked prediction is applied to all videos while tactile supervision is available only for a labeled subset, grounding the shared representation in measured contact and magnitude. With self-supervised pretraining alone, simple supervised readouts on frozen Touch-JEPA features outperform supervised baselines in contact discrimination and tactile magnitude estimation across three human-hand benchmarks, and transfer to robotic hands without robot tactile training data. Joint learning with limited tactile supervision further improves contact and magnitude estimation on the human-hand benchmarks. Together, these results show that hand-object video can provide scalable self-supervision for tactile representation learning, while limited tactile measurements provide complementary physical grounding.
authors: Minseong Kweon, Qiao Feng, Yiming Huang, Lingjie Liu
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited coverage of tactile measurements for learning contact and tactile magnitude.

Frozen pretrained features outperform supervised baselines on contact discrimination and tactile magnitude estimation across three human-hand benchmarks.
Transfers to robotic hands without robot tactile training data; limited tactile supervision further improves human-hand performance.

papers.abstract: Tactile-visual-language models combine vision and touch through a shared language space to recognize objects and materials. In real-world deployment, changes in lighting, contact quality or sensor hardware can shift visual or tactile inputs and degrade recognition performance. When both modalities contribute to a prediction, an unreliable modality can override correct evidence from the other. Since labeled data are generally unavailable during deployment, test-time adaptation offers a way to recover recognition performance from unlabeled observations. In this setting, we find that comparing accumulated observations with the text embeddings of candidate classes reveals modality reliability differences that confidence can miss. Refining features against competing classes also improves recognition beyond geometric alignment alone. These findings motivate SenseAlign, which uses a common semantic reference for test-time modality weighting and feature correction. Alignment Trust weights each modality according to its support for shared predicted classes. Anchor Realignment uses the same class text embeddings to fit a shared feature correction that separates predicted classes from alternatives. Both modules use the same unlabeled history while keeping all encoders frozen. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate strong recognition performance under both natural shifts and controlled corruptions.
authors: Chuyang Ye, Qinting Jiang, Jingyan Jiang
bullets: Addresses recognition degradation caused by lighting, contact-quality, and sensor-hardware shifts when labeled deployment data are unavailable.
Alignment Trust weights visual and tactile modalities by their support for shared predicted classes, revealing reliability differences that confidence may miss.
Anchor Realignment learns a shared feature correction that separates predicted classes from competing alternatives using class text embeddings.
Both modules reuse unlabeled observation history while keeping all encoders frozen.
Experiments across diverse datasets show strong recognition under natural shifts and controlled corruptions.

papers.abstract: Smart glasses can help users understand their activities and surroundings, but small vision-language models must preserve useful evidence within limited computation. This is difficult because redundant frames consume the visual budget, while aggressive spatial compression can discard relevant details. Although gaze identifies the wearer's focus, the question may require evidence from the surrounding scene. To address these constraints, we propose GazeLens, which combines frame selection with gaze- and question-guided token reduction. First, HOG transitions and image sharpness select frames before visual encoding. For each selected frame, Gaussian pooling then forms gaze-focused and complementary summaries. Because their relevance depends on the question, a lightweight gate blends them into a primary token. Together with a global scene token, this retains both focused and contextual summaries within two tokens per frame. On StreamGaze, GazeLens achieves higher macro and micro accuracy than the evaluated full-grid and token-reduction baselines, with lower input-forward FLOPs than the shared-backbone token-reduction baselines.
authors: Trong-Thang Pham, Anh Nguyen, Hien Van Nguyen, Ngan Le
bullets: Addresses limited computation in smart-glasses VQA while preserving both gaze-focused evidence and surrounding context.
Selects frames using HOG transitions and image sharpness before visual encoding.
Uses Gaussian pooling to create gaze-focused and complementary summaries, then applies a lightweight question-guided gate.
Represents each selected frame with a blended primary token plus a global scene token.
On StreamGaze, outperforms evaluated full-grid and token-reduction baselines in macro and micro accuracy while using fewer input-forward FLOPs than shared-backbone token-reduction baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed focus-aware, question-conditioned token reduction framework. (1) Dynamic Frame Selection. A continuous video stream is filtered using HOG transition and sharpness cues to retain informative frames while discarding small-change and blurry frames. This filtering process produces a dynamic input sequence V . (2) Focus-Aware Gaze Aggregation. Each selected frame is encoded into spatial features and combined with gaze (xt, yt) to produce a focus token gt, an unfocus token ct, and a global token mt. (3) Question-Conditioned Semantic Gating. Question token embeddings are mean-pooled and L2-normalized to t. A two-layer MLP and sigmoid then yield a scalar gate s ∈ [0, 1]. The gate modulates gaze-focused versus contextual information as pt = s · gt + (1− s) · ct. (4) Token Assembly and Training Objective. The per-frame tokens pt and mt are linearly projected, concatenated with the question, and fed into a language model to predict the answer, optimized with a cross-entropy (CE) loss.

Figure 1: Teaser of our gaze-driven adaptive token reduction framework for egocentric video QA. In the left panel, egocentric video and gaze data are inherently noisy and redundant, with dense frames and unstable gaze signals. In the middle panel, existing VLM approaches suffer from inefficient frame selection (too dense or too sparse) and often ignore gaze or rely on computationally expensive adaptive attention mechanisms. In the right panel, our approach combines (1) Dynamic Frame Selection, (2) Focus-Aware Gaze Aggregation, and (3) Question-Conditioned Semantic Gating. Together, these modules produce two visual tokens per frame. This design reduces the visual token budget and model computation while improving performance under strict token budgets.

papers.abstract: For efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs), methods of ultra-low-bit backbones reduce weight storage, memory traffic, and linear-layer execution cost, while multi-token prediction (MTP) methods reduce sequential decoding steps by predicting multiple future tokens in parallel. Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP
authors: Ning Zhang, Shihao Wang, Jinrui Zhang, Chaodong Xiao, Lei Zhang
bullets: Combines joint autoregressive and block-causal training so one model supports both regular generation and multi-token drafting.
Offers confidence-only, speculative-only, and hybrid decoding without separate draft and verifier models.
Uses accepted-prefix alignment, shared KV storage, and width-specialized CUDA Graph execution to reduce decoding overhead.
Reports 2.1–2.4× speedups on selected Bonsai models and up to 3.3× throughput on Jetson Orin across evaluated tasks and hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The BitMTP framework. (a) Joint NTP+MTP training supports mask-conditioned blockcausal drafting and an AR path in one model. (b) Confidence-only decoding commits a confidenceselected prefix. Speculative-only decoding verifies each block, while hybrid decoding verifies when the confidence prefix is too short. Verifier-based steps add a correction or bonus token. (c) The runtime executes accepted-prefix transitions with width-specialized low-bit operators and captured CUDA Graphs. Graphs reuse causal KV history through shared storage. In hybrid decoding, verifier inputs are prepared before the host branch decision.

Figure 3: Runtime mechanisms M1–M3. M1 selects packed operators by replay width M and input/output dimensions (K,N), while numerical role r selects the output projection π(r). M2 indexes captured graphs by (M,σ, r) and shares one KV buffer Bσ across widths and roles within each capacity segment. M3 moves verifier-input preparation ahead of the hybrid branch decision.
