papers.abstract: Learning latent dynamics is fundamental to building action-conditioned world models for planning. Among existing families, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a natural framework by modeling transitions directly in latent space rather than at the pixel level. However, two issues remain in JEPA-based world models: (i) physical grounding lacks explicit aggregation of temporal context and (ii) action planning always overly relies on generic sampling distributions. To this end, we propose $\mathcal{G}$-JEPA, which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and couples the learned models with prior-guided action planning. Specifically, during learning, we incorporate a shared causal temporal module that aggregates temporal context within observation and prediction sequences under physical state supervision, grounding both in task-relevant physical states. When planning, we further introduce action inference through stepwise conditioning of a generative action distribution on the current and goal latent representations together with their evolving discrepancy, yielding anchored proposals that guide model-based online refinement. Together, physical state supervision guides temporal representation learning, while the action prior guides search through the learned world model. Experiments demonstrate improved planning performance on manipulation tasks, including tasks with increasing temporal separation between initial and goal observations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/myl11045/G-JEPA.
authors: Yilei Man, Yang Chen, Jingcai Guo
bullets: Addresses missing temporal context in JEPA-based physical grounding and the reliance on generic action sampling.
Uses a shared causal temporal module to aggregate observation and prediction histories under physical-state supervision.
Infers actions by conditioning a generative action distribution on current and goal latents plus their evolving discrepancy.
Combines temporally grounded representations with prior-guided online model-based refinement.
Reports improved manipulation-task planning, including tasks with larger temporal gaps between initial and goal observations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of G-JEPA. World-model learning combines latent matching and SIGReg with (a) nuisance invariance under photometric augmentation and (b) temporal physical grounding. A shared S4D module aggregates temporal context separately within observed latents and aligned onestep predictions, supervising physical state estimates from both sequences. (c) During planning, the learned action prior is instantiated as a latent-conditioned diffusion policy that generates action proposals alongside Gaussian candidates. The frozen world model scores both sources using latent goal-matching costs, and a shared elite set updates the Gaussian search distribution. The policy remains fixed, while action execution provides new observations for subsequent planning rounds.

Labels report success and final position/orientation errors (pixels/degrees) for PushT or cube–goal distance (cm) for Cube. t counts environment steps, and Final marks each method’s stopping state in PushT.

(A) PhyLatent (Zeng et al., 2026) grounds individual latents in physical states, while PSG-JEPA (Yan et al., 2026) additionally supervises state changes between latent pairs. (B) Gaussian CEM generates action candidates from a proposal distribution adapted through online elite updates. (C) G-JEPA uses a shared causal grounding module to aggregate temporal context within encoded and predicted latent sequences under physical state supervision. (D) Learned action proposals supplement Gaussian candidates, with joint world-model evaluation and shared elite selection guiding subsequent Gaussian updates. Curves illustrate schematic candidate motion paths.

papers.abstract: Tracking large human-motion datasets has become the dominant route to general, expressive humanoid whole-body control, but scaling across many motions is expensive. Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute. SuperMimic amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient. In 3 hours on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than $1000\times$ and fails on only 25 of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures. From 1 to 264 hours of motion, the world model's prediction error stays stable, and GPU-hours to a target return grow slowly. Our policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions. SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control, making it practical to measure motion-tracking scaling laws.
authors: Qiayuan Liao, Yiyang Shao, Junfeng Long, Kevin Zakka, Roberto Horowitz, Pieter Abbeel, Koushil Sreenath
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of learning across large human-motion datasets.
Fits a shared differentiable dynamics model from simulator transitions and trains it jointly with the tracking policy.
Uses short imagined rollouts and backpropagation-through-time to provide analytic policy gradients.
On the reported benchmark, it exceeds a 7-day, 128-GPU baseline after 3 hours on one GPU, with 25 versus 179 failures; zero failures are reached after 9.8 hours on two GPUs.
Transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions, while maintaining stable prediction error as motion data scales from 1 to 264 hours.

(2) The differentiable world model is fit to k-step windows sampled from B (§3.2). (3) The policy is improved by backpropagation-through-time through the frozen world model over H imagined steps; a critic Vψ , trained in the same phase, bootstraps the return beyond H (§3.3). Two budget rows compare SuperMimic (dot) with SONIC (diamond): SuperMimic reduces wall-clock time by more than 50× and GPU-hours by more than 1000×. (b, c) On a shared dataset-length sweep, GPU-hours to target return (b) grow slowly while the world model’s 8-step prediction error (c) stays within 0.007–0.011 as the dataset grows from 1 to 264 h, consistent with one world model amortizing shared body and contact dynamics across motions. The prediction error counts the state only, is normalized by a predefined nominal error, and is measured online on policy rollouts.

Figure 5: Imagined rollouts are fast and differentiable. (a) On an H100, over the batch sizes used in practice (shaded, 2k–16k parallel environments), the world model runs more than 10× faster than MuJoCo Warp; the gap widens to 62× at 64k, where MuJoCo Warp has flattened. papers.abstract: Object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) requires an embodied agent to find an instance of a specified category in an unseen environment and stop near it. The agent typically relies on an object detector but must judge online from a limited egocentric video stream, sometimes a single frame, whether a detected candidate is the target. Detectors often confidently mistake similar objects, such as a sofa for a bed, and stopping at a false positive fails the episode. Prevailing systems also approach candidates greedily, leaving them occluded or partially observed. We present CLOSER, an evidence-aware active verification framework that treats stopping as closed-loop evidence acquisition, coupling vision-language model (VLM) verification with active perception. CLOSER fine-tunes an open-source VLM to label each view of a candidate tracked across frames as target, non-target, or uncertain, selects complementary views with an embedding-based diversity gate, and fuses their per-view probabilities with a lightweight network. If the fused judgment remains uncertain, a diffusion policy drives the agent toward the candidate using only the tracked mask and depth until the decision becomes decisive. CLOSER runs locally and plugs into existing ObjectNav systems without retraining them. On Gibson and Habitat-Matterport 3D, it raises average success rate by 3.6 points and success weighted by path length by 2.0 points, showing that verifying evidence before committing improves embodied navigation.

bullets: Addresses false-positive stopping caused by visually similar objects and limited egocentric views.

Uses a diffusion policy to approach uncertain candidates using only tracked masks and depth.
Improves success rate by 3.6 points and success weighted by path length by 2.0 points on Gibson and Habitat-Matterport 3D.

papers.abstract: People adapt how they talk to the person in front of them. However, chat models tend to respond in Standard English regardless of the dialect used by the user. A uniform answer can hide whether training treats these users alike, and output audits cannot tell as well. We trace how each post-training stage, from supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to preference optimization (DPO) and reinforcement learning, changes a model's tendency to match the user, and read what each update prefers from two content-matched replies, one matching the user and one not. Across 10 open model lineages, post-training standardizes replies to every informal cue, yet after adjusting for how likely each reply already was, the DPO update still favours matching British and Australian spelling over AAE and Singlish on 10 lineages, and models still produce AAE features when asked. We then introduce calibrated accommodation pairs (CAP), preference data that reward matching users' dialect density while preserving Standard English for Standard-English users. On a fully open model, CAP raises convergence on features it was not trained on without a detectable increase in dialect for Standard-English users or a cost in instruction following. In contrast, one-sided pairs reach a similar gain only by overshooting the user and imposing dialect. Our findings show that uniform replies can hide selective updates and audits should read the update as well as the output. Code: https://github.com/kouzhizhuo/cap-accommodation.

papers.abstract: While large-scale human motion capture datasets provide a rich source of demonstrations for humanoid robot learning, retargeting the diverse motions to different humanoid robots remains a nontrivial challenge. Existing kinodynamic trajectory optimization pipelines are computationally expensive and often require manual adjustments per motion. We present FRDV (Fast Retargeting with Dynamics Validation), a scalable framework consisting of rapid constrained kinematic retargeting and an additional dynamics validation pipeline. Its kinematic stage integrates a custom Sequential Quadratic Programming solver, Real-Time Iteration, and parallel chunk-based processing, achieving up to 9,156 frames per second, approximately up to 136 times faster than GMR and ProtoMotions, while robot-specific constraints are incorporated into the optimization to reduce common retargeting artifacts, such as ground penetration and self-collision. For motions requiring additional verification, a contact implicit iLQR controller is utilized to test the retargeted reference under full rigid body dynamics. This dynamics-based validation identifies dynamically infeasible motions and refines contact-related artifacts such as foot floating and foot skating. We evaluate retargeting quality by training motion tracking reinforcement learning policies using several state-of-the-art pipelines and comparing their tracking fidelity and success rates. Furthermore, sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated on a Unitree G1 humanoid. Videos and code are available at: https://daroslab.github.io/frdv/.
authors: Daniel Marew, Sangjun Park, Nisal Perera, Donghyun Kim
bullets: Addresses the computational cost and manual effort of adapting diverse human motion capture data to different humanoid robots.

Incorporates robot-specific constraints to reduce ground penetration and self-collision artifacts.
Applies contact-implicit iLQR dynamics validation to detect infeasible motions and refine foot floating or skating.
Evaluations include motion-tracking reinforcement learning and sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree G1 humanoid.

papers.abstract: General-purpose multimodal models have shown promise as direct robot action policies, yet whether they grasp the physics underlying real-world interactions and can apply that understanding to guide action remains underexplored. We investigate this question using contact-rich manipulation as a representative testbed, examining tactile understanding as a concrete instance of this broader capability. Contact-rich manipulation requires interpreting tactile feedback and adjusting actions after obstruction. Existing learned tactile policies acquire these capabilities through specialized pretraining and per-task optimization, with substantial data and training costs. We present GPT-as-Tactile-Policy, which summarizes expert demonstrations into task guidance and tactile references for contact assessment and corrective action. GPT-6-Astra combines this context with multimodal observations and interaction history to generate control commands and adjust actions through contact feedback. Without additional robotics-specific pretraining or per-task policy fine-tuning, our method achieves 93.8\% mean success across five UniVTAC tasks. Overall performance is comparable to state-of-the-art policies, with higher success on selected tasks. On Insert Hole, tactile feedback improves success from 31\% to 99\%. Execution analysis further demonstrates contact-guided probing and correction, supporting manipulation progress through explicit expert experience and online feedback.

papers.abstract: Omni LLMs can naturally locate key audio and visual evidence and integrate information across modalities for audiovisual reasoning. Existing audio-visual reasoning benchmarks that mainly rely on multiple-choice questions usually score models solely based on answer correctness, making it difficult to assess whether a model truly forms a reasoning chain from evidence to the correct answer. In addition, textual or unimodal shortcuts may allow models to answer correctly without analyzing the necessary audio-visual evidence, further weakening the reliability of evaluation benchmarks. To address these issues, we introduce EvaOmni, an evidence-grounded benchmark containing 392 videos and 1,027 purely human-annotated question-answer pairs, covering 15 capabilities and three levels: retrieval and localization, basic understanding, and complex reasoning. We design a series of rigorous annotation procedures in which experts annotate audio and visual evidence and construct video-based distractors; humans review whether questions meet strict inspection criteria, and finally models filter textual and unimodal shortcuts. Beyond high-quality question-answer pairs, we require models to simultaneously return the answer and supporting evidence intervals in order to evaluate the complete reasoning chain. We propose the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) to measure how much annotated evidence a model identifies, and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.) to penalize poor temporal localization in either modality; both are incorporated into answer correctness. Across 7 open-weight and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs, Gemini3.7-Flash achieved the highest overall accuracy (79.4%), C.G. (70.8%), and B.G. (35.1%). At Level 3, it reached 79.1% accuracy, but its B.G. was only 12.3%. These results show that even the most advanced models still have room for development in grounded audio-visual reasoning.
authors: Xiaoxing Hu, Wenxi Yao, Chaoyuan Shi, Ziqi Ye, Xiaorong Guo, Peixuan Li, Zhuoran Sun, Ziyang Gong, Peiyuan Zhang, Mingxin Liu, Shuran Ma, Hongbo Liu, Xiaomin Yu, Yu Tian, Wentao Wang, Zhenjie Yang, Jian Hu, Yunhang Shen, Haoyu Cao, Xue Yang

papers.abstract: Large Language Model inference over long contexts is increasingly bottlenecked by the cost of attending to a growing Key-Value (KV) cache. Sparse attention reduces this cost by accessing only a fraction of the cache, but existing methods face a trade-off between deterministic retrieval, which captures high-scoring tokens but discards residual attention mass, and sampling, which improves coverage at the cost of higher variance. Hybrid methods combine top-$k$ retrieval with uniform sampling, yet still exhibit a substantial gap from dense attention at aggressive sparsity. We introduce \emph{Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA)}, a unified framework combining deterministic retrieval with score-guided sampling. SSA deterministically attends to high-scoring tokens while sampling the residual using proxy attention scores and correcting for their inclusion probabilities, thereby recovering attention mass beyond the retrieval set. SSA encompasses top-$k$, top-$p$, and hybrid top-$k$+sampling as special cases. Across RULER, LongBench, LOFT, and AIME, and five models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters, SSA consistently improves over the baselines at matched sparsity. On RULER-HARD with Ministral-3-8B, SSA improves accuracy over the strongest practical baseline from 81.8\% to 84.2\% at 32K and from 63.8\% to 69.3\% at 128K under $50\times$ attention sparsity, recovering 94\% and 85\% of dense-attention performance, respectively. With optimized CUDA kernels, SSA achieves up to $2.96\times$ decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M context, demonstrating that its accuracy gains translate into practical long-context inference acceleration. We open-source our code at https://github.com/skylight-org/SSA-Paper-Code.
authors: Sahil Joshi, Prithvi Dixit, Aryan Katiyar, Agniva Chowdhury, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Anshumali Shrivastava, Aditya Desai, Kumar Krishna Agrawal
bullets: Targets KV-cache attention costs for long-context LLM inference, where sparse methods lose attention mass or suffer sampling variance.
Combines deterministic selection of high-scoring tokens with score-guided sampling of residual tokens and inclusion-probability correction.
Generalizes top-k, top-p, and hybrid top-k-plus-sampling methods.
Improves matched-sparsity performance across four benchmarks and five models, including stronger RULER-HARD accuracy at 50× sparsity.
With optimized CUDA kernels, reaches up to 2.96× decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M-token context.

papers.abstract: Classical robot navigation stacks are reliable but often require re-engineering for each new robot type and site. Learning-based navigation shifts this effort from hand-tuned parameters to data generation and training, where a policy adapts to each new embodiment or facility by fine-tuning in simulation. Whether policies adapted this way stay reliable on real industrial robots has seen little systematic testing. We study this for NVIDIA's X-Mobility and COMPASS workflow for training learned navigation policies on Idealworks robots. In simulation, we extend the COMPASS benchmark with two embodiments, the differential-drive iw.hub and an omnidirectional Humanoid Mobile Platform (HMP), and with a digital twin of the Idealworks R&D center. For the real world, we fine-tune X-Mobility on data from this digital twin, with and without sim-to-real variants generated by NVIDIA Cosmos, train COMPASS on top of it from scratch in the digital twin, deploy the resulting policies on the iw.hub's onboard Jetson AGX Xavier, and benchmark them in the Idealworks R&D center against COMPASS trained only on NVIDIA's environments and the existing Idealworks navigation stack on task success, efficiency, safety, smoothness and onboard compute. Running every static scenario both in a digital-twin replica and in the real facility measures the sim-to-real gap and how far Cosmos-augmented data closes it. Training in the digital twin with Cosmos sim-to-real augmentation raises the real-world success rate of learned navigation from 65.3% to 91.7% across four scenarios and nearly halves its weighted travel time compared with simulation-only training, bringing it within 8.3 points of the production navigation stack, fully onboard; with an integrated global planner, it also reaches far, occluded goals in every trial.

papers.abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied generalist policies by jointly modeling future world evolution and robot actions across diverse manipulation tasks. However, representing diverse futures is only the first step: a capable WAM must also generate futures that match the requirements of the current task and execution progress. In long-horizon manipulation where similar observation-action segments occur across different tasks and stages, existing approaches may generate locally plausible yet misdirected rollouts to drift toward wrong task stage, i.e., a phenomenon we term Stage Confusion. To address this problem, we propose TaskWAM, a closed-loop, stage-aware framework that represents fine-grained task requirements with Mode Tokens and tracks execution progress with State Tokens, forming a structured task state to steer world--action generation toward intended future. We further introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark with parameterized stage variations and automated evaluation.Extensive experiments on both simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM effectively reduces confusion and achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, TaskWAM provides strong plug-and-play transfer across heterogeneous WAM architectures and robot embodiments, including single-arm robots, dual-arm grippers, dexterous hands, and humanoid robots.

papers.abstract: Vision-language trackers (VLTs) accept descriptions intended to assist tracking, but accepting text does not establish that its content changes tracking decisions, particularly as visual evidence deteriorates. We introduce DISTRACT, a matched-intervention benchmark that holds video, target, and distractor fixed while crossing four text priors with four image degradations along a controlled severity axis. We evaluate five VLTs on four datasets using behavioral contrasts, layerwise representation probes, and activation patching. Molmo2 and JointNLT exhibit directed text use. Some effects contract under degradation, whereas others show no significant endpoint change after multiplicity correction. UVLTrack, MMTrack, and DUTrack respond only weakly to changes in text semantics, with no directed behavioral effect surviving FDR correction in the tested settings. Model-internal analyses reveal that at decision-near states, correct-versus-conflicting text is decodable in Molmo2 and JointNLT but not in the other three systems. In the responsive models, decodability peaks at late states where replacement produces little behavioral change, whereas replacing selected earlier states redirects conflict-associated trajectories toward the target. Because matched-correct donors do not significantly outperform unrelated donors, these interventions identify earlier intervention-sensitive states without establishing target-specific semantic rescue. DISTRACT thus exposes when and where text affects tracking under degraded visual evidence.

papers.abstract: Code-based video generation offers fine-grained control, targeted editing, and component reuse compared with direct video generation. This approach requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to translate visual and temporal requirements into executable programs that produce complete videos. However, existing code-based benchmarks primarily target specialized tasks, leaving complete video creation across diverse creative categories and input modalities insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a general-purpose benchmark for code-based video generation across text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and video-to-video (V2V) settings. Code2Video-Compass comprises 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and three complexity dimensions covering construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency. It combines tasks curated from textual instructions and visual references with corresponding T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks derived from complete professional and user-created videos. We propose a dual-level evaluation framework combining 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics. Objective evaluation covers operational performance, video quality, text-video alignment, and reference fidelity, while subjective evaluation uses an MLLM judge to evaluate instruction following and holistic video quality. Extensive evaluation of 15 recent proprietary and open-weight MLLMs from nine families reveals that even leading models face challenges in reliably generating high-quality complete videos aligned with textual and visual requirements, with performance generally declining as construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity increases. We anticipate that Code2Video-Compass will advance reliable, coherent, and controllable code-based video generation and inspire broader progress in programmatic visual creation.
authors: Zhenghan Chen, Zekai Shao, Xin Lin, Leting Cheng, Siming Chen
bullets: Addresses the lack of broad evaluation for complete code-based video creation beyond specialized tasks.
Includes 2,104 tasks across 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and construction, dynamic-animation, and state-dependency complexity dimensions.
Covers text-to-video, image-to-video, and video-to-video generation, using textual instructions and visual references from professional and user-created videos.
Combines 12 objective metrics with five subjective MLLM-judged metrics for operational performance, quality, alignment, fidelity, instruction following, and holistic quality.
Evaluation of 15 MLLMs shows persistent difficulty producing high-quality, requirement-aligned videos, with performance declining as task complexity increases.

papers.abstract: Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end-to-end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine-tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine-tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state-of-the-art foundation model pre-trained on substantially more data. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region-specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open-source package on https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.
authors: Spiros Maggioros, Guray Erus, Gareth Harman, George Aidinis, Alexander Getka, Aristeidis Sotiras, Christos Davatzikos
bullets: Pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted MRI scans pooled from multiple studies.
Supports both weight initialization for downstream fine-tuning and standalone feature extraction.
Improved brain-age prediction accuracy and convergence speed relative to random initialization.
Frozen embeddings outperformed anatomical volumetric features on four of five classification tasks and competed with a larger-data foundation model.
Latent features capture spatially localized, neuroanatomically meaningful information with region-specific effects on reconstructed anatomy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the Brain2Vec pre-training architecture and downstream applications. (Pre-training) Brain2Vec is a 3D Masked Autoencoder (MAE) pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted MRI scans from the iSTAGING consortium. Input volumes are divided into 8× 8× 8 patches, with 75% randomly masked. A 12-layer Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder processes only the visible patches to generate a 768-dimensional latent representation. Mask tokens are then introduced, and an 8-layer ViT decoder reconstructs the original scan. (Evaluation) The pre-trained encoder serves two complementary roles. First, it provides a robust weight initialization for end-to-end fine-tuning on a downstream task (brain age regression), accelerating convergence and improving accuracy relative to random initialization. Second, its frozen 768-dimensional embeddings serve as fixed features for lightweight downstream models, including a Support Vector Regressor (SVR) for brain age regression and SVMs for five binary classification tasks: CU vs. AD, elevated BMI, diabetes, smoking status, and hypertension. We additionally assess the quality and interpretability of these frozen embeddings via self-attention visualization, correlation with anatomically-defined Regions of Interest (ROIs), and latent-space manipulation, showing that Brain2Vec encodes spatially localized, neuroanatomically meaningful representations.

papers.abstract: We present our solution to the AKBC LM-KBC 2026 Shared Task, where we achieved a score of 0.6836 on the official leaderboard, more than double the baseline of 0.2964. This task requires generating all possible objects for subject-relation pairs using a language model with up to 32 billion parameters, with no retrieval or fine-tuning involved. We show that the prompting methodology is as important as the model architecture: while the instruction-tuned model version achieves 0.5681 with its chat interface, the base model achieves 0.6836 when prompted using text completion. Thus, instruction tuning decreases factual recall; we refer to this effect as the instruction tax, which is caused by the model's weights rather than the prompting method. Our final solution is fairly straightforward: we prompt the base model with some examples from the training data, generate 64--256 outputs, and retain only the repeated ones. Two specialized methods are then applied for each relation: one improves the recall of large answer sets, and the other verifies a person's vitality before predicting their place of death.
authors: Christophe Khalil, Aya Mourad
bullets: Achieved 0.6836 on the AKBC LM-KBC 2026 Shared Task, over twice the 0.2964 baseline.
The base model scored 0.6836 with text-completion prompting, versus 0.5681 for the instruction-tuned model using chat prompting.
The approach uses training examples in prompts, generates 64–256 candidates, and keeps repeated answers.
Relation-specific methods improve recall for large answer sets and verify a person’s vitality before predicting their place of death.
The findings suggest reduced factual recall is caused by instruction tuning in the model weights, not merely by prompting.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially improved spoken interaction and video understanding. Existing online and streaming benchmarks primarily assess causal multimodal perception through timestamped question answering, whereas real-world interaction requires models to continuously identify task-relevant multimodal cues and decide whether, when, and how to respond. This leaves open how well current models can sustain real-time interaction throughout an evolving multimodal stream. To address this gap, we introduce DIVE, a benchmark for evaluating full-duplex interaction with visual engagement under continuous and realistic multimodal streams. It organizes six tasks into three complementary interaction scenarios. (1) Proactive Intervention evaluates whether models can identify emerging visual or semantic cues and intervene at the appropriate moment. (2) Continuous Engagement evaluates sustained participation through continuous visual tracking and visually grounded query interaction. (3) Interaction Coordination evaluates how models coordinate listening and speaking under overlapping and multi-party interactions. DIVE contains 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and precise temporal metadata. Its evaluation protocol separates response quality, participation decisions, and response timing. We evaluate representative real-time models using response quality, window response rates, and reaction latency. Experiments show that leading real-time models achieve sub-second average response latency, yet their average window response rates remain at or below 53.77%. Response quality varies substantially across models and tasks, with adapting ongoing responses to newly arriving information remaining particularly challenging. We hope DIVE facilitates progress toward more natural and capable real-time multimodal interactive systems.
authors: Yuhang Chen, Guangyue Liu, Shilong Liu
bullets: Targets a gap in streaming benchmarks that focus mainly on timestamped question answering rather than deciding whether, when, and how to respond.
Defines six tasks across proactive intervention, continuous engagement, and coordination during overlapping or multi-party interaction.
Provides 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and temporal metadata.
Separately evaluates response quality, participation decisions, and timing using response quality, window response rate, and reaction latency.
Leading models respond in under a second on average, but window response rates reach at most 53.77%; adapting responses to new information remains difficult.

papers.abstract: As streaming video generation advances, enabling real-time interaction with generated video is becoming increasingly important. We introduce StreamEval, a unified benchmark for interactive streaming video generation spanning five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing. StreamEval comprises 300 scripted test cases lasting 15-300s, each specifying initial assets, incrementally arriving multimodal requests, and explicit requirements for state changes and content preservation. Performance is assessed along four evaluation dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination, instantiated through ten task-specific metrics on a 0-100 scale. Evaluating 37 distinct models across 300 test cases, we find that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. In particular, request execution remains challenging: the highest task-specific scores are 36.90 for Following among seven avatar-performance models, 25.93 for Following in text-conditioned world generation, and 15.00 for Edit Success among three reported reference-editing models. These findings identify reliable request execution under timing and preservation constraints as a central challenge for advancing omni-modal real-time interactive systems. The leaderboard is available at https://streameval.ai
authors: StreamEval Team
bullets: Covers five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing.
Uses 300 scripted 15–300-second test cases with incremental multimodal requests, initial assets, and explicit preservation requirements.
Evaluates task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination through ten task-specific metrics.
Results from 37 models show that visual quality and identity retention do not guarantee reliable request execution or sustained consistency.
Request execution scores remain low across evaluated tasks, highlighting a key bottleneck for real-time interactive systems.

papers.abstract: Visual tool use enables vision-language models (VLMs) to acquire task-relevant evidence, but its effectiveness can be limited by predefined visual operations and the tool-use strategies learned during training. Representing these operations and strategies as reusable external skills allows them to be refined through self-evolution without updating model parameters. However, skill refinement can introduce performance regressions. Meanwhile, inspecting accumulated task execution trajectories together with skill evolution history may lead to evolution evidence overload. To address these challenges, we propose VisualEvolve, a self-evolving framework that evolves executable visual operations and tool-use strategies for VLMs through a Select--Execute--Evolve--Evaluate cycle. Skill-Library Snapshot Selection uses performance on a fixed validation set disjoint from execution tasks to select an effective historical snapshot for subsequent evolution, limiting the propagation of performance regressions. Progressive Evidence Access (PEA) guides capability-gap diagnosis through a coarse-to-fine hierarchy comprising the Skill-Performance Report, Evolution Log, Trajectory Summaries, and relevant raw trajectory segments. Across four VLM backbones and six evaluation sets from three benchmarks, VisualEvolve improves over the Initial Skill Library in 23 of 24 settings, with a maximum gain of 15.1 percentage points on VisualProbe Hard using Qwen3.5-Plus. Ablation studies support the contributions of Snapshot Selection and PEA, while further experiments show that skills can be improved using experience from different data settings and directly reused across backbones. Moreover, VisualEvolve enables effective skill self-evolution with over an order of magnitude fewer task-solving trajectories than estimated for representative RL-based methods.
authors: Jiawei Wang, Yucun Li, Xueqi Li, Shenghao Wang, Xinquan Gong, Dan Zhang, Zheqi Lv, Yuquan Le, Shaozu Yuan, An Zhang, Da Cao, Tat-Seng Chua
bullets: Addresses limitations of fixed visual operations and training-learned tool-use strategies in VLMs.
Uses a Select–Execute–Evolve–Evaluate cycle to refine executable visual skills externally.
Skill-Library Snapshot Selection chooses robust historical skills using a separate validation set to reduce regression propagation.

papers.abstract: Head-dimension compression can reduce the memory required by the key-value (KV) cache, but existing methods often reconstruct full-dimensional representations during inference, adding significant decoding FLOPs overhead. We formalize the design considerations for converting pretrained attention into a natively reduced-dimensional form that reduces both KV-cache storage and attention computation using a calibration set. Specifically, we consider reductions that (1) apply a shared projection to queries and keys so that they remain in a common reduced feature space, (2) derive this projection jointly from query and key activations to better preserve their interaction, and (3) are compatible with the pretrained RoPE transformation. To obtain a reconstruction-free realization of this reduction, we restrict it to coordinate selection and theoretically show that RoPE compatibility then holds if and only if complete rotary pairs are retained. Building on this characterization, we introduce RACE, a post-training method that selects rotary pairs using their joint query-key activation energy. We theoretically show that this criterion minimizes a separable, calibration-dependent upper bound on post-RoPE query-key product approximation error. The resulting reductions are folded into the model weights and require neither runtime reconstruction nor specialized kernels. Across three model families and different compression levels, RACE outperforms structured pruning and remains competitive with reconstruction-based methods on language-modeling, zero-shot, and long-context tasks. At 50% KV-cache retention and 256K context, RACE reduces total inference FLOPs by 47.8%, yielding 1.79x higher throughput, 43.2% lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and 28.1% lower allocated GPU memory in comparison to an uncompressed model.
authors: Irene Tenison, Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Daniel Karl I. Weidele, Nima Dehmamy, Dan Gutfreund
bullets: Targets head-dimension reduction while avoiding the decoding FLOPs overhead of reconstructing full-dimensional keys and values.
Uses a shared query-key projection derived from calibration activations and retains complete rotary pairs to preserve RoPE compatibility.
Selects rotary pairs by joint query-key activation energy, minimizing a separable upper bound on post-RoPE query-key approximation error.
The folded, post-training method requires no runtime reconstruction or specialized kernels and outperforms structured pruning across evaluated tasks.
At 50% KV-cache retention and 256K context, it reports 47.8% lower inference FLOPs, 1.79× higher throughput, 43.2% lower TTFT, and 28.1% lower allocated GPU memory versus an uncompressed model.

papers.abstract: Training multimodal search agents requires tasks that make visually grounded search necessary for determining the answer. Textual identity clues and unused target evidence allow shortcuts in synthetic questions, weakening supervision for visual search and evidence integration. We propose RACE, an image-conditioned task synthesis framework that constructs dependencies from images to targets and from target-specific evidence to answers. Referential Abstraction (RA) replaces identity-revealing text with specific visual references or ambiguous relational references resolved by searching among depicted candidates. Compositional Evidence (CE) links retrieved facts about multiple entities in one image or entities from different images into joint questions whose answers require every designated contribution. Both operations also apply to images found during search, allowing new visual observations to determine subsequent search targets or supply answer evidence. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-27B on only 12K teacher-generated trajectories from RACE raises average accuracy across ten multimodal benchmarks from 53.5 to 56.0, a relative improvement of approximately 4.7% over the matched base agent. Our code, data, and model will be publicly available.
authors: Eric Tao, Minhao Sun, Liyan Liu, Zhijing Wu, Xiaohan Yu, Lang Mei, Li Huang, Chao Feng, Jinchao Ma, Sichen Kang, Siyu Mo, Chong Chen
bullets: Addresses shortcuts in synthetic multimodal search tasks caused by textual identity clues and unused visual evidence.

Applies both mechanisms to images discovered during search, enabling observations to guide later targets or provide evidence.
Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-27B improves average accuracy across ten benchmarks from 53.5 to 56.0, a reported relative gain of about 4.7%.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about safety is essential for embodied agents powered by large language models (LLMs). We introduce the Contextual Action and Plan Safety benchmark (CAPSafe), designed to evaluate safety reasoning at two levels: (1) an action-level dataset that tests whether a single action is safe given its environmental context, and (2) a plan-level dataset that evaluates whether agents can generate safe long-horizon plans for complex hazardous household tasks. CAPSafe models safety conditions where hazards are situational (inferred from object properties), multiple hazards can co-occur within the same environment, and each is annotated with a relative severity level for fine-grained analysis. Evaluating nine closed and open-source LLMs reveals a substantial gap between hazard recognition and safe long-horizon planning. Several models achieve high accuracy in recognizing unsafe actions (exceeding 90% in the best cases), yet safe long-horizon planning remains substantially harder. Gemini-3-pro achieves the highest safe success rate (78.19%), while other models remain below 65%. These results highlight that robust safety reasoning over long action sequences remains an open challenge.

papers.abstract: A growing body of work proposes dynamic expert-skipping methods for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that adjust the number of experts activated per token during inference, aiming to preserve model quality while further reducing the number of active parameters. These methods have added calibrated importance scores, inter-expert similarity metrics, or learned per-token allocators in order to identify experts to skip. However, different calibration regimes, different reductions in the effective number of experts, and evaluation suites make comparisons difficult. We classify four representative prior methods into a unified taxonomy and benchmark them against a natural, simple baseline: statically reducing the number of experts $k$ (i.e., same reduced $k$ across all layers and tokens). We provide a fair comparison of these methods at matched expert-compute budget, on two modern MoEs (Gemma4-26B-A4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B) in a text-only setting and a contemporary vision-language model (Qwen3-VL) in a multimodal setting. Surprisingly, we find that the simple baseline is hard to outperform consistently across models, modalities, benchmarks, and calibration settings. The methods we benchmark often underperform the baseline and achieved gains, when present, are minor. We further find that the effective $k$ achieved (or optimized for) in calibration can diverge from the effective $k$ in testing, resulting in over- or under-estimating the compute at inference time. Based on these findings, we recommend a calibration-free per-modality static $k$ reduction and validate this on a held-out model and modality. We further argue that a static control at matched measured compute is the baseline any dynamic skipping method must beat.
authors: Jakob Steimle, Thomas Elsken, Daniel Ehrhardt, Lukas Rinder, Daniel Cremers, Xi Wang
bullets: Unifies four dynamic expert-skipping methods and compares them with using the same reduced expert count across layers and tokens.

Calibration can produce an effective expert count that differs from testing, causing inference compute to be over- or underestimated.
Recommends calibration-free, per-modality static expert reduction and validates it on a held-out model and modality.

papers.abstract: Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) requires a robot to rearrange objects that block access to its goal. For a pushing robot, progress may depend on a setup push that enables a later opening without itself clearing a passage. The number of candidate sequences can grow exponentially with sequence length, making physics-based search costly. We introduce the Search-trained Push Action Ranker (SPAR), which learns to prioritize push primitives from simulated search outcomes. Searches over sequences of up to two pushes per object provide supervision that distinguishes immediate openings from setup pushes. A transformer trained with regression and ranking losses scores primitives using contact tokens conditioned on scene geometry and reachability regions. The same model guides simulator evaluations in SPAR Search and selects actions for direct execution in SPAR Policy. Both modes solve successive keyhole problems that open access to neighboring free-space regions within a NAMO planner. Across successful runs on $300$ simulated two-push keyhole problems, SPAR Search reduces median simulator calls by $7.0\times$, leading to a $3.8\times$ reduction in planning time relative to Random Search. Without retraining, the same ranker guides search on $600$ keyhole problems which have no solution within two pushes. At a depth limit of five pushes, SPAR Search achieves $50.7\%$ success within $100$ simulator calls, compared with $20.2\%$ for Random Search. These gains carry over to NAMO planning: on hard simulated scenes, SPAR Search achieves $47\%$ success within $100$ simulator calls, compared with $21\%$ for Random Search. In real-robot experiments, SPAR Policy succeeds in $37/40$ trials without a physics-based digital twin, compared with $33/40$ for SPAR Search and $27/40$ for Random Search.
authors: Dhruv Metha Ramesh, Tri-An Nguyen, Junshan Huang, Jingjin Yu, Kostas E. Bekris, Abdeslam Boularias

Trains a transformer with regression and ranking losses on searches involving sequences of up to two pushes per object, using scene geometry, reachability, and contact tokens.
Supports both search guidance (SPAR Search) and direct action selection (SPAR Policy) within a keyhole-based NAMO planner.
On simulated two-push problems, SPAR Search reduces median simulator calls 7.0× and planning time 3.8× versus Random Search.
On real-robot trials, SPAR Policy succeeds in 37/40 cases, compared with 33/40 for SPAR Search and 27/40 for Random Search.

papers.abstract: Object counting in videos remains a poorly characterized capability of multimodal large language models. Counting questions are included in many existing VideoQA benchmarks, but the ground-truth count distributions in these benchmarks are heavily skewed toward small values. Across the nine benchmarks we survey, the median ground-truth count is at most five, and the three most frequent values together account for between 45% and 93% of the videos. The resulting mean accuracy is then dominated by the most frequent counts; a value-dependent bias at a rare count contributes negligibly to the average and remains invisible. We introduce CountVideoBench, a benchmark of 2,600 synthetic videos covering 26 cardinalities in the interval [5, 50] (100 videos each), grouped into six clusters of consecutive counts that span the range while enabling near-neighbor comparisons. Each video contains a single class of static objects under a controlled camera motion, removing object motion and reducing recognition as confounds. We evaluate sixteen video-language models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting. No model exceeds 27.6% Exact Match. The dependence of accuracy on cardinality varies across models, ranging from monotonic decline to a non-monotonic peak-and-collapse pattern, which rules out increasing difficulty with cardinality as the dominant explanation of counting failure. Every model further concentrates its predictions on its own set of preferred integers, with accuracy peaks coinciding with these values and collapsing at adjacent counts. These findings highlight the need for balanced, diagnostic counting benchmarks to reliably assess this fundamental visual capability.

bullets: Existing VideoQA benchmarks are dominated by small ground-truth counts, masking errors at rarer cardinalities.

Sixteen video-language models are evaluated zero-shot; none exceeds 27.6% exact-match accuracy.
Accuracy varies unpredictably with cardinality, including monotonic declines and peak-and-collapse patterns.
Models favor particular integers, with performance dropping sharply at neighboring counts, motivating balanced diagnostic benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning asks a model to work out where objects are in 3D space, how they relate to one another, and how they move. Agentic VLMs have recently brought large improvements on such tasks by letting the model actively gather evidence with 3D perception tools instead of answering in a single pass. Even so, on many questions the tools return the right evidence and the model still does not arrive at the correct answer: the gap between model and tools, where raw readings become usable conclusions, is left unfilled. We present S-Agent 2.0, a spatial reasoning agent that equips an off-the-shelf general coding agent with a command-line perception toolkit, and we design the interface around one principle: help the VLM close the evidence loop: acquire scene evidence, remember it in a persistent scene memory, and interpret each reading in plain spatial language. This design keeps the full flexibility of a coding agent, and every reading it acts on stays grounded in the tools' geometry. On MMSI-Bench and ReVSI, the toolkit improves a strong open-source model, Qwen3.8-27B, by +13.9 and +20.5 points over the same agent without tools, and a strong closed-source model, Gemini-3.8-Flash, by +11.2 and +9.6 points. With the open backbone S-Agent 2.0 reaches 66.5 on MMSI-Bench and 82.3 on ReVSI, ahead of the specialized system SpatialClaw on the same backbone (62.6 and 74.5), and with Gemini-3.8-Flash it reaches 74.1 and 90.5 against its 67.0 and 79.7. Both tool gains shrink as the backbone grows more capable, but SpatialClaw's shrinks far more on ReVSI, from +13.2 to +2.7, while ours stays at +9.6. S-Agent 2.0 also works across different general coding agent harnesses, such as Codex and Claude Code.
authors: Rui Gong, Ruoyu Wang, Yalun Dai, Hao Li, Sidi Yang, Qihao Zhao, Hongyu Li, Zeyang Guan, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Kim-Hui Yap, Ziwei Liu

Improves Qwen3.8-27B by 13.9 and 20.5 points, and Gemini-3.8-Flash by 11.2 and 9.6 points on MMSI-Bench and ReVSI, respectively.
Works across coding-agent harnesses including Codex and Claude Code; gains decrease with stronger backbones but remain substantial.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from monocular video requires inferring motion from noisy and intermittently visible observations. Long-range tracks provide valuable geometric constraints, but integrating their fragmented temporal coverage into shared, continuous motion remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{RayCo4D}, a ray-conditioned continuous motion model for monocular 4D reconstruction that explicitly separates visual measurements from latent 3D motion states. Each track is associated with a reference-time 3D query constrained to its camera ray, and its image and depth observations constrain shared latent motion nodes through local many-to-many associations. Each node maintains an $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ pose and body-frame velocity at sparse support times. A white-noise-on-acceleration process prior couples neighboring states and defines continuous-time interpolation, allowing observations across visibility intervals to jointly constrain the same latent state sequence.The inferred shared motion is transferred to Gaussian primitives through dual-quaternion blending, while reference-anchored local $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ residuals capture fine-scale non-rigid deformation beyond the shared scaffold. Experiments on diverse monocular dynamic scenes show that RayCo4D achieves competitive novel-view synthesis quality, improves structural and temporal consistency under rapid motion and incomplete tracks, and supports continuous-time rendering.
authors: Yuanxiang Ni, Xianliang Huang, Ruihan Hou, Feng Xie, Hao Zhang
bullets: Addresses noisy, intermittently visible observations and fragmented long-range tracks in monocular dynamic reconstruction.
Uses camera-ray-constrained reference-time 3D queries and many-to-many associations to connect observations to shared latent motion nodes.
Models each node with an SE(3) pose and body-frame velocity, coupled by a white-noise-on-acceleration prior for continuous-time interpolation.
Transfers shared motion to Gaussian primitives via dual-quaternion blending, with local SE(3) residuals for fine non-rigid deformation.
Reports competitive novel-view synthesis and improved structural and temporal consistency under rapid motion and incomplete tracks, with continuous-time rendering support.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of RayCo4D. Given a monocular video, RayCo4D constructs ray-conditioned 3D queries from 2D tracks and camera-depth estimates to constrain shared latent motion nodes. Sparse SE(3) pose–velocity states are coupled by a WNOA prior to model continuous motion. The inferred motion is propagated to Gaussians via dual-quaternion blending, while reference-anchored local residuals capture fine-grained non-rigid deformation for dynamic rendering and optimization.

papers.abstract: Realistic few-shot adaptation of medical vision-language models (VLMs) can leave low-prevalence classes without any labeled support. The training-free SS- Text+ solver remains operational in this setting, but its zero-support prototypes receive no visual adaptation and fall back to a purely textual class prototype. We in- troduce Gated Knowledge-Guided Prototype Transfer (GProtoT), a pre-repulsion module that transfers supported-class visual residuals to missing classes using VLM similarity and an ontology-based clinical distance. A validation-free evidence gate scales transfer based on semantic relevance and residual agreement, thereby limiting unsupported extrapolation. In 50 paired realistic one-shot trials on MESSIDOR with FLAIR features, severe and proliferative diabetic retinopathy were absent from every support set. Relative to SS-Text+, gated ProtoT improved missing-class recall by 5.23 points, average class accuracy by 1.37 points, and the missing/supported recall harmonic mean by 1.83 points. It reduced negative- transfer frequency from 46-48% for ungated transfer to 2%, while at the cost of reductions of 1.20 percentage points in supported-class recall and 0.45 percentage points in top-1 accuracy. These results indicate that evidence-based gating provides a safety mechanism for the knowledge source. GProtoT is based on SS- Text+ and requires no gradients, validation data, or additional model inference, of- fering a low-compute path toward accountable adaptation under incomplete clini- cal supervision. Code is available: https://github.com/sumaiyaafridi/GProtoT
authors: Sumaiya Fazal, Rizwan Qureshi, Laleh Behjat, Samira Ebrahimi Kahou
bullets: Addresses zero-support classes in realistic few-shot medical VLM adaptation, where textual prototypes lack visual adaptation.
Transfers supported-class visual residuals using VLM similarity and ontology-based clinical distance.
Uses a validation-free evidence gate based on semantic relevance and residual agreement to limit unsupported extrapolation.
Across 50 paired one-shot trials on MESSIDOR, missing-class recall improved by 5.23 points and the missing/supported recall harmonic mean by 1.83 points.
Reduced negative-transfer frequency to 2%, with modest decreases in supported-class recall and top-1 accuracy.

papers.title: Gated Prototype Transfer for Zero-Support Medical Vision Language Model
papers.tldr: GProtoT safely transfers visual knowledge to medical VLM classes with no labeled support, improving missing-class recall while sharply reducing negative transfer without training or validation data.

papers.abstract: Autonomous video editing from open-world resources remains a challenging problem in multimedia content creation. Retrieval-based methods are constrained by fixed source material and lack creative flexibility, while generative models struggle with long-horizon coherence and often diverge from user intent. Both paradigms fail to replicate the structured, multi-stage reasoning that underlies professional post-production. To address these limitations, we present Auto-Director, a tool-augmented multi-agent framework that mirrors professional editorial workflows: a Planning Agent decomposes abstract topics into fact-grounded scripts via retrieval-augmented planning; a Material Agent indexes open-world footage through shot segmentation and visual tagging; an Editor Agent assembles semantically aligned clips with MLLM-driven spatial adaptation; and a Critic Agent governs an iterative Reflect-and-Revise loop that checks scene-level alignment and pacing. To rigorously evaluate this new paradigm, we introduce VEdit-Bench, a benchmark of 100 expert-curated topics with human-annotated Golden Scripts and a five-dimensional metric suite covering Narrative Logic, Factual Accuracy, Semantic Alignment, Compositional Quality, and Stylistic Cohesion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Auto-Director significantly outperforms baseline methods in both automated metrics and human evaluation, effectively bridging the gap between amateurs and professional-grade video production.
authors: Yuxia Chen, Wenbo Zhu, Yangguang Ji, Zhenxiang Jiang, Teng Zhong, Yu Zhang
bullets: Addresses limited creative flexibility in retrieval-based editing and poor long-horizon coherence or intent alignment in generative approaches.
Uses four specialized agents: Planning, Material, Editor, and Critic, coordinated through retrieval, visual tagging, semantic alignment, and iterative revision.
Introduces VEdit-Bench, a benchmark with 100 expert-curated topics, Golden Scripts, and five evaluation dimensions.
Reports better automated-metric and human-evaluation performance than baseline methods, narrowing the gap between amateur and professional video production.

papers.abstract: Trajectory tracking for compliant robots is challenging due to nonlinear dynamics and modeling uncertainties, often requiring learning-based methods to avoid explicit parameter identification. Iterative Learning Control (ILC) ensures theoretically high precision and preserves the passive compliance of the robot. However, traditional ILC requires a separate learning phase for each new trajectory. Conversely, Reinforcement Learning (RL) generalizes to new trajectories, but practically suffers from high sample complexity and limited tracking precision. This work proposes Reinforced Iterative Learning Control (RILC) that combines the strengths of both approaches to achieve fast adaptation and guaranteed tracking convergence across diverse trajectories. By establishing a concurrent coupling between the two controllers, RILC overcomes the high initial errors and slow adaptation of traditional ILC, enabling high-performance tracking from the very first trials. In this architecture, ILC provides high-quality samples, while RL contributes as a generalizing best-effort policy across iterations. Additionally, a theoretical proof is presented to show that the RL component preserves ILC stability and, under specific conditions, can also reduce the error bound asymptotically. The efficacy of this framework is demonstrated through simulation and experiments on an underactuated 4-degree-of-freedom serial elastic robot using different trajectories and modeling mismatches.
authors: Yuri De Santis, Michele Pierallini, Franco Angelini, Manolo Garabini
bullets: Addresses ILC’s need for trajectory-specific learning and RL’s high sample complexity and limited precision.
Concurrently couples ILC and RL: ILC supplies high-quality samples, while RL learns a generalizing best-effort policy.
Theoretical analysis shows RL preserves ILC stability and can asymptotically reduce the tracking-error bound under specific conditions.
Simulation and experiments on an underactuated 4-DOF serial elastic robot demonstrate tracking across trajectories and modeling mismatches.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires a model to decide not only what to answer but also when to answer. Evidence arrives progressively, and recent benchmarks identify premature responses, issued before the queried event has concluded, as a recurring failure mode. Existing approaches often learn response timing through additional training, while training-free alternatives typically rely on scalar gating signals that do not explicitly represent when an answer becomes final. We organize chunk-wise streaming errors into three patterns: sampling variation can make an answer unstable, a stable answer may lack support in the observed video, or an answer may be supported by the current evidence while the event remains unfinished. We propose PACE (Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit), a training-free framework designed around these three failure modes. Given a question, PACE drafts a plan specifying what to observe and what will signal completion. As the stream unfolds, it invokes an off-the-shelf video LLM at informative moments, evaluates each draft for stability, grounding in its cited frames, and completion, and records verified observations in an event ledger. Experiments on ProactiveVideoQA and OVO-Bench Forward show that PACE improves over the official protocols by up to 5.9 average PAUC points and 6.2 average accuracy points across proprietary and open-source backbones, yielding state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Siqi Guo, Yuxia Chen, Wenbo Zhu, Yangguang Ji, Zhenxiang Jiang, Teng Zhong, Yu Zhang
bullets: Targets premature responses and other timing errors in streaming video understanding.
Uses a question-specific plan to identify observations and completion signals.
Checks draft answers at informative moments for stability, frame grounding, and event completion.
Maintains verified observations in an event ledger while the video stream unfolds.
Improves official protocols by up to 5.9 PAUC points and 6.2 accuracy points across evaluated benchmarks and backbones.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) differ widely in pretraining objective, modality and resolution, and none leads across benchmarks. We ask whether their representations are complementary, and whether a single encoder can inherit that complementarity. We introduce Pangaea-Latents, an extension of the Pangaea benchmark providing frozen embeddings of $5$ GFMs over its $11$ datasets, along with reproduced baselines, and find GFM embeddings to be neither redundant nor disjoint. We then propose GeoMixture, a preliminary framework to align a ViT to several GFMs per dataset through a multi-representation alignment (mREPA) objective. Our encoder ties the best GFM in average rank across nine Pangaea datasets, trading peak performance for cross-task consistency.
authors: Arthur Ouaknine, David Rolnick
bullets: Geospatial foundation models vary in objectives, modalities, and resolutions, with no single model leading across benchmarks.
Pangaea-Latents provides frozen embeddings from five GFMs across 11 datasets and reproduced baselines.
The embeddings are complementary rather than fully redundant or disjoint.
GeoMixture uses a multi-representation alignment objective to align a ViT with several GFMs per dataset.
The encoder matches the best GFM in average rank across nine datasets, trading peak performance for consistency.

papers.abstract: Geometric Relative Positional Encoding has become the primary mechanism for injecting spatial inductive biases into multi-view transformers. Existing designs condition attention on camera-level frustums or ray-marched depth, associating cross-view tokens through the sensor geometry. Such sensor-centric formulations, however, describe only where a token is observed from, leaving the rich surface geometry of the scene region depicted by the token. In this paper, we advocate a shift toward surface-aware positional encoding that explicitly grounds patch tokens in the geometry of physical surfaces. We introduce HRoPE, which represents the local geometry of each patch as a slanted 3D plane, following the slanted support-window assumption of classical multi-view stereo. We inject token-level, plane-induced homographies into attention as relative transformations. This equips the transformer with a geometric prior for rectifying perspective distortions and aligning patch features across viewpoints. Our encoding requires no ground-truth geometry: the plane parameters can be predicted end-to-end under a view-synthesis objective alone, or derived from foundation models. Extensive experiments on RealEstate10K, CO3Dv2, and DL3DV show that our best variant of HRoPE consistently outperforms the evaluated geometric positional encodings for novel view synthesis. Extensive ablations and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed encoding. Please refer to our project page at: https://gaohchen.github.io/HRoPE
authors: Huachen Gao, Yang Yang, Xiaoqian Liang, Xingyu Chen, Youjia Zhang, Qi Zhang, Baorui Ma, Anpei Chen, Wei Yang
bullets: Targets the limitation of sensor-centric positional encodings, which model camera rays but not the depicted surface geometry.
Represents each image patch as a locally slanted 3D plane and injects its induced homography as a relative attention transformation.
Plane parameters can be learned end-to-end from view synthesis alone or obtained from foundation models, without ground-truth geometry.
Experiments on RealEstate10K, CO3Dv2, and DL3DV report consistent gains over evaluated geometric positional encodings for novel view synthesis.
Ablations and analysis support the effectiveness of the surface-aware encoding.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about fine-grained placement constraints, such as support and containment, is essential for realistic 3D scene creation. It remains a significant challenge for existing methods that rely on simplified object representations like oriented bounding box (OBB), which are blind to the detailed geometry. To address this limitation, we introduce GALA, a geometry-aware language model with explicit point cloud perception for controllable object placement. Our model performs autoregressively by predicting the 6D pose of one target object at a time conditioned on the scene context and placement instruction. We utilize a two-stage training strategy: the first stage aligns geometric and textual modalities through pretraining tasks, and the second stage fine-tunes the model for placement. To facilitate this task, we also curate a multi-source scene dataset covering diverse room types and fine-grained furniture arrangements, which will be open-sourced for community benefit. Experiments on our benchmark show our model significantly outperforms baselines without explicit geometric reasoning. We further develop a multi-stage plan-place-verify agent pipeline that uses the model for text-driven scene generation. Project Page: https://xccelephant.github.io/paper/gala/
authors: Chucheng Xiang, Runze Wang, Zhi Deng, Ruchao Bao, Yuanwei Zhang, Yuxuan Xie, Hanliu Wang, Liangzhen Fei, Wenzheng Wu, Cheng Wan, Peifeng Li, Zhongyuan Liu, Ligang Liu
bullets: Targets fine-grained constraints such as object support and containment, which simplified OBB representations may miss.
Autoregressively predicts one object’s 6D pose at a time from scene context and placement instructions.
Uses two-stage training to align geometric and textual modalities before placement fine-tuning.
Introduces a diverse multi-source scene dataset for room layouts and fine-grained furniture arrangements.
Also presents a plan-place-verify pipeline for text-driven scene generation; experiments report significant gains over methods without explicit geometric reasoning.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the geometry-aware placement model. Given the scene boundary, the already-placed objects (with poses, sizes, semantic categories, and point clouds), the new object (with size, semantic category, and point cloud), and a placement instruction, the multimodal LLM outputs a numeric 6D pose. The model performs placement autoregressively, adding each predicted object to the scene context before predicting the next one.

Fig. 12. Overview of the hand-crafted scene dataset used for geometry-aware object arrangement. The gallery illustrates the diversity of room types, object categories, and fine-grained support and containment configurations.

Fig. 10. Gallery results from the agent pipeline for scene generation. Given text prompts and polygon floor boundary, the planner decomposes the request into object-level placement steps, then GALA predicts poses for the target objects to produce complete 3D scene arrangements.

Fig. 8. Qualitative comparison with baselines on whole-scene inference results. Each method receives the object set and the per-step placement instructions of a held-out test scene and places the objects one at a time, so the comparison isolates placement quality from planning.
Fig. 6. Qualitative comparisons of instruction-conditioned single-object placement results across instruction-aware baselines and our method.

Fig. 3. Dataset construction pipeline. Multi-source scenes are first cleaned by physical plausibility checks and VLM-based quality assessment. Each retained scene is parsed into a scene graph containing absolute room-location edges (abs), dependency edges (on, within, under), and proximity edges (next to). We form a floor-rooted scene tree T by selecting dependency edges with priority on > within > under > abs. We obtain the placement order 𝝅 = BFS(T) by traversing from the floor root, sorting nodes at the same depth by edge priority and footprint area. For each placement step, the tree edge and nearby proximity relations are verbalized into an instruction paired with per-object point clouds and the target 6D pose.

Fig. 9. More autoregressive inference results of our model on held-out test scenes. Starting from scene-level object sets and placement instructions, our model sequentially predicts object poses and produces complete arrangements across different room types and layout complexity.
Fig. 5. Agent pipeline for automated scene generation, where a planner turns a user prompt into object-level steps, GALA places each object, and a verifier feeds back failures for correction.

Fig. 7. Qualitative ablation results on fine-grained placement. Each column shows one instruction, the predicted scene, and a zoomed crop around the target placement. Blue boxes mark inserted target objects.

Fig. 4. Dataset statistics. (a) Distribution of object counts per scene across data sources. (b) Proportion of placement instructions generated from each source. (c) Distribution of instruction relation types, including absolute, on, within, and under.

Fig. 11. Procedural expansion of SpatialLM layouts. Starting from a 3D-box semantic layout, we replace large proxy objects with compatible assets from a curated library and then enrich the scene with small objects placed according to the geometry and affordances of the instantiated furniture.

Fig. 13. Validation loss curves for the text-only and point-cloud variants used in the internal comparison. Both variants reach their minimum validation loss at step 6240 (epoch 2.67), the checkpoint used for the reported test metrics; the markers annotate the corresponding validation losses.

papers.abstract: VGL-stGen is a multimodal large language model adapted from a pretrained medical vision-language model using paired lung H&E and spatial transcriptomics with single-cell references. Training integrates image-expression and expression-cell-type pairs, and gene-conditioned pseudo-labels transfer transcriptomic cell-type supervision to histology images. One deployed checkpoint supports thirteen evaluated tasks spanning tissue and cell-type classification, gene prediction and conditional expression completion from combinations of histology, cell identity and observed gene expression. Task-specific decoding produces categorical labels, gene lists and structured expression levels. For conditional completion, fixing queried gene identities and predicting their levels autoregressively improves structured prediction. Controlled adaptation shows that restricting supervision to requested expression-level tokens can further improve image-conditioned completion. Image-permutation experiments indicate that correctly paired histology adds information beyond observed expression. External classification relies partly on computational references with shared annotation lineage, and some H&E sources were exposed during cancer training or model development. Within these conditions, VGL-stGen demonstrates how a medical vision-language backbone can learn from spatial transcriptomics and histology to connect tissue morphology and molecular states through shared generative modeling.
authors: Haenara Shin, Dongjoo Lee, Sungwoo Bae, Kwon Joong Na, Daeseung Lee, Hongyoon Choi
bullets: Adapts a pretrained medical vision-language model using paired lung H&E images, spatial transcriptomics, and single-cell references.
Transfers gene-conditioned cell-type supervision to histology images through pseudo-labels.
Supports classification, gene prediction, and conditional expression completion with task-specific outputs.
Autoregressive prediction of queried gene levels and supervision focused on requested expression tokens improve conditional completion.
Image-permutation tests suggest correctly paired histology contributes information beyond observed gene expression.

papers.abstract: Oddly Satisfying Videos (OSVs) can evoke strong viewer responses through repetitive motion, visual tactility, and ASMR-like sounds despite containing few explicit semantic emotion cues. This makes OSVs a challenging setting for Video Emotion Analysis (VEA), since most existing methods focus on semantic video content and under-model the physical sensory dynamics that shape viewer responses. To support Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis (OSVEA), we construct the Oddly Satisfying Video Dataset (OSVD), comprising 12,000 annotated 5-second clips. Each clip provides viewer-emotion labels under video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual conditions, together with explanations grounded in visual and acoustic sensory evidence. Building on OSVD, we propose PI-MLLM, a psychophysics-inspired multimodal large language model that integrates Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment (MSDA) and Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution (CAVA). MSDA uses auxiliary prediction objectives to align modality representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics. CAVA evaluates emotion scores across modality coalitions and applies Shapley attribution to identify the dominant modality and determine whether visual and auditory evidence is synergistic or conflicting. Experiments show that PI-MLLM improves both viewer-side emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality, suggesting the value of physical sensory cues to video emotion analysis.
authors: Yuheng Zhang, Jie Zhang, Yuecong Min, Yunwei Zhao, Meichen Liu, Qiankun Li, Shiguang Shan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of analyzing emotions in videos with few explicit semantic cues but strong sensory effects.

Uses Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment to align representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics.
Uses Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution with Shapley values to identify dominant modalities and audiovisual synergy or conflict.
Experiments report improved emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality.
