papers.abstract: Recent advances in visuospatial understanding and agentic reasoning enable direct robotic manipulation with general-purpose multimodal models, but their embodied capabilities remain poorly understood. This paper systematically evaluate GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation using a lightweight agent execution framework. We first probe three fundamental embodied capabilities-depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile understanding-and demonstrate that the model can exploit depth information, acquire simple manipulation strategies from contextual demonstrations, and use tactile feedback to correct its actions. We then evaluate GPT-6 Astra across five established manipulation benchmarks along six capability dimensions. Despite competitive performance on several benchmarks-26.92\% success on RoboDojo and 76.0\% on RoboTwin 2.0-our analysis reveals a pronounced gap between semantic reasoning and physical execution, particularly in consequence-aware action planning, precision, and complex motion coordination. To further examine these limitations, we introduce LIBERO-GeoMotion, a new benchmark of geometry-constrained tasks that require precise pose alignment, coordinated translation and rotation, and anticipation of physical action consequences. GPT-6 Astra achieves only 11.1\% zero-shot success, exposing the difficulty of translating spatial understanding into physically feasible motion. Real-world experiments corroborate these findings: zero-shot execution is feasible for simple tasks, yet persistent deficits remain in motion feasibility, precise control, and physical safety, while substantial inference latency further hinders practical deployment. Overall, our results characterize the emerging embodied capabilities of general-purpose multimodal models and delineate the key challenges toward safe, efficient, and reliable robotic manipulation.
authors: Youwei Zhou, Bohan Hou, Yankai Fu, Yaoxu Lyu, Yifan Ye, Shilin Shan, Chen Guo, Jiaming Liu, Ran He, Caifeng Shan, Shanghang Zhang, Jianfei Yang, Zhihe Lu

papers.abstract: Low-cost multi-zone single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) sensors provide compact time-of-flight measurements but are limited by sparse sampling and unreliable depth estimates near geometric discontinuities. This letter presents a reliability-aware reconstruction framework for V-shaped surfaces using two complementary TMF8821 acquisition configurations. Point-wise reliability is learned from sensor confidence, transient peak amplitude, and peak sharpness, and is incorporated into a graph-based depth optimization. The reconstructed geometry is evaluated by robust two-plane fitting and a perpendicular cross-section. Experiments on 60-degree, 90-degree, and 120-degree targets reduce the mean V-angle error from 11.21 degrees to 9.66 degrees (13.8%). For the representative 90-degree target, the combined point-to-plane RMSE decreases from 14.56 mm to 13.65 mm.

Across 60°, 90°, and 120° targets, mean V-angle error drops from 11.21° to 9.66%; the 90° target’s point-to-plane RMSE falls from 14.56 mm to 13.65 mm.

papers.abstract: This work presents SplatFlux, a feed-forward latent-to-4DGS framework for both video-based 4D reconstruction and conditional 4D generation. Our key observation is that observed videos and conditionally generated content can be represented in the same pretrained video latent space, allowing both tasks to be formulated as latent-to-4DGS decoding. To construct compact and temporally coherent 4D scenes, SplatFlux introduces a static-dynamic decoupled 4D Gaussian representation that explicitly predicts dynamic probabilities for Gaussian primitives. This representation separates static scene structures from moving regions, enabling complete 4D scene construction in a feed-forward manner through static aggregation and dynamic motion interpolation. To learn static-dynamic decomposition and dynamic Gaussian motion without costly annotations, we further develop an auxiliary distillation strategy that provides pseudo dynamic masks and optical-flow cues. Extensive experiments across 3D and 4D reconstruction and generation demonstrate that SplatFlux achieves state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Runmin Zhang, Binglin Ren, Zhu Yu, Fudong Wang, Jiangke Lin, Yichun Shentu, Si-Yuan Cao, Yi Yuan, Hui-Liang Shen
bullets: Unifies observed-video reconstruction and conditional 4D generation through a shared pretrained video latent space.
Uses a static-dynamic decoupled 4D Gaussian representation with dynamic probabilities for each Gaussian primitive.
Builds scenes via static aggregation and dynamic motion interpolation.
Employs auxiliary distillation to obtain pseudo dynamic masks and optical-flow cues without costly annotations.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across 3D/4D reconstruction and generation tasks.

papers.abstract: Adapting Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) to medical imaging via LoRA has become standard practice, yet model selection is guided almost entirely by downstream task metrics, treating backbones with similar performance as interchangeable. We investigate whether equal performance implies equal internal representational shift. We analyse four ViT-B/16 backbones, DINOv3, SigLIP2, MerMED-FM, and BiomedCLIP, pre-trained with different objectives (self-distillation vs. contrastive vision-language) and on different data domains (natural vs. medical images). We adapt each to brain tumour segmentation and evaluate on six datasets covering both segmentation and Alzheimer's disease classification. Using attention divergence, weight-change analysis, and activation patching, we find that the four models converge to similar segmentation performance (mean Dice 78-81%) through markedly different internal dynamics, yet diverge in cross-task transfer: segmentation adaptation improves Alzheimer's disease classification for DINOv3 but degrades it for the other three backbones. We reveal a dissociation between modification magnitude and causal importance: the most heavily modified layers are not the causally relevant ones, with early-to-mid layers identified as sufficient for segmentation recovery. Restricting LoRA to these layers matches or approaches full-layer segmentation while reducing classification degradation in the three affected backbones, providing a mechanistically grounded strategy that is more parameter-efficient and more robust than standard full-layer adaptation.
authors: Cecilia Diana-Albelda, Fiona Kekwick, Raghav Mehta, Aleksandra Kulbaka, Paul M. Matthews, Jesus Bescos, \'Alvaro Garc\'ia-Mart\'in, Wenjia Bai, Bernhard Kainz
bullets: Four ViT-B/16 backbones reached comparable segmentation performance despite distinct representational shifts.
Segmentation adaptation improved Alzheimer’s classification for DINOv3 but harmed it for the other three models.
Layer modification magnitude did not indicate causal importance; early-to-mid layers were sufficient for segmentation recovery.
Restricting LoRA to these layers matched or nearly matched full-layer segmentation while reducing cross-task degradation.
The findings support mechanism-aware model and layer selection rather than choosing backbones solely by task metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the adaptation and analysis pipeline. (Panel A) Four brain MRI modalities (T1n, T1c, T2f, T2w) are fused via a trainable 1 × 1 convolution into a 3-channel input, processed by a frozen ViT-B/16 encoder with trainable LoRA modules applied to the query (Q) and value (V) projections of every transformer block in the default all-layer configuration. Components marked with \ (fusion convolution, LoRA modules, and segmentation head) are jointly trained on BraTS-GLI. (Panel B) Segmentation is evaluated on three BraTS datasets. For classification, the full encoder (including LoRA weights) remains frozen and only a logistic regression classifier (\) is fitted on each classification dataset using mean-pooled features from 𝓁12; the fusion convolution is bypassed (T1n input only). Four mechanistic interpretability tools are applied per layer to analyse the adaptation process: JS divergence, weight-change ratio, off-brain attention fraction, and activation patching.

Figure 6: Layer-selective LoRA performance across segmentation and classification datasets. Top row (a–c): normalised segmentation recovery 𝑅(𝓁) on three BraTS datasets; values above zero indicate improvement over the frozen baseline, and values below zero indicate degradation. Bottom row (d–f): absolute classification AUC on three Alzheimer’s disease benchmarks (not normalised, since the frozen-to-adapted gap varies in sign across backbones); the logistic regression probe is refit on the patched features for each block. All metrics are averaged across patients and MRI slices. Shaded bands show ±1 standard deviation across 3 seeds.

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) minimizes empirical risk over observed preference comparisons, implicitly assuming that the training preference distribution matches the deployment preference distribution. In practice, this i.i.d. assumption often fails, as preference distribution shift exhibits a natural hierarchical structure across three levels: group-level shift, prompt-level shift, and preference-level shift. Such multi-level distributional mismatch poses a critical challenge for safe LLM deployment, yet existing robust DPO methods typically either model uncertainty over the joint preference distribution or focus on individual sources of shift, leaving the hierarchical structure of OOD preference shifts underexplored. We propose TPO, a tri-level distributionally robust framework for OOD preference alignment, which jointly models all three levels of distributional uncertainty through a hierarchically structured rectangular ambiguity set. By instantiating it with Wasserstein distance, we derive a tractable and interpretable objective that combines a closed-form preference-level margin penalty, prompt-level adversarial embedding perturbation, and worst-case group reweighting, each governed by an independent radius. We establish finite-sample convergence guarantees and empirically validate the effectiveness of TPO over existing robust DPO methods.
authors: Chengtao Jian, Kai Yang
bullets: Addresses DPO’s vulnerability to deployment preference shifts beyond the i.i.d. assumption.
Uses a hierarchically structured rectangular ambiguity set to jointly represent three shift levels.
Combines a closed-form preference-margin penalty, adversarial prompt-embedding perturbation, and worst-case group reweighting.
Provides finite-sample convergence guarantees.
Experiments report improved effectiveness over existing robust DPO methods, without details on datasets or numerical gains.

papers.abstract: Large language models can solve complex problems across a variety of subjects, such as mathematics and coding. For such complex analytical tasks, models with a long context perform better. Serving models with long context is currently mostly done on powerful systems with multiple GPUs, which are too expensive for most users. An alternative is local inference, or serving a model on a user's own machine, which removes per-token costs and rate limits, besides keeping sensitive data private and giving users full control over the models they run. The common understanding, however, is that local LLMs need compression (e.g., quantization) to run on a single GPU. In this paper, we set out to study the limitations that prevent serving long-context models for single users, besides the capacity issue. Rather than characterizing a single model on one GPU, we analyze how different models behave across several GPU generations. This lets us uncover not just individual bottlenecks but broader trends in where inefficiencies arise. Our analysis confirms that, as expected, self-attention dominates the runtime for long-context inference. More unexpectedly, our evaluation reveals that the current structure of self-attention leaves key GPU resources significantly underutilized, and the newest GPU is often the least well served. Many of these findings are fundamentally data management problems, from paging the KV cache to improving cache utilization and synchronization in the GPU, which is why we bring this study to the Data Systems community. To engage this community, we present our findings as a series of experimental observations and formulate recommendations for future work.
authors: Mattias D\"urrmeier, Alberto Lerner
bullets: Local inference can reduce serving costs and rate limits while improving privacy and user control.
The study analyzes multiple models across several GPU generations rather than focusing on one model-device pair.
Self-attention dominates runtime for long-context inference.
Self-attention underutilizes important GPU resources, with newer GPUs often receiving less effective utilization.
Key challenges include KV-cache paging, cache utilization, and GPU synchronization; the paper offers observations and recommendations for future work.

papers.abstract: We introduce JAXbounce, a continuous control pong-like benchmark designed to evaluate active inference beyond discrete, low dimensional environments. JAXbounce combines continuous states and stochastic dynamics in discrete time with flexible and composable observation models that allow representing the environment as a state vector or a pixel grid, corruptible through the rich family of noise models we provide. It is fully differentiable and parallelisable in JAX. We run over 10,000 agent simulations on our environment comparing a baseline deterministic solution, to a state-based active inference agent with Unscented Kalman Filter perception and expected free energy planning, and a pixel based agent whose measurement model is a pretrained neural network encoder. All agents are evaluated across three scenarios of increasing difficulty with eight different noise conditions. Our experiments characterise how performance of continuous state agents scales with planning, planning horizons, observation modalities and knowledge of the noise process, exhibiting preference-oriented behaviour even in the presence of increasing uncertainty. We release JAXbounce as a reproducible benchmark for continuous control active inference research.
authors: Chaitanya Kaul, Markus Klar, Sebastian Stein, Fraser C. Paterson, John H. Williamson, Roderick Murray-Smith
bullets: Targets active inference beyond discrete, low-dimensional environments using continuous states and stochastic dynamics.
Supports composable state-vector or pixel-grid observations with varied noise models.
Provides JAX-based differentiability and parallelisation for scalable, reproducible experiments.
Compares deterministic, state-based, and pixel-based agents across three difficulty levels and eight noise conditions.
Findings characterise effects of planning, horizon, observation modality, and noise knowledge, including preference-oriented behaviour under uncertainty.

papers.abstract: Object-centric reinforcement learning agents typically receive each object's position in a fixed global frame, even though their decisions usually depend on where objects are relative to one another. These absolute views often fail to capture the local context that is most relevant to the agent's behavior. As a result, an agent must relearn the same response at every location where a configuration can occur, and its performance collapses when the scene is merely shifted. In this work, we propose a shift toward Object-Relative Coordinates fixed to Anchor (ORCA), where entities are described in a relative frame of reference. To operationalize this idea, we introduce Object-Relative inductive-Bias Transformers (ORBiT), a transformer-based architecture for processing anchor-relative inputs in reinforcement learning. Our results suggest these relative representations improve performance for both MLP and transformer agents. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ORBiT outperforms the pixel-based PPO baseline, achieving an aggregate HNS IQM greater than 1.0 over 13 Atari games. ORBiT learns the game of Foosball from scratch, dominating all baselines. In our controlled Tag environment, we further show that ORCA extends to rotations, that ORBiT generalizes to unseen numbers of distractors, and that these gains require a decision-relevant anchor.
authors: Cedric Derstroff, Jannis Bl\"uml, Janosch Moos, Michael Girstl, Zihan Ye, Debora Clever, Kristian Kersting
bullets: Absolute coordinates force agents to relearn equivalent behaviors at different scene locations and can fail under simple shifts.
The proposed ORCA representation encodes entities in anchor-relative coordinates, while ORBiT uses a transformer to process them.
Relative representations improve both MLP and transformer agents; ORBiT also outperforms a pixel-based PPO baseline across 13 Atari games.
ORBiT learns Foosball from scratch and dominates the evaluated baselines.
In controlled Tag experiments, ORCA handles rotations and unseen distractor counts, but requires a decision-relevant anchor.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) supervises student-generated responses using sampled-token student-teacher log-ratios. A positive log-ratio penalizes a token that the student assigns higher probability to than the teacher, but its current value does not distinguish sustained high penalties from abrupt increases along a response. We examine these local changes by comparing consecutive blocks of tokens within the same response. Our diagnostic identifies penalty jumps, abrupt increases in average penalty that persist on held-out tokens. Across these jumps, penalties rise while teacher confidence decreases. We call this pattern penalty-confidence tension. Boundaries into high-penalty blocks do not exhibit comparable confidence changes, showing that local changes provide information beyond the current penalty value. Motivated by this observation, we propose Adaptive Pullback OPD (AP-OPD). At each detected jump, AP-OPD uses the preceding block as a local reference and uniformly scales all supervision coefficients in the following block so that its weighted average penalty matches the preceding block's original mean. This reference determines the scaling factor without an additional strength constant. AP-OPD improves performance on both mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Guangyu Liu, Siyuan Gan, Shilong Zhou, Linjian Meng, Boyan Wang, Jing Huo
bullets: OPD’s current penalty value does not capture abrupt local increases within a response.
Penalty jumps coincide with rising penalties and decreasing teacher confidence, a pattern termed penalty-confidence tension.
AP-OPD uses the preceding token block as a local reference at each detected jump.
It uniformly rescales supervision coefficients in the following block to match the reference block’s original mean penalty.
The method improves performance on mathematical reasoning and code generation.

papers.abstract: Token merging is an effective approach to reducing KV-cache memory consumption in autoregressive video generation by clustering temporally redundant tokens and retaining only a small set of representatives. Existing methods, however, typically apply a uniform merging ratio across all attention layers and heads. We observe that different layers and heads exhibit substantially different yet jointly correlated sensitivities to token merging, and that these sensitivity patterns remain consistent across prompts. Based on this observation, we introduce CALM, a Calibrated Allocation for Layer-Head Merging that uses offline calibration to improve online cache compression. Exhaustively evaluating all possible layer-head allocations is prohibitively expensive. To enable efficient calibration, we show that attention-output error strongly correlates with end-to-end video quality and can therefore serve as a lightweight proxy for allocation risk assessment. We evaluate different allocation strategies using this proxy and construct a fixed layer-head risk map offline. Given a cache budget at inference time, CALM uses dynamic programming to determine the best allocation of merging ratios. Experiments across three different autoregressive video models demonstrate that CALM consistently outperforms uniform token merging under the same memory budget, by reducing the LPIPS to original videos by around 21% with higher video-quality scores.
authors: Zhen Wang, Ning Lai, Qingtao Yu
bullets: Uniform token-merging ratios overlook substantial, prompt-consistent sensitivity differences across attention layers and heads.
CALM uses attention-output error as a lightweight proxy for end-to-end video-quality risk during offline calibration.
It builds a fixed layer-head risk map, then selects merging ratios dynamically for a given cache budget.
Across three autoregressive video models, CALM outperforms uniform merging, reducing LPIPS to original videos by around 21% while achieving higher video-quality scores.

papers.abstract: Pose-free 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) aims to bypass cumbersome Structure-from-Motion (SfM) by directly reconstructing scenes from unposed image sequences. In this work, we present CrossFit-GS, a deferred-commitment progressive framework that mitigates cumulative trajectory drift and breaks the self-reinforcing loop of distorted-map error propagation. Specifically, we partition the input sequence into interleaved subsets and maintain two complementary submaps. Each candidate pose is cross-refined against a frozen opposite submap that has never been optimized using the target frame, thereby providing an independent geometric reference for pose estimation. Checkerboard validation and spatial coverage safeguards further reject unreliable updates, and only verified poses are committed to their corresponding owner submap. Once the trajectory has been refined, the intermediate submaps are discarded and the final global representation is trained from scratch using the fixed refined poses. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that CrossFit-GS substantially reduces cumulative trajectory drift and consistently improves both camera pose estimation and novel-view synthesis over existing methods.
authors: Zijian Wu, Jinliang Wang, Mingfeng Jiang, Zidian Lin, Ying Song, Ziqian Lu
bullets: Targets pose-free 3DGS without relying on Structure-from-Motion.
Splits image sequences into interleaved subsets and maintains two complementary submaps.
Cross-refines candidate poses against an opposite submap that has not used the target frame.
Uses checkerboard validation and spatial-coverage checks to reject unreliable updates before commitment.
Evaluations on multiple benchmarks show improved pose estimation and novel-view synthesis over existing methods.

The frame subsequently contributes only to Map B. The roles of the two folds alternate, ensuring that a frame does not train the map used to assess its pose. Finally, a unified Gaussian representation is trained from scratch using all training images and the fixed estimated poses.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies increasingly reason before acting, but existing reasoning models compress this intermediate decision into a single representation. When several plans are valid, this commitment hides alternatives that could otherwise be selected or revised. We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (GPL), which represents the reasoning state as a low-dimensional conditional distribution over plans, such as which object, grasp, or route to use. This makes the reasoning state addressable: without retraining the VLA, plans can be sampled (coverage), selected on request (steering), and reweighted by deployment outcomes (outcome adaptation). We test all three on SimplerEnv manipulation with $\pi_0$, and extend the analysis to RoboCasa, LIBERO, and a maze domain. Steering the plan raises the fraction of executions that follow the request from 0.48 to 0.94, while the same guidance on the native action distribution shows no reliable gain. Finally, we show that an explicit plan is most useful when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.
authors: Matteo Cercola, Katie Z Luo, Milan Ganai, John Alora, Simone Formentin, Marco Pavone
bullets: Existing VLA reasoning compresses alternative valid plans into one representation, limiting revision and control.

In SimplerEnv, steering increased request-following executions from 0.48 to 0.94; native action-distribution guidance showed no reliable gain.
Explicit plans help most when they encode decision information not already determined by the observation.

papers.abstract: Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR.
authors: Xiaoxu Xu, Hao Li, Hongtao Zhang, Yili Tang, Jiafei Cao, Junhao Cai, Haoxiang Ma, Weixin Li, Weinan Zhang

papers.abstract: Existing feature lifting approaches for open-vocabulary segmentation rely on simple backprojection to assign features to primitives. In the case of 3D Gaussian splatting reconstruction, the primitives overlap heavily, leading to suboptimal reconstructions, governed by many primitives per ray. Backprojection, however, reduces to a least-squares solvable problem, exactly when no two primitives share a ray. Motivated by this insight, we propose OV-Foam, which uses PowerFoam as the underlying representation. This representation uses a power-diagram to partition the scene, resulting in zero overlap between primitives and a substantial reduction in primitives per ray, which ultimately simplifies the lifting problem and allows for closer-to-optimal feature assignment. We show that the space partitioning primitives of OV-Foam reach near-optimal assignment, and our experiments demonstrate improved open-vocabulary segmentation over Gaussian baselines.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, their reliability can degrade substantially when task conditions deviate from the nominal setting. Perturbations in object positions and task instructions may lead to complete task failure. Existing VLA policies generally lack an explicit runtime mechanism for distinguishing these failure modes and selecting an appropriate recovery strategy. To systematically mitigate this issue, we propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework for improving the robustness of VLA policies at inference time. FIT-MAC augments a VLA policy with an inference-time control layer. First, the Planner Agent parses the language instruction into a structured task specification that captures the manipulation goal and spatial constraints, and the Grounder Agent resolves each instruction-level reference to a visual target. Next, the Verifier Agent tracks phase-specific execution progress, distinguishes target-binding errors from local execution failures, and determines whether intervention is warranted. The Correction Agent then routes permitted interventions to target rebinding or bounded grasping or placement recovery, depending on the failure type. When no intervention is required, the pretrained VLA remains the default action generator. Extensive experiments on LIBERO-PRO demonstrate that FIT-MAC improves robustness across multiple VLA backbones, consistently increasing success rates and achieving state-of-the-art performance under diverse perturbations.
authors: Jiatong Li, Jisheng Dang, Qiangqiang Ma, Bimei Wang, Jingwen Zhao, Wenjun Ma, Juncheng Li, Hong Peng, Bin Hu
bullets: Targets VLA failures caused by deviations from nominal task conditions, including object-position and instruction perturbations.
Uses Planner, Grounder, Verifier, and Correction Agents to parse tasks, bind references, monitor execution, diagnose failures, and select recovery actions.
Retains the pretrained VLA as the default action generator when no intervention is needed.
Demonstrates improved robustness across multiple VLA backbones on LIBERO-PRO, with state-of-the-art performance under diverse perturbations.

papers.abstract: Wearable devices increasingly support personalized health and well-being applications, but post-deployment data can differ substantially from those used for training, while purely local adaptation may be limited by the data available on a single device during real-world operation. Conventional federated and decentralized learning rely on recurrent communication and stable connectivity, whereas existing opportunistic approaches often exploit available encounters without adequately considering their utility, compatibility, or communication cost. We propose PULSE, an event-driven framework for personalized opportunistic learning that treats each encounter as an online collaboration decision, selecting either no interaction or a promising nearby peer. Peer gradients are incorporated only when compatible with the local learning direction, while past interactions guide future peer selection. Across human activity recognition, fall detection, and stress recognition under synthetic and real contact traces, PULSE preserves or improves personalized classification performance, while reducing peer-assisted exchanges by 80-94% compared with opportunistic model averaging. On-device experiments further demonstrate its feasibility on wearable hardware: peer-assisted operations require limited energy, while the complete implementation occupies 149.8 KiB of RAM and 561.8 KiB of flash. The obtained results show that selective opportunistic collaboration can provide effective personalization while limiting communication and resource demands on constrained wearable devices.
authors: Mattia Giovanni Campana, Dariush Salami, H\"useyin Yi\u{g}itler, Stephan Sigg
bullets: Addresses distribution shift after deployment and limited data for purely local adaptation.

Maintains or improves personalized performance across activity, fall, and stress recognition tasks.

papers.abstract: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.
authors: Peisong Wen, Qianqian Xu, Minye Lei, Siran Dai, Yang Liu, Qingming Huang
bullets: Addresses redundant object-structure recovery, missing temporal correspondence, and displacement-insensitive pointwise losses in dense JEPA interfaces.
Decomposes representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks, then freezes this pretrained interface for downstream use.
Introduces a Transition Memory Predictor with slot-specific and shared cross-slot dynamics, retrieving transitions through corresponding-slot statistics.
Uses Unbalanced Optimal Transport to supervise mask prediction and compare predicted and goal masks based on spatial progress.
Features transfer across seven visual-understanding benchmarks and improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar and four robotic-arm tasks on REALM-JEPA.

papers.abstract: Multilingual evaluations often score a model's opening yes or no, a token that also carries model and language answering conventions. We ask when different ways of eliciting and reading an answer recover the same judgment, and when they measure an answer habit. We collect 1.1 million replies from eight models in six languages on up to 105 moral vignettes, varying the question's form, the answer constraint, and the reading of the reply, token or sentence, in both wordings (the FAR-6 battery). Story-level judgment profiles converge across the tested readouts and question forms, except for the yes/no token after a negative interrogative read under a preset mapping: on the same replies, token and sentence profiles agree at a median r = 0.67 across cells, while sentence profiles agree with free-sentence profiles at 0.94, a known linguistic variability. With each language's story consensus removed, a model's profile is nearest to its own in another language for 39 of 48 model-language cells under proposition labels and 15 under free sentences, against 5 expected by chance. Particle, position, and named-term preferences follow their own patterns. A model can keep its judgment and change its yes: scoring that token requires establishing which proposition it affirms.
authors: Haonan Huang, Yuwei Lu, Chengkun Cai
bullets: The study tests eight models in six languages across up to 105 moral vignettes, varying question form, answer constraints, and whether replies are read as tokens or sentences.
Story-level judgment profiles generally converge across readouts and question forms.

The main exception is a yes/no token following a negative interrogative under a preset label mapping; token and sentence profiles agree less strongly (median r = 0.67), while sentence and free-sentence profiles agree at 0.94.

After removing shared story consensus, models’ profiles are most similar to themselves across languages in 39 of 48 cells using proposition labels, versus 15 with free sentences; particle, position, and named-term preferences show distinct patterns.
Interpreting a yes/no answer requires identifying which proposition the model is affirming, rather than scoring the token alone.

papers.tldr: Language models largely preserve the same moral judgments across languages and elicitation formats, but a standalone yes/no token can reflect answering conventions rather than the affirmed proposition.

papers.abstract: The Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm has achieved remarkable success in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, when applied to long-horizon tasks, it faces severe challenges: i) Due to the high task complexity, the model struggles to sample enough successful trajectories, resulting in slow convergence. ii) Relying solely on sparse final rewards causes all steps to be updated indiscriminately, encouraging redundant step generation. When both the quantity and quality of successful trajectories become difficult to guarantee, the performance is severely constrained. This dilemma stems from the limitations: existing RL paradigms rely entirely on the reasoning capability of base models, lacking the ability to actively optimize trajectories. To address the above issues, we propose a novel trajectory evolution paradigm with hindsight credit assignment, termed TrajEvolve. TrajEvolve not only relies on the trajectory inferred by the model but also generates ``evolutionary trajectories'' by refining low-quality steps in historical trajectories, thereby exposing the policy to high-quality compositions that lie within the base model's support but are rarely sampled within practical training budgets. Furthermore, TrajEvolve reformulates step-level continuous credit assignment as a binary classification task, whether each step is necessary for task completion. This simplification not only reduces the learning difficulty but also enables step labels to be obtained through counterfactual verification, achieving precise identification of redundant steps. Extensive experiments on two datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.
authors: Yi Wen, Hao Chen, Wanyu Wang, Maolin Wang, Pengyue Jia, Derong Xu, Huize Tan, Yingyi Zhang, Wenlin Zhang, Weihong Luo, Xiku Du, Xiangyu Zhao
bullets: Addresses sparse-success sampling and indiscriminate updates caused by final-only rewards.
Generates evolutionary trajectories by refining low-quality steps in historical trajectories.
Recasts continuous step-level credit assignment as binary necessity classification.
Uses counterfactual verification to label whether each step is required for task completion.
Experiments on two datasets report superior performance, without details in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Understanding how supervision signals shape semantic visual representations remains challenging, particularly in fine-grained, low-data settings. Standard evaluations of vision models rely on downstream accuracy, which often fails to capture structural differences in learned representations. We propose a compact explainability-driven framework for comparing encoders trained with classification-only and caption-generation supervision on CUB-200. Using a controlled two-stage protocol in which both encoders are ultimately optimized for the same classification task, we enable a direct comparison of the resulting representations. Saliency maps are generated using attention rollout and gradient-weighted rollout and evaluated with five metrics covering faithfulness (positive and negative perturbation) and localization (keypoint emphasis, background attribution, and Earth Mover's Distance). Across random seeds and explanation methods, caption supervision yields representations that are more sensitive to the removal of salient regions, better aligned with annotated object parts, and less reliant on background regions, whereas classification supervision produces representations that are slightly more robust to the removal of low-saliency regions. An ablation study on the Oxford-IIIT Pet dataset shows consistent trends across key metrics. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework makes supervision-induced representational differences observable and quantifiable beyond downstream accuracy alone. More broadly, it provides a systematic basis for assessing learned representations and comparing alternative training and transfer-learning strategies.
authors: Md Raisul Kibria, S\'ebastien Lafond
bullets: Motivation: Downstream accuracy alone may miss structural differences in learned visual representations, especially in low-data fine-grained settings.
Method: Compare classification-only and caption-generation supervision under a controlled two-stage classification protocol using saliency-based faithfulness and localization metrics.
Caption-supervised representations are more sensitive to removing salient regions, better aligned with annotated object parts, and less dependent on background regions.
Classification-supervised representations are slightly more robust when low-saliency regions are removed.
Trends remain consistent in an ablation on Oxford-IIIT Pet, supporting the framework’s use for quantifying supervision-induced representation differences.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) consolidates expert capabilities into a single student by matching teacher and student final-layer distributions on student-generated rollouts. We investigate whether depthwise prediction transitions, the changes in predictions between layers, can provide additional task-relevant supervision. Our diagnostic study finds that stronger teacher--student agreement in intermediate transitions is associated with higher answer correctness within questions, with correct responses exhibiting lower mean transition KL across all measured intermediate layer pairs. These observations motivate On-Policy Transition Distillation (OPTD), which augments final-layer distribution matching by aligning teacher and student layer-to-layer log-probability increments on student-generated rollouts. Evaluations across three backbones and eight benchmarks spanning mathematics, coding, and instruction following show that OPTD achieves the best or tied-best overall performance in both dual- and three-domain distillation. In the three-domain setting, OPTD recovers $\approx 90\%$ of the overall teacher--student capability gap, compared with $\approx 75\%$ for OPD.
authors: Runyang You, Yongqi Li, Tiezheng Yu, Wenjie Li
bullets: Intermediate teacher–student transition agreement correlates with answer correctness, with correct responses showing lower transition KL.
OPTD augments standard on-policy final-layer distribution matching with layer-to-layer log-probability increment alignment.
Evaluated across three backbones and eight mathematics, coding, and instruction-following benchmarks.
OPTD achieves the best or tied-best overall performance in both dual- and three-domain distillation.
In three-domain distillation, OPTD recovers approximately 90% of the teacher–student capability gap versus approximately 75% for OPD.

papers.abstract: Panoptic scene graph generation (PSGG) represents scene entities with segmentation masks and directed relations. Equirectangular projection (ERP) panoramas challenge PSGG through distortion, latitude-dependent pixel areas, and an artificial seam. We propose a two-stage spherical geometry-aware framework that fuses overlapping perspective-view predictions using observation reliability, spherical overlap, and angular proximity. Relation reasoning combines spherical-area-aware aggregation, weighted no-relation supervision, and dual-longitude score fusion. We also construct a dataset of 340 high-resolution panoramas with 10,571 nodes and 6,632 directed relations. Against corresponding baselines, spherical fusion improves PQ by 36.03% under matched views, while relation reasoning improves mR@50 by 11.20% under PredCls with ground-truth masks and object labels. The full framework improves mR@50 by 52.99% under SGDet with predicted panoptic segments. These results demonstrate the value of spherical geometry for panoramic PSGG.

Uses spherical-area-aware relation aggregation, weighted no-relation supervision, and dual-longitude score fusion.
Introduces a dataset of 340 high-resolution panoramas containing 10,571 nodes and 6,632 directed relations.
Reports improvements of 36.03% in PQ, 11.20% in mR@50 under PredCls, and 52.99% in mR@50 under SGDet.

papers.abstract: Examining existing benchmarks for grounding in 3D VLMs reveals a pervasive "semantic leakage" in the evaluation and prompting protocols: a heavy reliance on bounding boxes as spatial prompts or representation primitives. Because bounding boxes are highly informative of object categories, they introduce a shortcut for the models to neglect visual information during 3D VLM training. We demonstrate this with a "blind" LLM that, prompted only with the box coordinates, can perform surprisingly well. To further analyze this shortcut, we propose point-based grounding prompting - querying models with a single 3D point instead of a box. Under this protocol, the accuracy of the blind LLM drops from 36.4% to 18.0% on ScanNet's Nr3D, and similarly degrades for 3D VLMs (e.g. LL3DA). Building on this insight, we introduce P$^3$-VLM, a novel tri-pathway 3D VLM that supports point-based prompts and achieves 52.1% state-of-the-art accuracy on location-grounded captioning under this setting. To achieve this, we redesign the architecture while keeping it detector-free, scene-centric, and suitable for 3D GS inputs. P$^3$-VLM utilizes three complementary pathways (location-, task-, and context-aware), enabling strong reasoning about scenes without any bounding box dependencies. The key benefit of point-based learning is a consistent improvement across settings: P$^3$-VLM achieves state-of-the-art performance under point-based grounding while also improving robustness, OOD generalization, and performance on ungrounded scene-centric 3D VQA benchmarks, reflecting its reduced reliance on bounding-box shortcuts and resulting stronger visual-spatial reasoning.
authors: Anna-Maria Halacheva, Jan-Nico Zaech, Sombit Dey, Luc Van Gool, Danda Pani Paudel
bullets: Existing 3D VLM grounding benchmarks risk semantic leakage because bounding boxes reveal object-category information.
A blind LLM using only box coordinates reaches 36.4% on ScanNet Nr3D, but falls to 18.0% with a single 3D point, exposing the shortcut.
P$^3$-VLM is a detector-free, scene-centric, tri-pathway 3D VLM designed for point prompts and 3D Gaussian Splatting inputs.
Its location-, task-, and context-aware pathways achieve 52.1% accuracy on point-based location-grounded captioning.
Point-based learning also improves robustness, out-of-distribution generalization, and ungrounded scene-centric 3D VQA performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3: P3-VLM architecture overview. Three complementary pathways process the voxelized 3D scene: the location-aware pathway extracts a single token at the queried point; the task-aware pathway produces prompt-guided scene tokens by first refining the task prompt tokens and subsequently utilizing them for visual refinement of the sparsified features; the context-aware pathway distills 8 global scene summary tokens via unconditional cross-attention. Notably, the context and task pathways operate on the sparsified features for efficiency gains.

papers.abstract: Camera design heavily influences perception task performance, yet cameras are typically designed by domain experts through costly experimentation, in isolation from the tasks they serve. Existing joint-design methods either rely on differentiable simulation limited to pre-captured 2D images, restricting them to optics or image-processing pipeline design, or use non-differentiable camera simulators optimised with derivative-free or reinforcement-learning methods that scale poorly with the number of design parameters. We present a differentiable framework for jointly designing complex camera systems and downstream perception tasks. We use it to design two coded-aperture depth-from-defocus cameras, a monocular and a stereo configuration, by jointly optimising the coded aperture mask, camera parameters, and a depth estimation network end-to-end. Our framework represents scenes with 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructed from real-world captures, providing a differentiable image formation process for gradient-based optimisation over design spaces intractable for prior differentiable approaches. Results demonstrate that our differentiable method improves over existing coded aperture design and non-differentiable camera design baselines, offering a step forward in automated and principled camera design for autonomous systems.
authors: Chengyang Yan, Donald G. Dansereau
bullets: Addresses the costly, task-agnostic process of designing cameras through manual experimentation.
Jointly optimizes coded aperture masks, camera parameters, and a depth-estimation network end-to-end.
Uses 3D Gaussian Splatting from real-world captures to enable differentiable image formation and gradient-based design optimization.
Demonstrated on monocular and stereo coded-aperture depth-from-defocus cameras.
Improves over existing coded-aperture and non-differentiable camera-design baselines, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 7. The stereo depth-from-defocus method. Per-view AiF proxy images are synthesised by fusing the Tikhonov-deconvolved focal stack using a differentiable Laplacian sharpness measure and passed to a frozen RAPIDFlow [29] network to estimate dense disparity. The disparity is then used to warp the right-view into the left-view coordinate frame via bilinear grid sampling. The left-view focal stack, the warped right-view focal stack, and a depth map derived from the disparity estimate are concatenated and fed into the monocular U-Net backbone with frequency injection, yielding the reconstructed AiF image and depth map for the left view.

Figure 1. We introduce a differentiable method that jointly optimises camera parameters and perception tasks, using 3DGS scenes reconstructed from real-world captures and a coded aperture simulation modelling depth-dependent optical blur. Camera parameters and the perception network are jointly updated via gradientbased optimisation of the task loss (red arrows), spanning geometric parameters (FoV, pixel count, multi-camera configurations) and high-dimensional optical parameters (coded aperture mask).

Figure 6. The monocular depth-from-defocus method. The backbone follows the U-Net of Ikoma et al. [16], which takes a coded aperture image and its Tikhonov-deconvolved focal stack as input and jointly predicts the AiF image and depth map. We augment this backbone with a frequency injection module. In this module, the input image is divided into patches, a 2D Fourier transform is applied to each patch independently, and the log-magnitude spectrum is computed to capture local, spatially-varying defocus strength. The per-patch spectra are encoded by a lightweight 3-layer convolutional network, reassembled into a 2D feature map based on each patch’s location, and injected at the bottleneck of the U-Net.

Figure 8. Qualitative comparison for the monocular experiment under the Noise×200 scenario. Our jointly optimised camera, mask, and perception model again produce sharp AiF images and accurate depth, while the fixed-camera baseline (Ikoma et al. [16]) and the derivative-free joint optimiser (TaCOS [43]) produce images with more defocus blur and lower depth accuracy in these regions.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison for the monocular experiment. Our jointly optimised camera, mask, and perception model produce sharp AiF images and accurate depth, while the fixed-camera baseline (Ikoma et al. [16]) and the derivative-free joint optimiser (TaCOS [43]) degrade noticeably in blurry regions.

Figure 9. Qualitative comparison of the proposed stereo method with a coded aperture dual-pixel camera method (CADS [12]) and the monocular alternative. Our method achieves better AiF reconstruction by combining varying focus planes across the two views, and better depth estimation by exploiting disparity as an additional cue.

Figure 4. Our method fuses photometric cues from a foreground-focused and a background-focused view for higher AiF quality and improves depth accuracy by leveraging disparity. Full comparisons with baselines are presented in the supplementary material.

Figure 2. A camera captures the real-world scene (blue arrow), which 3DGS models as a 3D Gaussian representation. At each step, this representation is rendered with the current geometric camera parameters into pinhole RGB images and depth maps; the coded aperture simulation then convolves these RGB renders with depth-dependent PSFs computed from the coded mask, focus distance, and f-number via a physical optics model, followed by a physics-based noise model. The resulting renders are fed to the perception task network, and the task loss ltask is backpropagated through both stages (red arrows) to jointly update all learnable parameters (green text).
Figure 5. Prototype of the optical system used for real-world validation and the real-world stereo results.

Figure 10. (a) The optimised coded aperture masks in both monocular and stereo experiments, the manufcatured masks, and their measured PSFs. (b) The captured coded aperture image, reconstructed AiF image, and estimated depth map for the monocular setup. The AiF and depth recovery on real hardware show plausible outcomes but with modest accuracy gap attributable to the sim-to-real domain shift and manufacturing tolerances.

[16], tested with their original Phase mask and with an Amp. (amplitude) mask matched to our settings) and a derivative-free joint optimiser (TaCOS [43]). Optimised parameters are marked•, fixed parameters•; our method outperforms both baselines under two noise scenarios.

The monocular row is our own strongest monocular configuration evaluated under the same narrow FoV, isolating the benefit of a second view; CADS [12] is the closest existing coded-aperture baseline, included despite its dual-pixel baseline being limited to the sub-mm aperture scale. papers.abstract: VLMs for medical image interpretation are typically evaluated on clean inputs, despite the progressive evidence loss that can occur in high stakes clinical settings. Existing robustness studies show that performance can degrade while confidence remains high, but do not establish when a previously reliable model-case pair ceases to behave reliably. We introduce a baseline-anchored framework that traces baseline-correct cases through progressive image degradation to identify an empirical evidence boundary, and define mirage as continued commitment at this boundary, regardless of correctness. Across three VLMs on three medical datasets, only MedGemma provides a sufficiently large baseline-correct pool for trajectory analysis. On VQA-RAD, the only dataset in which the question text varies, language-only answerability is associated with baseline correctness (AUROC 0.677) and with commitment at the boundary (AUROC 0.653 to 0.670). MedGemma's post-boundary behavior is heterogeneous, including direct mirage, correct recovery, mirage dissolution, consistent abstention, and oscillation, with mirage rates of 16.0 to 100.0% across dataset-modality pairs. Despite this behavioral heterogeneity, residual-stream probes decode commit-versus-abstain behavior at the boundary with AUROC of 0.895 to 0.994 under nested cross-validation. These results show that progressive evidence loss can produce persistent commitment that output entropy and abstention behavior do not consistently reflect, motivating boundary-aware evaluation, option-order controls, and improved abstention mechanisms for reliable medical foundation models operating under partial observation.
authors: Edric Castel C. Hao, Rez Samantha Z. Floresca
bullets: Introduces a baseline-anchored framework that tracks initially correct model–case pairs through progressive degradation to identify an empirical evidence boundary.
Defines “mirage” as continued answer commitment at that boundary, whether or not the answer remains correct.

Across three VLMs and datasets, only MedGemma had a sufficiently large baseline-correct pool for trajectory analysis; its post-boundary behavior varied widely, with mirage rates of 16.0–100.0% across dataset–modality pairs.
On VQA-RAD, language-only answerability was associated with baseline correctness and boundary commitment.

Residual-stream probes decoded commit-versus-abstain behavior at the boundary with AUROC 0.895–0.994 under nested cross-validation, motivating boundary-aware evaluation and better abstention mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Moving from controllable videos to genuinely playable worlds requires persistent world state, executable game rules, and low-latency interaction. We outline a roadmap for the next generation of Matrix-Game that separates game execution from visual generation through an executable game harness, and introduce Matrix-Game 4.0 as the first system built on this design. A lightweight game engine maintains world state and executes interaction rules, a multimodal coding agent translates player ideas into game code and dynamic scene captions, and a renderer based on autoregressive video model transforms engine-rendered low-poly proxies into detailed visuals, conditioned on dynamic captions and memory references. This framework provides continuous guidance for visual generation and enables natural-language creation and modification of scenes and gameplay. Our renderer is trained on aligned low-poly and high-fidelity video pairs and distilled into a causal generator that generates in four-frame chunks with one or two denoising steps. Together with targeted inference optimizations, Matrix-Game 4.0 enables 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on a single NVIDIA RTX5090 with a key-press-to-display latency of 112ms. Single-step generation achieves 83FPS steady-state throughput with 18.2GiB of peak GPU memory usage. With fixed prompts, steady-state throughput also reaches 67FPS on an RTX5080 and 58FPS on an RTX5070Ti. We demonstrate customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics, and release code, model weights, and low-poly game assets to support research and creation of playable game worlds.
authors: Jihai Zhang, Runjia Qian, Kaiqin Kong, Biao Jiang, Puyi Wang, Siru Chen, Tianle Li, Guanjie Chen, Junyi Wu, Chubin Chen, Yuanhang Li, Kaichen Huang, Haobo Zhang, Yangguang Li, Wei Yu, Guibin Chen, Yu Cheng, Yahui Zhou
bullets: Addresses the gap between controllable video generation and playable worlds requiring persistent state, executable rules, and low-latency interaction.

Separates game execution from visual generation: an engine manages state and mechanics, while an autoregressive video model renders detailed visuals from low-poly proxies, captions, and memory references.
A multimodal coding agent converts player ideas into game code and dynamic scene descriptions.
Demonstrates customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics.
Achieves 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on an RTX5090 with 112 ms key-press-to-display latency; code, weights, and assets are released.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Architecture of the rendering model. The noisy latent of one chunk (one latent frame, four video frames) and the low-poly proxy encoded by TAEHV are concatenated into 148 channels and patchified into 405 tokens per latent frame at 480×864. Thirty causal DiT blocks apply self-attention over a KV cache that holds spatial-memory frames, reference frames, and the latest 20 chunks, cross-attention to the cached text keys and values of the dynamic caption, and a feed-forward network, each modulated by the timestep through AdaLN. The output head predicts a velocity, one or two flow updates produce the clean latent, and TAEHV decodes four frames. The finished chunk is then re-run at t = 0 without the control input to write its keys and values into the cache.

(d) Self-attention is split into seven window ranges whose quantized keys and values are cached; the partial outputs are combined by log-sum-exp.

papers.abstract: Tactile representation learning for dexterous manipulation often requires substantial robot-side data collection, limiting its scalability across different hands and sensors. We explore whether large-scale human hand-object interaction (HOI) data can provide a useful prior for robotic tactile learning. To this end, we propose HuTact, a framework that pretrains tactile-aware hand representations from human HOI data without requiring real tactile signals during pretraining. HuTact transfers the interaction structure learned from human hand motions to robotic tactile observations and can be further adapted with a small amount of unlabeled robot interaction data. We evaluate HuTact on tactile perception and manipulation tasks, including grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning. Across these tasks, human HOI pretraining improves data efficiency and provides a strong initialization for downstream learning. Notably, with HOI pretraining followed by midtraining on unlabeled robot play data, HuTact achieves 88.26% Macro-F1 on grasp prediction using only 25\% of the labeled downstream data, comparable to training from scratch on the full labeled dataset (88.23%). These results suggest that human interaction data can serve as a scalable complementary source for robotic tactile representation learning.
authors: Yeonguk Yu, Jaehong Kim, Byungok Han
bullets: Addresses the need for costly, robot-specific tactile data collection across diverse hands and sensors.
Pretrains from human hand motions without real tactile signals, then transfers interaction structure to robotic tactile observations.
Can be adapted using a small amount of unlabeled robot interaction data.
Improves data efficiency across grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning.
With HOI pretraining and unlabeled robot play-data midtraining, reaches 88.26% Macro-F1 on grasp prediction using 25% of labeled data, comparable to 88.23% from full-data training.

Stage 2 optionally adapts the representation to real robotic tactile signals using unlabeled play data, and Stage 3 fine-tunes the encoder for downstream robotic tasks.

Fig. 2. Illustration of backbone architecture. Each frame is encoded from separate tactile and wrist-local fingertip coordinate token streams. The resulting frame-level CLS tokens are then aggregated across 15 frames by a temporal Transformer to produce a window-level representation for downstream tasks.

Fig. 3. Hardware setup and downstream tasks. We use a Unitree G1 humanoid equipped with a BrainCo Revo2 dexterous hand. Downstream tasks includes grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, cup destacking, and single-card sliding.

papers.abstract: Telecom language models must combine broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics while remaining practical to deploy as a single model. We present an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic training data from structured networking taxonomies and expert graphs, materializes 212,559 routed training records across fourteen networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers over one shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates their behavior into one deployable student adapter using Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD). In RSOD, the committed student generates each trajectory, the route-assigned specialist teacher-forces the exact native token sequence, compact teacher hidden states are reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, and only the student LoRA is updated. A controlled reconstruction validation shows mean absolute logit error of 7.26 x 10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. On four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, the completed 2,000-step run produced 16,000 trajectories with zero observed student-version or token- ID mismatches. Under the primary route-conditioned evaluation over 2,850 held-out questions, the raw Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model scores 12.8661/25 micro (13.0172/25 macro), the combined routed six-teacher system scores 21.7641/25 micro, and the consolidated RSOD student, released as Llama-CalixCLM v1, reaches 21.7112/25 micro (21.8006/25 macro) on the same five dimension LLM-judge rubric. Under a separate neutral deployment-like prompt, the same student reaches 20.0028/25 micro (20.0778/25 macro). The consolidated student remains within 0.0529 micro-score points of the combined routed-teacher system while retaining a numerically validated and auditable train-serve execution path.

Teacher-logit reconstruction achieved 7.26 × 10^-6 mean absolute error and 100% top-1 agreement; the completed run reported zero student-version or token-ID mismatches.
On 2,850 held-out questions, Llama-CalixCLM v1 scored 21.7112/25 micro versus 21.7641/25 for the combined routed teachers and 12.8661/25 for the base model.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon video generation requires retaining an ever-expanding history, but conditioning on its growing token sequence is costly. Existing methods restrict or compress historical context, potentially losing information needed for future generation. This work proposes ReCam, which groups local spatiotemporal blocks of historical latents into vectors and projects them directly into the high-dimensional hidden space of a Diffusion Transformer. The model learns to use the resulting memory tokens through native self-attention, reducing token count while retaining block-level access to the full history. To mitigate temporal drift during autoregressive rollout, we further introduce dual-pointer denoising with separate noise schedules for recent context and target frames. Among the evaluated methods, ReCam achieves the highest VBench-Long overall score of 80.1 and competitive static-scene revisitation performance on R2M-Bench. It also leads on all four consistency metrics for off-screen subject reappearance, including clothing consistency of 4.09 versus 3.03 for the best baseline.
authors: Yukuo Ma, Cong Liu, Junke Wang, Junqi Liu, Haibin Huang, Zuxuan Wu, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses the cost and information loss of conditioning on growing video histories.
Groups local spatiotemporal latent blocks into vectors and projects them into a Diffusion Transformer’s hidden space.
Uses native self-attention for block-level access to the full history with fewer tokens.
Introduces separate noise schedules for recent context and target frames to improve autoregressive stability.
Achieves the top reported VBench-Long score (80.1) and leads all four off-screen subject reappearance consistency metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of ReCam. Historical latents are grouped into local spatiotemporal blocks and projected into memory tokens by a lightweight MLP. The first frame remains a clean visual anchor. Native self-attention connects the historical memory and current chunk, while text cross-attention is applied only to the current chunk.

Figure 1 A coarse read on fine-grained history. We compare our method with other representative methods. Keyframe-based approaches, such as CaM [Yu et al., 2025], typically employ an external rule-based selector to retrieve a subset of frames as memory. In contrast, compression-based methods [Zhang et al., 2025] encode history into a compact representation through a separate reconstruction stage. Different from these approaches, ReCam allows the video model itself to learn how to represent history and how to retrieve it via its native attention mechanism.

papers.abstract: The Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) has achieved significant progress in Promptable Concept Segmentation (PCS) by processing short noun phrases to generate segmentation masks with unique instance identifiers. While SAM3 excels at single-concept segmentation, it falls short in complex, real-world environments where multiple concepts must be segmented simultaneously. In particular, SAM3 typically fails to simultaneously process concepts with semantic overlap, leading to semantic misclassifications and redundant mask predictions. Moreover, as the number of concepts increases, the independent inference paradigm introduces prohibitive inference latency. To address these limitations, we propose the Dense Competitive Representations SAM (DCR-SAM) framework. By decoupling cross-modal interactions, the proposed method alleviates the inference latency. To resolve semantic misclassifications, DCR-SAM dynamically aligns textual concepts with visual representations and incorporates a dense competition head to enforce explicit inter-class competition. Furthermore, a learnable background token is applied to absorb non-target objects dynamically. These mechanisms effectively suppress overlapping predictions and generate high-fidelity masks. Extensive experimental evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed framework: (1) achieves a 2.3% $\sim$ 10.7% performance improvement over state-of-the-art methods, (2) delivers a 33$\times$ inference speedup compared to the native SAM3, and (3) exhibits strong robustness across diverse scenarios.
authors: Wenbin Liao, Hao Zhu, Yike Ma, Hao Jiang, Feng Dai
bullets: Addresses SAM3’s semantic confusion, redundant masks, and high latency when segmenting multiple concepts simultaneously.
Decouples cross-modal interactions to reduce inference cost.
Dynamically aligns text concepts with visual features and uses a dense competition head for explicit inter-class competition.
Introduces a learnable background token to absorb non-target objects and suppress overlapping predictions.
Reports 2.3%–10.7% improvements over state-of-the-art methods and a 33× speedup over native SAM3 across multiple benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large (vision) language models have enabled computer-use agents that automate digital workflows via fine-grained keyboard and mouse operations. However, such agents remain fragile in long-horizon settings, where errors accumulate and executed actions leave unintended side effects, making the ability to recover from failures critical. Yet, existing remedies remain inadequate: environment resets are infeasible in proprietary settings, action replay is prohibitively expensive over long horizons, and API-based rollback is limited to web environments, leaving model-based recovery largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ReTrace, a scalable evaluation framework for systematically studying recovery behavior in computer-use agents. We formalize Transition-Consistent Recovery: identical downstream actions from the recovered and target states must yield identical outcomes. We operationalize this criterion through goal-oriented action replay following controlled error injection. Using ReTrace, we present the first systematic study of autonomous, model-based recovery, revealing that (i) ideal recovery can unlock model's latent task completion capabilities, (ii) current computer-use agents fail to exploit their latent recovery capabilities, and (iii) accurate model-based recovery yields measurable end-to-end gains. Together, these findings establish recovery as a fundamental capability for building reliable computer-use agents. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/BangProx/ReTRACE.
authors: Byeonghun Bang, Sangwoo Park, Jinheon Baek, Kangsan Kim, Youngwan Lee, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: Long-horizon computer-use agents are fragile because errors accumulate and actions can create unintended side effects.

Its goal-oriented action replay framework systematically evaluates autonomous, model-based recovery after controlled error injection.
The study finds that agents possess latent recovery capabilities but fail to use them effectively; accurate recovery improves end-to-end performance.

papers.abstract: Egocentric action transfer aims to decouple the semantic action from egocentric observations and reproduce them in new visual contexts, enabling scalable world simulation, embodied policy learning, and robotic data generation. Existing approaches to transferring actions rely on condition-guided video generation, which converts the observation video into explicit geometric controls (e.g., hand poses or meshes) to drive synthesis. However, these methods introduce geometric estimation errors, making it difficult to preserve physically plausible interactions when transferred to new scenes. Alternatively, motion transfer methods directly extract motion patterns from the observation video, yet motion-level features alone cannot encode rich contact dynamics, frequently leading to severe hand structural collapse and implausible contact layout. To address both limitations, we present EgoACT, a test-time framework for egocentric action transfer that operates directly on the denoising process of video diffusion models without requiring additional geometric estimators. EgoACT uses Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring to stabilize reference-consistent hand-object structure in the early denoising stage, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration to refine reliable local correspondences in the mid-to-late denoising stages. Together, these two components preserve transferable action semantics while improving temporal coherence and interaction realism. We further establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating action preservation, visual quality, and hand-object plausibility across diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios. Experiments show that EgoACT generates more coherent and physically plausible interaction videos than strong baselines.
authors: Yue Ma, Pengjie Song, Xinyu Wang, Yi He, Zeqian Long, Fangneng Zhan, Kaichen Zhou, Hongyu Liu, Hongfa Wang, Peihao Li, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan, Qifeng Chen
bullets: Existing condition-guided methods suffer from geometric estimation errors, while motion-only transfer often loses contact dynamics and causes hand collapse.
EgoACT is a test-time framework that operates directly during video-diffusion denoising.
Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring stabilizes hand–object structure early in denoising.
Sparse Correspondence Calibration refines reliable local correspondences in later denoising stages.
EgoActionBench evaluates action preservation, visual quality, and hand–object plausibility; experiments report more coherent and physically plausible videos than strong baselines.

Figure 16. More Comparison with Baseline. Our method consistently produces more coherent action transfer and more plausible handobject interactions than baselines, which often suffer from structural collapse, temporal inconsistency, or physically unrealistic interactions.

Figure 14. Failure case. Our method may struggle with actions involving very fast hand or object motion, which can lead to motion blur, temporal aliasing, or loss of hand-object correspondence. This limitation is primarily due to the base video diffusion model, which was not specifically trained to handle rapid egocentric dynamics and tends to produce temporally smoothed outputs when the inter-frame displacement is large.
Figure 8. Qualitative comparison. Compare with previous methods, our method preserves stable hand-object layout and object response.

(c) Our SCC performs sparse correspondence calibration only in the mid-to-late denoising stages, where the action layout has been established and local interaction details can be refined, improving temporal consistency and hand-object realism.

This confirms that VSA effectively anchors the hand-object skeleton through velocity-guided alignment, resulting in more structurally consistent attention patterns.

papers.abstract: Person re-identification (ReID) ranks an image gallery using either an image query or a textual query. In image-to-image (I2I) ReID, viewpoint, illumination, occlusion, and background changes can make distractors appear more similar than the true match. In text-to-image (T2I) ReID, incomplete or ambiguous descriptions may omit key visual evidence. We study this problem for vision-language model (VLM) based ReID, where attributes such as clothing color and carried objects provide useful fine-grained matching cues. However, directly using attribute-prompt similarities as retrieval scores is unreliable because templated prompts can be biased, correlated, and poorly calibrated. We therefore propose \textbf{PR}ompt-guided \textbf{A}ttribute-based \textbf{I}nference-time \textbf{S}imilarity \textbf{E}nhancement (\texttt{PRAISE}), a query-side test-time adaptation framework for VLM-based ReID. Instead of treating prompts as scores, \texttt{PRAISE} uses a transferable attribute-prompt bank to construct an \emph{Attribute-Conditioned Subspace} (ACS): a query-dependent low-rank subspace induced by the most compatible attribute prompts. ACS provides a controlled attribute-conditioned geometry for reshaping query--gallery affinities and guiding lightweight inference-time updates without identity or attribute labels. Experiments across multiple I2I- and T2I-ReID benchmarks show that \texttt{PRAISE} consistently improves VLM retrieval backbones and outperforms both generic and ReID-specific TTA baselines.
authors: Rajarshi Bhattacharya, Aryan Shukla, Shakeeb Murtaza, Christian Desrosiers, Jose Dolz, Maguelonne Heritier, Eric Granger
bullets: Addresses distractor similarity in image-to-image ReID and incomplete or ambiguous descriptions in text-to-image ReID.
Builds an Attribute-Conditioned Subspace from the most compatible prompts in a transferable attribute-prompt bank.
Uses this subspace to reshape query–gallery affinities and guide lightweight, label-free test-time updates rather than treating prompt similarities as direct scores.
Improves VLM retrieval backbones across multiple I2I- and T2I-ReID benchmarks and outperforms generic and ReID-specific test-time adaptation baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Method overview. PRAISE uses attribute prompts to construct a query-specific semantic subspace that stabilizes query-side adaptation under domain shift. Figure 1. Motivation and overview of PRAISE. (a) In I2I-ReID, raw visual similarity can retrieve distractors caused by camera, pose, or background bias. (c) PRAISE addresses both cases by selecting query-relevant attribute directions, orthogonalizing them into an Attribute-Conditioned Subspace (ACS), and using this controlled subspace to reshape query-gallery affinities during test-time.
