papers.abstract: Automated respiratory sound classification enables continuous, non-invasive respiratory assessment, yet long-term deployment remains challenging due to domain shifts from evolving recording devices and acquisition periods. When privacy and governance regulations prohibit replaying historical data, sequential learning easily overwrites previously acquired knowledge. Preserving dedicated domain experts prevents parameter interference, but selecting the correct expert at inference is difficult under overlapping acoustic distributions and absent domain labels. To resolve this dilemma, we propose APRIL, an exemplar-free domain-incremental framework for RSC. Built on a shared frozen BEATs backbone, APRIL sequentially inherits and isolates low-rank experts to enable new-domain adaptation without altering earlier models. A multi-level prototype router retrieves the top-two candidate experts and dynamically selects the final model by integrating domain-routing posteriors with classification confidence, adaptively weighted by matching ambiguity. We establish standardized device- and temporal-incremental benchmarks on the ICBHI and SPRSound datasets across forward and reversed domain orders. Evaluated over five random seeds, APRIL consistently achieves the highest final-session average Score among compared continual learning approaches, reaching 64.4% and 65.4% on ICBHI, and 83.1% and 82.2% on SPRSound under forward and reversed sequences, respectively. Crucially, average forgetting remains under 1.0% across all protocols, demonstrating robust domain adaptation and long-term knowledge retention without data replay. Overall, APRIL offers a reliable and privacy-preserving paradigm for deploying continuous respiratory sound classification across real-world healthcare settings.

papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) enable fast, flexible last-mile and emergency delivery, but their routing remains challenging as the number of clients varies. Classical approaches based on mixed-integer programming and heuristics can scale poorly or require problem-specific design, motivating learning-based alternatives. Reinforcement learning is particularly promising, provided a single policy can generalize across problem sizes without retraining. Although attention-based Pointer Networks are inherently size-agnostic, their solution quality degrades under both upscaling and downscaling. Using the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) as a controlled proxy, with fixed capacity reflecting drone payload constraints, we investigate this degradation and identify three contributing factors: shifts in node density, attention dispersion, and dilution of the mean-pooled graph context. We systematically compare architecture-wide, encoder-side, and decoder-side modifications to address these limitations and propose a learned, permutation-invariant graph-context aggregation mechanism, implemented as a weighted average and as Set2Set. Results reveal distinct requirements for transfer in each direction: entropy-based attention scaling reduces the CVRP20-to-CVRP100 performance gap by 1.41 percentage points, while the proposed aggregation methods achieve the largest improvement on the more challenging CVRP100-to-CVRP20 transfer, approximately 0.9 percentage points. Exploiting this complementarity, we introduce an approach selector that chooses the best model for each training-target size pair. The selector reduces cost relative to the reference model across all nine seen train-test pairs and eight of nine pairs involving unseen sizes (CVRP35, CVRP75, and CVRP200), achieving improvements of up to 3.2 percent.
authors: Sofiene Lassoued, Devara Tertia, Stefan Lier, Andreas Schwung
bullets: Pointer Networks are size-agnostic but lose solution quality when routing problems are scaled up or down.
The study attributes cross-scale degradation to node-density shifts, dispersed attention, and diluted mean-pooled graph context.
It compares architecture-, encoder-, and decoder-level changes, including entropy-based attention scaling and learned permutation-invariant graph-context aggregation.
Attention scaling improves CVRP20-to-CVRP100 transfer by 1.41 percentage points; aggregation methods improve CVRP100-to-CVRP20 transfer by about 0.9 points.
An approach selector lowers routing cost across all nine seen size pairs and eight of nine unseen-size pairs, with improvements up to 3.2%.

papers.abstract: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.
authors: Zhiyuan Liu, Sicheng Liu, Haiyu Wu
bullets: Addresses multimodal futures, where one observation can lead to several valid continuations.

papers.abstract: Real-world observations are noisy and often contain excessive task-irrelevant information. Effective world modeling and planning need to abstract observations into world state representations while filtering out irrelevant information. However, encoders in existing world models are typically non-adaptive, leading to state representations that are easily distracted by task-irrelevant information. As a result, the model may not selectively filter observations to cater to different task demands. To address this problem, we introduce ConfigWM, which realizes configurable perception through task-conditioned state extraction. Given a language description of the task at hand, ConfigWM uses it as a configuration signal to steer how visual embeddings are mapped into a task-specific state space, selectively preserving information relevant to the current task while suppressing task-irrelevant variations. Action-conditioned dynamics are then learned in this task-specific state space for planning. We evaluate ConfigWM in environments with increasing levels of distraction. While existing methods exhibit substantial declines in planning success rate as the environments become increasingly noisy, ConfigWM remains comparatively stable and outperforms the strongest competing method by 22.3% on average across diverse environments. Consistent gains in physical-quantity probing (+0.365 Pearson r) and distracted-to-clean retrieval (+75.5%) further indicate that ConfigWM learns states that preserve task-relevant information while remaining robust to distractors, supporting reliable world modeling and planning in noisy worlds. Project Page: https://configwm.github.io
authors: Yijun Shen, Delong Chen, Xianming Hu, Kai Zhang, Pascale Fung
bullets: Existing world-model encoders are non-adaptive and may retain task-irrelevant information.
ConfigWM conditions visual state extraction on a natural-language task description.
It learns action-conditioned dynamics in the resulting task-specific state space for planning.
Across increasingly distracting environments, ConfigWM remains comparatively stable and outperforms the strongest competitor by 22.3% on average.
Probing and retrieval results indicate stronger preservation of task-relevant information and robustness to distractors.

papers.abstract: Model compression makes large language models deployable, but today's evaluation tells an incomplete story. Standard practice measures retained task performance and stops there. This misses a critical fact: compression perturbs the distributed knowledge embedded across billions of weights, and task scores alone cannot reveal which underlying abilities survive and which quietly collapse. To solve this question, we introduce ACE-Compression, an ability-centric evaluation framework. Instead of asking only "does the compressed model still answer correctly?", we ask "which of its core abilities remain intact?" Our framework probes four deployment-facing dimensions: procedural reasoning and constraint execution, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition and affective understanding, and persona fidelity and stylistic consistency. Across more than 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs-covering quantization and pruning-we find that compression redistributes ability profiles. Coarse, local, and surface-level signals often persist, while fine-grained, long-tail, and context-dependent abilities become fragile. Quantization consistently outperforms pruning in retention, but the practical meaning of that gap depends entirely on which ability an application requires. Based on our findings, deployers can choose compression methods by the ability profile their application needs, not just by a leaderboard average. And algorithm designers gain diagnostic signals to build compression methods that preserve what matters. We believe that ACE-Compression turns compression from a black-box accuracy drop into an interpretable intervention-one we can measure, understand, and ultimately improve.
authors: Jiahui Ning, Liang Chen, Yuchen Liang, Yi Zhang, Fenglei Fan
bullets: Introduces an ability-centric framework covering procedural reasoning, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition, and persona/style consistency.
Evaluates over 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs using quantization and pruning.

Quantization generally retains abilities better than pruning, but the practical choice depends on an application’s required capabilities.
Supports capability-aware deployment decisions and provides diagnostics for designing more ability-preserving compression methods.

papers.abstract: Enterprise agents answer questions over workplace records that evolve through team collaboration. As information is shared, corrected, and revised across documents, chats, and figures, multiple versions of the same information accumulate in the workspace. Reliable question answering therefore requires agents to reason over sufficient evidence, resolve cross-source and temporal conflicts, and recognize when the available evidence is insufficient to establish an answer. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce MMEnterprise-Bench, a benchmark comprising 1,613 questions grounded in evolving multimodal records from simulated collaboration projects, covering three categories: Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution, and Unanswerability. We evaluate 10 proprietary and open-source multimodal LLMs and find that even the strongest models struggle when evidence contains cross-source or temporal conflicts or spans multiple images. Moreover, increasing the retrieval budget or employing a larger retriever improves evidence recall but does not consistently translate into higher answer accuracy. These findings highlight the persistent challenges of reasoning over evolving workplace records and establish MMEnterprise-Bench as a testbed for developing more reliable enterprise agents. Code and data are available at https://mlvlab.github.io/MMEnterprise-Bench/.

papers.abstract: Staged post-training of multimodal foundation models chains vision-language alignment, reasoning distillation, and domain tuning, yet how each phase trades capabilities against the others remains under-characterised. Tracking an 8.4B-parameter model from an un-fine-tuned baseline through three training phases on Japanese financial documents (evaluated on five text-input benchmarks), we find the phases interact non-additively: math-only distillation overwrites the financial knowledge acquired earlier even as procedural math skill survives, and the domain phase repairs more than it installs. A skip-phase ablation is best for domain knowledge but forfeits numerical-reasoning gains, so per-phase contributions are not decomposable and the best checkpoint is task-dependent, with implications for checkpoint retention and scheduling rather than added stages.
authors: Genshin Kakimoto, Atsushi Yanagisawa
bullets: Studies an 8.4B-parameter model across vision-language alignment, reasoning distillation, and domain tuning.
Math-only distillation erases previously acquired financial knowledge while preserving procedural math ability.
Domain tuning mainly repairs lost capabilities rather than adding entirely new ones.
Skipping a phase maximizes domain knowledge but sacrifices numerical-reasoning gains.
The best checkpoint depends on the task, favoring careful checkpoint retention and phase scheduling over simply adding stages.

Phase 2 (Mathematical Reasoning Distillation): P2-S1 updates the LLM via QLoRA on approximately 150K math problems with XML-structured chain-of-thought supervision from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 (vision encoder and projector frozen). papers.abstract: We investigate associative creativity in descriptions of abstract visual stimuli by humans and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). While conceptual association is central to human communication, it remains unclear how humans and models adapt when visual stimuli become increasingly difficult to map onto familiar semantic concepts. We evaluate several state-of-the-art MLLMs and human participants along two dimensions of creativity, originality and effectiveness, using two datasets with controlled manipulations of difficulty. SilCC varies naming difficulty through progressively more complex combinations of abstract shapes, and PixCC varies difficulty through increasing levels of random visual noise. Results show that humans produce more diverse associative descriptions than MLLMs, including greater semantic distance, higher entropy, and more novel expressions relative to reference lexica. As difficulty increases, effectiveness declines in SilCC, and humans increasingly shift from holistic associations to descriptions of low-level visual properties in PixCC.

bullets: Evaluates human and MLLM associative creativity using originality and effectiveness.

Greater difficulty reduces effectiveness in SilCC and shifts human descriptions toward low-level visual properties in PixCC.

papers.abstract: Endoscopic video contains state transitions induced by camera displacement, deformable tissue, and instrument interaction, yet existing pre-training methods treat dynamics implicitly. Inspired by action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive world models and by the observation that endoscopic optical flow contains both shared image-plane displacement and localized residual motion, we reformulate passive endoscopic video pre-training as causal motion-guided latent-state prediction. We present EndoWorld-JEPA, to our knowledge the first latent world-model pre-training framework designed for general-purpose endoscopic video representation learning. In place of recorded actions, calibrated poses, or robot kinematics, the model conditions prediction of the next latent state on motion observed up to the current state. Its Optical Motion-guided module separates dominant displacement from residual motion and converts the resulting evidence into an ordered temporal motion condition and spatial local-motion weights. Complementary global and motion-local predictors use these outputs: the temporal condition modulates both latent transitions, whereas the local weights define an auxiliary motion-local state that extends prediction from scene-level evolution to spatially selective dynamics. Patch-wise motion weighting emphasizes localized change while retaining anatomical context, and past-motion-window dropout randomly withholds the complete motion condition to reduce dependence on unreliable motion. This global--local formulation learns predictable visual--motion dynamics in representation space without reconstructing stochastic appearance artifacts. Evaluation shows that a common pre-trained checkpoint achieves strong transfer across four downstream benchmarks, supporting motion-guided global--local latent prediction as an effective pre-training paradigm for endoscopic video.
authors: Jie Wang, Shilong Yang, Tao Zhou, Juan Yu, Rong Qu, Jianfeng Ren, Zhicheng Zhang, Linlin Shen
bullets: Addresses the implicit treatment of camera, tissue, and instrument-induced dynamics in existing endoscopic pre-training methods.
Uses observed motion instead of recorded actions, calibrated poses, or robot kinematics to condition next-state latent prediction.
Separates dominant image-plane displacement from localized residual motion to form temporal motion conditions and spatial motion weights.
Combines global and motion-local predictors, with motion-window dropout to reduce reliance on unreliable motion cues.
A shared pre-trained checkpoint transfers effectively across four downstream benchmarks, supporting the proposed paradigm.

papers.abstract: Anticipating how users will interact with their surroundings is essential for proactive systems that provide timely assistance in AR, VR, and embodied applications. Prior work typically forecasts hand-object interactions directly from historical observations, leaving intention and contact geometry implicit. However, similar observation histories can precede semantically or geometrically distinct futures. Inspired by behavioral evidence that gaze can provide early cues for underlying intention, we propose Gaze2HOI, a gaze-aware framework that formulates hand-object interaction forecasting as a hierarchical problem comprising intention inference, contact grounding, and coupled hand-object motion generation. Specifically, Gaze2HOI first weights gaze cues by fixation strength and recency, and uses them to modulate the visual representations of a vision-language model (VLM) through Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation (TGSM), thereby reducing semantic ambiguity in intention inference. Subsequently, an Anticipatory Contact Grounding (ACG) module maps these structured intentions into explicit contact, support, and placement fields, effectively mitigating geometric ambiguity. Driven by these explicit conditions, a diffusion-based model jointly generates the 6-DoF object trajectories and future articulated motion of both hands. To evaluate Gaze2HOI, we further introduce EgoAIM, a phase-aware benchmark that organizes egocentric hand-object interactions into four phases defined by evolving hand-object relations and provides fine-grained intention annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Gaze2HOI achieves state-of-the-art performance in both intention inference and motion forecasting, even approaching oracle-level end-to-end performance in specific interaction phases. Project page: https://gaze2hoi.github.io/.
authors: Chuanyang Ma, Chenye Wang, Yixuan Wang, Huiling Zhou, Xingqun Qi, Muyi Sun, Man Zhang, Caifeng Shan, Zhenan Sun
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in predicting semantically and geometrically distinct futures from similar egocentric observation histories.
Uses fixation strength and recency to modulate a vision-language model via Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation for intention inference.
Maps intentions to contact, support, and placement fields with Anticipatory Contact Grounding.
Generates 6-DoF object trajectories and articulated motion for both hands using a diffusion-based model.
Introduces the phase-aware EgoAIM benchmark with fine-grained intention annotations; reports state-of-the-art intention and motion forecasting, with near-oracle performance in some phases.

papers.abstract: This paper shows that JEPA-style latent world models (LWMs) can learn across diverse domains and data sources by adopting the language-conditioned interface of video generation models. We establish this approach as an effective and efficient basis for planning with imagination and downstream policy fine-tuning. To this end, we introduce LaLa-World, a Language-conditioned Latent World model that learns from simulation and robot trajectories together with broader image and video data. Two designs make this work. First, we describe both numerical actions and visual changes in language, enabling joint training of a single future predictor across heterogeneous datasets. Second, we build the predictor on a language model, allowing it to interpret language conditions while predicting future latent states. The resulting predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than existing LWMs trained separately for each domain or task. Adding image and video data further improves average planning performance and robustness to action phrasing. In a matched comparison with an RAEv2-based video generation model baseline, LaLa-World reaches comparable planning performance with $6\times$ less training cost and $13.9\times$ faster planning. Beyond planning, the pretrained LaLa-World serves as an initialization for LaLa-Policy, which jointly predicts actions and future visual representations. LaLa-Policy performs competitively with Cosmos Policy on LIBERO and RoboCasa, with up to $5.5\times$ faster inference.
authors: Junha Song, Geonmo Gu, Jeongeun Park, Heejeong Nam, Lucas Maes, Byeongho Heo, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
bullets: Trains one language-conditioned future predictor on simulation, robot trajectories, images, and videos.
Uses language to unify numerical actions and visual changes across heterogeneous data.
Achieves higher average MPC planning performance than domain- or task-specific latent world models.
With additional image/video data, planning robustness to action phrasing improves.
Matches an RAEv2 video-generation baseline with 6× lower training cost and 13.9× faster planning; its policy initialization enables competitive performance with up to 5.5× faster inference.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of LaLa-World. (a) Language provides a shared interface for numerical actions and visual change, enabling joint training on control and video data. (b) A single predictor built on a language model uses encoded observations and language conditions to predict future visual representations. Fine-tuning the pretrained LaLa-World yields LaLa-Policy, which predicts actions as well as future visual representations. (c) The jointly trained predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than both separately trained LWM baselines and the generative world model baseline, RAEv2. (d) LaLa-Policy performs competitively with our adapted Cosmos Policy baseline on RoboCasa, while reducing average inference time per trajectory by a factor of 5.5×.

Each example shows the initial and goal observations, the predicted rollout under the selected language actions, and planning time. Decoded images from LaLa-World may have lower visual quality because it is not trained for pixel reconstruction. Both models predict plausible future states, while LaLa-World requires less planning time.

Figure 2: MPC planning with language actions. LaLa-World imagines future representations under candidate actions with MPC and selects the most promising action toward the goal. Because all actions share one language interface, a single LaLa-World predictor can plan across multiple domains, despite differences in action dimensionality and physical meaning. The predictor also supports language-based actions without numerical values (bottom two rows), as detailed in Section D.4.3. The visualized observations result from executing the selected actions in the simulator.

Figure 3: Examples of language-conditioned transition data. Each example consists of past observations, a language condition, and the next observation. Language conditions describe either numerical control actions from simulation and robotics or visual changes in images and videos. This shared interface enables training a single LWM across different action spaces and data sources.

Figure 7: Predicted future observations on LIBERO and RoboCasa. (b) We compare planning performance and average planning time per trajectory across four predictor depths, with all models trained on the same number of transition data. papers.abstract: Online Continual Learning (OCL) requires models to learn from non-stationary data streams under a strict single-pass constraint, making them highly susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. While existing studies have explored various strategies from data, architecture, and optimization perspectives, the optimizer often directly uses generic approaches such as SGD and AdamW. In this work, we reveal a new link between optimization dynamics and OCL needs by recasting Polyak-Ruppert averaging as the engine of "plasticity" and Primal averaging as the anchor of "stability". This inspires our novel optimizer, SPIN (Stability-Plasticity INterpolation), which explicitly decouples plasticity and stability by interpolating between a fast-moving "plasticity" sequence and an adaptive "stability" sequence. We theoretically demonstrate that SPIN implicitly employs an inverse Hessian approximation, providing crucial Tikhonov regularization to damp noisy, single-sample Hessian estimates and mitigate forgetting. More importantly, SPIN can be seamlessly integrated into existing OCL methods by taking resulted gradients as input and replacing standard optimizers. Extensive experiments show that using SPIN instead of standard optimizers yields consistent and significant performance gains across multiple OCL approaches, including the challenging rehearsal-free setting and under strict memory constraints.
authors: Yongyi Wu, Zheng Wang, Sen Lin
bullets: OCL must learn from non-stationary streams in a single pass, making generic optimizers vulnerable to forgetting.
SPIN interpolates a fast-moving plasticity sequence with an adaptive stability sequence, inspired by Polyak-Ruppert and Primal averaging.
Its dynamics implicitly approximate the inverse Hessian and apply Tikhonov regularization to suppress noisy single-sample curvature estimates.
SPIN can replace standard optimizers in existing OCL methods without changing their gradient inputs.
Experiments report consistent, significant gains across multiple OCL approaches, including rehearsal-free and strict-memory settings.

Figure 6: Trajectories of Polyak-Ruppert Averaging and Primal Averaging. Polyak-Ruppert Averaging computes the gradient at the current, fast-moving model iterate θt: gt = ∇L(θt). The final model is the average of this noisy sequence: θ̄T = 1 T ∑T t=1 θt. Primal Averaging computes the gradient at the averaged iterate over the current trajectory: gt = ∇L(θ̄t), where θ̄t = 1 t ∑t i=1 θi. This stable gradient is then used to guide the update.

papers.abstract: Action-free videos are an appealing substitute for costly teleoperated data. Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out-of-plane movements and potential occlusions. We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi-camera views using cross-attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions. The latent actions are fed into a policy in which a latent expert and an action expert are coupled by sequential flow matching around a frozen VLM backbone. We further evaluate in strict cross-embodiment settings where task-specific demonstrations come from other embodiments. We show that dual-view LAM pretraining improves the decodability of ground-truth 6D actions by 17% compared to single-view, while scaling single-view data by two orders of magnitude is not sufficient to fully recover out-of-plane motions. The downstream policy improves success rate by +13.5% compared to +6.2% for single-view LAM. A single cross-embodiment is sufficient for skill transfer, and adding a second viewpoint outperforms adding up to four further embodiments. The results transfer to hardware where demonstrations come from a human hand improving success rate by +20% over action-only policies in 850 rollouts. We show that video and robot data are complementary, and that benefits of learning from video are task-dependent. Website: https://learnsyslab.github.io/multiview_latent_action_pretraining/
authors: Oliver Hausd\"orfer, Felix Minzenmay, Mani Majd, Maximilian P. Christof, Shiyuan Zhang, Angela P. Schoellig
bullets: Single-view latent action models ambiguously infer 6D movements, especially out-of-plane actions and occluded interactions.
The proposed model combines cross-attention over multiple views with sequential flow matching between latent and action experts around a frozen VLM.
Dual-view pretraining improves 6D-action decodability by 17% over single-view and yields a +13.5% downstream success-rate gain versus +6.2% for single-view.
One cross-embodiment source is sufficient for skill transfer; adding a second viewpoint is more beneficial than adding up to four additional embodiments.
Hardware experiments using human-hand demonstrations improve success by 20% over action-only policies across 850 rollouts, with benefits varying by task.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Method: We combine latent action pretraining from in-domain cross-embodiment videos with a downstream flow-matching policy. First, latent actions are inferred from a large cross-embodiment video dataset. Second, a sequential policy is learned on the latent actions and a small set of demonstrations on the target embodiment. The LAM uses a spatio-temporal transformer to merge multiple viewpoints before computing the latents. The spatial block attends to patches of other viewpoints, yielding latent actions grounded in 3D space. Latent action labels and real robot actions are jointly used to train a hierarchical downstream policy. The policy uses sequential flow matching experts and outputs actions applied to the robot.
Fig. 8. Failure modes. Models struggle with object grasping (44% of failure cases). The push task requires precision to align the gripper with the milk.

Fig. 4. Real World Tasks: We evaluate the policies and skill-transfer on six tasks consisting of novel movements, novel background, novel objects, and novel placements. For each eval task, we collect 50 human demonstrations and evaluate under settings with 0–50 robot demonstrations per task. We additionally collect an off-task play dataset across 32 tasks, totaling 1000 human demonstrations and 600 robot demonstrations.

Fig. 3. Left: Latent Action Probing. An MLP probe reconstructs ground-truth robot actions from the latents. Adding the second view improves decodability in the directions that are only ambiguously observed by single-view. Right: Cross-embodiment Learning. t-SNE showing 2D correspondence of latent actions to embodiments. Separation by color indicates separate latent per embodiment before training, while mixed colors show a latent space shared between embodiments. Shared latents already occur for a single cross-embodiment present in pretraining.

Fig. 2. Scaling with Data. Policy success rate (SR) when scaling (left) the number of action-annotated demonstrations per task on the deployed embodiment Franka Panda, (middle) the fraction of LIBERO-90 used as off-task play data for latent video pretraining increasing task diversity. Top row shows mean success rate over all 40 tasks; bottom row split by in-distribution and heldout tasks (see Sec. IV). Successes on heldout tasks prove transfer from crossembodiment video demonstrations. (Right): The number of cross-embodiments contained in the video dataset (1 = iiwa, 2 = +kinova3, 3 = +sawyer, 4 = +ur5e) for single- and dual-view pretraining. Dual-view pretraining outperforms adding up to four cross-embodiments.

Fig. 6. Human to Robot Transfer. Left: We apply the latent action computed on a human frame to a robot frame from an eval rollout not seen during training: both yield the same movement to the right. Right: Motion decoded from the predicted latents for a human and a robot video. Both motions decode into similar motions in robot end-effector space. The multi-view LAM shows significantly better reconstruction of the ground-truth robot motion in y-direction. See more qualitative results in the supplementary video.

Fig. 5. Evaluation: Each datapoint represents 25 rollouts. Left: We observe successes without using any robot data for new tasks. On average, using human demonstrations without any robot demonstrations increases SR by +20%, and with 5 robot demonstrations by +19%. Tasks with novel placement locations ([place]) are easiest to solve, followed by novel objects ([obj]). Middle: Multi-view video pretraining scores 46% against 21% for single-view significantly increasing SR. Right: Scaling of SR with increasing robot demonstrations for one task: video and robot demonstrations are complementary.

papers.tldr: Multi-view latent-action pretraining uses synchronized cameras to improve cross-embodiment robot learning from action-free videos by resolving depth and occlusions.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models, but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands. Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings: general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B. Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 with a statistically significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval. We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
authors: Siyuan Ma, Yu Qi, Cheng Ye, Ruotian Peng, Xinyi Xu, Zitiantao Lin, Zedong Cai, Yijian Huang, Weiyang Liu, Siyuan Wang, Yandong Wen
bullets: RoboJudge-Bench evaluates MLLM judges on Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment using 800 human-annotated videos from 8 corpora, 10 generators, and varied hand embodiments.
Existing general-purpose and general-domain video judges show limited or inconsistent agreement with human judgments in embodied scenarios, especially for physical adherence.
RoboJudge-Train contains 12K videos with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales.
RoboJudge-9B is fine-tuned with supervised learning and reinforcement learning, achieving the highest reported agreement on the benchmark with a Pearson correlation of 0.719.
The trained judge also improves performance on external benchmarks and is used to evaluate video generation models.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and model for evaluating embodied video generation using MLLMs, directly addressing the evaluation of embodied world models and video generation.
papers.title: RoboJudge: Multimodal Language Models as Judges for Embodied Video Generation
papers.tldr: RoboJudge introduces a benchmark and trained 9B multimodal judge that better aligns with humans when evaluating the physical validity and instruction following of embodied video generations.

papers.abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve high-quality novel-view synthesis by representing a scene as a continuous volumetric radiance field. However, the geometry encoded by the density field of vanilla NeRF can be noisy and inaccurate, since different combinations of shape and radiance may explain the same input images. To reduce this ambiguity, we augment vanilla NeRF with a geometry-optimization branch based on self-supervised cross-ray consistency. Specifically, this branch samples candidate surface points from the density field, generates virtual rays that intersect at each point from different directions, and renders their appearance using the NeRF network. Based on the visibility-weighted color consistency across these rays, we constrain the implicit geometry. We further regularize the implicit geometry by penalizing opacity at candidates with inconsistent appearance predictions and encouraging local normal smoothness. These geometric constraints are derived from the NeRF predictions and require no ground-truth depth or surface-normal supervision. Experiments on eight Replica scenes show that the proposed method reduces the mean Chamfer distance by 30.8% compared with vanilla NeRF.
authors: Zongji Wang
bullets: Vanilla NeRF geometry can be noisy because shape and radiance ambiguities explain the same images.
The method samples candidate surfaces from density and evaluates appearance consistency along virtual rays from multiple directions.
Visibility-weighted color consistency constrains geometry without ground-truth depth or normal labels.
Additional regularization penalizes opacity for inconsistent predictions and promotes local normal smoothness.
On eight Replica scenes, mean Chamfer distance decreases by 30.8% versus vanilla NeRF.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed framework. The shared NeRF renders training views for RGB reconstruction and supplies the density field for candidate surface sampling. The geometry-optimization branch generates virtual cross-rays through each candidate, renders their appearances, and estimates visibility weights to reduce the influence of occluded rays. Cross-ray consistency, occupancy suppression, and local normal smoothness jointly regularize the field.

Fig. 3. Details of candidate sampling and visibility-aware cross-ray construction. (a) Uniform proposals and rendered-depth anchors are filtered by an intermediate opacity band to obtain candidate points. The curved patch schematically represents the current density boundary. (b) For a candidate x𝑖 , the auxiliary sphere is centered at x𝑖 + 𝑙0n𝑖 with radius 𝑟 . Its sampled locations õ𝑖 𝑗 determine ray directions, while the actual origins o𝑖 𝑗 are placed independently at distances 𝑙𝑖 𝑗 . All generated rays pass through the same candidate. (c) Opacity samples along each origin-to-candidate segment determine a continuous visibility weight: an intervening occupied region increases the opacity sum and reduces the ray’s influence. This segment is used for visibility estimation; appearance is obtained by standard volume rendering along the generated ray.

Fig. 4. Qualitative geometry comparison on Replica scenes. From left to right, each row shows the ground-truth geometry, vanilla NeRF, and the reconstruction after optimization with the proposed geometry-refinement objective.

Table 1. Chamfer distance on Replica scenes after 300,000 cumulative training iterations for both methods, multiplied by 100 and rounded to two decimal places (lower is better). Relative changes are computed from the unrounded distances with respect to vanilla NeRF; downward arrows indicate reductions. The lower distance in each scene and the entire mean row are highlighted in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Improves NeRF geometry via self-supervised cross-ray consistency, contributing to 3D scene reconstruction and world model representations.
papers.title: Geometry Regularization for Vanilla NeRF via Self-Supervised Cross-Ray Consistency
papers.tldr: A self-supervised cross-ray consistency branch regularizes vanilla NeRF geometry, reducing reconstruction ambiguity and mean Chamfer distance on eight Replica scenes.

papers.abstract: 3D Human Pose Estimation (3D HPE) is used in indoor environments, such as smart homes, to analyze human movement and monitor human states. Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar is suitable for this task because it is robust to lighting variations and does not capture images of human appearance. However, radar observations often provide insufficient information about certain body parts or contain overlapping reflections from multiple body parts, limiting accurate 3D joint localization. To address these limitations, we propose the Initialization-to-Refinement Pose Framework (I2R-Pose), comprising two stages: Motion-Aware Pose Initialization and Observation-Guided Refinement. In the first stage, joint-wise features are learned by incorporating temporal relationships across consecutive radar observations and human skeletal structure to compensate for insufficient joint information and estimate an initial 3D pose sequence. In the second stage, separately extracted radar observation features predict joint-wise positional corrections that refine the initial pose and generate the final pose sequence. The framework supports individual and fused inputs of time-Doppler/time-range (TD/TR) maps and radar point clouds (PCs). To evaluate performance across indoor activities, we construct the Radar Motion and Spatial Information for 3D Human Pose Estimation (RaMoS-Pose) dataset, providing synchronized TD/TR maps, radar PCs, and 3D joint ground truth (GT). Evaluations on RaMoS-Pose and the publicly available MVDoppler-Pose dataset show that I2R-Pose reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 39.50% on MVDoppler-Pose and by 15.13% on RaMoS-Pose with fused inputs, compared with the best-performing existing methods evaluated on each dataset.
authors: Woo-Jin Jung, Chan-Bin Lim, Seung-Hyun Kong
bullets: Addresses missing or overlapping mmWave radar reflections that hinder accurate 3D joint localization.
Uses a two-stage pipeline: motion-aware pose initialization followed by observation-guided joint correction.
Supports TD/TR maps, radar point clouds, and their fusion.
Introduces the RaMoS-Pose dataset with synchronized radar data and 3D joint ground truth.
With fused inputs, reduces MPJPE by 39.50% on MVDoppler-Pose and 15.13% on RaMoS-Pose versus the best evaluated existing methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the I2R-Pose framework. The TD/TR-only configuration with two observation views is illustrated as an example. The Motion Branch learns joint-wise features from radar observations, while the Pose Branch sequentially performs initial pose estimation using these features and pose refinement using separately extracted observation features. The GT-based Keypoint Motion Encoder and Keypoint HPE Head are used only during training, and Cross-Modal Motion Feature Alignment guides the learning of joint-wise radar features. For visual clarity, the feature tensors are illustrated with the temporal dimension (T ) along the X-axis, the joint or token dimension (J or NO) along the Y-axis, and the channel dimension (C) along the Z-axis.

Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison of 3D human pose estimation results on (a) MVDoppler-Pose and (b) RaMoS-Pose. Each row shows the ground-truth (GT) pose and the poses estimated by existing methods and I2R-Pose (Ours) for a representative motion. The numbers below each estimated pose indicate the MPJPE (mm) for the corresponding frame, with bold values indicating the lowest MPJPE in each row. RGB images in (b) are provided solely for visual reference.

Fig. 1. Conceptual overview of I2R-Pose. In the Motion-Aware Pose Initialization stage, joint-wise features are learned by incorporating temporal relationships across consecutive radar observations (TD/TR maps, PCs, or both) and human skeletal structure to estimate an initial 3D pose sequence. In the subsequent Observation-Guided Refinement stage, radar observation features extracted separately from the same radar input are combined with the joint-wise features used for initial pose estimation to predict joint-wise positional corrections. These corrections are applied to the initial pose to generate the final pose sequence. The refinement process and changes in MPJPE are illustrated using a representative frame, while RGB images are provided solely for visual reference.

Fig. 3. Main feature extraction and representation processes in I2R-Pose. (a) Generation of joint-wise radar motion features through TD/TR feature extraction and Time–Joint Cross-Attention. (b) Generation of PC spatial tokens through voxel-based feature extraction and global and local tokenization. The illustrated motion features are generated in the Radar Motion Encoder, while the same tokenization structure is independently used in the Radar Observation Encoder with separate weights. (c) Construction of joint-wise motion descriptors from GT joint sequences and their transformation into keypoint motion features.

Fig. 4. Data collection area and sensor configuration of RaMoS-Pose. The left panel shows the radar, camera, and LiDAR arrangement and the data collection area, while the right panel shows the actual sensor setup and relative distances between sensors.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a radar-based 3D human pose estimation framework (I2R-Pose) for indoor environments. This contributes to 3D perception (3D Vision) and provides a sensor modality for embodied agents.
papers.title: Radar-Based 3D Human Pose Estimation via Motion-Aware Pose Initialization and Observation-Guided Refinement
papers.tldr: I2R-Pose improves radar-based 3D human pose estimation by initializing poses from motion and skeletal context, then refining them with radar observations.

papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models have recently achieved remarkable progress in Real-world Image Super-Resolution (Real-SR). However, existing methods consistently exhibit a persistent seesaw effect: enhancing perceptual realism compromises structural fidelity. This effect, we argue, is not intrinsic to diffusion models, but largely stems from the architectural constraints of prevailing two-stage frameworks. To address this challenge, we propose PixelSR, a novel single-stage Pixel Diffusion Transformer for Real-SR that operates directly in pixel space. Specifically, PixelSR consists of two core designs: Pixel-space Conditional Diffusion and Orthogonal Flow Decoupling. The former establishes an effective pixel-space restoration framework by integrating spatially aligned LR conditioning, visual semantic guidance, and lightweight texture refinement, thereby bypassing VAE compression and enabling end-to-end optimization directly in RGB space. Complementarily, the latter decomposes the asymmetric flow target into a low-rank semantic component and a noise-free orthogonal texture component. By routing these components to specialized branches, it achieves decoupled optimization with reduced mutual interference. Benefiting from these designs, our PixelSR restores perceptually realistic details while faithfully preserving structural content. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PixelSR not only achieves competitive performance, but also effectively mitigates the fidelity--realism seesaw effect.
authors: Xiang Lv, Kai Zhao, Qiang Wang, Qiao Mo, Chao Zhou, Mingwen Shao
bullets: Targets the realism–fidelity trade-off attributed to architectural limitations in two-stage diffusion frameworks.
Uses pixel-space conditional diffusion with aligned low-resolution conditioning, semantic guidance, and lightweight texture refinement.
Introduces Orthogonal Flow Decoupling to separate low-rank semantic and orthogonal texture components into specialized branches.
Avoids VAE compression and enables end-to-end optimization directly in RGB space.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks show competitive performance and mitigation of the fidelity–realism seesaw effect.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed PixelSR framework. PixelSR comprises Pixel-space Conditional Diffusion (PCD) and Orthogonal Flow Decoupling (OFD). Left: PCD performs end-toend RGB-space restoration using spatially aligned LR conditioning, visual semantic guidance, and lightweight pixel-level texture refinement. Right: OFD factorizes the asymmetric velocity target into a projected low-rank component and a deterministic orthogonal residual, which empirically exhibit semantic- and texture-dominant characteristics, respectively. Their predictions are assigned to specialized DiT and PiT branches and recombined into the full velocity for flow matching, enabling task-aligned optimization with reduced interference.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on challenging real-world examples. PixelSR better preserves the text layout and feather structure while recovering fine-grained details consistent with the HR references, whereas several competing methods exhibit distorted characters, irregular textures, or over-smoothed results. Best viewed zoomed in.

Figure 5: Ablation of PixelSR components on RealSR. The bars and green curve report PSNR and MANIQA, respectively. Pixel-space x0-prediction provides a substantially stronger baseline than pixel-space v-prediction, while the successive PCD and OFD designs further improve fidelity and perceptual quality.

Figure 6: Frequency analysis of OFD branch specialization. Restoration results (top) and corresponding power spectra (bottom) under increasing orthogonal scale α. Larger α progressively strengthens fine textures and mid-to-high-frequency responses, while α = 1 denotes the default OFD output. All spectra share the same color scale.

Figure 10: Qualitative comparison on challenging real-world examples. PixelSR better preserves the original text layout and character structures while recovering fine-grained image details, whereas several competing methods exhibit distorted characters, irregular textures, or over-smoothed results. Best viewed zoomed in.

Figure 11: Qualitative comparison on challenging real-world examples. PixelSR better preserves high-frequency textures and fine structural details, whereas competing methods often produce oversmoothed surfaces, irregular patterns, or artificial artifacts. Best viewed zoomed in.

Figure 3: Visualization of orthogonal target factorization. With the Procrustes-aligned projector, the projected component mainly retains global content and coarse structures, while its orthogonal complement emphasizes edges, text patterns, and high-frequency textures.

Figure 9: t-SNE visualization of semantic and texture features. We sample 300 images from each of five ImageNet categories and visualize features from the two PixelSR branches. Semantic features form compact category-aware clusters, while texture features are more dispersed due to diverse local details, supporting the effectiveness of our OFD.

Figure 7: Representative image matrix of UGCSR benchmark. The benchmark covers ten semantic categories: humans, animals, text-rich images, natural scenes, urban scenes, indoor scenes, plants, food, tools, and everyday objects. Two representative degraded images are shown for each category.

Table 2: Ablation of pixel-space flow formulations on LSDIR. All variants use the same PCD network and parameter count. OFD improves over monolithic uA-prediction through explicit factorization and branch assignment.
Table 3: Implementation details of PixelSR.

Table 4: No-reference quality comparison of LR and HR images across real-world paired SR benchmarks. Results are reported as mean ± standard deviation. The best results among LR and HR images are highlighted in bold and underlined, respectively.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a pixel-space diffusion transformer and orthogonal flow decoupling for super-resolution, offering a novel approach to diffusion efficiency and architecture.
papers.title: PixelSR: Pixel-Space Orthogonal Flow Decoupling for Real-World Image Super-Resolution
papers.tldr: PixelSR is a single-stage pixel-space diffusion transformer designed to improve Real-SR perceptual detail without sacrificing structural fidelity.

papers.abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and optical imagery provide complementary structural and appearance information for remote sensing object detection. However, substantial cross-modal discrepancies and indiscriminate channel interaction inevitably introduce redundant or conflicting features. Since different feature channels encode heterogeneous semantic information and contribute unequally to cross-modal fusion, selectively highlighting task-relevant channels while suppressing redundant ones is essential. To address this issue, we propose the Channel Selective Interaction Fusion Network (CSIF-Net), which performs selective channel-level cross-modal interaction. CSIF-Net first employs a frequency decomposition module to construct frequency-aware SAR inputs, facilitating the separation of structural information from noise-related responses. It then models cross-modal channel relationships through a cross-attention channel selection module and dynamically partitions the features into shared and modality-specific components. Finally, a dual-branch fusion module performs cross-modal interaction and channel realignment for shared features while independently enhancing SAR-specific features, thereby exploiting complementary information and suppressing modality interference. Extensive experiments on the OGSOD 1.0 and M4-SAR datasets demonstrate that CSIF-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance in both horizontal and oriented object detection, surpassing the existing methods by 4.01% and 3.18% gains, respectively.
authors: Haojie Li, Yuanfei Huang, Lingfei Song, Jia Li, Lizhi Wang
bullets: Addresses redundant or conflicting features caused by indiscriminate interaction between optical and SAR channels.
Uses frequency decomposition to separate SAR structural information from noise-related responses.
Applies cross-attention channel selection to identify shared and modality-specific feature components.
Employs dual-branch fusion to realign shared features and enhance SAR-specific information independently.
Experiments on OGSOD 1.0 and M4-SAR show state-of-the-art horizontal and oriented detection, with reported gains of 4.01% and 3.18%.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overall architecture of the proposed CSIF-Net. FDM decomposes the SAR input into multiple frequency components to provide frequency-aware priors for feature extraction. CACS then models channel-wise correlations between the optical and SAR features and partitions them into shared and specific components. Finally, DBF enhances the shared components through cross-modal interaction while preserving modality-specific information in the specific components before multi-scale feature aggregation.

Fig. 3. Detailed architectures and data flows of CACS and DBF. Blue, red, and purple denote the optical stream, SAR stream, and fused information or module flow, respectively. CACS constructs the cross-modal attention matrix and selects shared and specific channels through statistical scoring and TopK selection. DBF performs cross-modal interaction and aligned grouped fusion on shared features, enhances SAR-specific features through self-attention, preserves optical-specific features, and concatenates the three outputs.

Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison of CSIF-Net against existing methods. The top two rows show horizontal bounding-box detection results on representative OGSOD 1.0 scenes, and the bottom two rows show oriented bounding-box detection results on representative M4-SAR scenes. Each row is one paired optical-SAR sample; the first two columns show the optical and SAR ground-truth annotations, and the remaining columns show the optical-view detection results of different methods. Red dashed boxes denote ground truth, yellow solid boxes denote incorrect predictions and green solid boxes denote correct predictions.

Fig. 1. We employ a simple 1×1 convolutional network for fusion and object detection, and track the accumulated gradients of each channel during training. The top-64 channels with the largest accumulated gradients are selected from the OPT and SAR modalities respectively to compute their channel correlation matrix. As can be observed, the accumulated gradients vary substantially across channels. Moreover, the cross-modal channel correlation matrix exhibits a pronounced banded pattern, with significant differences in correlation across channels.
Fig. 4. Feature-level analysis of CSIF-Net: (a) single-channel responses before and after fusion; (b) full-channel versus selected-channel fusion.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a channel-selective fusion network for cross-modal (Optical-SAR) data, relevant to spatial intelligence and multimodal representation learning.
papers.title: Revealing Inter-Channel Modality Discriminability: Channel Selective Interaction Fusion Network for Optical-SAR Object Detection
papers.tldr: CSIF-Net improves optical-SAR object detection by selectively interacting with informative channels while separating shared and modality-specific features to reduce cross-modal interference.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judgment assistants and as stand-in participants in psychology experiments, yet little is known about how much their probability estimates move in response to a single new piece of information. We pair premise-hypothesis items from $\delta$-SNLI with one strengthener and one weakener each, elicit the prior and the posteriors in separate calls, and measure the directional movement s: the mean posterior change signed by the annotated direction, so that the prior cancels out. We vary whether the update is stated ("Here is something else you learned") or reported ("Someone said that"), and whether the model gives one probability or five weighted estimates. We test seven configurations: two local models (Qwen3-8B, OLMo-2-7B; 240 pairs) and five configurations run through agent command-line harnesses (120 pairs), with hypotheses and analysis rules fixed before the formal runs (not publicly registered). Under stated, direct elicitation all seven move in the annotated direction (s = 18-28 percentage points). Reporting lowers s in all seven point estimates (significantly in six, by 2-5 points) and raises the share of reverse movements in all seven: the effect is consistent but small. Five weighted estimates lower the share of responses at $\leq$5% or $\geq$95% in all seven, but in the two local models they also reduce s by 43% and 68%, whereas in the harnessed configurations the point estimates of the change lie between -3.7 and +0.5 points. An elicitation format that reduces extreme values thus need not preserve sensitivity to evidence; the two should be tested separately. Because $\delta$-NLI annotates only direction, we make no claim about how large an update should be. Code, data and the frozen plan: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies
authors: An-Sheng Jhang
bullets: Across seven model/configuration settings, directly stated information consistently shifted probabilities in the annotated direction.
Framing information as something someone said produced smaller updates and more reverse movements, though the effect was generally small.
Requesting five weighted estimates reduced near-certain responses across all settings.
This multi-estimate format sharply reduced update sensitivity in the two local models but had little effect in harnessed configurations.
The study measures only whether updates follow the annotated direction, not whether their magnitude is normatively correct.
papers.selection_reason: Studies how framing and elicitation affect LLM probability updates. This is a linguistic study, but the findings on probability updates are relevant to the reliability of LLMs used as judgment assistants in embodied systems.
papers.title: Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates
papers.tldr: How an update is elicited substantially shapes LLM probability revisions: reported information weakens directional updating, while multiple estimates reduce extremes but may also reduce evidence sensitivity.

papers.abstract: Human-collected real-world robotic manipulation demonstrations often contain mixed-quality trajectories, including hesitant, indirect, or inefficient action segments. While diffusion- and flow-based policies can model such multimodal data, standard behavior cloning (BC) assigns equal likelihood to all demonstrated actions and may therefore reproduce suboptimal modes. Offline RL value estimates offer a natural signal for biasing policies toward higher-value behavioral modes, but directly fine-tuning the generative policy or using critic gradients for policy steering can amplify critic errors and induce prior drift. We propose Advantage-Weighted Latent Steering (AWLS), an offline post-training method for improving frozen one-step generative manipulation policies without updating their decoders. AWLS learns a residual noise shaper, an observation-conditioned residual correction to the policy's latent noise, and trains it with an advantage-weighted action reconstruction objective. The advantages are detached, scale-normalized, and used only as supervised weights on demonstrated actions, avoiding critic-gradient policy updates while preserving fast single-step inference. We further introduce a rollout-free decoder-sensitivity criterion for selecting pretrained checkpoints that remain responsive to latent-noise perturbations. Experiments on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks with clean and mixed-quality demonstrations show that AWLS improves over the frozen base policy while limiting drift from the pretrained behavior prior. Project page: https://awls-corl2026.github.io/
authors: Jiahong Tang, Jiaju He, Zhiyuan Yang, Ruyang Han, Haiyue Zhu
bullets: Addresses mixed-quality demonstrations where standard behavior cloning treats inefficient and high-quality actions equally.
Learns an observation-conditioned residual noise shaper using advantage-weighted action reconstruction.
Detaches and normalizes advantages, using them only as supervised weights to reduce critic-error amplification and prior drift.
Introduces a rollout-free decoder-sensitivity criterion for selecting checkpoints responsive to latent perturbations.
Experiments in simulated and real manipulation tasks with clean and mixed-quality data show improvement over the frozen base policy while preserving fast single-step inference.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of AWLS. Top: the one-step decoder Gθ is pretrained by behavior cloning. Bottom: with Gθ frozen, Tϕ reshapes the latent noise via advantage-weighted reconstruction using detached, normalized offline advantages.

Figure 5: The IQL critic ranks clean demonstrations above noisy ones (four 50/50 mixed DexArt datasets, MeanFlow backbone). papers.abstract: Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) face significant challenges in roundabout navigation due to dense traffic interactions and unpredictable agent behaviors, necessitating high levels of adaptability and safety. While the combination of Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Model Predictive Control (MPC) offers a promising approach, existing frameworks suffer from a structural mismatch where pointwise RL decisions fail to align with MPC's trajectory level optimization, and often lack rigorous safety guarantees. This work proposes RLTrajGen-PPMPC-CBF, a hierarchical framework for safe, smooth and comfort roundabout navigation, which regulates the coupling between RL-based planning and MPC-based control. We employ Prescribed Performance Constraints (PPC) to enforce a gradual, stable convergence between reference trajectories and control outputs, ensuring MPC tracking performance remains consistent with intended behavior from RL. Additionally, a Control Barrier Function (CBF) layer provides real-time safety corrections that are fed back into the RL process. Simulation results in the MetaDrive environment demonstrate that our method achieves a 6.25\% increase in average success rate and a 65.87\% reduction in Motion Sickness Dose Value (MSDV) compared to the optimal baseline, meanwhile accelerating training convergence.
authors: Wenhan Li, Yangrui Zhang, Hang Zhou, Peiran Liu, Yiding Ji
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between pointwise RL planning and trajectory-level MPC control, while targeting stronger safety guarantees.

In MetaDrive simulations, it improves average success rate by 6.25% and reduces Motion Sickness Dose Value by 65.87% versus the optimal baseline.
The approach also accelerates training convergence; evaluation is reported in simulation.

papers.abstract: Learned barrier certificates provide a principled mechanism for establishing safety of stochastic systems, but their validity may deteriorate during deployment when the underlying dynamics differ from those used for training. We propose an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits a learned barrier certificate using observed closed-loop trajectories. The monitor is intended to detect loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition; it does not by itself guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention. Specifically, the conditional barrier-drift condition is formulated as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test, and observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite-sample false-alarm control under arbitrary stopping times. Inspired by finite-horizon safety verification, we further introduce a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary, making the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon while preserving anytime-validity. The monitor is designed to detect statistical evidence that the safety certificate is no longer consistent with the observed dynamics, rather than to predict unsafe entry. To assess the monitor empirically, we evaluate empirical alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/runtime-barrier-monitor.
authors: Zhipeng Cao, Taoran Wu, Weiru Cui, Luke Ong, Bai Xue
bullets: Addresses degradation of learned barrier certificates when deployment dynamics differ from training dynamics.
Formulates the conditional barrier-drift condition as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test.

Adds deterministic temporal boundary shaping for greater conservatism early in a prescribed deployment horizon.
Empirically evaluates alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates; the monitor does not guarantee pre-unsafe-entry detection or subsequent safety.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon human-object-scene interaction (HOSI) is central to embodied AI, animation, and game development. Existing human-object interaction (HOI) and human-scene interaction (HSI) models excel in their respective domains, but none alone covers tasks requiring multiple interaction skills. Training unified HOSI models is hindered by scarce and costly data. We introduce World2HOSI, a multi-expert orchestration harness that generates continuous HOSI data from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes and natural language instructions. Our key insight is that long-horizon HOSI hinges not on a stronger single model but on orchestration. Given a shared, structured scene state and an orchestration harness grounded in it, existing experts can jointly accomplish tasks beyond the reach of any of them alone. World2HOSI realizes this insight as a closed loop around a persistent scene state built from decoupled background and object assets. A harness plans action stages over this state, invokes experts via their native conditioning interfaces, and writes each action's effects back, so that every invocation is grounded in the evolving world. To reduce physical artifacts, bounded residual optimization and contact-driven physics simulation further ensure the physical plausibility of human motion and object manipulation, respectively, while preserving interaction intent. Experiments and a perceptual user study show that World2HOSI achieves the best task completion and interaction quality on the evaluated HOSI tasks, while generating more diverse data.
authors: Jiushu Li, Haoran Wang, Yumeng Liu, Zhiyang Dou, Yuan Liu, Yuexin Ma, Cheng Lin
bullets: Addresses the lack of unified models and scarce, costly data for multi-skill long-horizon HOSI generation.

Experiments and a perceptual user study report the best task completion and interaction quality among evaluated methods, with greater data diversity.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in diffusion models have raised concerns about privacy, harmful content, and copyright violations. Concept erasure methods aim to address these risks by removing undesirable concepts from pretrained models without full retraining. However, existing approaches often degrade non-target generation quality through heuristic strength scaling (e.g., classifier-free guidance or negative prompt scaling), leading to uncontrolled and excessive semantic drift. To address this, we propose Push-Pull Attentional Anchoring (PPAA), a mechanism in the cross-attention space that displaces target representations while anchoring the scale of erasure via bounded cosine-similarity constraints. By using a relative similarity ratio instead of an absolute difference, our adaptive threshold represents a meaningful percentage of semantic retention, facilitating a single value to be applied uniformly across layers. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple concept categories, including celebrities, artistic styles, nudity, and intellectual property. Our method achieves favorable trade-offs against prior approaches on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and demonstrates its applicability to modern architectures such as FLUX.
authors: Nattanat Chatthee, Tagon Sompong, Ekapol Chuangsuwanich, Supasorn Suwajanakorn
bullets: Addresses semantic drift caused by heuristic erasure-strength scaling in existing concept-erasure methods.
Operates in cross-attention space, displacing target representations while constraining their cosine similarity.
Uses a bounded relative similarity ratio to express semantic retention and apply one adaptive threshold across layers.
Evaluated on celebrities, artistic styles, nudity, and intellectual property concepts.
Reports favorable trade-offs on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and applicability to FLUX.

ESD causes substantial semantic shifts in non-target concepts, whereas UCE fails to semantically erase Mickey Mouse. (b) Quantitative results. papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) reconstructs 3D scenes from images in a single forward pass, making it well-suited to applications that must operate within limited resource budgets. To further improve its practicality, recent budget-controllable FF3DGS methods allow the number of Gaussians to be adjusted at inference, so that the output meets a given storage limit or rendering-latency constraint. However, these methods overlook the cost of inference itself: to produce a representation with the target number of Gaussians, they first predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, requiring nearly constant latency and peak memory regardless of the budget. We therefore propose RLSplat, a resource-linear budget-controllable FF3DGS framework whose representation size, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget is reduced. Instead of pruning or selection, RLSplat learns a Gaussian allocation policy that distributes the budget across local scene regions, so that exactly the requested number of Gaussians is generated. These Gaussians are then refined through resource-linear Gaussian decoding, in which each Gaussian attends only to nearby Gaussians found via an efficient hierarchical neighbor search, so that the decoding cost decreases linearly with fewer Gaussians. In zero-shot evaluation, RLSplat outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, surpassing the strongest baseline even with 4$\times$ fewer Gaussians, while running up to 4.1$\times$ faster with 9.6$\times$ less peak memory at low budgets.
authors: Injae Kim, Minseok Joo, Jihwan Park, Sehyung Kim, Minseong Bae, Hyunwoo J. Kim
bullets: Existing methods generate a dense Gaussian set before pruning, so inference cost remains nearly fixed regardless of the final budget.
RLSplat learns how to allocate exactly the requested number of Gaussians across local scene regions.
A resource-linear decoder refines Gaussians using efficient hierarchical neighbor search and local attention.
In zero-shot evaluation, it outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, including a stronger baseline with 4× fewer Gaussians.
At low budgets, RLSplat runs up to 4.1× faster and uses 9.6× less peak memory.

papers.abstract: Semantic occupancy mapping supports embodied perception during exploration and detailed scene understanding afterward, giving rise to two complementary requirements: online incremental mapping for maintaining an up-to-date global map under causal constraints, and offline global map refinement for improving the completed scene representation with additional computation. We present VEOcc++, a unified voxel-centric framework that connects both stages through a persistent sparse voxel feature map. During exploration, the map expands with newly observed regions and integrates aligned local features through reliability-guided updates, while context-aware decoding produces the current semantic occupancy map. After exploration, cached local features are consolidated as complementary evidence and combined with the completed online representation for multi-scale spatial refinement. On EmbodiedOcc-ScanNet, VEOcc++ achieves 67.12\% IoU and 58.40\% mIoU, establishing new state-of-the-art performance for online incremental mapping. With the local predictor fixed, our online mapping pipeline outperforms VEOcc fusion by 3.70 IoU and 3.74 mIoU points, demonstrating substantial gains from the proposed global mapping design. Offline global map refinement further improves the completed map to 67.79% IoU and 59.37% mIoU using only the observations acquired during exploration. Zero-shot deployment on a mobile robot further demonstrates transferability to unseen environments, onboard feasibility, and scalability to large-scale indoor mapping. Project page: https://wryzju.github.io/VEOccpp/.
authors: Ruoyu Wang, Jiahan Li, Yong Liu, Kexin Zhang

On EmbodiedOcc-ScanNet, achieves 67.12% IoU and 58.40% mIoU online, with offline refinement improving performance to 67.79% IoU and 59.37% mIoU.
Demonstrates transfer to unseen environments, onboard feasibility, and scalable indoor mapping on a mobile robot.

papers.abstract: Large language models are expected to estimate their own uncertainty, with confidence signals used to guide retrieval, adaptive compute allocation, routing, and selective abstention. We investigate whether confidence signals measured at different temporal stages of problem solving encode distinct forms of epistemic information and remain reliable beyond English-centric settings. Inspired by classical meta-memory theory, we distinguish anticipatory pre-solve confidence (Feeling-of-Knowing, FOK) from retrospective post-solve confidence (Judgement-of-Learning, JOL). We evaluate these signals across two frontier LLMs, multiple reasoning domains, translated Marathi benchmarks, and a newly constructed benchmark of genuinely local Marathi factual questions. Across settings, the cheaper pre-solve signal remains weakly calibrated, while post-solve confidence generally provides stronger epistemic alignment despite its additional inference cost. Confidence behaviour transfers surprisingly well under direct language translation, with calibration trends largely preserved between English and Marathi, but degrades substantially on local Marathi knowledge, suggesting that linguistic transfer alone is insufficient for region-specific information needs. Finally, hallucinated responses maintain persistently elevated confidence after answer generation, highlighting important limitations of current LLM self-assessment mechanisms.

bullets: Studies confidence signals at two reasoning stages: pre-solve Feeling-of-Knowing (FOK) and post-solve Judgement-of-Learning (JOL).
