papers.abstract: 3D scene graphs support language-guided navigation by organizing physical entities and their containment and spatial relations into hierarchical maps. Building such structured maps requires a scene representation that consistently distinguishes semantic regions and object instances across viewpoints. To this end, we present PanoGraphGS, a unified framework that integrates panoptic 3D Gaussian representation learning with hierarchical 3D scene graph construction. The framework learns semantic and instance features on shared Gaussian geometry. Prototype-based semantic learning and association-based instance learning produce consistent panoptic predictions across viewpoints. The learned representation supports novel-view panoptic segmentation and direct Gaussian-level panoptic decoding. A semantic-aware scene graph module further recovers a floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy with containment and spatial relations. We further release NaviGS, a real-world dataset for panoramic scene understanding. The dataset provides 3DGS, mesh, RGB, semantic, and depth data. For 3D scene graph identification, PanoGraphGS outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in object-node accuracy by more than 50\% points on average across Replica and NaviGS. PanoGraphGS also achieves state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods in 2D panoptic segmentation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of PanoGraphGS in both hierarchical 3D scene understanding and 2D panoptic segmentation. The project website is available at: https://github.com/gaojh0333/PanoGraphGS.
authors: Jinghan Gao, Siyu Wang, Dongyu Feng, Yiyuan Pan, Rong Xiong
bullets: Uses shared Gaussian geometry with prototype-based semantic learning and association-based instance learning to maintain consistent panoptic predictions across viewpoints.
Supports novel-view panoptic segmentation and direct Gaussian-level panoptic decoding.
Builds floor–room–stuff–object hierarchies with containment and spatial relations through a semantic-aware scene graph module.
Introduces NaviGS, a real-world panoramic scene-understanding dataset containing 3DGS, mesh, RGB, semantic, and depth data.

Outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline by over 50 percentage points in average object-node accuracy across Replica and NaviGS, while achieving state-of-the-art 2D panoptic segmentation among evaluated methods.

papers.abstract: Long-video understanding with multimodal LLMs is fundamentally constrained by the mismatch between video length and the model's limited visual context budget, making frame selection essential for practical reasoning. Existing query-aware methods typically rely on heuristic pipelines: they assign one-dimensional query-conditioned scores to frames and then apply sampling, ranking, or extraction rules to form the final subset. While effective in practice, such methods are generally not derived from an explicit optimization objective and struggle to capture the heterogeneous evidence required for complex reasoning. In this paper, we revisit long-video frame selection from a principled optimization perspective. We formulate it as a structured evidence-allocation problem and propose OTFS, an optimal transport framework that maps multiple evidence sources onto video frames. To reflect the asymmetry of this problem---important evidence should be preserved, whereas redundant frames need not absorb mass---we instantiate this view with a semi-unbalanced entropic optimal transport objective and an efficient solver, OTFS-Sinkhorn. Combined with an exact dynamic program for coverage-aware subset extraction, OTFS yields a practical two-stage training-free pipeline. We further show that, in the single-source case, our formulation induces a Gibbs-type distribution over frames, making Q-Frame's temperature-scaled distribution a special case of our framework while also providing a broader perspective for understanding related prior methods. Experiments on three long-video understanding benchmarks show that OTFS consistently outperforms strong training-free baselines. Codes are available at https://github.com/barry664/OTFS.
authors: Ziwei Zhao, Yuhang Liu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between long videos and multimodal LLM context limits, where heuristic query-aware selection may miss heterogeneous evidence.
Maps multiple evidence sources to video frames using a semi-unbalanced entropic optimal transport objective.
Uses an efficient OTFS-Sinkhorn solver followed by exact dynamic programming for coverage-aware subset extraction.
Provides a training-free two-stage pipeline and shows that Q-Frame’s temperature-scaled distribution is a special single-source case.
Outperforms strong training-free baselines across three long-video understanding benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Simulation-ready world reconstruction demands physical interactivity beyond visual realism, which existing black-box 3D generation fails to deliver. We present NeoWorld-3, a coding-agent framework that reconstructs interactive 3D worlds from visual observations via tunable, executable programs. At its core, NeoSDK provides the underlying computational engine for low-level geometries, part composition, differentiable parameter refinement, and physics validation. At the same time, NeoMCP exposes these capabilities as structured, tool-callable APIs for vision-language agents to visually inspect, edit code, and iteratively refine programs. Through a hierarchical coordinator-worker architecture, the framework scales seamlessly from standalone articulated objects to complex compositional scenes. Evaluations across object-level and scene-level reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate that NeoWorld-3 achieves state-of-the-art geometric fidelity and physical readiness. Crucially, manipulation trajectories planned within our reconstructed twins achieve successful zero-shot execution on a physical dual-arm robot, completing the Real-Sim-Real loop.
authors: Eachen Soong, Zijian Niu, Haoran Xu, Yihong Dong, Yunbo Wang, Xiaokang Yang
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually realistic 3D generation and simulation-ready physical interactivity.
Uses NeoSDK for geometry, composition, differentiable refinement, and physics validation.
Uses NeoMCP tool APIs with vision-language agents to inspect, edit, and iteratively refine reconstruction code.
A hierarchical coordinator-worker design scales from articulated objects to complex scenes.
Reports state-of-the-art geometric fidelity and physical readiness, with successful Real-Sim-Real execution on a dual-arm robot.

Object- and scene-level feedback loops guide reconstruction and revision, producing simulation-ready scenes for sim-based policy optimization and sim-to-real deployment.

papers.abstract: Bipedal humanoids can change their effective footprint by adjusting body yaw, enabling both narrow-passage traversal and socially aware yielding. This paper presents a posture-aware navigation framework centered on \emph{Adaptive Traversal Tubes} (ATT), \emph{Interval Velocity--Heading} (IVH) control, and a sidestep-enhanced AMP locomotion prior. ATT represents a behavior-feasible corridor width field along a reference path, unifying geometric clearance and social comfort into a continuous signal. IVH maps this width to a continuous frontal-to-sidestep posture schedule and omnidirectional velocity commands. A velocity-conditioned AMP policy, trained with GVHMR-retargeted frontal/sidestep motions and coupled \((v_x,v_y)\) tracking rewards, is designed to improve transition stability over a generic locomotion controller while remaining interchangeable with the default onboard policy. This preprint presents the full method; a planned evaluation protocol on a Unitree G1 is outlined, with quantitative results to follow. Demo videos of MuJoCo simulation and real-robot deployment are available at: github.com/lborogzj997/Humanoid-Navigation-in-Crowds-and-Narrow-Spaces.
authors: Zijian Ge
bullets: Adaptive Traversal Tubes represent behavior-feasible corridor width, combining geometric clearance with social comfort.
Interval Velocity–Heading control converts corridor width into continuous posture transitions and omnidirectional velocity commands.
A sidestep-enhanced, velocity-conditioned AMP locomotion prior uses retargeted motions and coupled planar-velocity tracking.
The method is presented with MuJoCo and real-robot demonstrations, while quantitative evaluation on a Unitree G1 is planned.
Quantitative results are not yet reported in the abstract.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. System overview. Mid-360 LiDAR localization supports global A* and local Hybrid A* planning. ATT builds a behavior-feasible width field w(s) along the reference path from geometric clearance and social comfort; IVH maps w(s) to a frontal–sidestep heading schedule and body-frame (vx, vy , ωz) for a sidestep-enhanced AMP locomotion policy. Offline, GVHMR+GMR provide frontal/sidestep reference motions for AMP training; a generic onboard controller remains a compatible fallback.

Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed idea. Top: ATT width field (green→ red as the tube narrows) for a geometric squeeze-through (left) and social comfort compression (right). Bottom: corresponding real-robot behaviors on a Unitree G1, where IVH schedules a frontal-to-sidestep posture response.

Fig. 3. Qualitative illustration of the intended behaviors on a Unitree G1 (not a quantitative benchmark). (a) Socially aware pedestrian encounter: comfortspace compression narrows the tube and IVH schedules a frontal-to-sidestep yield. (b) Narrow-corridor traversal: geometric clearance shrinks w(s) at the gap, triggering a sidestep squeeze-through and recovery to frontal gait. Controlled comparisons against a frontal-only baseline are left to the evaluation protocol in Section IV.

papers.title: Adaptive Traversal Tubes for Posture-Aware Navigation of Bipedal Humanoids

papers.abstract: In object goal navigation (ObjectNav), an embodied agent must find a target object (e.g., "find a bed") in a previously unseen environment, relying on spatial commonsense such as object co-occurrence. Large Language Models (LLMs) encode this commonsense, but deploying them on robots exposes a trade-off between reasoning quality and efficiency: cloud-based models incur latency and privacy risks, whereas small on-device LLMs are fast but prone to hallucinated spatial judgments. Hybrid reasoning LLMs offer both a fast non-thinking mode and a slow thinking mode, which raises a key question for embodied agents: when is slow thinking worth its cost? We propose CovNav, a training-free framework that answers this question with Conformal Prediction (CP), turning dual-process (System 1 / System 2) inference into an uncertainty-aware decision. Much like recent decision models such as Jev, CovNav casts each spatial query as a structured binary decision rather than free-form generation: a local LLM in fast mode judges whether the target is likely near an observed object, CP converts its token probabilities into a prediction set, and only ambiguous queries are escalated to slow chain-of-thought reasoning. The object-pair formulation keeps calibration tractable and supports open-set objects through off-the-shelf detectors. Experiments on Gibson and HM3D show that CovNav surpasses the strongest zero-shot baseline by 0.8 and 1.7 percentage points in success rate on HM3D v1 and v2, while invoking slow reasoning for only 12.4% of queries and retaining most of the gain of always-on thinking at a fraction of its latency. Real-robot experiments on a TurtleBot 4 further validate the approach. CovNav shows how calibrated uncertainty can decide when an embodied agent should think slowly, offering a principled form of adaptive test-time reasoning for LLM-based robots.
authors: Pengying Wu, Zhejia Wen, Kang Ding, Kangjie Zhou, Chunxuan Jiao, Wei Pan, Xiangli Nie, Chang Liu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–reliability trade-off between fast, error-prone on-device reasoning and slower, more capable thinking.
A fast local LLM makes binary object-pair proximity judgments; conformal prediction identifies ambiguous cases for escalation to chain-of-thought reasoning.
The training-free design supports open-set objects detected by off-the-shelf detectors and keeps calibration tractable.
On Gibson and HM3D, CovNav improves HM3D success by 0.8 and 1.7 percentage points over the strongest zero-shot baseline while using slow reasoning for 12.4% of queries.
TurtleBot 4 experiments further validate the approach in real-robot navigation.

figures.caption: Fig. 6. Visualization of Real World Experiments. The figure depicts the navigation trajectory of the TurtleBot 4 platform (setup shown in top-left) searching for a toy. The system dynamically switches between Fast and Slow modes based on uncertainty. During the initial approach (Steps 11-27), the agent operates in Fast Mode for efficient exploration. At Step 42, high uncertainty at a semantic transition triggers the Slow Mode, enabling the agent to infer the correct path into the bedroom. The agent then reverts to Fast Mode (Step 60) and successfully localizes the target (Step 73). This demonstrates the efficacy of the adaptive fast-slow inference mechanism in handling real-world ambiguities.

Fig. 1. We propose a Conformal Prediction (CP)-guided fast-slow inference paradigm for object goal navigation using Qwen3-8B as the local LLM. CP monitors the local LLM’s output confidence to adaptively switch Qwen between its fast direct inference mode and slow deliberative reasoning mode. Clear Case: When observing a bathtub, Qwen confidently predicts a toilet will be nearby (logits: 0.9 vs 0.1), so CP accepts the fast direct inference. Ambiguous Case: When observing a sofa and querying about a bed, Qwen shows low confidence (logits: 0.6 vs 0.4), so CP triggers its slow deliberative reasoning mode for more reliable spatial analysis.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating how the environment will change. Existing world-action models explore future image prediction and latent dynamics modeling. However, generating complete future images can be computationally expensive, while highly compressed latent representations may obscure local changes. To address these challenges, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially structured patch-level future latent change from the current multimodal input, preserving local information about expected environmental changes. We introduce patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize regions undergoing larger changes and a future-to-action interface that explicitly incorporates predicted future latent change into action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Long show that PLaCA achieves a 79.0% success rate, improving upon the Action-only baseline by 5.0 percentage points. On CALVIN, PLaCA improves the average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564. These improvements are achieved while updating only 2.95% of the model parameters during the second training stage, demonstrating the effectiveness of future latent change modeling for downstream robotic manipulation.
authors: Zhan Yi, Yuchen Wang, Chao Li, Lei Hong, Boyuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the cost of full future-image prediction and the loss of local detail in heavily compressed latent dynamics.
Predicts spatially structured future latent changes from visual and language inputs.
Uses change-aware supervision to emphasize regions expected to change most.
Feeds predicted future changes into action generation through a future-to-action interface.
Achieves 79.0% success on LIBERO-Long and raises CALVIN average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564, while updating 2.95% of parameters in the second training stage.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our world-to-action framework. The shared multimodal backbone produces action-query representations, from which a future-change decoder predicts patch-level future latent change. During training, a frozen visual encoder provides change-aware supervision using current and future observations. The predicted future latent change is then incorporated into the action representation through a gated future-to-action interface to generate the full action chunk. Future observations are not required during inference.

Figure 3. Patch-level future latent change and change-aware supervision. (a) A frozen visual encoder extracts patch-level features from current and future observations. Their differences at corresponding patch locations define the ground-truth future latent change ∆Z∗ t , preserving the spatial structure across camera views. (b) The magnitude of each ground-truth change vector is used to compute patch-wise supervision weights, assigning larger relative weights to patches with greater changes. (c) The predicted future latent change ∆̂Zt is supervised against ∆Z∗ t using weighted regression and directional losses. All patches contribute to the training objective with different weights.

Figure 1. Motivation for spatially structured future latent change. (a) In robotic manipulation, future changes are often concentrated around the robot arm and manipulated objects, while much of the background remains unchanged. (b) Highly compressed state representations do not explicitly preserve the spatial locations of these changes, whereas patch-level future latent change retains their spatial structure and provides future information for action generation.
Figure 4. Per-task success rates on LIBERO-Long. Comparison between the Action-only baseline and PLaCA across all 10 tasks, with 20 closed-loop rollouts per task.

papers.abstract: Medical visual grounding requires models to align clinical descriptions with spatial evidence across heterogeneous imaging domains. However, existing multi-domain post-training strategies typically rely on fixed domain sampling and shared parameter updates, overlooking the need to adapt both which domains receive training and where their updates are applied. To address this issue, we propose PACE-MoE, a policy-guided framework that jointly performs adaptive domain sampling and domain-specific adaptation for medical visual grounding. PACE dynamically assesses the training value of each imaging domain from current-policy feedback and progressively adjusts domain coverage through domain admission, replay, and final all-domain balancing. Meanwhile, domain-specific LoRA adapters route updates to the corresponding imaging domains while preserving the pretrained backbone and visual encoder. This coordinated design aligns training-data allocation with parameter adaptation without modifying the original reward formulation or Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective. Experiments across seven medical imaging domains show that PACE-MoE consistently improves grounding performance over fixed-domain training, achieving a 3.64% relative improvement in mean box IoU over the Vanilla baseline. Under matched domain-specific adapter architectures, adaptive sampling alone further improves mean box IoU by 2.07%, demonstrating the benefit of policy-guided domain allocation. These results establish coordinated data-parameter routing as an effective strategy for multi-domain medical visual grounding.
authors: Zhenxuan Wang, Jisheng Dang, Ronghao Lin, Bimei Wang, Jingwen Zhao, Wenjun Ma, Bin Hu, Qi Tian, Tat-Seng Chua
bullets: Addresses fixed domain sampling and shared updates in heterogeneous medical imaging.

Routes domain-specific LoRA updates while preserving the pretrained backbone and visual encoder.
Across seven imaging domains, improves mean box IoU by 3.64% relative to the Vanilla baseline.
Adaptive sampling alone yields a further 2.07% mean box IoU improvement under matched adapters.

papers.abstract: Temperature scaling is typically applied as a post-hoc transformation of model probabilities. In posterior-induced flow language models, this creates two mismatches. First, posterior tempering implicitly changes both the endpoint distribution and the distribution of intermediate noisy states, while the denoiser remains trained on the original states. Second, the tempered posterior weights are combined with transport dynamics derived for the untempered flow. These mismatches are reflected empirically: lowering temperature improves GSM8K performance much less reliably in flow LMs than in discrete diffusion LMs. We introduce Bayes-Consistent Tempering (BCT), which makes temperature explicit in both the distributions and dynamics of the generative flow. Its learned realization trains the denoiser on tempered intermediate states and tempers the endpoint distribution using the corresponding tempered dynamics. We also derive training-free variants for conventionally trained checkpoints. Across hyperspherical flow LMs with two denoiser architectures and a von Mises--Fisher flow LM, BCT improves GSM8K generation across broad temperature ranges and achieves the strongest tempering performance. The gains also extend to Sudoku, demonstrating benefits on tightly constrained generation. At very low temperatures, the learned realization is also markedly more robust than the training-free variants, supporting temperature as a property of the generative flow across training and inference rather than a post-hoc probability adjustment. Code and model weights are available at https://daioba.github.io/bct .
authors: Daisuke Oba, Hiroki Furuta, Naoaki Okazaki
bullets: Post-hoc temperature scaling mismatches the intermediate noisy states and transport dynamics used by posterior-induced flow LMs.
BCT trains denoisers on tempered intermediate states and uses matching tempered endpoint distributions and dynamics.
Training-free BCT variants adapt conventionally trained checkpoints without retraining.
Across hyperspherical and von Mises–Fisher flow LMs, BCT improves GSM8K and Sudoku generation across broad temperature ranges.
The learned variant is notably more robust at very low temperatures, indicating temperature should be treated as part of the generative flow.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models show strong vision-language capabilities, yet their geometry-centric reasoning remains insufficiently understood. Existing mathematical benchmarks typically rely on rasterized figures and cover limited geometric knowledge areas and response formats, making it difficult to assess whether models reason over geometric structures or exploit superficial visual patterns. We introduce TriGeoBench, a geometry-centric multimodal benchmark constructed from Chinese middle- and high-school mathematics examinations. TriGeoBench contains 7,000 question-answer pairs and 12,235 geometric figures with TikZ code, spanning plane geometry, solid geometry, analytic geometry, function, and vector geometry across diverse response formats. Each instance forms a {question-answer pair, image, TikZ} triplet: question-answer pairs are stored in LaTeX, images as RGB figures, and TikZ preserves geometric topology, symbolic annotations, and relational structure. We evaluate representative open- and closed-source MLLMs through image-to-TikZ and multimodal reasoning probes. Results reveal persistent fine-grained structure and image-text alignment challenges. Oracle experiments with human-curated reference TikZ suggest that accurate executable representations provide complementary geometric cues; they do not evaluate an end-to-end conversion pipeline. TriGeoBench offers a testbed for structure-aware mathematical reasoning.
authors: Jing Wang, Yitong Yang, Hao Dou, Yaomin Wu, Shuting He, Tingfei Shen, Jia Wu, Jiaqi Li, Yinglin Wang

Evaluates image-to-TikZ reconstruction and multimodal geometry reasoning in open- and closed-source models.
Finds persistent challenges in fine-grained geometric structure and image-text alignment.
Human-curated TikZ oracle experiments provide complementary geometric cues but do not assess an end-to-end conversion pipeline.

papers.abstract: Handheld demonstration devices decouple data collection from the robot, but conventional designs burden the hand with a wrist camera, cables and a pose tracker (SLAM, an IMU, a VR controller, or a fixed external camera that the collector's body occludes), and burden the pipeline with as many data streams to timestamp, synchronise and cross-calibrate. We show that a single egocentric camera (USD 122) worn on the collector's head replaces the wrist camera, the pose tracker and their separate streams with one. It reads printed fiducials on an electronics-free glove (USD 22) against paper tiles taped around the workspace, giving the 6-DoF gripper pose and the jaw width from the same frames the policy will see; at deployment the same camera rides a low-cost (USD 120) arm beside the robot that mimics the collector's head from the robot's joint state. Against the robot's encoders the labels are accurate to 6.5 mm and 1.6 degrees median with 93-100% frame coverage, and a policy trained on them instead of encoders pays 3% in validation loss. Adding 194 glove demonstrations to 48 teleoperated episodes lifts rollout success from 10/25 to 17/25, level with 172 teleoperated episodes alone (18/25), and the full co-trained head-camera policy succeeds in 20/25 against 15/25 for the wrist-camera recipe, whose policies drop the object when the goal leaves their view, and 12/25 for a fixed camera.
authors: Yosub Shin, Yuan Liu, Igor Molybog

papers.abstract: Visual manuals communicate procedural knowledge through stepwise diagrams, but translating these instructions into reliable long-horizon robotic execution remains challenging. We introduce JARVIS, a method-agnostic benchmark for autonomous visual-manual-guided execution without additional language instructions. JARVIS comprises 236,679 LEGO assembly tasks across 8,987 scenes, with a carefully curated JARVIS-v1 suite of 50 tasks for interactive robotic evaluation. Tasks span varying initial structural complexities and assembly horizons, requiring agents to interpret manuals, ground actions in an evolving workspace, and execute the intended procedure. A structure-aware evaluation protocol captures geometric accuracy, structural relations, construction order, partial progress, and completion. We further introduce JARVIS-agentic, a tool-grounded embodied agent that composes robot primitives into executable programs and uses execution feedback for verification and recovery, without task-specific action trajectories or model parameter updates. Across nine multimodal and reasoning models, task-oriented primitives increase the average assembly score. Performance nevertheless declines sharply with assembly horizon, and execution errors remain difficult to correct. Prior-task experience improves initial performance, while repeated reflection provides inconsistent benefits, highlighting persistent limitations in connecting visual procedural reasoning with reliable physical execution.
authors: Fan Ding, Fucai Ke, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Xuewen Luo, Wenyu Liang, Vishnu Monn Baskaran, Hamid Rezatofighi, Yan Wu
bullets: Introduces a method-agnostic benchmark for autonomous assembly from visual manuals without extra language instructions.
Includes 236,679 tasks across 8,987 scenes and a 50-task interactive evaluation suite, JARVIS-v1.
Evaluates geometric accuracy, structural relations, construction order, partial progress, and completion.
JARVIS-agentic composes robot primitives into programs and uses execution feedback for verification and recovery without parameter updates.
Across nine multimodal and reasoning models, task-oriented primitives improve average assembly scores, but performance drops with longer horizons and repeated reflection is inconsistent.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the benchmark construction and evaluation pipeline. Visual LEGO instructions are first aligned with their corresponding 3D structural models. Long construction procedures are then decomposed into consecutive, self-contained episodes, each defined by an initial state, a set of required bricks, and a target state. These episodes are instantiated as physically interactive robotic assembly environments in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. During evaluation, a method observes the current scene, produces robot actions, and receives updated observations through closed-loop interaction. Performance is measured from the resulting construction state using the proposed Soft Score.
Figure 2: Overview of JARVIS-V1. The framework integrates multimodal task context, agentic code generation, simulation execution, evaluation, and self-reflection in a closed-loop assembly process.

papers.abstract: LiDAR-based 3D object detection is a core perception service for autonomous driving, but deployment requires robustness to point-cloud corruption while meeting latency and memory requirements. Existing approaches address robustness and resource efficiency separately, resulting in compact detectors that are fragile under corruption or robust detectors that remain costly to deploy. We therefore formulate LiDAR perception provisioning as constructing a detector that remains accurate under point-cloud corruptions while meeting constraints on inference latency and peak GPU memory. To achieve robustness, we first craft corrupted samples that mimic extreme weather conditions. Then we train candidate detectors offline by ordering clean and corrupted samples by perturbation sensitivity, through which detectors learn more from hard corrupted samples. We estimate perturbation sensitivity using an ensemble of seven heterogeneous 3D detectors by tracking changes in confidence, BEV overlap, and unmatched detections. To improve efficiency, we narrow the network and use offline neighborhood-density measurements to determine how many points and neighbors each sampling stage processes. We evaluate our method using AP (Average Precision) under clean and corrupted conditions, inference latency, and peak allocated GPU memory. On KITTI for Car detection with PointRCNN, our method improves Moderate AP under corruption by 3.32 points over the original detector while reducing mean latency by 19.8% and peak allocated GPU memory by 53.9%. Across two datasets, two detector architectures, and three object classes, our method improves AP under corruption by 4.03 points on average over the corresponding original detectors, while reducing mean inference latency and peak allocated GPU memory by 14.4% and 38.0%, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/drunklibai/robust-efficient-lidar-perception.
authors: Tingxu Han, Zijie Shen, An Guo, Lyuke Wang, Chunrong Fang, Zhenyu Chen, Wei Song
bullets: Targets the deployment trade-off between point-cloud corruption robustness and resource efficiency.
Generates extreme-weather-like corruptions and prioritizes hard samples using perturbation sensitivity.
Estimates sensitivity with an ensemble of seven heterogeneous 3D detectors using confidence, BEV overlap, and unmatched detections.
Narrows the network and uses offline neighborhood-density measurements to reduce processed points and neighbors.
Across two datasets, two architectures, and three classes, corruption AP rises 4.03 points on average, while latency and peak GPU memory fall 14.4% and 38.0%.

papers.abstract: Visual navigation in cluttered environments requires robots to recover previously observed structure and infer obstacles and free space that remain occluded. We present a framework that combines temporal aggregation and occupancy completion in an evidential bird's-eye-view (BEV) representation predicted from short RGB sequences. A decoder adapts frozen VGGT-Omega features and combines historical residual proposals using cellwise weights and a learned no-update option. The BEV predictor produces a local map in the latest ego frame without depth or camera-pose inputs or explicit geometric warping. The evidential model treats observed free space separately and predicts occupancy with associated confidence across the remaining supported region. We train the predictor on simulated RGB sequences paired with complete and visibility-masked occupancy annotations. Our experiments evaluate navigation in simulation and on a wheeled robot, with additional demonstrations on quadruped and humanoid robots. In simulated sequential two-goal navigation, our system achieves 89.6% success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 32.5 percentage points. Across 60 wheeled-robot trials in 20 scenes, it achieves 73.3% success, compared with 33.3% for the strongest evaluated baseline.
authors: Diwen Liu, Yiyang Shao, Borui Wang, Chi Zhang, Yunhui Liu
bullets: Addresses navigation failures caused by occlusions and previously observed but currently hidden structure.
Aggregates temporal RGB observations with frozen VGGT-Omega features, historical residual proposals, cellwise weighting, and a learned no-update option.
Predicts a local ego-frame BEV occupancy map without depth, camera poses, or explicit geometric warping.
Separately models observed free space and predicts occupancy with confidence over the supported region.
Achieves 89.6% simulated sequential two-goal success and 73.3% success across 60 wheeled-robot trials in 20 scenes.

Right: predicted occupancy with paths to example goals, planned path projections into the latest RGB view, and uncertainty 1− cj .

In the predicted maps, dark blue, blue-gray, and off-white denote occupied, free, and unknown cells, respectively.

papers.abstract: Can embodied task agents use tactile experience to perform fine manipulation without task-specific model training? We investigate this capability through Tactile-ETA, a system that incorporates tactile experience into an embodied task agent through in-context learning. Successful expert demonstrations show how contact changes during manipulation. We pair each recorded robot movement with its camera views and bilateral tactile observations. We keep tactile observations at the start and end of each movement and add two neighboring time points when the tactile images change markedly in between. The agent combines these demonstrations with current vision, tactile observations, and proprioception to select actions through general-purpose robot tools, without updating model parameters. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, adding tactile observations to the same two expert demonstrations increases average success from 15.75% to 24.00%, with current sensing and execution interfaces held fixed. Further experiments show that performance depends on the sensory content and representation of demonstrations, while comparing agent models on Lift Bottle reveals substantial differences under the same system configuration. On the real-robot tasks, demonstrations with aligned visual and tactile observations increase the task success rate from 0% to 60%. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using tactile experience in context for fine manipulation and suggest a path toward extending embodied task agents to additional sensory inputs.

papers.abstract: Current state-of-the-art segmentation models still produce anatomically implausible shapes, such as broken vessels and fragmented glands, on the structures that are hardest to segment. Learned shape representations capture what structures look like and can help correct these errors, but most cover a fixed set of anatomical classes. Extending this coverage across classes and imaging modalities is costly because it often requires new voxel-level annotations. We propose Diffusion for Anatomical Reshaping with Text (DART), which learns a shared shape representation from segmentation probabilities. It uses anatomical descriptions to correct these probabilities without receiving medical images. Across 13 public benchmarks, absolute Dice gains reach 31% for individual gallbladder cases in CT and 10% for individual prostate cases in MRI. Using existing segmentation predictions, we scale a single shape representation from 50 to 377 anatomical classes without new voxel-level annotations for correction training. The shared representation also corrects four lesion classes absent from training and transfers from CT to MRI without retraining. Corrected labels also improve segmentation models, raising one model's Dice from 57.1% to 67.5%. The same pipeline supports annotations for 45,000 CT scans. These results suggest that sharing shape information within and across classes can reduce the need for new voxel-level annotations when extending segmentation to more anatomical classes and imaging modalities. The model is available at https://huggingface.co/Koushik45/DART-Seg
authors: Koushik Swarna, Pedro R. A. S. Bassi, Lam Ngo, Wenxuan Li, Jiancheng Yang, Alan Yuille, Zongwei Zhou

Scales from 50 to 377 anatomical classes using existing predictions, and transfers across CT and MRI without retraining.
Across 13 public benchmarks, reported Dice gains reach 31% for individual gallbladder CT cases and 10% for individual prostate MRI cases.
Corrected labels improve downstream segmentation, including one model’s Dice increase from 57.1% to 67.5%, and support annotation of 45,000 CT scans.

Inference (bottom): probabilities are thresholded at 0.5 only to locate the crop. Their original values within the crop are resized, noised up to t∗, and denoised under the same description. The final result is thresholded to obtain a segmentation mask. Blue components are contributed by this work.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction from sparse posed monocular frames requires reasoning over observations that vary jointly in viewpoint and time. Existing methods either predict Gaussian primitives from observation-aligned features or aggregate multi-frame information through compact latent queries. However, the former tightly couples Gaussian allocation to individual frames, while the latter does not explicitly structure observed evidence according to its temporal relation to the requested timestamp. Consequently, evidence across spatial scales, viewpoints, and timestamps can be difficult to align and integrate. We present \textbf{HiQGS}, a query-based hierarchical framework for feed-forward Gaussian scene reconstruction from sparse monocular frames. HiQGS introduces a \textbf{Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Encoder} that organizes multi-resolution geometry-appearance visual features according to image location, observation time, and camera pose, thereby preserving complementary appearance and structural cues. Our \textbf{Time-Adaptive Decoder} use target timestamp queries the resulting hierarchical representation to retrieve relevant spatiotemporal evidence and predicts the corresponding Gaussian scene state. Experiments on static and dynamic scene reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate strong rendering quality and geometric accuracy, validating the effectiveness of hierarchical visual encoding and target-time-aware Gaussian querying.
authors: Qiaowei Miao, Qifeng Cheng, Yijing Guo, Yuru Xiao, Ziqian Ni, Sheng Yang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of aligning visual evidence across spatial scales, viewpoints, and timestamps in feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction.
Uses a Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Encoder to organize multi-resolution geometry and appearance features by image location, observation time, and camera pose.
Employs a Time-Adaptive Decoder that queries the representation at the requested timestamp and predicts the corresponding Gaussian scene state.
Experiments on static and dynamic scene benchmarks show strong rendering quality and geometric accuracy.
The method is designed for sparse monocular observations and explicitly targets both temporal and viewpoint variation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of HiQGS. Given sparse posed frames from a monocular video, the Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Encoder (HSE) organizes complementary multi-level geometry features and fine-grained appearance features into a hierarchical context. TP-RoPE grounds the context tokens by patch location, observation timestamp, and camera pose. The Time-Adaptive Decoder (TAD) adapt a scene-level Gaussian queries on the requested timestamp and retrieves evidence from both feature streams to predict the corresponding Gaussian scene state G(t∗). The resulting Gaussians are rendered from the target camera, while the target-independent context representation can be reused to decode multiple timestamps.

Figure 2: Qualitative comparison on RealEstate10K under the interpolation setting. HiQGS reconstructs the scene and renders held-out intermediate viewpoints with coherent geometry and fine-grained appearance details.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on the Waymo dataset. The target at +0.4 s lies within the temporal range of the context frames and evaluates temporal interpolation, whereas the target at +1.2 s lies outside this range and evaluates temporal extrapolation.
Figure 4: Qualitative depth comparison under sparse depth supervision. HiQGS recovers object geometry and delineates object boundaries more accurately than the baselines.
Table 3: Quantitative comparison of RealEstate10K interpolation and extrapolation with two context views. For baseline methods, we use the published results reported in TokenGS.

Table 1: Quantitative comparison of Waymo original-view RGB synthesis with 4 context frames and 16 target frames per 20-frame clip. For baseline methods, we use the published results reported in StreetForward.
Table 4: Ablation study on the Waymo dataset. PSNR and SSIM are reported on full-image evaluation.

papers.abstract: As model parameters scale up, sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches have become essential for model scaling. However, mainstream models currently adopt hierarchical architectures, where experts in different layers, although topologically independent, exhibit substantial similarity and redundancy in their stored content. Compared to the hierarchically arranged \textbf{Local Expert} in existing mainstream models, we hypothesize that inter-layer shared \textbf{Meta Expert} hold greater potential. To this end, we conduct a multi-dimensional empirical comparison between Local and Meta Experts, and find that models incorporating Meta Experts exhibit lower parameter redundancy, together with lower cross-entropy loss and higher downstream task accuracy. With the activated quantity and the expert granularity held fixed, \textbf{our model matches the performance of Vanilla MoE using only 70--80\% of the experts}, substantially improving the model's scaling potential. Beyond removing inter-layer redundancy among experts and improving information storage efficiency, our theoretical analysis further shows that, compared with Local Experts, Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible residual pathways, thereby improving information retrieval efficiency.
authors: Ermo Hua, Xiangyu Hong, Baiting Wu, Che Jiang, Haozheng Hou, Yicheng Gu, Hanjing Wang, Qirui Zeng, Ming Zhang, Ning Ding, Qipeng Guo, Youbang Sun, Biqing Qi, Bowen Zhou
bullets: Problem: Hierarchically local experts across layers can store redundant information, limiting MoE scaling efficiency.
Method: Replace or augment layer-specific Local Experts with cross-layer shared Meta Experts and compare their properties empirically and theoretically.
Result: Meta Expert models show lower parameter redundancy, lower cross-entropy loss, and higher downstream task accuracy.
Efficiency: With fixed activation quantity and expert granularity, the approach matches Vanilla MoE performance using 70–80% of its experts.
Insight: Cross-layer Meta Experts provide more flexible residual pathways, improving hidden-state information retrieval.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison between Vanilla and Meta-Expert models. All models are trained under the optimal setting of the Vanilla model, at varying depths and scales. Models with Meta Experts achieve comparable loss to the Vanilla baselines with only 70–80% as many experts, or 75–90% as many parameters, and the savings in both experts and parameters grow as the models get deeper and larger, indicating the favorable scalability of Meta Experts.

Figure 6: Pilot experiments on the Meta/Local Expert topology. We vary where Local Experts are used exclusively (the first and/or the last 1/2/4/8 layers), and how the Meta Experts are hierarchically organized (2/4/8 sub-pools, accessed in a looped manner, either chunked or interleaved). Both interventions generally degrade the loss, corroborating the benefit of Meta Experts, while a lighter degree of intervention—only the first and the last two layers restricted to Local Experts, or the Meta Experts looped only twice—slightly improves it.
Figure 2: The Implementation of Local and Meta Experts. In contrast to the layer-private Local Experts, Meta Experts are shared across all layers.
Figure 3: The Quantitative and Topological Comparison between Meta and Local Experts.

Figure 7: Scaling-ladder on the Meta/Local Expert topology. We scale the two best pilot configurations—Local Experts exclusively at both shallow and deep ends, and interleaved sub-pool partitioning of the Meta Experts—across training compute (FLOPs). Restricting the first two and the last two layers to Local Experts, together with 2 sub-pools, achieves the best performance at every compute budget; as the model becomes deeper, more Local-Experts-only layers and a larger hierarchy of Meta Experts further help, suggesting that deeper models call for a larger hierarchical expert topology.

Table 2: Per-depth architecture of the scaling ladder. Every rung uses 128 routed experts plus one gated shared expert, top-8 routing, a period-4 GDN/full-attention pattern (one quarter full attention), and a head dimension of 256. Widths scale jointly with depth. The table specifies the shared vanilla backbone at each rung; the Meta Experts variants replace only the routed-expert layers and keep the same 128×L routed-expert budget, so every variant at a given rung shares these dimensions. papers.abstract: While feed-forward models excel in static 3D geometry estimation, extending them to dynamic 4D scenes requires modeling visual geometry as a causally evolving state. Current methods typically rely on unordered temporal aggregation, which lacks the directional structure of physical time. Furthermore, existing supervision often treats geometry and motion as disjoint objectives, failing to exploit their inherent physical coupling. Consequently, they lack a unified constraint to effectively supervise temporal state transitions, leading to inconsistent 4D scene representations. To address this, we propose a feed-forward framework for causal 4D visual geometry learning from monocular videos. At its core, Causal Spatiotemporal Mamba augments temporal aggregation with directional state propagation. Through complementary Temporal-Spatial and Spatial-Temporal Scans, CSM continuously propagates geometry-aware states across frames to model spatiotemporal evolution. To align this causal state evolution with observable dynamics, we introduce Unified Motion Supervision. Rather than treating motion as an independent objective, UMS leverages geometry-aware predictions from the camera and depth heads to construct a unified forward motion field that is consistent with the underlying 3D structure. This geometry-grounded supervision explicitly constrains inter-frame state transitions, enabling stable states propagation across frames. Extensive evaluations on dynamic benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across video depth, camera pose, and optical flow estimation. These results validate that the synergy between the directional state propagation of Causal Spatiotemporal Mamba and Unified Motion Supervision effectively captures continuous scene evolution, significantly reducing temporal drift and reinforcing spatial-temporal consistency in 4D representation learning.
authors: Qiaowei Miao, Yijing Guo, Lipei Zhang, Qifeng Cheng, Yuru Xiao, Ziqian Ni, Sheng Yang
bullets: Targets temporal inconsistency in dynamic 4D reconstruction caused by unordered frame aggregation and separate geometry–motion supervision.
Causal Spatiotemporal Mamba propagates geometry-aware states directionally across frames using complementary temporal-spatial and spatial-temporal scans.
Unified Motion Supervision derives a geometry-consistent forward motion field from camera and depth predictions to constrain state transitions.
Evaluations on dynamic benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance for video depth, camera pose, and optical flow, with reduced temporal drift and improved spatiotemporal consistency.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our causal spatiotemporal state evolution framework. Given an ordered monocular video, the model first extracts geometry-aware tokens with global context, and then applies Causal Spatiotemporal Mamba (CSM) to propagate these tokens through causal spatiotemporal state evolution. Complementary Temporal-Spatial Scan (TS Scan) and Spatial-Temporal Scan (ST Scan) update geometry-aware states across temporal and spatial dimensions while preserving the temporal order of scene evolution. The updated spatiotemporal representations parameterize camera extrinsics, intrinsics, pixel-aligned 3D point maps, and forward optical flow. Unified Motion Supervision (UMS) constructs a unified forward motion field with geometry-grounded supervision mechanism, enforcing geometry-aligned inter-frame state transitions.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of dynamic geometry reconstruction. Our method produces more accurate and temporally coherent geometry in dynamic regions, with sharper structures and fewer artifacts than existing feed-forward 4D methods.

Figure 2: Comparison of 4D modeling paradigms. Attention-based methods [25, 37] aggregate context through pairwise token affinities, while Image/Video Mamba [15, 14] applies generic bidirectional scans for visual representation learning. In contrast, CSM introduces geometry-aware causal scans that propagate states along the temporal order of the video. The complementary TemporalSpatial Scan and Spatial-Temporal Scan jointly model temporal evolution and spatial structure, enabling ordered spatiotemporal state propagation for monocular 4D visual geometry.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of optical flow estimation. Benefiting from our unified motion supervision, our model yields highly accurate motion fields with sharp boundaries. Notably, in the middle columns where moving objects occupy a small proportion and share high visual similarity with the background, Flow3r struggles to effectively detect the foreground optical flow. In contrast, our approach successfully disentangles these challenging motions.

papers.abstract: When unique pretraining data is scarce, models see the same tokens many times and are thought to memorize. Random-token replacement, an input-corruption augmentation, is one remedy reported to lower validation loss, but a lower loss alone does not reveal which source of error it reduces. On a controlled source whose entropy rate is known in closed form, we show that replacement shrinks predictions toward the corpus average. We also introduce a decomposition that separates validation loss into approximation, estimation, and memorization terms. This shrinkage view predicts that replacement's bias cost needs no memorization but its benefit does. Memorization raises validation loss after its minimum, so we report the effect at two points, the minimum validation loss and the end of a fixed budget. Where replacement helps, it reduces this rise by about 60%. At the end of the budget, it turns from harmful to helpful as the controlled source becomes less predictable; at the minimum, it helps at no predictability level under the fixed recipe. On Korean and Japanese web text, replacement removes about a third of the loss rise after the minimum by the end of the budget, but its effect at the minimum is much smaller. Across ten real corpora, replacement lowers the final loss on nine. It harms only the census corpus, program-generated JSON that is the most redundant of the ten and much more redundant than any of 64 further prose and code corpora we measure.
authors: Wonsup Shin, Jingu Kim
bullets: Repeated data causes memorization that raises validation loss after its minimum; random replacement counteracts part of this rise.
A known-entropy analysis decomposes loss into approximation, estimation, and memorization terms, showing replacement trades bias for reduced memorization.
At a fixed training-budget endpoint, replacement reduces the post-minimum loss rise by about 60% where it helps and becomes beneficial as the source becomes less predictable.
On Korean and Japanese web text, it removes about one-third of the post-minimum loss rise; across ten real corpora, it lowers final loss on nine.
The exception is highly redundant, program-generated JSON, indicating that extreme redundancy can make replacement harmful.

papers.abstract: LLM agents have become capable kernel engineers on mainstream GPU stacks, but they struggle on emerging accelerators such as Ascend NPUs, whose programming model is barely represented in pretraining data. Recent NPU agents address this gap largely through experience: they accumulate memory from their own generation and optimization trials and reuse it on later tasks. We argue that experience alone is not enough for kernel generation. An agent can only remember what it has tried, and it rarely tries a mechanism it does not know. As a result, such memory offers little help when a new operator calls for a different mechanism, and even familiar operators raise unseen situations as optimization proceeds. We present ASCENDEVOLVE, which grounds every step of an evolutionary kernel search in a large external knowledge base built from platform documentation, toolkit headers, and operator repositories. Because this corpus far exceeds any context window, ASCENDEVOLVE indexes it and routes each agent to a small, task-specific slice of evidence instead of the corpus itself. The retrieved knowledge seeds diverse implementation strategies, guides repair when a candidate fails, and constrains how strong candidates are recombined. On 53 Ascend C operators from CANN-Bench spanning four difficulty levels, ASCENDEVOLVE achieves an overall score of 71.39, improving over Reflexion and OpenEvolve by 11.6% and 17.2%.
authors: Xi Chen, Ming Shen, Haotian Yan, Ruoyu Sun, Tianjun Yao
bullets: Experience-based NPU agents may miss unfamiliar implementation mechanisms and optimization situations.
The method indexes documentation, toolkit headers, and operator repositories, then retrieves task-specific evidence for each search step.
Retrieved knowledge seeds diverse implementations, supports candidate repair, and constrains recombination of strong kernels.
Evaluated on 53 Ascend C operators across four difficulty levels, it achieves an overall score of 71.39.
It improves over Reflexion and OpenEvolve by 11.6% and 17.2%, respectively.

papers.abstract: Online adaptation of the cornering stiffness keeps a model-based sideslip estimator valid as tires change, but competes with learned model correction for the same filter innovation. A corrector with enough parameters can absorb the innovation pattern that a stiffness change produces, and adaptation is suppressed while the fit improves. We propagate the stiffness sensitivities of the predicted measurements through the vehicle states and construct a corrector orthogonal to them. A null-space parameterization enforces the constraint without a penalty coefficient and preserves the static least-squares stiffness estimate on each identification segment. In full-vehicle simulation, the stiffness response of the unconstrained corrector declines as its parameter count grows, whereas the orthogonal corrector responds at least as fully as the uncorrected filter at all sizes and lowers sideslip error by 12.7% to 22.0%. In a simulated drive with a stiffness step, the orthogonal corrector adapts as quickly as the uncorrected filter and lowers sideslip error during and after the transient. On public real-vehicle data, the 430-parameter unconstrained corrector loses most of its response to deliberate offsets of the filter's nominal stiffness, whereas the orthogonal corrector of the same size retains most of it, with a sideslip error slightly above the uncorrected filter's.
authors: Kyoungtae Ji, Dongyeol Won, Kyoungseok Han
bullets: Problem: Flexible learned corrections can absorb the innovation caused by tire-stiffness changes, suppressing stiffness adaptation.
Method: Propagate stiffness sensitivities through the vehicle model and constrain the corrector to their null space using a penalty-free parameterization.
Contribution: The approach preserves the static least-squares stiffness estimate on each identification segment while separating correction from stiffness adaptation.
Results: In simulation, it reduces sideslip error by 12.7%–22.0% and adapts as quickly as the uncorrected filter during stiffness transients.
Scope: On public real-vehicle data, it retains most stiffness response for a 430-parameter corrector, though sideslip error is slightly higher than with the uncorrected filter.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex speech agents must update persistent memory while listening and speaking, yet it remains unclear which events should be stored, revised, or excluded. Existing benchmarks isolate interaction timing from memory outcomes, obscuring the state transitions behind a correct answer. We introduce DuplexLedger, a bilingual benchmark of 1,094 persistent sessions aligning four full-duplex scenarios with event-level Write/Update/Ignore/Retain supervision, explicit pre/post memory states, and 6,564 same-session questions and checks. Evaluating five full-duplex models reveals an interaction-memory gap: no system combines strong boundary control with coherent final-state memory, and the best final-state fact coverage is 2.01%. We propose ACT-Mem, an 8.92M-parameter sidecar comprising an event controller, a versioned transactional ledger, and a typed retriever coupled with a frozen MiniCPM-o 4.5 backbone. On 219 held-out sessions, ACT-Mem increases latest-value accuracy from 4.11% to 8.68% while reducing stale assertions and distractor adoption. It improves interaction boundaries but slows interruption stopping. These results motivate selective, auditable full-duplex memory rather than indiscriminate transcript retention. Code is available at https://github.com/lyx-researcher/DuplexLedger.

Proposes ACT-Mem, an 8.92M-parameter sidecar with event control, a versioned transactional ledger, and typed retrieval over a frozen MiniCPM-o 4.5 backbone.
On 219 held-out sessions, ACT-Mem raises latest-value accuracy from 4.11% to 8.68% and reduces stale assertions and distractor adoption.

papers.abstract: Factual recall is a lookup: some representation inside the network serves as the key, and what that key is made of decides which queries can retrieve the fact, what an edit must cover, and what a retriever can read. We call it the factual access state. In autoregressive (AR) models the subject position enriches attributes largely independently of the relation, and relation-specific selection happens later, at the readout position. In masked diffusion language models (DLMs) we find the state is assembled differently, and much earlier: in the first attention layer the wording of the relation is routed into the position of whichever entity is visible and the early feed-forward layers look the fact up on this fused representation. The state therefore varies with the relation's surface form and with the query direction, so the queries about one fact occupy a region of state space rather than a point, and an operation on the fact succeeds only for queries that enter it. We treat the state as an interface to a DLM's factual knowledge, and put it to two uses. Writing to the state gives a knowledge editor: from one declarative statement, Multi-View Edit fits one shared value per direction across that region and installs it in the early-MLP block, preserving source-prompt reliability while substantially improving paraphrase and reverse question answering, where AR editors gain near zero. Reading it suggests a complementary use: the state at each entity position can serve as a relation-specific retrieval vector with no training, returning both pieces of evidence for two-entity queries on which pooled, prompted and lexical retrievers almost never return both.
authors: Yuchen Guo, Zhuoyuan Mao, Yiwen Guo
bullets: In autoregressive models, relation-specific selection occurs late; in diffusion language models, relation wording is fused with entity representations in the first attention layer.
Because the access state varies across relation surface forms and query directions, one fact corresponds to a region of state space rather than a single point.
Multi-View Edit writes a shared value across this region in the early MLP block, improving paraphrase and reverse-question answering while preserving source-prompt reliability.
The same state can act as a relation-specific retrieval vector without training, retrieving both evidence pieces for two-entity queries where pooled, prompted, and lexical retrievers usually fail.
The findings are specific to masked diffusion language models and emphasize how their factual representation differs from autoregressive models.

papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to understand user-generated videos by integrating multiple modalities. Existing methods often treat modalities as symmetric, overlooking the fact that language provides a dominant semantic prior while nonverbal signals are complementary and noise-prone. To address this, we propose a Text-Anchored Modality Experts with Uncertainty-Guided Routing, termed TAME, that reformulates MSA as an uncertainty-guided refinement paradigm, where the language prior is calibrated and enhanced by selectively trusted nonverbal evidence. Specifically, TAME adopts an asymmetric Mixture-of-Modality-Experts framework, in which textual features act as a fixed and always-activated shared expert, while audio-textual and video-textual cross-modal branches serve as dynamically routed auxiliary experts. Furthermore, we introduce lightweight Prophet Heads to quantify the sample-level predictive uncertainty of each individual modality, and this uncertainty metric is further incorporated into the modality router to realize reliability-aware expert aggregation and fusion. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS datasets demonstrate that TAME achieves state-of-the-art performance on the majority of metrics while reducing parameter count by up to 78.7% and FLOPs by up to 41.2% over the mixture-of-expert baseline. %These results confirm that asymmetric expert construction with uncertainty-guided routing is an effective paradigm for MSA.
authors: Xiaohua Huang, Bingrui Lei, Xiuyan hao, Ling Zhou, Yuan Zong, Wenming Zheng, Guoying Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitation of treating text, audio, and video as equally reliable, despite language providing a stronger semantic prior.
Uses an asymmetric mixture-of-modality-experts design with an always-active text expert and dynamically routed audio-textual and video-textual experts.
Introduces lightweight Prophet Heads to estimate modality-specific, sample-level uncertainty for reliability-aware expert routing and fusion.
Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS report state-of-the-art performance on most metrics.
Compared with a mixture-of-experts baseline, reduces parameter count by up to 78.7% and FLOPs by up to 41.2%.

papers.abstract: Depression assessment from counseling speech requires integrating textual and acoustic psychological evidence across turns, yet existing end-to-end classification approaches lack explicit multimodal evidence interpretation and context-aware reasoning. We propose AudiPsy, an evidence-grounded omni-LLM for depression assessment over spoken counseling conversations. AudiPsy employs an Observation-Assessment-Summary (OAS) paradigm to integrate dialogue transcripts, textual and acoustic emotions, and textual-acoustic emotion incongruence into structured reasoning. OAS incrementally organizes multimodal observations, performs contextualized assessment, and maintains an evolving dialogue summary for subsequent turns. To support this framework, we construct AudiPsy-Counsel, a synthetic spoken counseling conversation corpus with multimodal context augmentation, and develop a unified three-stage curriculum for depression-oriented reasoning. Experiments on DAIC-WOZ demonstrate superior depression assessment performance over specialized depression detection methods and general-purpose speech/omni-LLMs, along with improved reasoning quality, while supplementary evaluation on EATD-Corpus supports AudiPsy's applicability to naturalistic conversations.
authors: Chuanbo Zhu, Run Luo, Weibo Zhao, Yue Li, Kun Qian, Qiang Qu, Yike Guo, Minghuan Tan, Wei Xue
bullets: Addresses the need to jointly interpret transcript content, textual and acoustic emotions, and their incongruence.
Uses an Observation–Assessment–Summary (OAS) process to organize evidence, assess context, and maintain evolving dialogue summaries.
Introduces AudiPsy-Counsel, a synthetic multimodal counseling corpus, and a three-stage curriculum for depression-oriented reasoning.
Reports stronger assessment performance and reasoning quality than specialized detectors and general-purpose speech/omni-LLMs on DAIC-WOZ.
Additional evaluation on EATD-Corpus supports applicability to naturalistic conversations.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used within everyday applications where their responses have significant downstream impacts. For responsible deployment of such systems, we desire insight into how much we can trust their individual outputs. A popular approach for estimating LLM confidence is to train probes on the hidden states of the LLM's tokens to predict the correctness of the model's output. These probes typically read hidden states from tokens that are already in the model's vocabulary. In this work, we introduce a new approach to confidence probes that learn a new readout token and utilize its hidden states to train the probe. We show that our learned readout approach ScratchProbe outperforms its existing-token counterpart on a variety of datasets and LLMs. We also extend our method to a multi-token approach which we show provides further performance improvements. Finally, since the learned readout changes only the position a probe reads from, any existing probe can adopt it. Applied to a state-of-the-art probe, it improves AUROC on every backbone, in domain and out of domain.
authors: Nima Seifi, Martin Ester
bullets: Addresses the need to assess whether individual LLM outputs can be trusted.
Introduces a learned readout token in place of hidden states from existing vocabulary tokens.
Extends the approach to multiple learned readout tokens for further improvements.
Outperforms existing-token probes across varied datasets and LLMs.
Improves AUROC for a state-of-the-art probe across every tested backbone, both in- and out-of-domain.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal LLM (MLLM)-based anomaly detection (AD) methods can generate textual explanations that help interpret their predictions. However, reliably and efficiently evaluating these explanations remains challenging. While LLM judges can assess explanations through structured rubrics, they often require substantial token generation, making evaluation costly and difficult to scale. We instead propose to anchor evaluation in the available ground truth by extracting verifiable claims from each explanation and verifying them against the corresponding annotations. We instantiate this idea as AnomalyJev, a lightweight framework that extracts verifiable claims from contextualised representations using ground-truth-defined queries and pointer based heads, without token generation. The claims are then verified against the ground truth to score faithfulness and completeness. For evaluation, we construct a human-annotated set of 640 explanations with over 1,600 expert ratings across in-domain and cross-dataset settings. Despite its compact design, AnomalyJev achieves stronger agreement with human annotators than most open MLLM judges and approaches that of flagship MLLM judges, at a fraction of their runtime and resources.
authors: Qizhou Wang, Jiawen Zhu, Guansong Pang, Christopher Leckie
bullets: Addresses the costly and hard-to-scale evaluation of textual explanations from MLLM-based anomaly detectors.
Extracts verifiable claims from contextualized representations using ground-truth-defined queries and pointer-based heads, without token generation.
Scores explanation faithfulness and completeness by checking claims against available annotations.
Introduces a human-annotated benchmark of 640 explanations with over 1,600 expert ratings across in-domain and cross-dataset settings.
Shows stronger human agreement than most open MLLM judges and near-flagship-judge agreement with substantially lower runtime and resource use.

The extracted claims are verified against the ground truth to score faithfulness and completeness.

papers.abstract: Generating high-fidelity, city-scale 3D environments plays a crucial role in applications such as virtual reality, gaming, and urban digital twins. However, the scarcity of real-world city-scale 3D training data forces existing methods to either stitch independently generated assets or learn from synthetic urban corpora, often sacrificing realism and global consistency. In contrast, 2D image data and their corresponding generative models are abundant and encode rich visual priors. To bridge this gap, we propose CityPaint, a novel framework that leverages 2D diffusion models to generate globally consistent city-scale 3D textures without relying on city-scale 3D training data. Specifically, CityPaint integrates geometric priors with the generative power of 2D diffusion models, introducing a robust top-$K$ camera baking strategy for iterative texture projection. To address the artifacts of 2D-to-3D projection, we further propose a decoupled refinement mechanism that separately optimizes terrain and building textures. Extensive experiments show that CityPaint produces globally coherent textures with fine local details and achieves favorable results against strong baselines in both visual quality and cross-view consistency.
authors: Yuchen Zou, Lihuang Fang, Siyu Zhu, Xiao Hu
bullets: Addresses the lack of real-world city-scale 3D data and the resulting realism and consistency issues.
Combines geometric priors with 2D diffusion models for iterative texture projection.
Introduces robust top-K camera baking to guide texture generation across views.
Uses decoupled refinement to separately optimize terrain and building textures, reducing projection artifacts.
Experiments show fine local detail, global coherence, and favorable visual quality and cross-view consistency versus strong baselines.

The generated views are accumulated into a global UV atlas using a face-wise top-𝐾 camera baking strategy to suppress artifacts from grazing angles.

papers.abstract: Memory-based temporal graph neural networks (TGN) rely on recurrent node memories to capture evolving interaction histories. However, temporal mini-batching introduces a trade-off between computational efficiency and temporal fidelity: when a node appears multiple times within the same batch, later interactions are evaluated using stale pre-batch memory because the intermediate memory updates have not yet been committed. This problem becomes more severe as temporal batch size increases. To overcome this challenge, we propose AnchorRM, an anchor-based residual memory mechanism that reconstructs event-specific intra-batch node states without executing sequential recurrent updates. AnchorRM treats the last committed node memory at the beginning of each batch as a pre-batch fixed anchor and uses causally preceding same-batch interactions to infer the missing state evolution relative to that anchor. The learned residual then calibrates the anchor to reconstruct an event-specific node memory for each interaction. Because each event-specific residual is predicted directly from the fixed anchor and its causal history, reconstructed states do not depend on previously reconstructed states and can therefore be computed in parallel within the batch while preserving temporal causality. Experiments across four temporal graph datasets and three memory-based backbones demonstrate that AnchorRM achieves an average 6.16x training speedup (up to 10.05x) and 28.67x batch scaling (up to 40x). These results demonstrate that AnchorRM substantially improves the scalability and training efficiency of memory-based temporal graph learning while maintaining competitive predictive performance.
authors: Haroon Gharwi, Kai Shu, Yue Dai
bullets: Addresses stale pre-batch memory when nodes appear multiple times within a temporal mini-batch.
Uses the last committed memory as a fixed anchor and predicts residual updates from causally preceding same-batch interactions.
Reconstructs each event-specific state independently, allowing parallel computation without sequential recurrent updates.
Across four temporal graph datasets and three memory-based backbones, reports 6.16× average training speedup and 28.67× batch scaling on average.
Maintains competitive predictive performance while improving scalability and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Safety pretraining has emerged as a promising paradigm for embedding safety deeply into a model during pretraining, yielding robustness to subsequent fine-tuning that conventional safety post-training often lacks. We refer to this safety acquired during model pretraining as native safety. Yet native safety is expensive to acquire, confined to the model in which it was pretrained, and often accompanied by lower general utility. In this work, we rethink the practical value of safety-pretrained models and introduce, for the first time, the native safety reuse problem: Can native safety be transferred from a specialized, potentially smaller, safety-pretrained "teacher" to standard-pretrained "students," enabling them to inherit its robustness while preserving their general utility? We show that native safety can "travel" through on-policy distillation. A standard-pretrained student generates responses to safety-pretraining prompts, while a small safety-pretrained teacher supervises the student's token-level predictions along its own generated trajectories; cross-tokenizer alignment further enables transfer across model families. The resulting students exhibit substantially greater safety robustness than their safety-post-trained counterparts while retaining higher general utility than the teacher: subsequent fine-tuning raises the average attack success rate (ASR) of the 1.7B student by only 5.00%, compared with 11.58% for safety post-training, and its average utility of 48.20% far exceeds the aligned teacher's 27.42%. Unlike conventional large-to-small knowledge distillation, our framework enables selective, small-to-large safety transfer: it reuses the robust safety expertise of a smaller pretrained teacher without inheriting its utility limitations. These findings establish native safety as a reusable model property rather than one permanently tied to the originally pretrained model.
authors: Bingqi Shang, Yang Zhang, Yiwei Chen, Changsheng Wang, Shiyu Chang, Bingquan Shen, Sijia Liu
bullets: Introduces the native safety reuse problem: transferring safety learned during pretraining across models.
Uses student-generated trajectories, teacher token-level supervision, and cross-tokenizer alignment for cross-family transfer.
Transferred students show greater safety robustness after fine-tuning than safety-post-trained counterparts.
The 1.7B student’s ASR increase after fine-tuning is 5.00%, versus 11.58% for safety post-training.
The student reaches 48.20% average utility, exceeding the aligned teacher’s 27.42%.

papers.abstract: Code agents increasingly work on evolving real repositories, and memory systems aim to help them reuse earlier experience. However, such experience is diverse and evolving, so it remains unclear how memory systems organize it and thereby affect code agents. Existing benchmarks cannot answer this reliably because they lack either temporally valid histories or control over prior-task relevance. In this paper, we present MemDev-Bench to evaluate how memory systems affect code agents over diverse repository histories. It pairs each task with relevance-annotated earlier tasks from the same repository to build histories with controlled relevance. We also build an automated pipeline that reliably makes these earlier tasks executable and verifiable, producing 4,869 historical tasks for 555 base tasks. Based on MemDev-Bench, our systematic evaluation of memory systems across diverse development scenarios yields three main findings. (1) Memory mainly improves fine-grained localization and editing, increasing functional correctness. (2) Memory also causes failures on otherwise solvable tasks even with related history, and unrelated history tends to increase such failures. These failures mainly stem from agents reusing memory without reassessing its applicability. (3) Compared with using memory systems, directly providing agents with raw historical trajectories substantially reduces their steps. Further analysis suggests that agents save these steps by reusing process information that compressed memories tend to omit. These results suggest that future memory systems should preserve process information and reassess memory applicability against current task context.
authors: Guorui Chen, Tao Liu, Zhenzhen Huang, Yidan Zhang, Liyu Jiang, Shuoyuan Wang, Hanchen Sun, Xu He, Dong Li, Yihan Hu, Jianye Hao, Lei Feng
