papers.abstract: Omnidirectional cameras provide surround-view information, significantly overcoming the field-of-view constraints for traditional visual localization systems. However, existing localization systems fail to fully exploit the characteristics of omnidirectional cameras, struggling to deliver accurate and robust localization performance amidst scene content variations and illumination-induced appearance changes. In this work, we propose OmniVLoc, a surround-view localization system based on a topo-metric framework. By integrating state-of-the-art global place recognition and monocular depth estimation methods, we introduce a multi-constrained visual localization paradigm. By solving a scale-aware pose graph and performing precise spherical bundle adjustment, we accurately recover the metric-level pose for each query frame.Furthermore, a hierarchical verification mechanism is designed to filter out erroneous outputs across different stages, effectively bolstering the overall system robustness. Extensive experiments on both public and our custom datasets validate the superior accuracy and reliability of OmniVLoc. To benefit the community, our source code and dataset will be made publicly available upon publication.
authors: Zhuo Yu, Shuyang Zhang, Huihua Zhu, Wenjia Ouyang, Zuo Zuo, Jianhao Jiao, Yilong Zhu, Xiaopin Zhong, Zongze Wu
bullets: Addresses the limited field of view and robustness challenges of conventional visual localization systems.
Combines global place recognition and monocular depth estimation in a multi-constrained localization pipeline.
Recovers metric-level poses through scale-aware pose-graph optimization and spherical bundle adjustment.
Uses hierarchical verification to reject errors across localization stages and improve reliability.
Experiments on public and custom datasets validate its accuracy and robustness; code and data are planned for release.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our system. System front-end processes omnidirectional images to obtain monocular depth with scale uncertainty, global place candidates, and their feature associations with the query frame. The back-end utilizes a factor graph to eliminate scale uncertainty, followed by pose optimization with temporal constraints and bundle adjustment. Across the entire pipeline, we enforce strict consistency checks on intermediate outputs to avoid system degradation.

Fig. 1. Comparison between our topo-metric map and traditional 3D feature map. Traditional 3D mapping relies on multi-view triangulation and suffers from geometric degeneracy and complex updates. Our topological map treats pose-annotated reference panoramas (orange) as independent database keys for the query (red), eliminating rigid geometric constraints, enabling effortless map management and continuous updates.

papers.abstract: Despite advances in photorealism, semantic fidelity, and aesthetics, text-to-image generation and image editing remain understudied in a human-centered dimension: whether their outputs feel psychologically comforting. Grounded in cognitive evaluation theory, we define psychological comfort as an affective response shaped by viewers' appraisal of restorative and emotionally supportive visual cues. We introduce HealBench, a fine-grained benchmark of 30,000 high-quality image-text pairs spanning 19 categories and 92 subcategories, selected from 100,000 candidates through a human- and expert-in-the-loop pipeline combining vision-language model matching, human preference models, expert filtering, and exemplar-guided augmentation. We also construct HealBench-Eval, a feature-clustered evaluation set of 1,095 instances. Using HealBench-Eval, we conduct objective and subjective evaluations of 14 representative image generation models and prompt-rewriting strategies. Results reveal a gap between conventional visual quality and perceived comfort: strong semantic alignment and aesthetics do not guarantee emotionally restorative images. Reinforcement learning experiments further show that HealScorer can serve as a reward signal for assessing and improving the emotional and restorative quality of generated images. These findings establish psychological comfort as a distinct dimension of human-centered image generation and position HealBench as a foundation for affect-aware generative models.
authors: Junjie Xu, Yuzhe Yang, Rui Yang, Luwei Xiao, Wenxin Wu, Xingjiao Wu, Liang He
bullets: Targets an understudied human-centered dimension: whether generated or edited images feel psychologically comforting.
Defines comfort through restorative and emotionally supportive visual cues grounded in cognitive evaluation theory.
Provides 30,000 image-text pairs across 19 categories and 92 subcategories, plus a 1,095-instance evaluation set.
Evaluates 14 generation models and prompt-rewriting strategies with objective and subjective assessments.
Shows that HealScorer can provide a reinforcement-learning reward signal to improve emotional and restorative quality.

papers.abstract: Pretrained Vision-Language Models (PVLMs) achieve strong zero-shot recognition but often suffer performance degradation under target-domain shift. Unsupervised adaptation provides a practical way to improve target-domain performance without labeled data, but it remains challenging because pseudo-labels generated by the model can be unreliable and no labeled validation set is available for model selection or early stopping. We propose a simple framework for unsupervised PVLM adaptation that combines progressive margin-based subset selection with cascaded consistency learning. The subset selection strategy constructs a class-balanced pseudo-labeled set using prediction margins and gradually expands it during training, enabling adaptation to start from reliable supervision anchors before incorporating broader target-domain data. Cascaded consistency learning further exploits unlabeled samples by using temporally smoothed teacher predictions on weakly augmented views to supervise student predictions on strongly augmented views, with confidence filtering to reduce the influence of uncertain pseudo-labels. To preserve the pretrained embedding structure, the framework updates only normalization parameters in the visual encoder and class prototypes initialized from text prompts. Experiments across multiple recognition benchmarks with both CLIP and SigLIP backbones show consistent improvements over zero-shot baselines and competitive performance against recent unsupervised PVLM adaptation methods. These results suggest that progressive pseudo-label selection and teacher-guided consistency provide an effective and lightweight strategy for adapting PVLM classifiers without labeled target data.
authors: Hao Yan, Guanghui Wang
bullets: Addresses unreliable pseudo-labels and the lack of labeled validation data during target-domain adaptation.
Builds a class-balanced pseudo-labeled subset from prediction margins, starting with high-confidence samples and expanding it progressively.
Uses cascaded consistency learning with temporally smoothed teacher predictions, strong/weak augmentations, and confidence filtering.
Updates only visual-encoder normalization parameters and text-initialized class prototypes to preserve pretrained representations.
Across multiple benchmarks with CLIP and SigLIP, consistently improves over zero-shot baselines and remains competitive with recent unsupervised methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed unsupervised vision-language model adaptation framework. The teacher model selects a class-balanced pseudo-labeled subset based on prediction margins. The student is trained with supervised learning on the selected subset and cascaded consistency learning on unlabeled data via weak and strong augmentations. The teacher parameters are updated as an exponential moving average of the student parameters, producing stabilized pseudo-labels that progressively improve subset selection and consistency learning.

papers.tldr: A lightweight unsupervised adaptation framework improves vision-language model recognition under domain shift by progressively expanding reliable pseudo-labels and enforcing teacher-guided consistency.

papers.abstract: 4D scene graphs require persistent object identity when an object disappears inside an opaque carrier and later reappears as a fresh detection. When appearance and target-centric motion are unavailable, identity recovery must rely on relational history. We formulate cross-visibility-gap identity persistence as historical-node recovery through a remembered target--carrier binding. We introduce CVG-SGM, a perception-frontend-compatible transfer--maintain--read memory. Geometry-weighted cross-node interaction transfers target-specific evidence into carrier states, a shared per-node GRU maintains this information during transport, and a two-time readout combines stored carrier--identity compatibility with current detection--carrier geometry to recover the historical identity. In the controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting, CVG-SGM achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy, compared with 0.570 for both no-memory and parameter-count-matched no-write controls. It also generalizes to scene-disjoint, unseen longer visibility gaps. On real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level episodes, it correctly re-links 36/36 held-out detections, compared with 28/36 for the strongest fixed carrier--identity control. Counterfactual carrier-memory swaps redirect predictions according to the swapped bindings, supporting the role of stored relational information in identity recovery. The current approach remains limited by shared-carrier identity ambiguity and does not provide end-to-end raw-video re-identification.
authors: Jiahui Hu, Li Gao, Yu Liu, Pengzhan Zhou
bullets: Addresses identity recovery when objects disappear inside opaque carriers and later reappear as new detections.
Uses geometry-weighted target-to-carrier transfer, per-node GRU memory during transport, and a two-time compatibility readout.
Achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy in the controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting, versus 0.570 for both no-memory controls.
Correctly re-links 36/36 held-out real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level detections, compared with 28/36 for the strongest fixed-binding control.
Generalizes to unseen longer gaps, but remains limited by shared-carrier ambiguity and lacks end-to-end raw-video re-identification.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CVG-SGM. (1) Identical targets disappear with separately trackable carriers and reappear without continuous target tracks. (2) Nodes from GT, SAM2, or 4DSG pass through a track-indexed encoder and masked intra-frame attention. (3) Geometry-weighted cross-node transfer lets target-specific evidence enter a carrier’s recurrent state, updated by a shared GRU that maintains it through the gap; an auxiliary relation head reads these states under relation supervision. (4) At reappearance, routing weights rkc from current detection–carrier geometry combine with identity compatibility Bci from end-of-carry memory as ski = ∑ c∈C rkcBci to recover the historical identity.

Figure 1: Cross-visibility-gap identity persistence through remembered carrier relations. (a) Controlled 2t2c diagnostic: two identical targets bind to carriers cA and cB , are occluded while the carriers swap, and reappear near their current carriers at locations that are uninformative with respect to their own pre-gap positions. (b) The bindings persist as memory through the gap, re-linking each fresh detection to its identity; on unseen long gaps, FULL improves re-link accuracy from 0.576 (NOMEM) to 1.000. (c) Complementary human-operated cup-shuffle videos provide offline carrier-recovery evidence, while full real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level 2t2c re-linking is reported in Table 4.

papers.abstract: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.
authors: Daniel Weiner, Raj Korpan
bullets: Evaluates Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC against published general-purpose VLM baselines.
Outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error and competence detection but underperforms on detailed social-attribute judgments.
Adding a visual frame improves one task while degrading the other.
Performance differs between judgments based on observable cues and those requiring inference about internal states.
Results are preliminary and model-family differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents aim to improve from their own experience rather than remain fixed after deployment, but naturally collected trajectories often lack ground-truth solutions or verifier-derived rewards. We introduce Retrospective Self-Distillation (RSD), a multi-round framework that turns such experience into dense supervision using privileged retrospective context. For each on-policy trajectory, the same underlying model acts as both student and teacher: the teacher re-scores the student's realized actions while conditioning on cross-task precedents and lessons, together with turn-level reflection and future hindsight from the completed trajectory. The resulting teacher distribution is distilled back into the policy through on-policy self-distillation. Across rounds, the experience bank grows and the retrospective context is refreshed, allowing the model, its data, and its supervision to co-evolve. We further introduce frontier-guided context-policy evolution, where a stronger frontier model proposes constrained edits to how privileged context is constructed. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SearchQA with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, RSD improves performance by up to 59.7% relative to the base model, while frontier-guided context-policy evolution adds up to a further 44.7% relative improvement over a fixed context policy. These results show that naturally accumulated experience can be converted into persistent model capability without ground-truth trajectories or verifier-derived rewards for the core policy update.
authors: Yuhang Zhou, Yifan Wu, Bo Peng, Mingyi Wang, Jiayi Liu, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang, Zhuokai Zhao
bullets: Addresses the lack of ground-truth solutions or verifier rewards in naturally collected trajectories.
Uses the same model as student and teacher: the teacher re-scores actions with precedents, lessons, reflections, and future hindsight.
Distills these teacher distributions into the policy across multiple rounds while the experience bank and supervision co-evolve.
Adds frontier-guided evolution to improve how privileged context is constructed.
Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SearchQA, RSD improves performance by up to 59.7% relative to the base model; context-policy evolution adds up to 44.7% further relative improvement.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RSD. At self-evolution round r, the current policy π(r) first collects on-policy interaction experience, which is incorporated into the accumulated experience bank. Privileged retrospective context is then constructed from past experience: precedents and lessons, together with reflection and future hindsight from the completed current trajectory. The same underlying model retrospectively re-scores the student’s realized actions under this privileged view, and the resulting distribution is distilled back into the student to obtain π(r+1). Repeating this process jointly evolves the policy, accumulated experience, and retrospective supervision. In the stronger-access extension, a frontier model additionally adapts the context-construction policy ϕ(r) across rounds.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Agents through Privileged Retrospective Distillation
papers.tldr: Retrospective Self-Distillation enables agents to improve from their own unverified experience by using hindsight and privileged context to create training supervision.

papers.abstract: Mitigating catastrophic risks from large language models requires excising hazardous operational capabilities, such as cyberwarfare exploitation and pathogen enhancement, without degrading benign scientific utility. In these dual-use domains, legitimate defensive science and malicious attacks share vocabulary, syntax, and internal model representations, causing standard unlearning methods to induce severe collateral damage (concept bleeding). In this work, we present Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning (OBU), a mathematically grounded framework designed to eliminate collateral damage on benign dual-use capabilities. OBU extracts a domain-matched capability subspace from paired calibration queries via singular value decomposition on empirical activation covariances, and restricts parameter updates strictly to the orthogonal null space. This guarantees that benign representations experience zero parameter perturbation along the spanned calibration subspace. We present two complementary realizations of OBU: Projected LoRA, which applies the orthogonal constraint during iterative gradient-based fine-tuning, and Closed-Form Weight Surgery, which directly edits model weights in a single analytical step without training. Across four modern open-weight foundation models (Gemma-3-4B, Qwen3.5-4B, SmolLM3-3B, and Granite-4.2-3B), OBU achieves strong dual-use concept separation, substantially mitigates in-context priming attacks, and demonstrates durable resistance against adversarial relearning without degrading benign domain competence.
authors: Niccol\`o Ronchetti
bullets: Targets concept bleeding, where malicious and defensive capabilities share language and internal representations.
Extracts a domain-matched capability subspace from paired calibration queries using SVD of activation covariances.
Restricts parameter updates to the orthogonal null space, providing zero perturbation along the spanned benign calibration subspace.
Implements the approach through Projected LoRA and training-free Closed-Form Weight Surgery.
Evaluated on four open-weight models, it mitigates in-context priming attacks and resists adversarial relearning without degrading benign competence.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Dual-Use Representation Manifold and Benign Subspace Identification. In language model activation space Rd, capabilities reside on a continuous representation manifoldM partitioned by an operational safety boundary B into hazardous capabilities Mhazard (activations {h(i)f }, where subscript f denotes the forget set) and benign science Mbenign (activations {h(i)b }). Because dual-use pairs lie in close proximity across B, isolating benign capabilities requires identifying their local geometry. OBU passes domain-matched calibration queries Db through the model to extract benign activations {h(i)b }, computing the principal linear subspace Vboundary = span(Vr) spanned by their leading r empirical singular vectors to tightly enclose the local benign capability manifold.

Figure 2: Operator Subspace Geometry and Orthogonal Projection in OBU. Parameter updates ∆W ∈ Rdout×din are depicted via their principal input singular direction in Rdin , where ProjVboundary (·) denotes the component of the update acting on the benign subspace Vboundary (its shadow on the blue plane).

papers.title: Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning for Dual-Use Concepts in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning removes hazardous dual-use capabilities while preserving benign scientific competence by constraining model updates away from benign capability representations.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image models can generate visual concepts that their prompts never mention, and recent work shows that such associations can be implanted so that ordinary prompts trigger them. Auditing this behavior requires recovering the description that a prompt omits. Existing prompt optimizers are not well suited to this task. Gradient-based methods require backward access to the scoring encoder. Discrete evolutionary search treats semantically unrelated tokens as equally close. Language-model-guided search requires one inference call per candidate, which limits exploration. This paper presents EmbGA, an embedding-space genetic algorithm that recovers concepts present in a set of images but absent from the prompt that generated them. EmbGA keeps the population structure of genetic search but applies its operators in the token embedding space. Crossover interpolates between parent embeddings, and mutation moves an embedding toward a randomly drawn vocabulary embedding. Each offspring is then projected back to discrete tokens before scoring, so every evaluated candidate is a valid token sequence. We evaluate EmbGA on two benchmarks against six optimizers under two exploration budgets. EmbGA achieves the highest alignment when the exploration budget is large, recovers the most grounded tokens on natural images, and runs much faster than language-model-guided search.
authors: Zhengfeng Zheng, Minghong Fang
bullets: Addresses auditing of implanted or implicit prompt-to-image associations.
Uses a genetic algorithm with embedding-space crossover and mutation, then projects candidates back to valid tokens.
Avoids gradient access and reduces the cost of language-model-guided candidate search.
Evaluated on two benchmarks against six optimizers under two exploration budgets.
Achieves the highest alignment with large budgets, recovers the most grounded tokens on natural images, and is faster than language-model-guided search.

papers.abstract: Adapting a forecasting system to a changing world classically means retraining. We ask whether the task of continually learning regimes for time series forecasting can be represented by a piece of text: a guidance block, evolved by outcome-driven reflection and used in a frozen LLM forecaster's prompt. On a refreshed multimodal benchmark (weekly search indices, daily currencies, daily commodities, each window paired with web-retrieved news), we run GEPA-style prompt evolution under strict contamination control to prevent the data leakage common in timeseries benchmarks: the forecaster's knowledge cutoff predates every evaluated window. A 900-word evolved guidance carried by Llama-3.3-70B beats TimeSeries Foundation Models (TSFMs) on held-out data (GM MASE 0.776 vs. 0.898 for TabPFN-TS-3), transfers to more recent models without measurable loss, and costs dollars rather than GPU-days to update. We characterize the loop: out-of-loop gains concentrate in the first reflection, in-loop improvements overstate out-of-loop gains 2-3x unless an untouched monitor arbitrates, and error-only objectives silently suppress the text modality. We provide two extensions. First, compiling the guidance into executable code with a TSFM as a callable tool recovers most of the gain deterministically. Second, ablations show the advantage widens at short horizons and that removing the news text does not hurt the guided forecaster, consistent with the text's value being distilled into policy during learning. We argue that continual prompt evolution is a practical, training-free alternative to retraining for multimodal forecasting.
authors: Laurent Mombaerts, Jonathan Taws, Jacopo Gargano, Dinesh Gaddam, Kevin George, Srijan Tiwari, Shreyas Rajesh
bullets: Prompt evolution uses outcome-driven reflection to update a roughly 900-word forecasting policy.
On a refreshed benchmark of search indices, currencies, commodities, and paired news, the method achieves GM MASE 0.776 versus 0.898 for TabPFN-TS-3.
Performance transfers to newer models without measurable loss and updates cost dollars rather than GPU-days.
Untouched monitoring is important: in-loop gains can overstate out-of-loop gains by 2–3×, while error-only objectives suppress the text modality.
Code compilation recovers most gains deterministically; benefits are larger at short horizons, and removing news does not hurt after policy distillation.

papers.abstract: On-policy learning is central to post-training: training on a model's own generations limits distribution shift and helps preserve existing capabilities. On hard problems, however, on-policy RL provides no reward-based learning signal when all attempts fail. On-policy distillation provides next-token supervision from a teacher, but on hard problems, if a rollout goes wrong early, subsequent supervision is conditioned on prefixes that already contain the mistake. Correct behavior can instead come from a gold or teacher solution, but such off-policy targets can differ substantially from the model's generations and, as we show, may erode existing capabilities. We therefore treat on-policyness as a continuum and propose projected distillation, which minimally edits the student's failed attempts into correct targets. The method uses contrastive updates to favor corrections over failed attempts and refreshes these corrections as the student evolves, enabling near-on-policy learning even when all student attempts fail. Theoretically, we prove that the student's learning regret grows with the edit size: it scales linearly with the horizon under minimal correction, as in DAgger, and quadratically under full-answer replacement, as in behavior cloning. Empirically, across two students (Qwen3-8B and OLMo-2-7B) and five domains spanning math, code, science, and tool use, projected distillation gives the highest area under the specialization-retention frontier (best on 8 of 9 cells against GRPO and OPD, and 7 of 9 against SPOT and SODA). Our ablations highlight the importance of online corrections, the contrastive loss, and on-policyness: moving targets farther off-policy steadily worsens the specialization-retention trade-off, with retention falling from 0.916 to 0.744 when minimal corrections are replaced by student-agnostic gold solutions.
authors: Shripad V. Deshmukh, Christian Bock, Kangrui Ruan, Abhijeet Awasthi, Vijay Lingam, Rein Houthooft, Manish Prajapat
bullets: Hard problems can yield no reward signal when all on-policy attempts fail, while teacher or gold solutions may be too far off-policy and cause capability erosion.
The method edits failed student attempts into minimally corrected solutions, using contrastive updates and refreshing corrections as the student changes.
Theory links learning regret to edit size: minimal corrections scale linearly with horizon, whereas full-answer replacement scales quadratically.
Across two students and five domains, it achieved the best specialization–retention frontier in most reported comparisons against GRPO, OPD, SPOT, and SODA.
Ablations show that online corrections, contrastive loss, and on-policyness matter; farther-off-policy targets reduce retention.

papers.abstract: Agent platforms are starting to improve their own agents: they read a deployed agent's execution traces, derive a change, have an automated verifier approve it, and release it with no human author. How much of this loop can safely run without a human? We propose two quantities a platform can measure. Verifier strength $\sigma$ is how well the available verifier -- often an LLM judge -- agrees with a trusted reference verifier; it limits how much a step can improve the agent. Recoverability is how cheaply a bad change can be undone: whether undoing it needs a new verifier approval, and how much of the old behavior a rollback restores. A step should run unattended only if both are adequate. On our platform this rule allows prompt, tool and skill edits to run unattended and keeps weight updates under human sign-off. Our main contribution is these two definitions and how to measure them. We built a platform that applies the rule and tested it in two ways: on the platform's own approval gate, and in controlled experiments on the $\tau^2$-bench agent benchmark. On verifier strength, the platform's LLM judge sometimes gave the same score no matter what it was shown (9 of 37 settings) and reported no error, so a verifier can look healthy while approving anything; its strength must be measured, and two simple tests catch the failure. On recoverability, restoring a saved copy brought the agent back to its original behavior, but a regenerated undo did not, so only changes whose old version is kept can be reversed without a human; and while a change was deployed, it altered the outcome of 17 percent of tasks beyond normal run-to-run variation, which no undo repairs. Together these support the rule: a change can run unattended only when its old version is kept and its verifier's strength has been measured.
authors: De Wang, Peng Qi
bullets: Verifier strength measures agreement with a trusted reference and bounds how safely a change can improve an agent.
Recoverability depends on whether rollback avoids new verification and restores prior behavior, including effects during deployment.
The proposed rule permits unattended prompt, tool, and skill edits, while requiring human approval for weight updates.
Experiments found an LLM judge could give unchanged scores across inputs without reporting errors, so verifier health must be tested.
Saved-copy rollback restored behavior, but regenerated undo did not; deployed changes also affected 17% of tasks beyond normal variation.

papers.title: Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) attaches small low-rank matrices to a frozen backbone, and public repositories host many LoRAs per backbone, each for a different concept or task. Combining several LoRAs in one generation forces a trade-off. Merging their weights into one update needs a single forward pass, but LoRAs trained for different concepts interfere and quality drops. Running each LoRA in its own forward pass (composite) preserves quality, but inference time grows linearly with the number of active LoRAs. We study a property of LoRA pools overlooked by prior multi-LoRA work. In real LoRA pools, the stacked low-rank factors need far fewer directions than their summed ranks. Using singular value decomposition, we find the minimal subspace that keeps 99% of the factor energy. On three diffusion pools, only 46% to 57% of the summed LoRA ranks is needed, and the subspace grows sub-linearly with pool size. A 48-LoRA sub-pool of LoRA-Hub on FLAN-T5 tasks shows comparable overlap (62%), while the diversity-curated LoRA-Retriever benchmark sits near the no-overlap baseline (96%), so pool composition rather than modality predicts where compression is large. We build on this overlap with LoRASpace, a training-free method that computes the subspace once per pool and reuses it in two inference modes, a static mode at merge cost and a dynamic mode for input-dependent routing. On the diffusion pools, static LoRASpace matches composite quality at merge cost, and dynamic LoRASpace is more than 6x faster than composite with six active LoRAs on a 17-LoRA pool, mainly because it runs one backbone pass instead of six. In an ablation, static variants at the same rank match LoRASpace, so the quality gain does not depend on the pool-wide basis. On the near-orthogonal LoRA-Retriever benchmark, compression is small and gains come from coupling with external retrieval.
authors: Thamirawaran Sathiyalogeswaran, Navindu De Silva, Chamikara Siriwardane, W. K. Alwis, Jason Mars, Udaya Sampath K. Perera Miriya Thanthrige, Ranga Rodrigo
bullets: LoRA pools often occupy a subspace much smaller than their summed ranks, but compression depends on pool composition.
It computes one shared subspace per pool and supports static merging or dynamic, input-dependent routing without training.
Static LoRASpace matches composite quality at merge cost; dynamic inference is over 6× faster than six separate LoRA passes in one reported setting.
Compression is substantial for overlapping pools but limited for near-orthogonal, diversity-curated pools.
Ablations indicate the quality gain comes from the method’s coupling, not specifically from using the pool-wide basis.

papers.abstract: Solving reasoning tasks supported on graphs typically requires providing a Language Reasoning Model (LRM) with a serialized description of the graph. This approach results in the input length growing with the number of edges, which limits the size of the problems that can be solved. Furthermore, even when graphs fit in context, performance sharply decays as the graphs grow. We propose to address this by augmenting LRMs with scalable and permutation equivariant graph positional encodings that modulate attention logits. An additional post-fusion-style module incorporates structural information into hidden states. We compute these positional encodings using a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer. This eliminates the need for serialized adjacencies, reducing the context burden to $O(N)$. We jointly fine-tune the positional encoder and the LRM LoRA adapters using optimal solutions generated by graph-theoretic solvers, resulting in a computationally efficient method. Trained on small graphs, the model exhibits improved size-generalization across graph-theoretic tasks on graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, and produces fewer tokens than a conventional LRM. Additionally, we observe that our model remains robust to node relabelings. Evaluations on graph-theoretic benchmarks also show that performance on small graphs is preserved.
authors: Javier Porras-Valenzuela, Arush Arora, Alejandro Ribeiro
bullets: Serialized graph descriptions scale with the number of edges and cause reasoning performance to degrade on larger graphs.
The method uses permutation-equivariant positional encodings from a GNN and Graph Transformer to modulate attention, plus a post-fusion module for structural information.
The positional encoder and LRM LoRA adapters are jointly fine-tuned using solver-generated optimal solutions.
Trained on small graphs, the model generalizes to graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, uses fewer tokens, and remains robust to node relabeling.
Performance on small graphs is preserved on graph-theoretic benchmarks.

The LRM’s attention layers are masked by the graph adjacency. Node tokens only attend the tokens of their neighbors.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention limits the keys used by each query, but finding those keys can still require a full-prefix scan at every layer. We introduce \textbf{MLIPS (Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing)}, a training-free method that shares candidate search while retaining each consumer's own scoring and selection. A producer publishes a top-$M$ pool larger than the attention budget $K$; subsequent layers select their own top-$K$ from that pool. Measurements across three sparse-attention model families show substantially higher coverage from broad pools than overlap between final selections. We implement layerwise sharing, persistent decode reuse, and a coarse producer in vLLM for DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Across four long-context suites, three consumer layers per producer give $1.14$--$1.40\times$ speedups and $14.8$--$27.4\%$ lower GPU energy, with observed accuracy changes of $-1.49$ to $+0.29$ percentage points in single runs. More extensive sharing exposes task-dependent quality losses. Sampled prefill traces also reveal recurring selected KV positions across query groups and layers. We characterize this shared working-set structure and use it to motivate Top-$G$, an exploratory bounded pool construction for prefill. Its deployment, task accuracy, and serving benefits remain open.
authors: Samkit Jain, Sai Kishan Pampana, Shlok Agarwal
bullets: Sparse attention still incurs costly full-prefix key searches at every layer.
A producer publishes a top-M candidate pool; each consumer independently selects its own top-K keys.
Implemented in vLLM for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, sharing three consumer layers per producer improved serving efficiency across four long-context suites.
Single-run accuracy changes ranged from −1.49 to +0.29 percentage points; more aggressive sharing can reduce quality.
Recurring KV-position reuse motivates Top-G, an exploratory prefill method whose deployment and benefits remain open.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free sharing of sparse-attention candidate search improves long-context LLM serving efficiency and GPU energy.
papers.title: MLIPS: Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing
papers.tldr: MLIPS accelerates sparse attention by sharing broad candidate-key pools across layers, achieving 1.14–1.40× speedups with 14.8–27.4% lower GPU energy but task-dependent quality trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models already make a sparse choice for every token: which experts should process it. We ask whether a sparse dictionary should reuse that choice. NR-SAE gives each routed expert a small dictionary and opens only those the frozen router selects. At block 15 of Gemma 4 26B-A4B, after ten million C4 training tokens and across three seeds, the expert-aligned autoencoder explains 0.518 of the variance in router-weighted expert outputs on a fixed evaluation capture. A rank-addressed control with the same parameters but sixteen times as many candidates reaches 0.481, a candidate-matched control 0.458, and an architecture-matched control with randomized expert identity 0.387. A transcoder variant also leads all three controls: 0.432, against 0.347, 0.371, and 0.118. Part of this advantage is architectural: each expert writes into a subspace of at most a quarter of the model width, so naming the expert names the subspace. How much it explains, we have not measured. At this layer and budget, the router already knows something a dictionary would otherwise have to learn. Our implementation did not train faster, and semantic interpretability, downstream loss, and causal faithfulness remain untested.
authors: Andrew Bistras, Marty Johnson
bullets: MoE routing decisions can be reused to select dictionary components, creating the Neural Router Sparse Autoencoder (NR-SAE).

papers.abstract: 3D point clouds generation requires capturing both part-level layout and surface detail while preserving permutation equivariance. Existing latent generative models often encode an entire shape into a single vector, which limits their ability to retain part-level structure. We propose TokenFlow, a hierarchical flow matching framework that represents each shape as a set of latent tokens and couples a rectified flow over these tokens with a conditional flow over points. A bottleneck of $M \ll N$ learnable tokens aggregates global context through cross-attention at $O(NM)$ cost. On ShapeNet, TokenFlow achieves the best MMD and coverage across airplane, car, and chair, while obtaining 1-NNA comparable to the strongest baselines. On ModelNet, its learned latent set reaches the best reported linear-evaluation accuracy on ModelNet10. These results show that representing a shape as a set of latent tokens, aggregated at $O(NM)$ cost, provides an effective representation for 3D point cloud generation.
authors: Linhao Wang, Dongjin Huang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of retaining part-level structure when encoding an entire point cloud into one latent vector.
Represents each shape with M ≪ N learnable latent tokens and uses cross-attention to aggregate global context at O(NM) cost.
Combines rectified flow matching over latent tokens with conditional flow matching over points.
On ShapeNet, achieves the best reported MMD and coverage across airplanes, cars, and chairs, with 1-NNA comparable to leading baselines.
On ModelNet, the learned latent set attains the best reported linear-evaluation accuracy on ModelNet10.

figures.caption: Figure 1. TokenFlow pipeline. The prior flow transports Gaussian noise to a set of latent tokens over a Transformer encoder with several layers whose output is rescaled by a time-conditioned γ. The conditional point flow then decodes those tokens into a point cloud. A shared per-point MLP embeds each point and feeds two separately projected branches that are added, a code path in which the pooled token set and the time embedding give the scale and shift of an adaptive layer normalization over the point features, and a token path that cross-attends from the points to the latent tokens.

papers.abstract: A failed gaming trajectory reveals that an agent needs intervention, but not necessarily how its execution harness should change. Effective harness adaptation therefore requires gathering diagnostic evidence, rather than merely proposing alternative recovery rules. We present KPHarness, a framework that adapts the external execution harness of a frozen vision-language-action model through knowledge-probing co-evolution. Recovery knowledge supplies context-specific intervention hypotheses that guide active probing; probe outcomes reveal when these hypotheses apply and provide evidence for refining both recovery knowledge and later probe selection. This reciprocal process allows the harness to improve not only which interventions it applies, but also how it investigates failures. KPHarness separates fast policy execution from a slow research loop that translates accumulated knowledge and probing evidence into bounded harness revisions. Each revision is compared with the incumbent under matched sandbox conditions and accepted only when the paired evaluation shows improvement. Recoveries supported by further validation are retained for cross-task reuse, while immediate interaction feedback and delayed episode-success credit update action- and knowledge-probing policies during adaptation. Experiments on Minecraft tasks spanning mining, combat, and crafting show improved task coverage over bare policy execution, a manually specified fixed harness, and knowledge-only harness evolution with non-adaptive probing. Evaluation on previously unseen tasks further shows improved task completion with the evolved harness, knowledge bank, and probing policies held fixed,
authors: Zhikang Chen, Yueqing Sun, Sen Cui, Ziang Ye, Yu Wang, Yan Feng2, Xierui Song, Yu Zhang, Tingting Zhu
bullets: Uses failure-driven diagnostic probing to determine when recovery hypotheses apply and refine future investigations.
Separates fast policy execution from a slower research loop that makes bounded harness revisions.

Updates action- and knowledge-probing policies using immediate feedback and delayed episode-success credit.
Improves Minecraft task coverage and unseen-task completion over bare execution, fixed harnesses, and knowledge-only evolution.

papers.abstract: Reliable quadrotor flight in disturbed environments requires predictive models that remain accurate as unmodeled aerodynamic effects change during deployment. We introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) framework that preserves an offline-identified nominal model while learning only a disturbance-induced correction online. A reference-dependent KCF is first learned from simulation data and calibrated using limited hardware data. During deployment, the nominal KCF remains fixed while a lightweight residual ensemble learns a low-dimensional disturbance correction from causal state-command-state transitions. The Adaptive DA-KCF model is incorporated into MPC, where disturbance corrections are evaluated along the prediction horizon to optimize position and yaw references sent to the onboard stabilizing controller. Hardware experiments on a nano-quadrotor under uniform wind and a spatially varying wake demonstrate that online adaptation improves multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, while satisfying real-time control requirements.
authors: Stella Kombo, Masih Haseli, Alejandro A. Stefan-Zavala, Peter I. Renn, Morteza Gharib, Joel W. Burdick
bullets: Addresses model mismatch from unmodeled, spatially varying aerodynamic disturbances during deployment.
Learns an offline nominal Koopman Control Family model, then updates only a lightweight, low-dimensional residual correction online.
Uses causal state-command-state transitions and evaluates disturbance corrections across the MPC prediction horizon.
Hardware tests on a nano-quadrotor in uniform wind and a spatially varying wake show improved multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbances increase.
Designed to satisfy real-time control requirements while preserving the nominal model.

papers.abstract: Although deep learning-based point cloud denoising methods have demonstrated impressive results in recent years, their effectiveness usually degrades substantially in real-world scenarios where the noise distribution of test point clouds deviates from that of the training set. To address this challenge, we propose a test-time adaptive denoising (TTAD) framework that enables existing denoising approaches to adapt to unknown noise patterns at test time without relying on additional supervision or retraining from source data. Taking a pre-trained denoising model and a test noisy point cloud as input, TTAD first employs a residual-driven noise modeling (RDNM) module to estimate the sample-specific noise distribution through analyzing the deviation between the noisy input and its pseudo-clean version denoised by the initial model. Then, a noise-aware contrastive adaptation (NACA) module is designed to build sample-specific noisy-noisier test-time training pair from the denoised point cloud, and update the model parameters over a few adaptation steps per sample at test time through contrastive learning. Furthermore, TTAD naturally extends to a continual TTAD (CTTAD) setting, facilitating efficient progressive refinement across sequential test samples with consistent noise distributions, while reducing the computational cost per sample. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the generalization ability of existing denoising models under unseen noise, achieving superior performance across multiple evaluation metrics.
authors: Kun Jiang, Shida Fu, Fanhao Yi, Weiqing Li, Zhiyong Su
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when test-time noise differs from training noise.
Uses residual-driven noise modeling to estimate each input’s sample-specific noise distribution.
Constructs noisy–noisier training pairs for noise-aware contrastive adaptation over a few test-time steps.
Extends to continual TTAD for efficient progressive refinement on sequential samples with consistent noise.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report improved generalization across multiple metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed TTAD framework. (a) The input noisy point cloud Xt is first denoised by a pre-trained model fθ to produce a pseudo-clean output Ỹ . (b) The residual-driven noise modeling (RDNM) module utilizes the residual noise N̂t = Xt − Ỹ to estimate the test-time noise distribution p(n) of Xt via a lightweight Gaussian mixture model (GMM). (c) The noise-aware contrastive adaptation (NACA) module generates a sample-specific noisy-noisier pair (X̃(1) t , X̃ (2) t ) of Ỹ . Within each test-time adaptation step, we first use the reconstruction loss Lrecon, identity loss Lid, and consistency loss Lconsist to update the online model fθonline via gradient descent at each iteration step. After that, the target model’s parameters θtarget are updated as an exponential moving average (EMA) of the online model’s parameters θonline. Finally, we can use the final θtarget to obtain the adapted denoised result Yc = fθtarget (Xt).

Figure 1: Illustration of existing point cloud denoising methods and the proposed test-time adaptive denoising (TTAD) framework. The source model (PointFilter [13]) fθ is trained on synthetic datasets with Gaussian noise. fθ performs well on noisy point clouds with seen (Gaussian) noise (a), but fails under unseen noise (b). The proposed TTAD framework significantly enhances the denoising performance of fθ by adapting it to unseen noise distributions during test time (c).

Each group compares three strategies: Baseline (blue), Fully Update (orange), and EMA (green), evaluated by Chamfer Distance (top row) and Point-to-Mesh Distance (bottom row). Across all noise types, the adaptation strategy with EMA consistently improves generalization to unseen noise while maintaining source-domain performance on Gaussian noise.

papers.abstract: LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by storing experience from their own executions in external memory and reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. Retaining these abstractions allows agents to reuse strategies without repeatedly deriving them from raw trajectories. However, errors in stored abstractions can propagate to subsequent decisions through retrieval and reuse. They can also shape execution trajectories, which then become the basis for new abstractions that reproduce the original errors. We term this feedback mechanism error reproduction: errors are regenerated through a cycle of abstraction, execution, and re-abstraction, extending their persistence beyond direct reuse of the original faulty knowledge. We propose Anti-Persistence, a memory design that accumulates trajectories and outcomes while reconstructing task-specific guidance on demand. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to decide whether and how to synthesize guidance, which is discarded after execution. This prevents its direct reuse as a stored object, although indirect feedback through retained trajectories remains possible. Across different benchmarks and backbones, Anti-Persistence achieves higher overall held-out success and the lowest average LLM-call cost among the evaluated memory designs. These results support separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence in memorybased self-improvement.
authors: Ruhan Wang, Kishan Panaganti, Dongruo Zhou
bullets: LLM agents can self-improve by storing execution experience without changing model parameters.
Stored rules, summaries, and skills enable strategy reuse but may propagate errors through retrieval and reuse.
The paper identifies “error reproduction,” where faulty abstractions influence executions that generate further faulty abstractions.
Anti-Persistence stores trajectories and outcomes but synthesizes task-specific guidance only when needed, discarding it afterward.
Across benchmarks and backbones, it achieves the highest overall held-out success and lowest average LLM-call cost among evaluated memory designs.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving beyond reactive responses toward proactive assistance that anticipates user needs without explicit requests. However, existing proactive agents primarily address immediate needs, while many everyday situations involve delayed intentions that can only be acted on hours or days later. Humans handle such intentions through prospective memory, the ability to remember to act on an intention when the right moment arises. In this paper, we introduce ProMemAgent, the first proactive agent to incorporate prospective memory over everyday sensory contexts for long-horizon proactive assistance. ProMemAgent organizes past sensory perceptions (e.g., egocentric video and audio) into context-aware memory, generating prospective cues and linking earlier events with subsequent developments for future retrieval. Given the current context, it retrieves relevant past events and performs memory-augmented proactive reasoning to determine whether assistance is needed. We further introduce CPMBench, the first benchmark for evaluating long-horizon proactive assistance over sensory contexts, comprising 1,000 instances across eight everyday categories. Extensive experiments show that ProMemAgent achieves the best memory retrieval performance and consistently outperforms all baselines on long-horizon proactive assistance.
authors: Lilin Xu, Linyang He, Kaiyuan Hou, Yuang Fan, Minghui Zhao, Xuhai Xu, Xiaofan Jiang
bullets: Addresses the gap between immediate-response agents and delayed everyday intentions that require action hours or days later.
Organizes egocentric video and audio perceptions into context-aware memories with prospective cues linking earlier events to later developments.
Retrieves relevant past events from the current context and performs memory-augmented reasoning to decide whether assistance is needed.
Introduces CPMBench, a benchmark with 1,000 instances across eight everyday categories for evaluating long-horizon proactive assistance.
Experiments report the best memory retrieval performance and consistent improvements over all evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Learned post-training quantization (PTQ) calibration fits quantizer parameters on a small calibration set, and for a text embedder the natural supervision is retrieval relevance. We ask two questions that are usually conflated: how far to calibrate, and whether to calibrate at all. Across three embedders (e5-base-v2, BGE-M3, EmbeddingGemma-300m) at 4-bit weight quantization, 161 calibration runs, the outcome of a fixed procedure ranges from a gain to catastrophic degradation, and the driver is the dose of the update, measured as the functional displacement D_func of the quantized model from its uncalibrated start. On EmbeddingGemma the same learning-rate grid gives +1.47 to -71.53 points of in-domain NDCG@10 change; a label-free cosine objective collapses at the same dose (-69.52 vs -71.63), so the collapse is a property of learnable calibration rather than of retrieval supervision. Objective sensitivity is heterogeneous: on e5, ranking calibration is substantially more robust than cosine at matched displacement (+14.16 +/- 4.34 pp, 95% t-CI [+3.37, +24.96], three paired slates), whereas on BGE-M3 the ordering is directionally opposite but unresolved ([-5.18, +2.38]). Dose is the main axis but not a sufficient statistic: equal D_func reached along different paths differs by up to 1.61 pp. We therefore treat calibration as an optional intervention. A pre-registered rule that accepts a checkpoint only when a per-query paired confidence interval on a 25% calibration-validation split clears the uncalibrated baseline was run on 6 independent slates and five arms. It never selected a checkpoint below its slate's baseline (0 harmful selections in 30 decisions), retained 8 of 11 beneficial updates, and paid a mean oracle regret of 1.52 pp with one abstention that forfeited 11.13 pp, a safety-opportunity trade-off, not a free improvement. We report what remains open, including label efficiency.
authors: Hyojung Han, Ryangkyung Kang, Youngeun Kim, Seung-Hun Jeon
bullets: Across three embedders and 161 4-bit calibration runs, outcomes ranged from gains to severe degradation, largely tracking functional displacement from the uncalibrated model.
On EmbeddingGemma, the same learning-rate grid produced changes from +1.47 to −71.53 NDCG@10 points; a label-free cosine objective showed a similar collapse at the same dose.
Objective robustness varied by embedder: ranking calibration was more robust than cosine on e5, while BGE-M3 showed an unresolved opposite trend.
Functional displacement was the main risk axis but not sufficient: equal displacement reached through different paths differed by up to 1.61 points.
A validation rule made 0 harmful selections in 30 decisions, retained 8 of 11 beneficial updates, and incurred mean oracle regret of 1.52 points, including one missed 11.13-point gain.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes post-training quantization calibration for text embedders, directly relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: When PTQ Calibration Helps or Hurts: Dose-Driven Collapse and Validation-Gated Abstention in Quantized Text Embedders
papers.tldr: PTQ calibration can greatly improve or catastrophically damage quantized text embedders, so validation-gated abstention offers a safer—but opportunity-costly—way to deploy it.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video generative models trained on successful, goal-directed demonstrations tend to ignore the commanded action, rendering a plausible expert-like future regardless of what is asked of them. We trace this failure to training data that lack sufficient action influence. We analyze this metric and prove that it upper bounds the action influence that any model trained on that data can express. Expert demonstrations, whose narrow action distributions let next states be predicted without attending to the action, set a low ceiling that no amount of model capacity alone can raise. Raising it requires collecting different data. We introduce Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an algorithm for actively collecting training data for improving dataset action influence. We compare the performance and data-efficiency of AIM against exploration heuristics and intrinsic-motivation methods on simulated navigation and manipulation tasks. In pixel-based manipulation, AIM is the only method that consistently improves controllability: 500 actively collected episodes added to 3k demonstrations match a world model trained on 300k expert episodes on end-effector controllability, an $85\times$ reduction in data.
authors: Samuel M. Bateman, Tenny Yin, Chongyi Zheng, Lei Huang, Brian Wang, Benjamin Eysenbach, Jaime Fern\'andez Fisac, Dhruv Shah
bullets: Expert demonstrations often have narrow action distributions, allowing models to predict plausible futures without using the commanded action.
The proposed action-influence metric upper-bounds the influence a trained model can express, so model capacity cannot overcome insufficiently influential data.
AIM actively collects training episodes to maximize dataset action influence.
Across simulated navigation and manipulation tasks, AIM is compared with exploration and intrinsic-motivation methods.
In pixel-based manipulation, 500 AIM episodes added to 3,000 demonstrations match the controllability of 300,000 expert episodes, an 85× data reduction.

figures.caption: Figure 5 | Improving Controllability via Active Data Collection. Across discrete-action navigation (FourRooms: left) and continuous-action manipulation (Push-T: center, right), AIM improves controllability with just a few hundred episodes. While Random is ideal when uniform state sampling is possible (FourRooms), AIM approaches this performance with more data; in more realistic scenarios (Push-T), AIM is the only method that improves controllability. Most notably, AIM with just 500 new episodes matches the performance of a world model trained with 300K expert episodes.

Figure 7 | Latent Diffusion Forcing Model Architecture: We train DreamerV4-like [26] latent diffusion forcing [18] action-conditioned causal autoregressive video world models with VideoRoPE [98] positional encodings and Stable Diffusion VAE [20] latent representations. These represent a strong world model architectural baseline which is held fixed in architecture and training recipe across generated datasets. These models generate human interpretable videos which help to identify degradations in the model, allowing us to focus on the impact of the data the model is trained on rather than specific architectural details.

Figure 4 | State-Action Coverage. Near-expert policies concentrate coverage around successful task execution, while random policies provide broader but less structured coverage. AIM targets action-informative regions useful for improving world model controllability.

Figure 12 | AIM Behavior Cloning Push-T Extended Results: While End-Effector controllability is significantly improved by AIM, we see all model variants struggle with improving Tee pixel recall, a measure of simulator fidelity. Nearly all exploration data collection policies we evaluate see noticeable improvement in tee recall, but even the top line 300k expert demonstration model struggles with performant tee manipulation. We hypothesize that this is a combination of poor coverage of tee positions in the dataset, as well as a lack of broad pre-training datasets in our experiments to improve extrapolation beyond the existing dataset. Additionally, we note that AIM shows significant improvement in full image pixel recall, outperforming the competing methods, and that pixel RMSE remains a strong metric of model fidelity in deterministic, nearly fully observable MDP settings despite the prevailing focus towards distributional evaluation metrics for generative world models [32, 33, 35].

Figure 2 | AIM is an algorithm that uses an information maximization objective to collect high-utility experimental transitions to improve controllability of learner policies similar to the prior demonstrations.

Figure 1 | Action-Conditioned Video Generative Models trained on near-expert data suffer from expert success bias and low controllability. The center panel shows a world model trained on expert data ignoring input actions and hallucinating a state closer to success. The right panel shows a world model trained with AIM data which remains faithful to the commanded action.

Figure 6 | Data Scaling Trends for World Models: We compare the simulation fidelity of world models trained on near-expert data (different types of PPO policies), recovery data, and random data on FourRooms [76] and Push-T [83] environments. Four Rooms Sim Realism estimates predicted states through maximum likelihood and enumerates the state-action space exhaustively for full evaluation reference distribution coverage. For Push-T, such exhaustive coverage is infeasible, so instead we evaluate the pixel recall of the ground truth sim end effector mask on H=10 horizon rollouts with on-policy Behavior Cloning and off-policy "Push Away" expert rollouts.

Figure 8 | Exhaustive Evaluation of World Model Action Sensitivity in Four Rooms: This figure compares the evaluation results of one step action sensitivity of two data scales of a Four Rooms world model trained on expert data via the above “Dozen plots". Each quarter slice in the figure represents a state (grid position and direction of the agent), and within that slice it is split into 3 triangles representing each commanded Four Rooms action: forward, left, right. The color, as denoted in the top right, represents the action corresponding to the actual observed transition by the learned world model. One can see that, in low data regimes, the world model collapses to a near deterministic action policy where the model follows the most likely policy action regardless of action conditioning. However, the same model with more of the same data distribution becomes a near perfect action sensitive world model.

Figure 13 | AIM Anti-Push-T Extended Results: We see similar results to that of Figure 12, though dampened due to the significantly more off-policy nature of the “Push Away" Push-T task which results in actions which are significantly more counter factual to those which exist in the pretraining data and thus harder to reproduce. This results in the worst data efficiency scaling from all of the active collection methods.

Figure 11 | The Need for Trust Regions for Density-Based Intrinsic Motivation in Push-T: In this experiment, we initialize the robot arm in the workspace in a grid and collect 4 transitions at each spot, one for each cardinal direction, then evaluate these transitions with the learned AIM reward model. We then plot the max AIM reward on the above heatmap. We see that the learned AIM intrinsic motivation reward provides significant reward for regions outside of the nominal action workspace, and unbounded policy optimization would likely encourage unfocused state coverage similar to prior work [44, 54, 55]. In contrast, the AWR [72, 97] weighted reward focuses in a narrow region around pre-existing behavior, favoring task relevant information before broader exploration.

Figure 10 | AIM Four Rooms Extended Results: We provide the full side-by-side metric results from batch online active data collection in Four Rooms. Of note is the similar quality of RMSE as an ordered quality metric compared to the state-focused Sim Fidelity in this simple environment, which is in contrast to conventional wisdom around evaluating generative models. Additionally, we see that measured world model action influence grows proportionately with the evaluated sim realism, a metric computed by enumerating all actions, rolling them out in both the world model and the simulator, and evaluating their state extractive simulation consistency, weighted according to the action influence evaluation measure.
Figure 3 | Action information and fidelity. Explained action information correlates with state-extracted simulation fidelity in Four Rooms, across dataset scales (𝑟 = 0.979).

Figure 9 | AIM-over-Random Fixed-Start Visitation Ratios: In this figure, we fix the initial state of data collection rollouts to the pose of the green triangle in all figures. Then, we compare state visitations in Four Rooms between rollouts generated by either successive AIM iterations or from a random policy as a heatmap of the clipped log ratio of their empirical state occupancy. More red represents more frequent AIM visitation, and more blue represents more frequent Random visitation. Pseudocounts with 𝜖 = 10−6 were added for normalization of the log ratios. One can see AIM provides significantly better medium and long horizon state visitation compared to pure random, which leaves the initial top left room less frequently. Additionally, each iteration shows AIM providing coverage of largely different subsets of the state space, showing the value of AIM iteration and its ability to avoid revisiting previously explored regions.

Table 3 | Policy hyperparameters. All models share a frozen, per-domain–finetuned SD-VAE encoder [20] (bf16 activations, fp32 params), 144×144 inputs encoded to 18×18×4 latents (81 tokens/camera), 2D sin–cos position embeddings [85, 86], and pre-LN transformer blocks with QK-norm [87] and SwiGLU FFNs [88]. IQL [71] variants add a cross-attention decoder on the shared BC backbone. Only the VAE is frozen across tasks.

Table 5 | World model hyperparameters. Both share a frozen, per-domain–finetuned SD-VAE (bf16 activations, fp32 params), 144×144 inputs encoded to 18×18×4 latents, pre-LN transformer blocks with QK-norm and SwiGLU FFNs, and a flow-matching velocity-MSE objective (EMA-normalized, 𝛼 = 0.99). Neither uses a target network; only the VAE is frozen. For human evaluation and ablations in Section 4.3, we instead train the Push-T models at 256×256 inputs to make them easier to evaluate.

Table 4 | SD-VAE [20] decoder-only finetuning hyperparameters. One recipe produces the per-domain tokenizers shared by all policy and world models; only augmentation and frame budget differ across domains.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes action influence maximization to improve controllability of action-conditioned video world models, directly targeting interactive world-model training.
papers.title: Training Controllable World Models via Action Influence Maximization
papers.tldr: Action Influence Maximization collects data that makes world models more responsive to commanded actions, substantially improving controllability with far less data than expert demonstrations alone.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now autonomously complete long-horizon tasks, such as repository-level coding, through hundreds of think-act steps, yet the experience each run produces is rarely reused on the next. Prior memory systems concentrate on retrieval, finding the most relevant past trajectory. Retrieval cannot observe the running agent, so it cannot decide whether the agent needs an experience, at which point, or for how long. We introduce REM (Reusable Experience Memory), a framework that manages the memory lifecycle from inside the agent's think-act loop through three explicit decisions. What to store: each completed trajectory is consolidated into a phase-structured document, two orders of magnitude smaller than the trajectory. When to recall: the document is injected at the start of the task; the costlier implementation record is withheld until an in-loop gate detects the agent struggling. What to forget: the record is evicted after a single exposure. On repository-level bug fixing (SWE-ContextBench Lite), REM retrieves the related trajectory more accurately than every state-of-the-art memory system (68.7% vs. 55.6% match@1) and improves, in every replicate, end-task resolution (27.6% vs. 24.9%) at 17% lower cost. Injecting the same experience as a summary or raw trajectory, even when oracle-retrieved, does not. Ablating any of the three decisions reduces resolution. Altogether, these results demonstrate that the bottleneck in experience reuse is not retrieval fidelity but how experience is stored and governed across its lifecycle, opening a control-theoretic perspective on agent memory.
authors: Xinyi Lisa Chen, Pedro Herrero-Vidal, Xiaohan Chen, Xiaojing Yu, Cris Liu, Bingqing Song, Bin Xu, Suleiman A. Khan, You-Lin Chen
bullets: Targets the failure of retrieval-only memory systems, which cannot observe when an agent needs past experience or how long it should retain it.
Consolidates completed trajectories into compact, phase-structured documents; exposes detailed implementation records only when an in-loop gate detects difficulty.
Evicts implementation records after one exposure to prevent unnecessary persistence.
On SWE-ContextBench Lite, REM achieves 68.7% match@1 retrieval accuracy and 27.6% end-task resolution, at 17% lower cost than the comparison system.
Ablations and oracle-retrieved summary/raw-trajectory variants show that lifecycle governance—not retrieval alone—is critical to effective reuse.

figures.caption: Figure 1: REM manages the memory lifecycle in three stages around the agent’s think-act loop. Left: the write path consolidates each completed trajectory into a phase-structured document (localize, understand, fix pattern, verify); the extraction fields come from a domain module discovered automatically from example trajectories. Top right: the read path retrieves candidates by cosine similarity, reranks with one LLM call, and injects the top document at the start of the run. Bottom right: the in-loop recall node recalls the implementation record on a struggle signal and evicts it after one exposure.
