papers.selection_reason: Explicit memory-lifecycle framework for reusing coding-agent experience; directly targets LLM agent memory.
papers.title: REM: What to Store, When to Recall, What to Forget in Experience Memory for Coding Agents
papers.tldr: REM improves coding-agent experience reuse by controlling what to store, when to recall it, and when to forget it within the agent’s loop.

papers.abstract: In joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA), an encoder and a predictor are trained together to produce a representation that minimizes the error in predicting the representation of the next observation. Because the representations of both the current and the next observation are learned, it is unclear which features they will include. Earlier characterizations describe the features JEPA selects in terms of their individual predictability, raising the concern that unpredictable features, like a traffic light, will not be encoded into the representation. However, the prediction error is also affected by the relationships between features, e.g., the light's color helps predict whether the traffic will stop. We propose the predictive closure characterization, which accounts for these relationships. Based on a reformulation of the JEPA training objective, we show that selection depends on properties of feature sets. This view agrees with earlier works when features evolve independently, but makes new predictions when they do not, for instance that a feature like the traffic light can still be retained. We test this characterization in controlled experiments, which show that unpredictable features can become better represented when they help predict other features, and that changing one feature's predictive relationships can affect how well others are represented. We also demonstrate implications for steering feature selection: targeting one feature with an auxiliary objective, or supplying it to the predictor as side information, can strengthen the representation of another feature whose future values it helps predict, so steering can be indirect.
authors: Mosh Levy, Aly Lidayan, Yoav Goldberg
bullets: Earlier analyses based on individual predictability may incorrectly suggest that features such as traffic lights are omitted.
The proposed predictive-closure characterization reformulates JEPA’s objective to account for dependencies among features.
Controlled experiments show that unpredictable features are better represented when they improve prediction of other features.
Changing one feature’s predictive relationships can alter the representation quality of others.
Feature selection can be steered indirectly through auxiliary objectives or predictor side information.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Will the traffic light be included in the latent representation? The top row shows successive observations, and the rows below show their latent representations with the light kept or dropped; crosses and dashed frames mark the resulting prediction errors. In the first step, the light changes color at random, so keeping it costs an error on its own next color. In the second step, the light’s current color helps predict whether the cyclist will ride or stop next, so dropping the light costs an error on the cyclist. Earlier characterizations judge the light only by whether its own next color can be predicted, and so would drop it; they disregard what its current color contributes to predicting the cyclist’s next move, which is what can make the light worth keeping. Cyclist artwork adapted from Scott McCloud’s Understanding Comics (1993).

Figure 4: Feasibility dependence: adding images to a cycle can reverse which images’ features are more strongly represented. Mean decoding accuracy across the competing cycle’s positions decreases as N grows, despite unchanged average copying probabilities; at N = 16, the fixed A/B pair is better represented. Dashed line: 50% chance.

Figure 2: Cross-subsidization: the unpredictable light becomes more decodable when it helps predict the images. Increasing q makes the current light more useful for predicting which images persist, while its future remains unpredictable. Dashed line: 50% chance accuracy.

Figure 3: Set switching: changing predictive relationships reverses which pair is more strongly represented. Increasing pD strengthens decoding of C/D and weakens A/B, whose predictive relationships remain fixed; neither pair helps predict the other. Dashed line: 50% chance.

Figure 9: Changing group size. Enlarging the C/D group reduces its decoding accuracy in every run at every regularization weight. At N = 16, A/B becomes better represented in all three runs at r = 0.10, 0.20, but only one of three at r = 0.05. We average decoding accuracy across positions within each group; dashed lines mark 50% chance accuracy.

Figure 10: Auxiliary reconstruction. Reconstructing C can also strengthen its predictive partner D, which receives no reconstruction supervision. At β = 0.36, C/D is better represented than A/B at every pD and regularization weight. Increasing β does not always improve decoding: at r = 0.20, pD = 0.75, both C and D decline from β = 0.135 to β = 0.36. All four images remain visible to the encoder. Cells show decoding accuracy from one training run, using a shared 50–90% color scale; numerical values below 50% remain visible.

Figure 11: Predictor side information. Supplying C strengthens representation of A and D while weakening B at pD = 0.75, 0.85 in all three runs at every regularization weight. The effect varies across the sweep and does not uniformly replace the A/B pair with C/D. Colored curves supply C to the predictor; gray curves omit side input. All probes read the main latent without access to the side input; supplying C also adds encoder capacity. Panels show decoding accuracy with standard errors across three runs; dotted lines mark 50% chance accuracy.

Figure 12: Worst- and best-position readouts show the same reversal. Both measures favor the competing cycle at the smallest size and A/B at the largest, showing that the reversal also holds for the least and most decodable positions within each group. Curves show means across three training runs; error bars show standard errors. Probes are trained on collages from images held out from encoder training and evaluated on separate collages. The dashed line marks the chance image-detection accuracy of 50%.

Figure 7: Cross-subsidization. The current light becomes more strongly represented as q increases, although stronger regularization weakens this effect. Dashed lines mark 50% chance light-decoding accuracy.

Figure 8: Changing predictability. Increasing pD from 0.60 to 1 changes the better-represented pair from A/B to C/D in all three runs at every regularization weight. Stronger regularization reduces the separation between the pairs. The change need not be monotonic: at r = 0.20, mean decoding accuracy for C/D decreases from pD = 0.95 to pD = 1. Dashed lines mark 50% chance accuracy.

Table 1: Predictors distinguish actual next observations from incompatible alternatives. Values are percentage correct, reported as mean ± standard error across three training runs. Chance is 50% for choosing between the actual next observation and the alternative. Each system is evaluated in its own learned latent space. The side-information condition supplies the current C image while keeping it visible in the main input.

papers.selection_reason: Characterizes feature selection in JEPA, a predictive world-model objective, with implications for learned environment dynamics.
papers.title: Predictive Closure: A Set-Level Characterization of JEPA's Feature Selection
papers.tldr: JEPA feature selection depends on predictive relationships among feature sets, allowing individually unpredictable features to be retained when they help predict others.

papers.abstract: Scaling laws suggest that increasing model size, training data, and compute generally yields monotonic performance improvements. While this often holds at the aggregate level, we present systematic evidence that vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit inverse scaling at the subtask level: specific question categories on which larger models perform worse than smaller counterparts within the same model family. We evaluate 19 models from four distinct model families across eight multimodal benchmarks (nine evaluation splits), answering 29,386 questions per model, 558,334 model-question evaluations in total. Using per-question pairwise analysis across all model pairs in each family, we identify 375 subtask-model-pair combinations exhibiting inverse scaling, spanning 4,342 unique queries where a smaller model answers correctly but a larger model fails, and we find that these patterns replicate across independently developed architectures. We identify 13 subtask-dataset pairs that show inverse scaling across multiple families, consistent with the phenomenon being task-driven rather than model-specific. The most affected domains in our study include multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and university-level STEM knowledge, with accuracy gaps exceeding 20 percentage points in several cases, while diagram understanding appears comparatively resistant. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing model size uniformly improves multimodal capabilities and suggest that model selection should be task-aware.
authors: Rohit Saxena, Alessandro Suglia, Marek Rei, Pasquale Minervini
bullets: Analyzes 19 models from four families across eight benchmarks and nine evaluation splits.
Finds 375 inverse-scaling subtask–model-pair combinations involving 4,342 queries where smaller models succeed and larger ones fail.
The effect replicates across independently developed architectures and appears in 13 subtasks spanning multiple model families.
Multi-image spatial reasoning, visual perception, and university-level STEM knowledge are most affected; diagram understanding is comparatively resistant.
Results support task-aware model selection rather than assuming the largest model is always best.

papers.abstract: Checking whether a text complies with a body of law is slow when done by hand and fragile when done with keyword rules. This paper presents ComplianceAgent, the legal compliance sub-agent of COMPASS, a multi-agent framework that evaluates texts along four axes: digital sovereignty, carbon impact, compliance, and ethics. The agent relies on a large language model that scores a text on a fixed rubric, grounds its judgment in a reference legal corpus, and, when the score falls at or below a critical threshold, runs a corrective chain made of self-healing rewrites, a compliance label, an explainability report, and escalation to a human reviewer. We describe what the language model does at each step, how the memory of the agent is organized, and how the same implementation can be pointed at different reference corpora. We evaluate the agent in a Canadian and Quebec context, on a corpus of thirteen legal instruments that brings together federal and provincial texts, international treaties, and municipal documents of the City of Trois-Rivi\`eres. The evaluation relies on a hand-annotated gold standard of fifteen texts and combines classification metrics, a repeated-query stability test, retrieval precision, and a composite score. On this gold standard the agent separates every conforming text from every non-conforming one, its scores remain stable under repeated queries, and the index returns relevant passages.
authors: Soukaina Alaoui Ismaili, Jean-Sebastien Dessureault
bullets: Addresses the slowness and fragility of manual and keyword-based legal compliance checks.
Scores texts against a fixed rubric grounded in a configurable reference legal corpus.
Triggers self-healing rewrites, compliance labels, explainability reports, and human escalation for critically low scores.
Evaluated on 13 legal instruments and 15 hand-annotated texts using classification, stability, retrieval, and composite metrics.
Separated all conforming from non-conforming texts in the evaluation, with stable repeated-query scores and relevant retrieval results.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have advanced rapidly in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain limited on tasks requiring fine-grained understanding of small or easily overlooked image regions. Recent thinking with images approaches mitigate this limitation by allowing models to inspect images through operations such as zooming, cropping, or code execution. While effective, their multi-turn interactions with VLMs introduce redundant token computation and slow inference, and separate region inspection from the reasoning step that depends on it. To address these issues, we propose Look Before You Reason (LoRe), an implicit visual thinking framework for efficient visual reasoning within a single-turn VLM interaction. Given an image and a question, LoRe predicts the most relevant image region, aligns it with the corresponding image patch features, and strengthens the associated key-value (KV) cache entries, enabling subsequent decoding to directly exploit the selected visual cues without additional visual inputs or explicit tool calls. We further employ reinforcement learning to guide the VLM toward identifying informative image regions and leveraging them during reasoning. To support fine-grained evaluation of multimodal reasoning, we introduce COCO-ObjQA, a large-scale benchmark for object-centric multimodal reasoning. Experiments on three challenging multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that LoRe consistently improves VLM reasoning performance with low additional inference overhead.
authors: Zerui Chen, Changrui Chen, Fei Ni, Jiankang Deng
bullets: Addresses overlooked small image regions and the inefficiency of zooming, cropping, or code-based visual inspection.
Predicts a relevant region, aligns it with image-patch features, and strengthens corresponding KV-cache entries in a single interaction.
Uses reinforcement learning to encourage selection and use of informative visual regions during reasoning.
Introduces COCO-ObjQA for fine-grained, object-centric multimodal reasoning evaluation.
Improves reasoning across three challenging benchmarks with low additional inference overhead.],

papers.abstract: In real-time autonomous field applications, GNSS is often unreliable and inaccurate. A possible solution is localizing against a prebuilt map like a satellite image, as it is georeferenced and already surveyed. In this work, we localize a spinning radar measurement against overhead RGB imagery with a learned observation model. We use a radar representation pretrained by masked reconstruction and align it to features from a satellite image. A particle filter propagated by radar odometry proposes candidate poses, and our observation model provides a likelihood over these poses. We evaluate our method over 31 distinct routes, over 8 datasets spanning both urban and offroad conditions using only ground radar and a coarse local prior. We also examine the robustness over changing weather using repeated traversals over the same route over 13 months, in both urban and offroad conditions.
authors: Shaunak Kolhe, Peng Jiang, Kasi Viswanath, Srikanth Saripalli
bullets: Targets real-time autonomous navigation when GNSS is unreliable or inaccurate.
Pretrains a radar representation via masked reconstruction and aligns it with overhead RGB imagery features.
Uses radar odometry to propagate particle-filter pose hypotheses and a learned observation model to score them.
Evaluated across 31 routes and 8 urban/offroad datasets using ground radar and only a coarse local prior.
Tests robustness to weather and seasonal change through repeated traversals over 13 months.

papers.abstract: Test-case generation is critical but remains challenging for language models. Existing test-time scaling methods either isolate candidates or aggregate traces, which do not scale to long-horizon tasks. We present TEX, a collaborative test-time scaling framework based on execution-driven cross-validation. TEX parallelizes agents to generate tests and patches, cross-executing each test against every patch to form a $K \times K$ feedback matrix. Agents use their matrix slices for refinement, enabling objective validation without verbose trace sharing. On SWT-Bench Verified, TEX achieves 86.4%, establishing a new state-of-the-art and improving +9.0% over single-agent baselines. Moreover, even random selection from TEX outputs (84.4%) surpasses the previous SOTA (84.0%), showing collaborative execution feedback improves solution quality, not just best-case samples. Our results highlight execution-grounded feedback as an effective scaling mechanism for long-horizon agentic tasks.
authors: Akash Gokul, Srijan Bansal, Yingbo Zhou, Semih Yavuz
bullets: Addresses the scalability limits of existing test-time scaling for language-model test generation.
Parallel agents generate tests and patches, then execute every test against every patch to build a K×K feedback matrix.
Agents refine their outputs using matrix slices rather than sharing verbose execution traces.
Reaches 86.4% on SWT-Bench Verified, improving 9.0 percentage points over single-agent baselines.
Random TEX output selection achieves 84.4%, indicating execution feedback—not only best-sample selection—drives gains.

We perform cross-validation by running all generated code patches against all generated test files. Each agent receives execution feedback from running its code & test against all other tests & code, then continues sampling in the next round.
Figure 2: Ablation on SWT-Bench subset shows crosscandidate feedback (TEX) outperforms self-feedback under identical compute (K = 4, R = 3).

papers.title: TEX: Test-Time Scaling Testing Agents via Execution-based Cross-Validation
papers.tldr: TEX improves long-horizon code-agent test and patch generation by having agents cross-execute one another’s outputs for objective feedback.

papers.abstract: The development of embodied models of animal behavior is a major goal of the neuro-AI community. Embodied models will enhance our ability to make direct comparisons between biological and artificial agents. To make such comparisons effective, though, we need embodied models that actually move like animals. Previous work has developed virtual animal bodies and techniques for training realistic motion through imitation. However, to date, there is no system for embodied animal modeling that produces natural movements both during trained goal-directed behavior, and during exploration driven by random generation. Here, we introduce Simulated Control via Augmented Motor Priors for Embodied Reinforcement learning (SCAMPER), a system for training an embodied virtual rat model, enabling natural movements during both goal-directed behavior and random exploration. SCAMPER uses a variational architecture with two distinct priors, a motion prior for control and a behavior prior for exploration. We show that combining both of these priors allows SCAMPER to generate realistic behavior during exploration and exploit the task structure effectively. SCAMPER can also learn from sparse rewards as a result of the diverse movements induced by the behavior prior, allowing the system to model realistic sparse-reward tasks from experimental neuroscience. Altogether, SCAMPER provides the neuro-AI community with an effective new system for training embodied models of rodents on realistic tasks.
authors: Aidan Sirbu, Charles Y. Zhang, Yuanjia Yang, Bence P. \"Olveczky, Talmo D. Pereira, Blake A. Richards
bullets: Addresses the lack of embodied animal models that produce realistic motion across both trained behavior and exploration.
Uses a variational architecture with separate motion and behavior priors for control and exploration.
Combining the priors supports realistic exploratory behavior while exploiting task structure.
The behavior prior enables learning from sparse rewards by inducing diverse movements.
Designed for modeling rodents performing realistic neuroscience-inspired tasks.

papers.abstract: Large language models can detect vulnerable code, yet the form of vulnerability encoding in their representations remains unclear. We analyze 8 code models spanning 6.7B-15B parameters on C programs using three datasets (DELTASECOMMITS, SVEN, and PRECISE-BUGS), comparing two diagnostic tasks on the same representations: identifying what patterns the code instantiates, and determining whether it is vulnerable. Models encode the first with high fidelity. Under the studied paired C-code datasets and linear-probing setup, vulnerability information is more accessible as a paired relational signal-whether code A is riskier than code B-than as a globally separable categorical label. This structural difference has implications for classification: the model reliably ranks which code is riskier but standard classifiers on isolated samples achieve limited accuracy because vulnerable and secure samples form overlapping distributions in representation space.
authors: Rui Melo, Andre Catarino, Claudia Mamede, Corina Pasareanu, Rui Abreu
bullets: Analyzes 8 code models (6.7B–15B parameters) on C programs across three datasets.
Models represent code-instantiated patterns with high fidelity.
Vulnerability is more accessible through paired comparisons—whether code A is riskier than code B—than through globally separable labels.
Linear classifiers perform poorly on isolated samples because vulnerable and secure representations overlap.
Findings are scoped to the studied paired C-code datasets and linear-probing setup.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Projection distributions (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, mean-token pooling). Left: Distribution of pair-wise projection differences (hvuln−hsecure)·d̂ across layers. Most pairs exhibit small positive differences concentrated near zero, with ∼13% negative. Right: Vulnerable versus secure projections. The tight clustering around the diagonal and strong overlap between distributions indicate modest per-pair separation and no global linear decision boundary.

The 12 CWE types include memory violations (CWE119, CWE-120, CWE-125, CWE-787), injection attacks (CWE-78, CWE-89), path traversal (CWE-22), and resource leaks (CWE-401). Most pairs are highly separable (90–100% AUROC, dark green), with weaker separation between similar memory-related types (58–72% AUROC, yellow/orange). Color scale: green indicates strong separation, yellow indicates chance-level performance. This pattern reflects strong functional encoding of vulnerability categories across diverse CWE types.

papers.selection_reason: Shows vulnerability information in code LLMs is encoded relationally rather than linearly separable; relevant to LLM representation analysis.
papers.title: When Models Know but Can't Linearly Say: Relational Encoding Limits Linear Vulnerability Classification in Code LLMs
papers.tldr: Code LLMs encode vulnerability information relationally, making them better at ranking which code is riskier than linearly classifying isolated samples as vulnerable or secure.

papers.abstract: Analyzing merchant transaction histories requires dynamic temporal filtering, entity resolution, and aggregation over irregular event streams--operations poorly captured by static tabular or time-series forecasting benchmarks. We introduce TxnQA, an analytical QA benchmark comprising 27 task families (81 templates) alongside a 5-scenario fraud-risk reasoning suite that evaluates both verdicts and supporting evidence over synthetic, privacy-mitigated transaction data. Ground-truth answers are computed programmatically, and model performance is decomposed into format-following rate (FFR), conditional content accuracy (CA), and end-to-end correctness (E2E). Evaluating prompted proprietary baselines and six LoRA-adapted open-weight models shows that adaptation reliably enforces output schemas but leaves arithmetic bottlenecks: Gemma-4-31B-IT and Qwen3-8B attain E2E scores of 0.867 and 0.816, whereas evaluated MoE checkpoints reach only 0.632-0.713. Furthermore, on the 500-instance fraud suite, verdict accuracy frequently exceeds 80%, yet joint accuracy (requiring exact evidence attribution) collapses to at most ~23%. These findings identify schema compliance, semantic calculation, and evidence attribution as three distinct bottlenecks in transaction-sequence QA.
authors: Rabimba Karanjai, Yiming Bian, Yun-Shiuan Chuang, Jenna L. Ballard, Zijie Pan, Shivani Shekhar, Yixi Li, Yirou Ge, Avinash Thangali, Richard Williamson, Linsey Pang, Prakhar Mehrotra
bullets: Introduces a benchmark with 27 analytical QA task families, 81 templates, and a five-scenario fraud-risk reasoning suite.
Tests temporal filtering, entity resolution, aggregation, verdicts, and supporting-evidence attribution over synthetic, privacy-mitigated transaction data.
Separates performance into format-following rate, conditional content accuracy, and end-to-end correctness using programmatic ground truth.
LoRA adaptation improves output-schema compliance, while arithmetic remains a bottleneck; evaluated models achieve E2E scores from 0.632 to 0.867.
Fraud verdict accuracy often exceeds 80%, but joint verdict-and-evidence accuracy reaches at most about 23%.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of the TxnQA benchmark framework. Starting from real merchant transaction data, we generate privacy-mitigated synthetic merchant profiles and irregular transaction sequences using REaLTabFormer. Each transaction sequence is converted into natural-language context and paired with automatically generated questionanswer pairs. Model performance is assessed using three complementary metrics together with fine-grained analyses across question categories, answer formats, and model architectures.

papers.abstract: Hallucination stress tests can yield similar average scores across language models even when different prompts elicit hallucinations in each model. We develop a procedure that iteratively edits source-grounded seed prompts to expose hallucinations in a target model. An LLM editor revises each prompt in response to the target's answer and a judge's category-specific score and explanation. In the main setting, the target also receives feedback on its previous response. Experiments cover 500 seeds from seven datasets and ten topics, with intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations evaluated across open-weight and closed-source models. Editing substantially increases judge-rated severity over the seeds. In the baseline configuration, retained responses fall in the judge's strong-hallucination bin in 77.2% of runs targeting extrinsic hallucination and 74.2% targeting intrinsic hallucination. Later editing rounds account for more than half of the mean score increase. Among 219 prompts that pass model-assisted source-validity checks, 89 elicit responses containing unsupported claims. Across five models, 200 curated prompts yield similar average severity scores, although pairwise Spearman correlations between prompt-level scores are only $\rho=0.0387$ to $0.1897$. Curated prompts can be reused across models, but their diagnostic value depends on source validity and the failures they expose in each model.
authors: Jiho Lee, Bingquan Zhang, Lin Ting Liang, Soroush Vosoughi, Weicheng Ma
bullets: Curated prompts produce substantially more severe judge-rated hallucinations than source-grounded seeds.
The method targets both intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations across seven datasets, ten topics, and open- and closed-source models.
Later editing rounds contribute more than half of the average severity improvement.
Across models, curated prompts have similar average severity but weak prompt-level score correlations, indicating model-specific diagnostic value.
Prompt usefulness depends on source validity and the particular failures exposed by each model.

papers.abstract: Enterprise adoption of LLMs in agentic workflows is gated by evaluations that span a wide arc of abilities: CRM operations, heterogeneous-document retrieval, personal data understanding, multi-turn planning, tool use, function calling, long-horizon research, and long-context software engineering. These evaluations live today in separate repositories with divergent runners, dependencies, and scoring conventions, which makes cross-benchmark comparison difficult and obscures what a single aggregate number actually represents. We release EGI-BENCH, a unified LLM agent benchmark suite that consolidates eight enterprise facing agent benchmarks (CRMARENA, HERB, PERSONABENCH, USERBENCH, MCP-UNIVERSE, MCPEVAL, BENCHFORCE, LOCOBENCH) behind a single command-line interface with two runtime-budgeted execution modes. On top of the suite we define the Enterprise General Intelligence (EGI) Score, a six-dimensional framework (M1-M6) whose buckets are populated by fine-grained sub-metrics routed from each benchmark rather than by benchmark-level averages. We describe the suite, the sub-metric routing, and the quick/deep budgets, and report results for fourteen frontier and cost-efficient LLMs spanning the GPT, Claude, and Gemini families under quick mode. Top-line EGI ranges from 39.6 (GPT-4o mini) to 65.6 (gpt-5.5), and no single model dominates every capability axis: gpt-5.5 leads task outcome, planning, and retrieval grounding; Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads tool actioning and safety/abstention; and Claude Haiku 4.5 leads engineering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/egi-bench.
authors: Zhiwei Liu, Zhujun Lan, Jielin Qiu, Zixiang Chen, Liangwei Yang, Ming Zhu, Akshara Prabhakar, Wenting Zhao, John Emmons, Jason Wu, Shafiq Rayhan Joty, Junnan Li, Shelby Heinecke, Silvio Savarese, Huan Wang
bullets: Covers CRM operations, document retrieval, personal-data understanding, planning, tool use, research, and long-context software engineering.
Provides a single CLI with quick and deep runtime-budgeted execution modes, replacing disparate runners and scoring conventions.
Routes fine-grained sub-metrics into six capability dimensions rather than averaging whole benchmarks.
Evaluates 14 GPT, Claude, and Gemini models; results show different models lead different capability axes rather than one universal winner.
Code is publicly available at github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/egi-bench.

The best M2 (Tool Actioning, 87.17) and M5 (Safety & Abstention, 80.28) are held by Claude Sonnet 4.5, while the best M1 (Task Outcome, 82.95), M3 (Planning, 30.89), and M4 (Retrieval & Grounding, 54.86) are all held by gpt-5.5, illustrating that top-line EGI can mask capability-level specialization.

papers.abstract: Medical workflows often require multiple interdependent analyses, but existing specialist and generalist AI models are not designed to coordinate them. We introduce MMedAgent-Plus, a multimodal medical tool-use agent that combines a vision-language planner with 18 leading specialist models spanning 12 tasks and 8 modalities. Through a unified tool interface, the planner selects specialists, executes them in sequence, and synthesizes responses grounded in their outputs. The planner is instruction-tuned on 208,928 samples from 32 public medical benchmarks, covering single- and multi-tool interactions across single and multiple rounds. We separately evaluate tool orchestration, response synthesis, and end-to-end execution on held-out samples. MMedAgent-Plus achieves tool-call accuracies of 91.0%, 98.1%, and 80.7% in single-tool multi-round, multi-tool multi-round, and multi-tool single-round settings, respectively. Given correct tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus achieves scores of 14.4-14.8 out of 15 for faithfulness, completeness, and conciseness across 600 evaluation samples. In end-to-end execution without pre-supplied tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus correctly invokes the required specialist in 90.6% of 350 evaluation cases spanning seven tasks. Its final-answer accuracy reaches 0.98, matching the dedicated leading specialist and exceeding the strongest baseline (0.28).
authors: Ruoxin Wang, Yuanting Pan, Binxu Li, Ruiyang Ji, Yaqian Chen, Jiayuan Ding, Qifan Wang, Lifu Huang, Mingjie Li, Yu Zhang, Ehsan Adeli, Kilian Pohl, Zhe Xu, Zihao Lin, Haoyu Dong, Yixin Wang
bullets: Addresses the need to coordinate multiple interdependent medical analyses across modalities and workflows.
Uses a vision-language planner with a unified tool interface to select, sequence, and synthesize specialist-model outputs.
Instruction-tuned on 208,928 samples from 32 public medical benchmarks covering single- and multi-tool interactions.
Achieves 90.6% correct specialist invocation in 350 end-to-end cases and 0.98 final-answer accuracy, versus 0.28 for the strongest baseline.
Scope: evaluations cover held-out samples, seven end-to-end tasks, and synthesis given correct tool outputs.

papers.abstract: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.
authors: Tao Jiang, Benjamin Navet, Yousouf Taghzouti, Fabien Gandon, Louis-F\'elix Nothias, \'Elise Dumont
bullets: Integrates computational protocols, lab notebooks, and chat logs across docking, molecular dynamics, and quantum chemistry.
Uses three memory tiers: session observations, project-level learnings, and human-validated cross-project rules.
Demonstrated across four chemistry case studies, tracking 317 runs and producing 116 project-tier entries and four promoted rules.
In controlled replays, memory-enabled runs passed checks that memory-free runs failed, including docking-configuration checks.
Combines automation, reproducibility, direct analysis, and human-in-the-loop feedback; its scope is illustrated by four case studies.

papers.abstract: Recent work has explored continuous representations in place of discrete tokens during Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, often referred to as soft CoT. This is motivated by the idea that a mixture of token embeddings can represent a superposition of multiple reasoning possibilities within a single step. However, it remains challenging to train large language models to realize this potential. Existing work has explored reinforcement learning (RL)-style training for soft CoT. However, these approaches treat soft tokens as actions in a Markov decision process rather than as differentiable intermediate computation steps. Thus, they do not propagate gradients across the soft tokens and miss out on the signal of how the choice of one soft token affects the next. In this paper, we propose a sparse relaxation method for RL (called SpaRLax), which leverages the differentiability of soft-CoT reasoning over time steps and makes training more stable and effective. We adopt an entmax sparsity method that adaptively determines the degree of softness, which truncates long-tail noise at confident steps while retaining multiple plausible candidates when uncertain. Across nine reasoning benchmarks, our method achieves the highest average performance compared with baseline methods. Further analyses validate the effective use of soft-token superposition in our approach, and also demonstrate the contribution of adaptive sparsity in our approach.
authors: Jiabin Fan, Matthias Lindemann, Zita Marinho, Andr\'e FT Martins, Lili Mou
bullets: Soft-CoT methods use mixtures of token embeddings to represent multiple reasoning possibilities, but are difficult to train effectively.
Prior RL approaches treat soft tokens as discrete-like actions, missing dependencies between successive soft tokens.
SpaRLax uses differentiable reasoning across time steps with entmax-based adaptive sparsity.
Adaptive sparsity suppresses noise at confident steps while preserving multiple candidates under uncertainty.
It achieves the highest average performance among compared baselines across nine reasoning benchmarks, with analyses supporting both soft-token superposition and adaptive sparsity.

papers.abstract: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables models to recognize new classes over time while retaining prior knowledge, but many real-world problems are compositional, where visual concepts arise from combinations of primitives such as states (i.e., red, shiny) and objects (i.e., shoe, car). Standard CIL methods treat each composition as an independent class, ignoring shared primitives and providing no mechanism to stabilize their representations as new compositions arrive. This causes parameter updates to entangle primitives and induce drift that degrades performance on earlier compositions. Compositional Incremental Learning (composition-IL) formalizes this setting by introducing new state-object compositions across tasks. In this paper, we propose Layer-Specific Adaptation with Prototype-Anchored Adapter-Space Transport (LSA-PAST), a parameter-efficient method tailored to composition-IL. LSA integrates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into a frozen ViT with depth-specialized adapters for states, objects, and compositions. PAST then maps past, anchored prototypes into the current adapter space through a rehearsal-free affine transform fit on current-task data, enabling old prototypes to remain compatible with new adapters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LSA-PAST achieves state-of-the-art (SOA) accuracy-forgetting trade-off performance for composition-IL.
authors: Kyle Stein, Andrew Arash Mahyari, Guillermo Francia III, Eman El-Sheikh, Jiangpeng He
bullets: Composition-IL introduces new combinations of shared primitives, but standard CIL treats each composition independently and causes representation drift.
LSA applies depth-specific LoRA adapters in a frozen ViT for states, objects, and compositions.
PAST uses a rehearsal-free affine transform to map anchored old prototypes into the current adapter space using current-task data.
Experiments report state-of-the-art accuracy–forgetting trade-offs for composition-IL.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Accuracy–forgetting trade-off on composition-IL benchmarks for adapter- and prompt-based methods.

Figure 2. (A) We adapt a frozen ViT with depth-specialized LoRA feeding three heads. (B) Post-training, empirical prototypes are blended with primitive directions (PGS) and stored. (C) Subsequent tasks instantiate fresh adapters for new compositions. (D) Using currenttask images as transient correspondences, AST fits an affine map ϕt′→t to transport past prototypes into the current adapter space without rehearsal. (E) Inference ensembles cosine similarities across all adapter spaces, recognizing both new and previously learned compositions.

papers.abstract: The Jetson AGX Orin is a common computer for robots and vehicles, yet measured accuracy, speed and energy of current depth estimators on it are hard to find. We benchmark nine model families as of October 2026: the monocular Depth Anything V2 and 3, Depth Pro, MoGe-2, Metric3D v2 and UniDepth V2, and the stereo methods libSGM, NVIDIA ESS and Fast-FoundationStereo. Every method runs on the Orin as a TensorRT FP16 engine or native CUDA code at up to three input sizes, up to the full 5.7 MP, and is scored for metric accuracy against Middlebury 2014 ground truth (non-occluded pixels of the 10 scenes whose disparity stays below 256 px), GPU time, energy and licence. Stereo is far more accurate. At 30 fps, NVIDIA's ESS reaches 0.70% AbsRel in 8.6 ms and libSGM 0.73% in 25 ms; with more compute, Fast-FoundationStereo reaches 0.33%. The best monocular models reach 12% with the true focal length (Depth Anything 3 Metric-L in 33 ms, Depth Pro in 803 ms), and 3.8-4.0% only with an oracle per-image scale (MoGe-2-L, UniDepth V2-B, Metric3D v2-L). Stereo error falls as the input resolution grows; no monocular model improves, and the metric scale of most drifts away from the truth outside their training resolution. At depth discontinuities, which AbsRel barely registers, the monocular models scatter 17-46% of the edge points between foreground and background, learned stereo 2-9% and libSGM at full resolution 1%. We give recommendations per frame-rate budget and release all code, per-scene results and engine build scripts.
authors: Leaf Jiang
bullets: Benchmark covers nine monocular and stereo depth model families on Orin using TensorRT FP16 or native CUDA, across resolutions up to 5.7 MP.
At 30 fps, NVIDIA ESS achieves 0.70% AbsRel in 8.6 ms and libSGM 0.73% in 25 ms; Fast-FoundationStereo reaches 0.33% with more computation.
With true camera focal length, the best monocular models reach about 12% AbsRel; oracle per-image scaling improves selected models to 3.8–4.0%.
Increasing resolution improves stereo accuracy but not monocular accuracy, whose metric scale often drifts outside training resolution.
At depth edges, foreground/background assignment errors are 17–46% for monocular models, 2–9% for learned stereo, and 1% for full-resolution libSGM.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks monocular and stereo depth estimators, which are core 3D perception methods relevant to 3D vision and embodied platforms.
papers.title: Which Depth Estimator for Jetson AGX Orin? A 2026 Benchmark of Monocular and Stereo Methods
papers.tldr: On Jetson AGX Orin, stereo depth methods are substantially more accurate and more reliable than monocular models, while meeting real-time budgets more effectively.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for structured extraction from financial documents, but their behavior under visual ambiguity is poorly understood. We study CARLAR (Courtesy Amount Recognition and Legal Amount Recognition) influence: a model returns the same amount for both cheque fields even though their annotations differ, including cases with a blank annotation encoded as zero. Across ten visual prompting conditions, we evaluate GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet on 243 primary cheques (124 with two observed unequal amounts) and 598 strict mismatches from two additional datasets. Under courtesy redaction, GPT-4.1 CARLAR reaches 73.7 percent (95 percent bootstrap interval: 68.3 to 79.0; p below 0.001 versus baseline). Model-reported confidence can remain high when predictions agree; expected calibration error reaches 0.93 among CARLAR cases. We also test a compressed-image few-shot intervention that presents examples as one visual table without model fine-tuning. On the 243-case cohort, Claude's Control condition increases paired joint extraction accuracy by 11.5 percentage points (95 percent interval: 6.2 to 16.9; adjusted p = 0.00054), but its strict-124 gain is smaller and not significant after correction. The intervention's effect on predicted-field agreement is model-dependent: it decreases for Claude and increases for GPT-4.1. These results motivate validation methods that account for visual context and dependencies between extracted fields.
authors: Joong Ho (Joshua), Choi, Aditya Paul, Nidhi Singh
bullets: The study examines CARLAR influence: identical predictions for courtesy and legal amounts despite differing annotations, including blank-as-zero cases.
Across ten prompting conditions, GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet were evaluated on primary and additional cheque datasets.
Under courtesy redaction, GPT-4.1 showed CARLAR behavior in 73.7% of cases, with severe miscalibration among affected predictions.
A compressed-image few-shot table improved Claude’s paired extraction accuracy by 11.5 percentage points in the 243-case cohort.
Intervention effects on field agreement differed by model, motivating validation that considers visual context and dependencies between fields.

papers.title: CARLAR Influence: A Structured Hallucination Risk in Multimodal Cheque Extraction and an Exploratory Compressed-Image Countermeasure
papers.tldr: Multimodal LLMs can systematically copy one cheque amount into both CARLAR fields under visual ambiguity, often with overconfident predictions, while compressed-image examples help Claude but have model-dependent effects.

papers.abstract: Modern language models are increasingly asked to handle several tasks within a single prompt. Doing so requires solving each task correctly while integrating the resulting answers into a coherent response. In this paper, we identify a fundamental limitation in this process, where models make substantially more errors when tasks are composed, even when they can solve every constituent task reliably in isolation. This degradation cannot be fully explained by the accumulation of independent errors. Across both open-weight models and the frontier model Claude Opus 5, our findings instead point to an implicit thinking budget underlying this effect. In particular, under composition, models use substantially fewer tokens per task than in isolation, even when the full sequence remains well within the context window. Tasks that require longer solution traces in isolation are consequently more $\textit{fragile}$ under composition, i.e., models make more errors on prompts containing these tasks. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than they need and waste compute. However, by grouping tasks according to their fragility, the implicit budgeting can be manipulated to reduce token usage by $43$\% across a range of math and linguistic tasks while also preserving accuracy.
authors: Chenpan Li, Thies Brockmoeller, Stefanie Jegelka, Sharut Gupta, Nikolaos Karalias
bullets: Models make substantially more errors on combined tasks even when they solve each task reliably in isolation.
The degradation is not fully explained by independent error accumulation.
Under composition, models spend fewer tokens per task despite having sufficient context-window capacity.
Tasks requiring longer reasoning in isolation are more fragile, while non-fragile tasks may receive excess computation.
Grouping tasks by fragility reduces token usage by 43% across math and linguistic tasks while preserving accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Identifies implicit reasoning-budget effects in LLM task composition and a way to reduce token usage; relevant to LLM reasoning and efficiency.
papers.title: On the Fragility of Tasks under Composition: Implicit Budgeting in Language Models
papers.tldr: Composing multiple tasks makes language models fragile because they implicitly divide their reasoning budget, especially harming tasks that need longer solution traces.

papers.abstract: Few-step trajectory distillation aims to learn accurate global updates from dense local supervision along a teacher's sampling trajectory. Existing approaches construct within-step dynamics using specific trajectory parameterizations or discrete interval predictions, tying the learned update to a prescribed temporal structure. We propose \method, which directly learns a continuous trajectory primitive representing cumulative displacement along the teacher trajectory. By supervising finite differences of the primitive with local teacher velocities, \method learns the accumulated motion directly, while obtaining global updates through endpoint differences. This formulation avoids prescribing a temporal basis or fixed query grid and instead learns the temporal evolution of cumulative displacement from local supervision. We further establish a local-to-global error bound to characterize how local regression errors affect full-interval displacement accuracy, and introduce endpoint absorption to eliminate the auxiliary primitive branch while preserving one-network-evaluation inference. Experiments on large-scale text-to-image generation show that \method achieves a T-FID of 20.92 and an HPSv2 score of 28.35 at one NFE, improving both metrics over a trajectory-distillation baseline. After endpoint absorption, it retains comparable performance, achieving a T-FID of 20.86 and an HPSv2 score of 28.33.
authors: Hongyi Fang, Benjia Zhou
bullets: Targets few-step trajectory distillation, where global updates must be learned from dense local supervision.
Learns cumulative displacement directly and obtains global motion from endpoint differences, avoiding a prescribed temporal basis or query grid.
Provides a local-to-global error bound linking local regression errors to full-interval displacement accuracy.
Endpoint absorption removes the auxiliary primitive branch while retaining one-network-evaluation inference.
On large-scale text-to-image generation, reaches T-FID 20.92 and HPSv2 28.35 at one NFE; endpoint absorption remains comparable at 20.86 and 28.33.

papers.selection_reason: Trajectory primitives for few-step distillation improve generation efficiency and dynamics modeling, relevant to video generation and efficient AI.
papers.title: PRIMFLOW: Learning Trajectory Primitives for Few-Step Distillation
papers.tldr: PRIMFLOW learns continuous cumulative trajectory primitives from local teacher velocities to enable accurate one-step diffusion distillation without a fixed temporal parameterization.

papers.abstract: Multimodal question answering (MMQA) is based on integrating heterogeneous data sources, selectively leveraging relevant modalities, and ignoring distractors. Existing approaches based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) improve performance by splitting the task into intermediate steps, but do not quantify how each modality contributes to reaching the final answer. We argue that quantifying the effect that each modality has on the answering process improves process traceability and final performance. Thus, we propose Entropy-Driven Multimodal Answering (EDMA), which uses logical entropy to formalise multimodal QA as an iterative process of entropy reduction and to quantify the contribution of each modality in distinguishing correct from incorrect candidate answers. This enables the construction of quantifiable answering trajectories, where each step is associated with a measurable entropy reduction. EDMA introduces (i) modality-conditioned partitioning to estimate unimodal entropy reduction, (ii) entropy-driven multimodal fusion to capture complementary information across modalities, and (iii) entropy-based selection of the answering trajectory that minimises the most logical entropy. Evaluated across standard MMQA benchmarks, EDMA outperforms competitive prompting baselines, with average gains of 12.8 F1 and 4.6 LLM-J points over Planning Prompting and 18.6 F1 and 8.3 LLM-J points over Chain-of-Thought. Moreover, EDMA outperforms self-consistency baselines and is competitive with the multi-agent system baseline. Moreover, we show that higher entropy correlates with more false positives and, through controlled trajectory selection, demonstrate that logical entropy serves as an effective, monotonic selector for correct reasoning paths, validating entropy level as a reliable proxy for performance.
authors: Emanuele Mezzi, Gertjan Burghouts, Fabio Massacci, Mengyuan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of quantitative traceability for how individual modalities contribute to MMQA answers.
Models answering as iterative entropy reduction and constructs trajectories with measurable uncertainty decreases.
Uses modality-conditioned partitioning, entropy-driven multimodal fusion, and entropy-based trajectory selection.
Outperforms prompting and self-consistency baselines across standard MMQA benchmarks, while remaining competitive with a multi-agent baseline.
Finds that higher entropy correlates with more false positives and that entropy can reliably select correct reasoning paths.

papers.abstract: LLM agents perform tasks over multiple steps and revise their actions based on feedback. As the total reasoning budget is often limited and must support future steps, the agent must choose between short and long reasoning before each action. Longer reasoning may improve the final task outcome by preventing later errors, but it also uses budget capacity that may be needed for future decisions. This creates two challenges: estimating the downstream value of long reasoning and deciding when that value is worth using the remaining budget. We propose Paired Outcome-guided Reasoning Allocation (PORA), which learns this decision by comparing short and long reasoning from the same interaction state. During training, \method{} completes the task twice from each selected state, once with a short reasoning allowance and once with a long allowance, and compares their final quality and total processing to estimate when longer reasoning is valuable. During inference, a controller weighs this estimate against learned prices on remaining-budget pressure and chooses either short or long reasoning without running both alternatives. We evaluate PORA across application, memory, code, retail, and mathematics tasks, achieving strong results across all settings. On BFCL memory, it exceeds the strongest existing method by 17.4--32.9 percentage points. Within the same agent, it matches or exceeds always using long reasoning on code and mathematics with 50.6% fewer actor tokens and 31.2% fewer model requests, respectively.
authors: Bo Yan, Qi Zhang, Zhen Tan, Tianlong Chen, Song Wang
bullets: LLM agents must balance deeper reasoning against saving budget for later decisions.
PORA learns the value of longer reasoning by comparing short- and long-reasoning outcomes from the same state.
At inference, a controller combines this value with remaining-budget pressure to select one reasoning length without running both.
It performs strongly across application, memory, code, retail, and mathematics tasks.

On BFCL memory, it improves over the strongest existing method by 17.4–32.9 percentage points; on code and mathematics, it matches or exceeds always-long reasoning with 50.6% fewer actor tokens and 31.2% fewer model requests, respectively.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting grows a dense scene from a sparse initialization through adaptive density control (ADC), driven by per-Gaussian statistics gathered during rendering. These statistics pass a frustum-based visibility filter blind to occlusion: fully occluded Gaussians still count as observed, diluting the averaged gradient signal and suppressing densification precisely where geometry is occluded. We correct this with an occlusion-aware filter that restricts densification statistics to views in which a Gaussian actually contributes, and replace the criterion's raw view-count normalizer with an average-contribution one. Integrated into a StopThePop-based framework, the two together improve every image-quality metric over the occlusion-blind baseline on occlusion-heavy scenes (up to 6% lower LPIPS), at less than half the Gaussians a view-count normalizer requires. Under the longer schedules these large scenes require, the count stays bounded where most criteria diverge, and on smaller benchmarks our method stays competitive at a fraction of the competitors' count.
authors: Marcel Rogge, Ren\'e Schuster, Didier Stricker
bullets: Frustum visibility can count fully occluded Gaussians, weakening gradient statistics and suppressing needed densification.

It uses less than half as many Gaussians as a view-count normalizer and keeps counts bounded during longer training schedules.
On smaller benchmarks, it remains competitive while using a fraction of competitors’ Gaussian counts.

papers.abstract: Recent Omni LLMs (OLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in joint audio-visual reasoning, yet cross-modal hallucinations remain a major challenge. Existing mitigation methods mainly operate at the output level, overlooking the entanglement of grounding evidence and learned priors within fused representations. To address this issue, we propose Omni-Woodpecker (OWP), a training-free framework that shifts hallucination mitigation from output-level manipulation to conflict-conditioned representation rebalancing. Specifically, OWP first identifies cross-modal conflicts from complementary modality-specific views. It then employs orthogonal decomposition to separate grounding evidence from competing priors within the hidden states. Finally, OWP adaptively rebalances fused representations by suppressing misleading priors and restoring ignored evidence before decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and strong cross-architecture generalization of OWP. Using Qwen2.5-Omni-7B as the backbone, OWP improves performance by 12.9 and 8.6 points on CMM and AVHBench, respectively, while consistently achieving gains of 0.67-2.25 points across four general OLLM reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, OWP generalizes effectively to VideoLLaMA2-AV, improving performance by 4.6 and 3.9 points on the same benchmarks. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZiiJianLiu/Omni-Woodpecker
authors: Zijian Liu, Chaoyou Fu, Yan Yang, Caifeng Shan, Ran He
bullets: Targets hallucinations caused by entanglement between cross-modal evidence and learned priors, rather than only editing outputs.
Detects conflicts using complementary modality-specific views.
Uses orthogonal decomposition to separate grounding evidence from competing priors, then adaptively suppresses misleading priors and restores ignored evidence.
Training-free and generalizes across architectures, including Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and VideoLLaMA2-AV.
Reports gains across hallucination and general reasoning benchmarks, including 12.9 and 8.6 points on CMM and AVHBench with Qwen2.5-Omni-7B.

papers.abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and answers from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system, combining structured-data keys, observed outcomes and language-model supervision across clinical notes, diagnostic reports and patient timelines. It answers multiple typed questions in a single forward pass without task-specific retraining, and each answer carries a probability that can route uncertain cases to human review. On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks scored independently of its training teacher. Across 21 external data sets, its aggregate performance approached that of the strongest tested 27-billion-parameter model, with 6.4-fold faster inference in a matched workload. Integrating CS1-4B with a language model agent produced cited answers over complete multi-year patient histories and screened a patient population against the eligibility criteria of 17 registered clinical trials, placing four times as many judged-eligible patients among its top 20 candidates as keyword search while using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than a language model reading every record. These findings support a division of labour in clinical AI, with small decision models performing repeated record reading and generative models formulating questions and synthesizing evidence.

papers.abstract: Scientific method figures often provide researchers with a clear visual entry point into a paper's methodology and core contributions, yet their dense layouts and complex information flows are difficult for Vision Language Models (VLMs) to interpret. Existing benchmarks predominantly focus on coarse-grained tasks, such as context-based retrieval or holistic comprehension, overlooking the fine-grained content and inter-module relations within complex methodological diagrams. To address these overlooked aspects, we introduce Scientific Figure Benchmark (SciFigBench), a benchmark for evaluating core capabilities required for scientific method figure understanding. Specifically, it targets three capabilities: dense content perception, visual relation comprehension, and information-flow tracing. For this purpose, we curate 4,352 scientific method figures from real-world research papers and construct 40,670 QA pairs to operationalize these capabilities as measurable question-answering tasks. All annotations are generated by dedicated pipelines and then manually verified. We further propose SciFigCue, a training-free visual prompting module that externalizes arrow-induced dependencies as visual relational evidence for method-figure reasoning. Experiments across open-source and proprietary VLMs show that even strong models remain substantially limited in visual relation comprehension, while SciFigCue improves performance across several tasks without parameter updates. The code and related resources are available at https://github.com/LeNcyer/SciFigBench.
authors: Lijia Wu, Zheng Li, Yuxuan Liu, Jingwen Zhang, Penghai Zhao, Xiang Li
bullets: Targets dense content perception, visual relation comprehension, and information-flow tracing.
Contains 4,352 real-world scientific method figures and 40,670 manually verified QA pairs.
Evaluations show that even strong open-source and proprietary VLMs struggle with visual relation comprehension.

Code and resources are publicly available on GitHub.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in unified visual editing have begun to consolidate image and video editing within a single model, while 3D scene editing remains largely separate and constrained by scarce paired training data. Given the rich image and video editing supervision now available and the common editing semantics shared across modalities, a natural question is whether this knowledge can be transferred to data-scarce 3D editing. We present VitronEdit, a universal framework for image, video, and 3D scene editing. VitronEdit adopts a shared sequence representation and progressive multimodal training to transfer editing knowledge across modalities. We further introduce geometry-aware post-training, which leverages a pretrained geometry reconstruction model to provide depth and camera-pose supervision. Surprisingly, applying geometric supervision only to 3D samples yields the best overall performance, while image and video editing also improve despite receiving no direct geometric supervision, suggesting that geometric regularization transfers through the shared backbone. Our analysis further shows that image and video training mainly transfers editing semantics to 3D, whereas 3D supervision primarily improves multi-view consistency. The project page: https://vitron-llm.github.io/VitronEdit/.
authors: Jing Wang, Yanlin Li, Mong-Li Lee, Wynne Hsu, Shengqiong Wu, Hao Fei

Uses a shared sequence representation with progressive multimodal training.
Adds geometry-aware post-training using depth and camera-pose supervision from a pretrained reconstruction model.

Image/video data mainly transfers editing semantics to 3D, while 3D supervision improves multi-view consistency.

papers.abstract: As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine-checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation protocols are also not always aligned with how modern coding agents operate. We therefore introduce ReuF2F, a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), spanning entry-level open research problems across a broad range of mathematical subfields. We expect these less prominent open problems, which tend to attract less attention and may remain unsolved for longer, to be better suited for held-out evaluation of end-to-end open problem resolution in Lean. We adopt a standard coding-agent evaluation setting, placing each problem and its logical negation into a Lean project in a Docker container. We also build Leanimum-agent on mini-SWE-agent to provide a unified harness for fair comparisons across models. Our evaluation finds that even the best-performing model resolves only ~40% of the problems, leaving substantial room for improvement on formalized open research problems.

papers.abstract: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).
authors: Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen, Tianfan Xue, Bin Zhao, Bingqi Jiang, Zihan Guo, Zicai Cui, Yang Li, Ming Zhou, Xinyuan Chen, Lihe Ding, Xiao Chen, Yujin Wang, Shi Guo, Junting Dong, Tao Lu, Xing Shen, Haoyu Guo, Yao Mu, Haiyong Yu, Haoxiang Ma, Fuxian Huang, Qiaojun Yu, Yunsong Zhou, Kailin Li, Zirui Wang, Yufei Xue, Weishuai Zeng, Tao Huang, Zhigang Wang, Junli Liu, Pengyuan Wu, Pingrui Zhang, Haotian Wang, Dongzhan Zhou, Jiafei Cao, Feng Yuan, Xinyi Ye, Quanli Xuan, Mulin Yu, Shangding Gu, Kaiwen Song, Dong Wang, Jiarui Li, Kehui Liu, Zhongjie Jia, Dongjiang Li, Jiacheng Bao, Haoran Yang, Zhaoqing Chen, Yiming Sun, Bowen Zhou

papers.title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges

papers.abstract: When given an image and a text prompt, vision-language models (VLMs) can produce seemingly sophisticated text responses. However, they are also prone to hallucinate objects in their output, which can have detrimental consequences in safety-critical applications. To detect these hallucinations, certain methods interestingly leverage internal signals from the VLM as it generates the text response; potentially, these methods use the same signals that led to a hallucination to detect it. We conduct an in-depth analysis to understand the robustness of these detection methods. First, we show that a naive baseline of a generated word's token position in the VLM text response achieves competitive performance. Further, we reveal how some detection methods rely on token position and use this heuristic as a shortcut. Second, we explore detection methods' sensitivity to language and vision modalities. Our experiments suggest that strong detection performance is often driven by detecting language-based hallucinations, and when methods rely on token position, they tend to be less visually grounded and exhibit reduced robustness when hallucinations occur earlier in a text response. Lastly, we demonstrate that different detection methods can carry complementary signals; when ensembling methods together, adding weaker methods to an ensemble of higher performing ones still offers performance improvements. Altogether, while there may be useful internal VLM signals to detect hallucinations, our investigation reveals important limitations of the current methods that try to leverage them.
authors: Allison Chen, William Yang, Salma Abdel Magid, Jonathan Williams, Olga Russakovsky, Esin Tureci
bullets: A simple baseline based on a generated word’s token position achieves competitive hallucination-detection performance.
Some existing methods rely on token position as a shortcut, weakening robustness when hallucinations appear earlier in responses.
Detection performance is often driven by identifying language-based rather than vision-grounded hallucinations.
Different detectors provide complementary signals, so adding weaker methods can still improve ensembles.
The results highlight important limitations in current internal-signal approaches, despite evidence that useful signals exist.

papers.abstract: Learned image compression (LIC) has achieved promising rate-distortion performance, but most methods lack scalability for diverse platforms with varying computational and storage constraints. Existing slimmable LIC methods achieve flexible complexity via consecutive-channel activation but suffer from two limitations: forced consecutive-channel selection degrades narrow-model performance at low bitrates, and the lack of stable variable-rate control limits adaptability to varying bandwidth. We propose a channel-level mask-guided slimmable image compression method. A learnable channel-wise mask with sparsity-promoting regularization enables non-contiguous top-w channel selection, letting narrow models use the most informative channels. After training, mask merging and channel reordering convert the model into a standard slimmable network via Mask-to-Slimmable (M2S) conversion, enabling efficient inference without architectural changes. For variable-rate control, we combine lambda- and width-conditioned modulation with quantization-step scaling and a progressive training pipeline stabilized by a freeze-then-fine-tune strategy. Experiments on Kodak across E2E, Hyperprior, and Checkerboard backbones show superior rate-distortion performance across widths and bitrates, with large gains for narrow models at low bitrates. At w=48, it achieves up to 19.22%, 24.11%, and 22.76% BD-rate savings over the same-width Slimmable baseline on E2E, Hyperprior, and CKBD, respectively. A single VBR model replaces 40 independent models, reducing storage by 14.8x to 15.9x. Code: https://github.com/sjtu-tcloud/MGSIC.
authors: Chen Chen, Chenggang Wu, Yongbiao Chen, Weidong Qiu, Zhengwei Qi, Haibing Guan
bullets: Addresses poor low-bitrate performance from forced consecutive-channel selection and unstable variable-rate control.
Learns sparse channel masks to select informative non-contiguous channels for narrow models.
Uses Mask-to-Slimmable conversion, channel reordering, and modulation with quantization-step scaling for efficient variable-rate inference.
Progressive freeze-then-fine-tune training stabilizes the combined width- and rate-conditioned model.
On Kodak across three backbones, reports stronger rate-distortion performance; one VBR model replaces 40 models with 14.8×–15.9× lower storage.

papers.abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. We first evaluate a static baseline and three frozen language models: SmallThinker, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 whose performance varies substantially between exact-game and six-player evaluation. We therefore propose Strategic Preference Optimization with KL-anchored Equilibrium (SPOKE), combining teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision, and compare it with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO. Across three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, SPOKE achieves the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn (0.213) and Leduc (1.081) and the highest six-max top-1 agreement (0.775), while maintaining teacher KL comparable to SFT (0.522 vs 0.523). These results provide preliminary evidence that strategic preference optimization can improve strategic quality while preserving teacher-consistent behavior.
authors: Phurinat Polasa, Thanapon Thanadunpremdet, Phatthanasak Kraiduang, Saksorn Ruangtanusak
bullets: Poker agents may make legal moves that are strategically weak, especially in multi-player settings.
The study evaluates a static policy and three frozen language models, finding performance varies between exact-game and six-player evaluation.
SPOKE combines teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision.
Compared with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO, SPOKE reports the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn and Leduc and the highest six-max top-1 agreement.
Results are preliminary and focus on three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, with teacher-consistent behavior measured through KL divergence.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems improve performance on clinical tasks, and that improvement is often read as evidence of a more trustworthy system. However, the two are not the same claim. A clinician acts on the stated reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so whether collaboration reduces hallucination, and what decides when it does, has to be measured in the reasoning too. Yet most evaluations score only the final answer. We evaluate four systems (a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies) across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring hallucination, under a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy, inside the rationale each system generates and reporting it alongside the task metric. We report that collaboration buys task performance but not lower hallucination as a rule, and no topology is reliably better than another. The effect differs by model: of the $36$ model--system--task comparisons, $12$ are large enough to resolve --- four decreases and eight increases, with no model on both sides. What sets the level, and the direction of any change, is the model rather than the topology or the number of agents. A self-correction experiment is consistent with this: shown its own flagged errors, every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination; the one model for which collaboration lowers hallucination gains the most, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the model whose hallucination it amplifies most, does not reduce its hallucination at all. We find that collaboration redistributes what its models can already do; it does not supply what they cannot.
authors: Won Seok Jang, Harry Bhaskar Joshi, Hong Yu
bullets: Evaluates a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies across four models and three clinical tasks.
Measures hallucination in generated rationales using factuality and faithfulness criteria, alongside final task performance.
Collaboration improves task performance but has no consistent effect on hallucination, with no topology reliably outperforming another.
Across 36 comparisons, notable effects included four decreases and eight increases in hallucination; effects varied by model.
Self-correction reduced hallucination for all but Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, suggesting collaboration redistributes existing model capabilities rather than adding missing ones.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have become a mainstream way to scale Large Language Models (LLMs), because each token activates only a small subset of experts, reducing inference cost. However, MoE decode remains highly memory-bound and exhibits strongly skewed, time-varying expert loads. 3D-stacked DRAM near-memory processing (NMP) provides the bandwidth that decode demands, yet its tiled organization makes load balancing expensive: expert parallelism (EP) preserves locality but suffers from hotspot-induced imbalance, while more distributed strategies weaken locality and increase NoC traffic. To address this locality-balance conflict, we observe that domain-specialized token routing creates offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps, a property we call expert complementarity. Using this insight, we propose 3D-MoE, a hardware--software co-designed system for MoE decode on 3D-stacked NMP. 3D-MoE uses offline, one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping to establish coarse-grained inter-group balance, handles residual intra-group hotspots through a lightweight Collaborative Memory-Network (CMN) that streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path, and uses cost-aware online remapping to remain robust to workload drift. Across MoE models, 3D-MoE achieves an average 4.63$\times$ MoE-layer speedup over EP and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.58$\times$--1.86$\times$ over the strongest NMP baselines, with 2.11\% additional logic-die area.
authors: Yudong Pan, Lian Liu, Shixin Zhao, Yintao He, Kaiyan Chang, Tianhua Han, Chenyang Ai, Haonan Zhu, Mengdi Wang, Yinhe Han, Ying Wang
bullets: MoE decode is memory-bound, with skewed and time-varying expert loads that make tiled NMP load balancing difficult.
The approach exploits complementary expert-load fluctuations across decode steps for offline inter-group balancing.
A Collaborative Memory-Network streams hot experts’ weight tiles once to helper cores, mitigating residual intra-group hotspots.
Cost-aware online remapping adapts the system to workload drift.
Across MoE models, it reports 4.63× average MoE-layer speedup over expert parallelism and 1.58×–1.86× end-to-end throughput gains over NMP baselines, with 2.11% additional logic-die area.
