papers.abstract: Latent world models let an agent plan in latent space. The planner searches for an action sequence that minimizes a cost, and that cost is often the $\ell_2$ distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent. The latent, however, is partly noise: the regularizer that prevents collapse during world model training promotes variance in the directions carrying no signal. We show that the same regularizer also supplies the structure to prune that noise in the latent. SIGReg drives the latent marginal to a standard Gaussian at every step, and assuming further that the latent sequence is a Gauss-Markov process, the transition is linear with its covariance pinned by the map itself, $z' \mid z \sim \mathcal{N}(Az,\, I - AA^\top)$. Fitting the state dynamics $A$ therefore yields the covariance at no additional cost, and in its eigenbasis each latent direction carries its own uncertainty. Furthermore, constraining $A$ to be a normal matrix fixes that basis across timesteps, so one eigenbasis measures the uncertainty over an arbitrary number of steps and serves as a stable basis to compute the planning cost on. We then restrict the $\ell_2$ cost to the $k$-dimensional subspace the state dynamics carry forward with the least uncertainty. The correction is post hoc: the encoder, the predictor, the rollout, and the planner are all left untouched, and only a single constrained matrix, $A$, is fit. We evaluate across six environments and show large gains on the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, raising success rate over the plain $\ell_2$ cost by up to $+54.7$ points under a harder planning setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yjang43/lp2.
authors: Yoo Sung Jang, Michael Ryoo
bullets: Latent world-model planning often uses terminal ℓ2 distance, but learned latents contain noise in directions unrelated to task signal.

Planning cost is restricted to the k-dimensional subspace propagated with the least uncertainty; the encoder, predictor, rollout, and planner remain unchanged.
Across six environments, the approach shows its largest gains on TwoRoom and PointMaze, improving success by up to 54.7 percentage points in a harder setting.
Scope: effectiveness is especially demonstrated on 2D navigation tasks and depends on the stated Gaussian and Gauss-Markov assumptions.

papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning is a fundamental capability for educational applications of Large Language Models (LLMs), where reliable problem solving requires not only correct answers but also coherent and verifiable reasoning processes. Multi-agent systems (MASs) have shown growing potential in this domain by leveraging collaboration and verification among multiple LLM agents. However, existing evaluations primarily focus on the correctness of final answers in text-only settings, offering limited insight into multimodal reasoning capabilities, the reliability of intermediate reasoning steps, and robustness against reasoning errors. To address these limitations, we introduce MAMath-Bench, a process-aware benchmark designed to evaluate the multimodal mathematical reasoning capabilities of MASs. MAMath-Bench comprises 1,003 problems spanning 11 mathematical categories, multiple difficulty levels, and several modalities, including text, images, and audio. It features fine-grained milestone annotations to evaluate systems across three dimensions: problem-solving correctness, reasoning-process reliability, and robustness to adversarial reasoning-chain perturbations. Our evaluation yields three key findings. First, multi-agent collaboration does not consistently improve final-answer accuracy over strong single LLMs. Second, collaboration can substantially enhance the coverage of intermediate reasoning, but such gains may come at the cost of increased reasoning redundancy. Third, current systems remain vulnerable to adversarial reasoning errors, particularly those involving subtle structural perturbations. The dataset is available at https://github.com/mira-ai-lab/AgentMath.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are enabling agents to move beyond predefined workflows toward autonomous planning and execution, creating new opportunities for smart manufacturing. However, dynamic environments, complex physical constraints, and stringent reliability requirements hinder the direct deployment of general-purpose agents in smart manufacturing. This article presents a systematic overview of LLM-driven industrial agents. First, we analyze five key challenges and discuss the concept and core characteristics of industrial agents. We then establish a unified taxonomy covering application scenarios, embodiment forms, and five capability levels. Next, we propose a four-layer system architecture and detail its core modules and operational mechanisms for closed-loop task execution. Finally, we review representative applications across the industrial lifecycle and outline future research directions. This article provides a structured reference for the design, development, and application of industrial agents.

papers.abstract: With the rapid expansion of online video content, video temporal grounding has become essential for localizing moments based on user-specific queries, comprising two subtasks: moment retrieval (MR) and highlight detection (HD). While recent approaches adopt DETR-style decoders or temporal pyramid architectures, they rely on single-scale feature maps or uniformly downsampled representations, limiting their ability to capture semantic boundaries and variable-length events. In this paper, we present SuperClip Video Temporal Grounding (SCVTG) built on a multi-scale temporal hierarchy that better captures distinctive events at various granularities. SCVTG constructs a SuperClip pyramid by grouping adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments, termed SuperClips. Further, to aggregate these SuperClips having variable duration and temporal location, we introduce a temporally adaptive kernel that aggregates SuperClips through temporally conditioned weights, enabling flexible aggregation. On top of this, we design relative saliency losses to guide the model in learning inter-clip importance, enhancing its ability to distinguish relevant events. Extensive experiments show that SCVTG achieves the best performance across five video temporal grounding benchmarks with promising gains.
authors: Sanghyeok Lee, Juyeon Ko, Joonmyung Choi, Jongha Kim, Dohwan Ko, Ji Soo Lee, Hyunwoo J. Kim
bullets: Targets moment retrieval and highlight detection in long, variable-length videos.
Builds a multi-scale SuperClip pyramid by grouping adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments.
Uses a temporally adaptive kernel to aggregate SuperClips with location- and duration-aware weights.
Introduces relative saliency losses to learn the importance of different clips.
Achieves the best performance across five video temporal grounding benchmarks, with promising gains.

Figure 5. Qualitative results of SuperClip Pyramid. The interval indicated by the red arrow denotes the ground-truth moments. The SuperClip highlighted with a red hatched region perfectly aligns with the ground truth, serving as an ideal candidate for temporal grounding.

(b) Next, each clip is projected using its corresponding weight generated by the temporally adaptive kernel (TA-Kernel), followed by pooling and a linear layer. (c) Unlike fixed convolutional kernels, which cannot handle varying lengths or temporal characteristics, we generate TA-kernel weights for SuperClips, considering the temporal information (ϕ(fi)) of its constituent clips.

papers.abstract: Treatment planning is intrinsically counterfactual: clinicians must compare how a patient's tumor and survival would evolve under competing regimens, whereas a retrospective cohort records only the regimen received and one follow-up scan. A treatment-conditioned generator trained on such data can therefore reproduce historical treatment allocation rather than simulate the interventional disease dynamics needed to rank regimens. We introduce \textbf{CaMeWM}, a causal medical world model for supported post-TACE tumor evolution and treatment planning. CaMeWM implements one intervention-to-decision loop rather than three independent prediction tasks: it first admits a queried regimen only for clinically comparable histories with empirical treatment support; it then generates a distribution of lesion-local follow-up worlds through an action-conditioned response descriptor, deterministic anchor, and residual 3D diffusion transition; and it finally maps sampled worlds to restricted mean survival time (RMST) with a response-Cox utility model. Under pre-treatment adjustment and positivity, this loop estimates a prespecified, support-restricted g-formula target; all selection and nuisance estimation are fold-local, and the induced policy is evaluated by cross-fitted, censoring-adjusted doubly robust estimation. Across 79 paired out-of-fold episodes, CaMeWM achieves 0.618 SSIM and 0.528 change-map SSIM for follow-up CT transition, while its generated-world survival pathway attains a 0.615 C-index; factual-only AIPW estimates a 9.60-week RMST gain (95\% CI 0.61--18.13) for the frozen policy. CaMeWM provides an inspectable basis for retrospective, support-restricted treatment planning.

Targets a support-restricted g-formula under pre-treatment adjustment and positivity, with fold-local nuisance estimation and cross-fitted doubly robust policy evaluation.
Across 79 paired out-of-fold episodes, follow-up CT transition achieved 0.618 SSIM and change-map transition 0.528 SSIM; the generated-world survival pathway achieved a 0.615 C-index.
The reported policy showed a 9.60-week RMST gain using factual-only AIPW estimates, with a 95% CI of 0.61–18.13 weeks.

papers.abstract: Temperature-field reconstruction and prediction are important for condition monitoring, process analysis, and state assessment in industrial and dynamic environments. This work aims to recover a four-dimensional spatio-temporal thermal state field directly from two-dimensional observations, without requiring a predefined 3D model, prescribed thermodynamic equation, or predefined heating/cooling trajectory. To this end, we propose the Gaussian Thermal State-Space Model (GTSM), which represents thermal evolution through a shared scene-level latent process and Gaussian-specific local thermal states. The resulting continuous dynamics are propagated using differentiable RK2 integration, allowing thermal evolution to be inferred from multi-view and multi-temporal observations and continuously extrapolated beyond the observed interval. GTSM is designed as a backbone-agnostic thermal dynamics module for Gaussian representations and can be integrated with both static 3D Gaussian Splatting and dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting, supporting thermal reconstruction and prediction under both static and time-varying target geometry. The reconstructed representation further enables novel-view thermal rendering and future-time thermal-state prediction. Experiments on real infrared sequences and synthetic dynamic thermal data demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and substantially stronger temporal extrapolation than representative baselines, while also validating the applicability of GTSM to deforming targets.
authors: Yunpeng Zhao, Haoxiang Zhang, Chao Liu
bullets: Models thermal evolution using shared scene-level and Gaussian-specific local latent states.

Works with both static 3D and dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting, including deforming targets.
Supports novel-view thermal rendering and future-time thermal-state prediction.
Experiments on real infrared and synthetic dynamic data show improved reconstruction and stronger temporal extrapolation than representative baselines.

papers.abstract: Online action detection (OAD) identifies ongoing actions in streaming videos. Many existing OAD systems combine RGB appearance with optical flow, but dense-flow extraction remains a major computational bottleneck. Codec motion vectors (MVs) are available during decoding, avoiding a separate optical-flow computation. On THUMOS'14, optical flow exceeds MVs by 11.2 mAP points with motion-only inputs, whereas the gap narrows to 3.7 points after RGB fusion, with the largest reduction in action-category discrimination. We propose CodecMotion-OAD, which replaces optical flow with decoder-provided MVs while retaining existing temporal detector architectures. Its two-stage training first aligns MV features with a pretrained flow-feature interface without action labels and then trains RGB+MV detectors using ground-truth labels and soft predictions from a frozen RGB+Flow teacher. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of codec MVs to frame-level OAD. On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, CodecMotion-OAD achieves 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow, while reducing decoder-to-prediction processing time by 11.48-fold on CPU and 2.04-fold on GPU.
authors: Zepeng Sun, Naichuan Zheng, Hailun Xia, Junjie Wu
bullets: Optical-flow extraction is a major OAD bottleneck; codec motion vectors are available directly during video decoding.
The method retains existing temporal detector architectures and uses two-stage feature alignment and teacher-guided RGB+MV training.
On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, it reaches 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow.
Decoder-to-prediction processing is 11.48× faster on CPU and 2.04× faster on GPU.
Scope: evaluated on THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD; performance remains below the optical-flow counterpart.

papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment requires AI systems to learn from diverse populations whose preferences may reflect heterogeneous or even conflicting objectives, and to personalize their behavior to individual users. Existing approaches in pluralistic alignment often assume access to annotator identities and rely on powerful pretrained representations to model individual preference variations. We propose Preference-PCA Pluralistic Learning (P3L), a novel framework for pluralistic alignment that jointly learns trajectory embeddings and the shared basis of preference directions via PCA decomposition from heterogeneous crowd feedback without requiring annotator identities. At test time, our approach enables rapid and accurate personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization. Experiments across multiple embodied control tasks demonstrate that P3L enables steerable personal alignment that generalizes beyond the offline dataset to out-of-distribution new users and attains competitive RL and test performance, while substantially reducing computational cost and supporting variable adaptation query budgets.

bullets: Addresses pluralistic alignment when user preferences are heterogeneous and annotators are anonymized.

Achieves competitive reinforcement-learning and test performance while reducing computational cost.

papers.abstract: Long-video understanding often requires answering many questions about a single video whose evidence is distributed across extended temporal contexts. Conventional video-language models repeatedly encode frames or retrieve visual evidence for every question. Parameterized video memory offers a write-once alternative, but existing methods rely primarily on synthesized text and fixed adaptation configurations, leaving open where video knowledge should be written and how visual evidence should shape the memory. We introduce Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training (MIT^3), a per-video adaptation framework that writes each long video into compact, video-specific adaptive parameters for video-free, text-only question answering. Under compact multi-scale supervision, causal tracing measures the causal memory utility of each model layer for video-grounded answering and selects video-specific adaptation locations. Visual memory distillation then trains the text-only memory to reproduce the representation change induced by the relevant video clip, preserving the internal effect of visual evidence beyond textual supervision. Across LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, MIT^3 achieves data-efficient video-free question answering with substantially fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods, demonstrating that effective video internalization depends on both where knowledge is written and how visual evidence is distilled into the model.
authors: Haonan Zhao, Jiaxuan Chen, Qingyang Liu, Shuochen Chang, Siyu Sun, Jiangtong Li, Li Niu
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of re-encoding or retrieving video evidence for every question.
Uses causal tracing to identify video-specific model layers for memory adaptation.
Distills the representation changes caused by visual clips into a text-only memory under compact multi-scale supervision.
Evaluated on LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, achieving data-efficient video-free QA with fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods.
Scope: memory is adapted separately for each video, so it is not a universal video memory.

papers.abstract: In generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation, support annotations are often compromised by sparsity and occlusion. Blindly adapting to such low quality samples risks learning spurious geometric patterns rather than robust novel concepts. Although 3D Vision-Language Models have been introduced to sup plement supervision, the potential of uncertainty to actively govern adaptation dynamics remains underexplored. Existing signal-level methods like loss reweight ing fail to prevent unreliable episodes from steering the optimization trajectory. To address this, we propose Uncertainty-Gated Adaptive (UGA), to the best of our knowledge the first framework that elevates uncertainty to update-level gating for generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation. The core mod ule, Uncertainty-Gated Update (UG-Update), estimates episodic reliability via intra-class dispersion over merged support and pseudo-labeled novel supervision, and selectively gates residual gradient updates. This encourages the model to learn novel semantics from reliable episodes while attenuating updates during unreliable ones. Complementing this, we introduce an Uncertainty-Based Pseudo Label Filter (UB-Filter) to enforce learning from high-confidence dense signals. On ScanNet200 and ScanNet++ (1-/5-shot), UGA sets new state of the art with an average +3.08 HM IoU over the strongest prior baseline.
authors: Yifei Zhao, Fanyu Zhao, Shengtang Wu, Han Zhang, Ruike Cao, Yinsheng Li
bullets: Problem: Low-quality few-shot support samples can cause models to learn spurious geometric patterns.
Method: UG-Update estimates episode reliability from intra-class dispersion and selectively gates residual gradient updates.
Method: UB-Filter retains high-confidence pseudo-labels to provide denser, more reliable supervision.
Result: On ScanNet200 and ScanNet++ under 1-/5-shot settings, UGA reports a +3.08 HM IoU improvement over the strongest prior baseline.
Scope: The approach targets generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation with unreliable support and pseudo-labeled supervision.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models support planning and policy evaluation by predicting future states. However, learning an accurate one-step predictor can require substantial training computation. We introduce Beckmann World Models (BWM), which learn a direct map from noise, visual history, and actions to future frames without a pretrained generative teacher. We adapt the terminal-map conservation law of Beckmann Transport Models to action-conditioned video prediction, training directly from noise-data pairs without conditional populations of generated samples required by DriftWorld. However, transport consistency on interpolated inputs does not ensure accurate prediction from the pure noise used at inference. We address this gap with endpoint-aligned training that directly supervises the source prediction, emphasizes motion and spatial structure, and teaches recovery from generated histories. All components train the same map and retain one network call per future chunk. On PushT and Robomimic Can, the final model reduces 64-frame prediction MSE by 68% and 57%, respectively, relative to same-backbone regression baseline. For policy evaluation, BWM achieves the lowest mean IoU error among the evaluated models, 0.0100, at 24.8 ms per four-frame PushT prediction. On Robomimic Can, the BWM stage trained with motion supervision and generated histories achieves 3.3 times higher throughput and 78% lower peak memory than local one-step DriftWorld. In a latent-space extension to RT-1 and Bridge-V2, equal-update controls show that feature supervision under generated histories improves perceptual prediction. These findings show how terminal-map learning can combine efficient training with accurate one-step visual prediction.
authors: Adam Lee, Shobhit Agarwal, June Pyo Suh
bullets: Addresses the high training cost of accurate one-step visual world models.
Maps noise, visual history, and actions directly to future frames without a pretrained generative teacher or conditional generated-sample populations.

Reduces 64-frame prediction MSE by 68% on PushT and 57% on Robomimic Can versus same-backbone regression baselines.

Achieves 0.0100 mean IoU error at 24.8 ms per four-frame PushT prediction; on Robomimic Can, motion-plus-generated-history training provides 3.3× throughput and 78% lower peak memory than local one-step DriftWorld.

papers.abstract: Due to the rapid growth of the global population, traditional construction methods are gradually unable to meet the current housing demand. The advancement of machine learning algorithms has encouraged researchers to explore their applications in the construction industry, leading to more intelligent and efficient building processes. In particular, the rise of large language models in recent years has provided more possibilities for the transformation from traditional construction to smart construction. In this study, a large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction method is proposed. An enhanced soft actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm is developed to plan actions for a mobile crane according to construction tasks. Robot kinematics and control algorithms are used to ensure that the actions generated by the reinforcement learning algorithm can be executed by the crane. In addition, a customized embedding model is developed to extract information from the construction environment according to user interests. Then, a large language model, ChatGPT 5, is used to update construction progress, provide safety information to control system, and generate construction progress reports. The feasibility of proposed method is verified through several full-scall retaining wall construction experiments.
authors: Yifei Xiao, Huasheng Lin, T. Y. Yang
bullets: Addresses the need for more intelligent and efficient construction processes.
Uses an enhanced soft actor-critic algorithm to plan crane actions for construction tasks.
Combines robot kinematics and control algorithms to make learned actions executable by a mobile crane.
Applies customized environment embeddings and ChatGPT 5 to track progress, provide safety information, and produce reports.
Feasibility is demonstrated through full-scale retaining-wall construction experiments.

papers.abstract: Creating photorealistic human heads typically involves trade-offs between representation power, efficiency, and generalizability. Traditional mesh-based solutions relying on 3DMMs generally sacrifice representation power but are efficient to render. On the other hand, NeRF-based methods improve representation power and fidelity while sacrificing efficiency. Gaussian splatting methods attempt to resolve these trade-offs by offering both high representation power and efficiency with real-time rendering. However, their efficiency nonetheless depends on the number of rasterized Gaussians, and the time needed to optimize and prepare the head (the enrollment time) is often high. In light of this, we propose EGGHead, which introduces a novel Gaussian allocation algorithm that efficiently assigns Gaussians to the head's semantic regions given a fixed Gaussian budget. Our algorithm reduces the number of Gaussians needed while minimizing the impact on representation power. EGGHead operates in a single forward pass and outperforms previous single-image face modeling methods in reconstruction quality, novel view synthesis, and rendering speeds.
authors: Pilseo Park, Andrew Hou, Michel Sarkis, Ning Bi, Yiying Tong, Xiaoming Liu
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between Gaussian-splatting fidelity, rendering efficiency, and enrollment time.
Introduces semantic-region-aware Gaussian allocation under a fixed Gaussian budget.
Generates the head in a single forward pass, reducing preparation requirements.
Reports improved reconstruction quality, novel-view synthesis, and rendering speed over prior single-image face-modeling methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Training Pipeline. We propose a single-image, generalizable, and lightweight Gaussian head model that adaptively allocates M Gaussians with minimal impact on rendering quality. Secs. 3.1–3.4 constitute the main reconstruction pipeline: GAM first allocates M Gaussians from the source image, Voronoi tessellation provides sparse geometric priors, and image/depth features are used to predict Gaussian attributes for rendering and refinement. Sec. 3.5 is trained in parallel to predict a density map supervised by the GAM-derived density map. It is independent of the main reconstruction pipeline during training and is used at inference time for density-based Gaussian allocation.

papers.abstract: Sparse routing reduces per-token computation but leaves the full expert bank resident in memory. We study expert pruning for speech-centric omni-modal models, where pooling calibration statistics can obscure the different expert demands of acoustic-input processing and text-answer generation. We propose PW-Pruning, a phase-aware extension of DO-ACP that constructs separate importance-weighted kernels for acoustic-prefill and teacher-forced answer tokens, then combines phase-weighted log-determinant marginal gains to select one static expert bank. On Qwen3-Omni, retaining 32 of 128 experts per layer improves MMAU-mini and MMSU accuracy over matched pooled selection by 3.20 and 4.38 percentage points, respectively, after supervised fine-tuning, averaged over three runs. Single-phase and shuffled-label controls on this public backbone suggest that semantic phase information contributes to these gains. Experiments on a non-public Qwen3.5-Omni backbone and English-only zero-shot evaluation of Nemotron provide complementary evidence. Across the tested Qwen budgets, AU gains are larger under stronger pruning, without inference-time mask switching.
authors: Junjie Cao, Fengping Tian, Wenjie Zhou, Xuanfan Ni, Chenyang Lyu, Siyou Liu, Longyue Wang, Weihua Luo
bullets: Pooling calibration statistics can miss the distinct expert needs of acoustic-prefill and answer-generation tokens.
The method builds phase-specific importance-weighted kernels and combines log-determinant marginal gains to choose one static expert bank.
On Qwen3-Omni, retaining 32 of 128 experts per layer improves MMAU-mini and MMSU accuracy by 3.20 and 4.38 percentage points over pooled selection after fine-tuning.
Controls indicate that semantic phase information contributes to the gains, which increase under stronger pruning across tested Qwen budgets.
The approach avoids inference-time mask switching; additional evidence comes from non-public Qwen3.5-Omni and English-only zero-shot Nemotron evaluations.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.
authors: Rui Shi, Xunjian Yin, Jiacheng Sang, Zichuan Liu, Shuyan Zhou

On eight deep-research benchmarks, reports 6.2% higher average accuracy than full fine-tuning and 27.5% higher than static LoRA merging.
Supports modular continual adaptation by adding or updating individual adapters without changing the backbone or other capabilities.

papers.abstract: Systems that combine several large language models (LLMs) often use one context for many questions. When the context is passed between models as text, the receiving model processes all of its tokens again for every question. Avoiding this cost requires a context representation that is compact, reusable across questions, and readable by a different LLM. Existing compression and latent communication methods each provide only some of these properties. We introduce LatComm, a Latent Communication interface that provides all three by separating encoding from reading: the context is encoded once without the question, and the receiver selects what to read for each question. A frozen context encoder LLM compresses the context into a fixed-size packet and sends it to a different frozen receiver LLM, which reads the packet through cross-attention, with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice question-answering datasets, LatComm improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points. On QuALITY, it reduces the receiver's input by 57x and answers the questions of an article 3x faster.
authors: Huawei Lin, Jinting Liu, Tan Yu, Weijie Zhao
bullets: Addresses the repeated token-processing cost of passing shared context between LLMs.
Uses a frozen encoder to create a fixed-size latent packet and a different frozen receiver that reads it via prompt-conditioned cross-attention.
Combines compactness, cross-model readability, and reuse across multiple questions.
Improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points across 12 multiple-choice QA datasets.
On QuALITY, reduces receiver input by 57× and answers article questions 3× faster.

figures.caption: Figure 2: LatComm overview. (a) The encoder reads the context; the receiver reads a task prompt. LatComm connects selected layers and adds context information after each paired receiver block. Both LLMs remain frozen. (b) For one layer pair, a context compressor produces reusable slots Zi. The gates compare a summary of the receiver’s prompt states with the compressed slots. The reader combines the gated slot values and adds the result to the receiver state.

Figure 5: Training loss of (a) Stage 1 and (b) Stage 2 against the number of context tokens processed, for the configurations of Table 10. Each column changes one setting, and the solid orange line is the default configuration. The token count is the number of processed examples times the mean context length of the training set. The curves are running means over 50 updates in Stage 1 and 100 updates in Stage 2. Dotted lines mark the ends of the first and second epochs of Stage 2.

Figure 3: Two-stage training of LatComm. (a) In Stage 1, the receiver gets an instruction to reproduce the context x and can read it only from the packet Zϕ(x). The reconstruction loss Lrec trains the compressors, readers, and gates. (b) In Stage 2, the receiver gets the question with its answer choices, and the task loss Ltask on the answer y trains only the readers and gates. The compressors are fixed, so the packet of each training context is computed once and stored. Both LLMs stay frozen in both stages.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces LatComm, a reusable context compression method for LLMs, which reduces memory requirements and processing time by compressing context into a fixed-size packet.

papers.abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.
authors: Anamaria-Roberta Hartl, Levente Z\'olyomi, Michael List, G\"unter Klambauer, Sebastian B\"ock, Sepp Hochreiter
bullets: Extends the xLSTM family with memory revision that corrects targeted associations along a single matrix-space direction.
Reduces interference with stored information compared with standard delta-rule updates.

Experiments find performance competitive with or often better than linear attention baselines, especially on long-context benchmarks.
Code and pretrained models are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Beyond basic tool use and coding skills, effectively incorporating visual references into agentic generation is equally essential for applying AI agents to real-world productivity tasks. We study this crucial capability through webpage development, a practical and readily evaluable setting in which existing benchmarks remain largely idealized: they typically focus on reconstructing visual targets or generating webpages from textual instructions alone, overlooking the more common workflow of developing from visual examples. Specifically, we introduce RefCraft, a benchmark comprising 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks that combine natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively interpret and utilize these references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their outputs. We evaluate the resulting open-ended artifacts using independently verifiable keypoints and complementary programmatic and VLM judges. Across nine frontier (M)LLMs, the strongest system achieves an overall score of only 52.12 out of 100, revealing that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation remains a substantial challenge for current models in practical webpage-development settings.
authors: Yuchi Wang, Rongyao Fang, Weihao Yu, Xilin Wei, Tiancheng Gu, Dingkang Yang, Hang Zhang, Dayiheng Liu, Hongsheng Li, Shuai Bai

Across nine frontier MLLMs, the strongest system scores 52.12/100, showing the task remains challenging.

papers.abstract: Expert human readers process large inputs (e.g., code repositories and long documents) by skimming to closely read only what matters. On the other hand, language models process all input tokens through each model layer, resulting in significant processing costs for long-context inputs. We introduce TokenGate, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning over long-context inputs for fast and memory-efficient prefill. To enable end-to-end learning despite the non-differentiable top-K operator for token pruning, we introduce token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits using token importance scores. Across diverse tasks, TokenGate achieves $1.4$-$11.3\times$ faster time-to-first token (TTFT) and $1.5$-$3.4\times$ lower peak memory at no accuracy degradation for prefill in transformers. Compared to the best-performing prior methods for token-pruning, TokenGate gives up to $6.4\times$ faster prefill and $2\times$ lower peak memory. TokenGate natively extends both standard transformers (e.g., Qwen3) and hybrid-attention models (e.g., Qwen3.5) with simple lightweight adaptation comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We make our code available at: https://github.com/tokengate-models/TokenGate.
authors: Liana Patel, Rishabh Ranjan, Ion Stoica, Matei Zaharia, Carlos Guestrin
bullets: Addresses the high cost of processing every token across all layers during long-context prefill.
Uses a small drop-in component that learns token importance and prunes less relevant tokens.
Introduces token-gated attention to enable end-to-end training despite non-differentiable top-K pruning.
Reports 1.4–11.3× faster time-to-first-token and 1.5–3.4× lower peak memory with no accuracy degradation.
Supports standard and hybrid-attention transformers through lightweight adaptation.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes TokenGate, a learnable token pruning mechanism for LLMs, to achieve fast and memory-efficient prefill, directly addressing token pruning and memory efficiency.
papers.title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
papers.tldr: TokenGate adds lightweight learned token pruning to existing LLMs, substantially reducing long-context prefill time and memory without degrading accuracy.

papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.
authors: Saurav Jha, Qianli Liao, Robert Vernon, Sarath Chandar, Quentin Fournier
bullets: Addresses the cost and memorization risks of scaling protein language models, while adapting test-time scaling to masked encoders.
Uses a weight-tied Transformer core that repeatedly refines residue representations over an adjustable number of cycles.
With 155M unique parameters, recAMPLIFY outperforms the larger AMPLIFY-350M on CASP contact recovery and three of four supervised tasks, including a 22.5% fold-accuracy gain.
Introduces Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), which combines hidden states across recursion cycles using learned residual gates for adaptive depth.
GMR reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, but accuracy trade-offs vary by task; halt depth also tracks biological properties.

figures.caption: Figure 1: recAMPLIFY architecture. A non-recurrent prelude maps input embeddings to a residue-aligned latent state 𝑧𝑘, a weight-tied Transformer core iteratively refines this state, and a non-recurrent coda maps the refined state to the output space. Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR) decodes from a probability-weighted mixture over the recurrence trajectory, with a per-sequence residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension channel resolution controlling how much of each cycle’s proposed update is accepted. Blue circles illustrate these channel-level parameterizations.

Figure 3: recAMPLIFY at varying recurrence depths. (a) For 1M-step recAMPLIFY, the coda embeddings become progressively more class-separable (5-NN accuracy) with larger test-time depth 𝐿eval. (b) For 100K-step recAMPLIFY, as 𝐿eval increases past the trained depth (𝐿 = 6), the fixed-𝐿 model (red) degrades while the variable-𝐿 variant (blue) remains largely stable.

Figure 5: Dynamics of recurrent block layer ℓ on stability prediction upon training with 𝐿 = 6 cycles (vertical dashed lines). (a) The successive difference norm ∥zℓ 𝑘 − zℓ 𝑘−1∥2 shows gating drives each layer’s step size toward zero beyond the trained depth. (b) The normalized difference to each layer’s deepest recorded state highlights the rate and timing of decay as key convergence diagnostics. depth as the mean of the model’s predicted halting distribution: 𝔼[𝑘] =∑ 𝑘 𝑘 𝑝𝑘. This characterizes the learned allocation policy rather than measured wall-clock savings, since our evaluation decodes the full mixture ∑ 𝑘 𝑝𝑘z𝑘 over the cycle budget. Gate resolution has no consistent effect on zero-shot calibration (KL (T) 49.7–50.4 across variants), but gated variants lead the 100K block on CASP and Stability (scalar) and on Localization (per-dim). Halt-only GMR reaches the shallowest expected depth (𝔼[𝑘] = 3.57, i.e., 2 + 3.57×8 + 2 ≈ 33 layers) while matching AMPLIFY-350M on SSP. To understand where gating helps, we next examine whether the gates produce an empirical fixed point of the recurrent state (§5.1.1); whether recursion preserves the depth-heterogeneous layerwise mixing profile of a feedforward Transformer (§5.1.2); and what the GMR halt signal encodes about proteins (§5.1.3).

(a) Successive-difference norm: gating drives each layer’s step size toward zero past the 𝐿 = 6 cycles seen during training. (b) Normalized operator residual to each layer’s deepest recorded state zℓ𝐿 (taken as an approximate fixed point) over 𝑘 ∈ {1, . . . , 𝐿 − 1} cycles shows the key diagnostic being the rate and timing of decay. Scalar and per-dim gates reach near-zero residual within a few cycles of the trained horizon, whereas halt-only and rank-16 decay only slowly and remain substantially non-zero at intermediate cycles. (c) Cosine similarity to zℓ𝐿: alignment is near-perfect for every variant, so cosine is an indirect diagnostic and must be read jointly with (a) and (b). Read together, only the scalar and per-dimension gates deliver empirical fixed-point convergence.

Without the injection, the state diverges by three orders of magnitude within a few cycles. Input injection thus helps keep the recurrence bounded, matching the finding of Blayney et al. [2026] on causal-LM looped Transformers. We note that this boundedness does not imply convergence. Each cell (𝑘, 𝑘′) is ∥𝐴𝑘 − 𝐴𝑘′ ∥𝐹 averaged over 𝐵 = 4 probe sequences from the stability prediction task, and the dashed line marks the trained halt horizon at 𝑘 ≈ 7. papers.selection_reason: Introduces recursive pretraining for protein language models (recAMPLIFY) and a Gated Mixture Recurrence framework, representing a foundation model approach for biological sequences.
papers.title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models
papers.tldr: recAMPLIFY scales masked protein language modeling through recursive, weight-tied refinement, achieving strong task performance with fewer parameters and enabling adaptive computation via GMR.

papers.abstract: Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx 5005$, the selected primes' period product.
authors: Anxin Guo, Tianlong Huang, Chenxiao Yang, Zhiyuan Li
bullets: Repeated tokens make local content insufficient for determining copying position and termination.
A two-layer transformer uses small-prime periodic VO-rotations to encode delimiter distances modulo multiple primes.
The Chinese Remainder Theorem combines these encodings to distinguish distances up to a chosen horizon using low precision and width.
The paper proves saturation-based impossibility for models relying on eventually constant additive attention biases, including NoPE and recursive ALiBi.
In synthetic experiments, VO models generalize to near-perfect copying up to about length 5005, while baselines fail on long repeated strings.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes LLM copying behavior and introduces a novel Position Hashing mechanism using RoPE rotations to handle repetition, providing insights into LLM architecture and attention mechanisms.
papers.title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing
papers.tldr: VO-rotations with Chinese Remainder Theorem distance encoding enable compact transformers to copy and terminate correctly on highly repetitive strings, addressing failures of standard positional mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical abstraction is a fundamental principle across many data modalities, enabling complex sequences to be represented compositionally at multiple levels. Learning such hierarchies directly from data, without explicit structural supervision, remains a central challenge in representation learning. We investigate whether meaningful hierarchical structure can emerge from compression alone. While autoencoders learn compressed representations through reconstruction, this objective does not necessarily favour meaningful compositional structure. We study this challenge through unsupervised grammar induction, where the underlying hierarchy can be evaluated explicitly. We introduce a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder that recursively combines adjacent tokens into increasingly abstract representations, compressing entire sequences through a variational information bottleneck. The model jointly learns representations and hierarchical structure by marginalising over possible binary trees using dynamic programming. To address training instability, we combine independently trained models through unsupervised consensus and distillation. Experiments on a synthetic, ambiguous grammar demonstrate the emergence of meaningful hierarchical structure without structural supervision. The resulting model achieves 93% grammatical parse-validity and 93% exact reconstruction on held-out sequences, compared with 42% parse-validity for the strongest trivial baseline. These findings establish a proof of concept for hierarchical token merging as a mechanism for unsupervised structure discovery and abstraction learning.
authors: Murat Guney Kemal, Robert Lieck
bullets: Addresses unsupervised discovery of meaningful compositional hierarchies without structural supervision.
Recursively merges adjacent tokens into abstract representations through a variational information bottleneck.
Marginalises over possible binary trees with dynamic programming to jointly learn representations and structure.
Uses unsupervised consensus and distillation across independently trained models to improve training stability.
On held-out synthetic sequences, reaches 93% parse validity and exact reconstruction, versus 42% parse validity for the strongest trivial baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The three-stage pipeline. The same architecture is used as the base model in Stage 1 and as the distilled model in Stage 3; only Stage 1 uses the chart, while Stage 3 trains on the fixed silver trees.

Figure 3: The seed lottery. Held-out parse-validity of the 24 base models in each of the four seedvarying pools (labelled by their seeds, so s52-75 is pool 52–75). The spread within a pool is wide even though the models differ only in random seed.

Figure 5: Cosine similarity between the nineteen word embeddings, ordered by category, for the best base model (held-out parse-validity 1.000) and the distilled student (0.989). The base model groups words by category; the student does not, yet both parse well. A sweep of the student’s KL weight (holding latent size fixed) does not reproduce the clustering, so it is a by-product of how the base models induce structure, not of the bottleneck and not a prerequisite for parsing.

Figure 2: One chart cell for span (i, j) at split k. The two child spans are merged into a candidate parent, which the unmerger tries to invert; the negative squared error (“energy”) is the local score. The span score is the log-sum-exp over splits, and the highest-scoring split is stored as a back-pointer for parsing.

Figure 6: The four networks of the base model, with layers and dimensions. The lifter maps each token id to a leaf latent through two embedding tables (a mean and a log-variance) and the reparameterisation trick. The merger is the encoder step, a two-layer perceptron with a ReLU that combines two child latents into a parent; it is applied bottom-up at every internal node of the tree. The unmerger is the decoder step and an approximate inverse of the merger, predicting the two children from a parent, applied top-down; its squared error against the true children is the one-step energy that also scores splits in the chart. The unlifter is a single linear layer that reads a recovered leaf latent back to a distribution over the vocabulary. A single merger and a single unmerger are shared across all tree depths.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder for unsupervised grammar induction, which is a form of token-level compression and structure discovery relevant to token pruning and efficiency.
papers.title: Hierarchical Token Merging with Recursive Autoencoders for Unsupervised Grammar Induction
papers.tldr: A recursive autoencoder learns hierarchical grammatical structure from compression alone, achieving 93% parse validity and exact reconstruction on a synthetic ambiguous grammar.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive language models emit one token per forward pass. This causes high inference latency, in particular as models are scaled up for quality. In this paper, we introduce Parallel Language Models (PLMs), which generate mutually consistent tokens in one forward pass by routing dependencies through latent auxiliary variables. PLMs are trained using a variational bound that reduces to an autoregressive loss plus a parallel decoding loss. Empirically, PLMs are on a faster and better Pareto frontier than autoregressive and discrete diffusion baselines. Pretrained PLMs achieve near-autoregressive pretraining loss on model scales of 80M to 3B parameters, and speedup follows a power law in model size. When post-trained, our 1.3B model matches or exceeds an identically trained autoregressive model on math, coding, and instruction-following benchmarks, speeding up inference $2.3\text{-}5.7\times$. Together, we show that parallel generation can be trained from a single training objective at autoregressive quality. We will make our code available at https://github.com/mandt-lab/plm.
authors: Felix Draxler, Robin C. Geyer, Daniel Geyfman, Farrin Marouf Sofian, Justus Will, Philipp Hildebrandt, Giosue Migliorini, Prakhar Srivastava, Gagan Sai Trinadh Duggaraju Peddiraju, Kushagra Pandey, Jorge da Silva Gon\c{c}alves, Elijah Tavares, Jan Niklas Groeneveld, Yang Meng, Julia E. Vogt, Stephan Mandt
bullets: Addresses the latency of autoregressive models, which generate one token per forward pass.
Routes token dependencies through latent auxiliary variables so multiple tokens can be generated in a single forward pass.
Uses a variational objective combining autoregressive and parallel-decoding losses.
Achieves near-autoregressive pretraining loss from 80M to 3B parameters, with speedup increasing with model size.
A post-trained 1.3B model matches or exceeds an identically trained autoregressive model while providing 2.3–5.7× faster inference on math, coding, and instruction-following benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a parallel autoregressive language model architecture via variational decoding, a substantive LLM architecture contribution with inference speedup.
papers.title: Parallel Language Models via Variational Decoding
papers.tldr: Parallel Language Models use latent variables and variational training to generate mutually consistent tokens in parallel, achieving near-autoregressive quality with substantially faster inference.

papers.abstract: Experience generated during deployment offers an opportunity for robots to improve policy reliability through learning from their own executions. However, learning through human corrections requires teleoperators to monitor execution and intervene when policies fail, a demand that is difficult to meet as robot fleets grow. We introduce collective experience learning (CEL), a learning paradigm in which deployed robots share their execution experience to improve a common policy. We realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), which uses failure contexts from robot executions to retrieve relevant trajectory segments from the fleet's shared successful experience and uses their actions as supervision for policy updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates experience collection, policy optimization and policy distribution despite local interruptions within the robot fleet. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and FERT generally achieves higher success rates across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots increases success from 79.2% to 98.3%. These results support collective experience as a practical basis for scalable robot learning and a path towards improving policy reliability during deployment without collecting additional expert corrective actions.

Method: FERT retrieves relevant successful trajectory segments using failure contexts and fine-tunes the policy with their actions as supervision.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS). a, The SwarmLink data plane connects robot workers at the edge to shared cloud inference and assembles streamed trajectory fields for training. The HotSwarm control plane manages membership and worker identity, and recovers failed workers. b, Synchronous collection makes each policy update wait for every robot, which leaves faster robots idle. In asynchronous collection, robots continue independently. c, HotSwarm restarts the worker of a failed robot in place while the other robots continue, and the action computed for the failed worker (#1) is discarded. d, Inference data and execution records are joined in the cloud, and an episode is released to training only after its required fields and outcome arrive. e, Robot time available for collection after fault handling, measured for FATS in the 96-robot run and modeled for restarting the entire system after each fault event with restart times between 2 and 10 min (Appendix D.4). Durations in b and c are illustrative.

Figure 1 Sources of experience for robot policy learning: human demonstrations, expert corrections and collective experience generated within a robot fleet. In our realization of collective experience learning (CEL), successful robot executions supply action supervision for further policy updates after expert-supervised initialization. FERT realizes this paradigm by using failure contexts to retrieve relevant successful experience. Episode outcomes can be labeled by human annotators or a learned reward model; our experiments use human-provided outcome labels and environment resets. The requirement for expert action supervision decreases from left to right.

Figure 4 Overview of the five manipulation tasks performed with AgiBot G2 robots: Flower Arrangement, Clothes Folding, Phone Charging, Stool Assembly and Phone Packaging. A detailed step-by-step description is provided in Appendix E.

Figure 2 Failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning. Robots asynchronously collect autonomous experience with binary task-outcome labels. Observations are encoded using visual and proprioceptive features. Failure contexts retrieve related segments from successful trajectories, and these segments receive increased sampling priority during policy fine-tuning. Updated policies return to the fleet to generate further experience.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a collective learning paradigm (CEL) and a specific fine-tuning method (FERT) for robot fleets, directly addressing robot manipulation and learning from deployment experience.
papers.title: Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots
papers.tldr: Collective experience learning lets robot fleets improve a shared policy from deployment failures and successful trajectories without additional expert corrections, achieving high reliability across manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Data-driven learning for general-purpose robotic manipulation presents a fundamental trade-off between data-collection cost and adaptability to real-world environments. Imitation learning (IL) requires costly human demonstrations, whereas simulation-based learning is vulnerable to sim-to-real gaps in dynamics and sensor observations. We propose ReDOA (Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment), a framework that decouples control learning from perception learning to learn image-based policies in the real world. A state-based teacher policy trained in simulation is executed on a real robot, and its control knowledge is distilled into an image-based student policy using the collected trajectories. Observation Alignment resolves observation mismatches between data collection and deployment. This framework collects successful, efficiently executed trajectories paired with real-world visual observations, without requiring demonstrations from human experts. In real-robot experiments on three non-prehensile manipulation tasks, including bimanual manipulation, our method achieves better overall performance when jointly considering task success and execution efficiency than both IL based on human demonstrations and policy distillation in simulation. https://isri-aist.github.io/redoa-project-page/
authors: Kotaro Kajitsuka
Masaki Murooka
Fumio Kanehiro
bullets: Addresses the cost of human demonstrations and the sim-to-real gap in dynamics and visual observations.
Uses a state-based teacher trained in simulation to guide an image-based student through real-robot trajectories.
Observation Alignment bridges mismatches between observations during data collection and deployment.
Evaluated on three real-robot non-prehensile manipulation tasks, including bimanual manipulation.
Reports better combined task success and execution efficiency than human-demonstration IL and simulation-based distillation.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes ReDOA, a real-world distillation framework for image-based manipulation policies that decouples control from perception, addressing sim-to-real gaps in robotic manipulation.
papers.title: ReDOA: Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment for Image-Based Manipulation Policy Learning
papers.tldr: ReDOA distills a simulation-trained state policy into a real-world image-based policy by aligning observations, avoiding human demonstrations while improving manipulation success and efficiency.

papers.abstract: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form similar representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that manipulate internal activations in open-weight language models. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale successfully inferred unstated relationships between entities and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across model and task families, models generated abstract representations of relational structure and combined them additively with representations of entity identity, binding entities to roles within that structure. Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried, rather than prospectively positioning each entity in a global coordinate system. Binding was mediated by a sparse, distributed set of key--value pairs; by perturbing these pairs, we implanted "false memories" that altered model behavior in predictable ways. Overall, our findings reveal an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map that explains how language models reason with limited information.
authors: Albert Qin, Jonathan Cohen, Gautam Reddy
bullets: Models larger than 10 billion parameters inferred unstated relationships and generalized them to synthetic entity names.
Causal activation experiments found abstract relational structure combined additively with entity-identity representations.
Models represented relationships as pairwise links composed at query time, rather than as positions in a global coordinate system.
Entity–role binding relied on sparse, distributed key–value representations; perturbing them produced predictable false memories.
These findings suggest an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map for reasoning with limited information.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates internal relational representations and key-value binding in large language models, contributing to LLM understanding and interpretability.
papers.title: Cognitive Map in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Large language models can build cognitive-map-like relational representations that support flexible inference and targeted memory manipulation.

papers.abstract: Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining requires substantial robot data and computation. To transfer these capabilities from pretrained EFMs to policies without action pretraining, we introduce TILDE (Teacher-In-the-Loop Distillation from EFMs), which synergizes on-policy distillation at student-induced states with learning from teacher-executed recovery trajectories. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates recovery-trajectory collection by more than $2\times$ compared with the human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher's corrective behavior, TILDE improves task performance by up to $4.1\times$ over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.
authors: Yuxiang Lu, Yantong Liu, Jinghua Hou, Xueli Sun, Ruihua Han, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Targets the high data and compute costs of reproducing EFM action pretraining.
Combines learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher-executed recovery trajectories.
Introduces AutoDAgger, which uses a robotic reward model to detect progress and autonomously trigger teacher intervention.
Collects recovery trajectories over 2× faster than a human-in-the-loop approach.
Improves task performance by up to 4.1× over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and enables cross-architecture distillation.

papers.tldr: TILDE distills robust manipulation skills from pretrained Embodied Foundation Models into policies without requiring action pretraining or human-supervised recovery collection.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly judged by how well they rank plausible futures, yet plausibility alone is the wrong target. The same scene can evolve under many latent rules, and a future that is smooth and physically valid under one rule can be incoherent under the rule actually in force. We formalize the resulting failure, operator-blindness, and show that it is systematically hidden by standard evaluation: a scorer can attain near-perfect generic ranking while separating current-world from other-world futures no better than chance. We introduce Operator-Mismatch Contrastive (OMC) learning, whose semantic hard negatives are valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories, and a matching protocol that measures world-relative coherence directly. On a controlled synthetic benchmark with in- and out-of-distribution operator parameters, across two trajectory-scoring backbones, and on feature-level external validation with CoPhy ballsCF, OMC raises operator-sensitive scoring far above a chance baseline that nonetheless achieves 0.99 generic top-1. We prove that the wrong-operator negative is necessary both for the protocol to detect the failure and for the objective to fix it, and position OMC as an auxiliary coherence signal (a trajectory-coherence scorer, not a generative model, planner, or control agent) that can be attached to existing world-model representations.
authors: One Octadion, Firmansyah Sundana, Novanto Yudistira
bullets: Standard plausibility ranking can miss operator-blindness: generic ranking may be near-perfect while world-relative discrimination remains at chance.
OMC uses valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories as semantic hard negatives.
A matching protocol directly measures coherence with the operator governing the current world.
Across synthetic in- and out-of-distribution settings, two scoring backbones, and CoPhy ballsCF validation, OMC substantially improves operator-sensitive scoring.
The analysis proves wrong-operator negatives are necessary both to expose and correct the failure; OMC is an auxiliary scorer, not a generator, planner, or controller.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces operator-sensitive trajectory coherence scoring with wrong-operator hard negatives, directly targeting world-model evaluation and representations.
papers.title: Operator-Mismatch Contrastive Learning for World-Relative Trajectory Coherence
papers.tldr: OMC learning trains world-model scorers to distinguish futures that are valid under the current world dynamics from those valid under a different operator.

papers.abstract: Hybrid architectures offer a promising approach to efficient language modeling by combining a small number of full-attention layers with a larger number of efficient sequence layers, such as sparse attention and recurrent layers. While full-attention layers maintain a KV cache that grows linearly with sequence length, efficient layers typically rely on separate, fixed-size states rather than accessing this richer existing memory. Recent work has begun exploring ways to allow efficient layers access to the KV cache, but the theoretical benefits of such access, and the extent to which existing approaches can realize them remain poorly understood. We investigate these questions by analyzing the expressive power of individual hybrid blocks on function composition, a well-studied task in sequence-model expressivity associated with multi-hop reasoning. We first establish that both conventional hybrid blocks and those with top-$\kappa$ KV-cache access require $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ capacity to compute even two-function composition over a domain of size $n$. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the \emph{Multi-hop Retrieval Attention} (MuRA) hybrid block, a simple architecture that enables multi-hop retrieval from a shared KV cache while preserving asymptotic computational and memory efficiency. We prove that a single fixed size $m$-hop MuRA block can compute $m$-function composition, whereas computing $(m+1)$-function composition with the same retrieval depth requires polynomial model size, establishing a strict expressivity hierarchy in retrieval depth. Synthetic experiments support this hierarchy, showing that increasing retrieval depth enables learning progressively deeper compositions, substantially outperforming existing hybrid architectures. Together, our results identify multi-hop retrieval as a promising mechanism for improving the expressive power of efficient hybrid architectures.
authors: Yam Eitan, Gilad Yehudai, Haggai Maron
bullets: Hybrid models combine a few full-attention layers with more efficient sparse-attention or recurrent layers, but efficient layers typically cannot exploit the full KV cache.
Conventional hybrid blocks and top-κ KV-cache access require Ω(√n) capacity even for two-function composition over a domain of size n.
The proposed Multi-hop Retrieval Attention (MuRA) block supports multi-hop access to a shared KV cache while preserving asymptotic computational and memory efficiency.
A fixed-size m-hop MuRA block can compute m-function composition, while computing (m+1)-function composition at the same depth requires polynomial model size.
Synthetic experiments support a retrieval-depth hierarchy, with deeper retrieval enabling progressively deeper compositions and outperforming existing hybrid architectures.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a multi-hop retrieval attention block for efficient hybrid language architectures, improving expressivity while preserving asymptotic efficiency.
papers.title: Improving the Expressive Power of Hybrid Sequence Models via Multi-Hop Retrieval
papers.tldr: Multi-hop retrieval substantially increases the expressive power of efficient hybrid sequence models, enabling deeper compositional reasoning with fixed-size retrieval depth.

papers.abstract: Federated learning for capacity-heterogeneous clients and federated continual learning are each well studied on their own, but their intersection -- clients holding differently sized models while every client's data stream also drifts over time -- remains underexplored. We study this setting directly, training a ResNet-18 fleet from scratch on Split-CIFAR-100 (10 tasks, class-incremental), and introduce DROD (Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout), which builds on FjORD's Ordered Dropout by using two independent reduction axes to extract sub-models: a shortcut ratio and a branch ratio. On a shared parameter/FLOP budget ladder, DROD achieves the highest mean accuracy among the heterogeneous-model federated learning strategies we compare. Its advantage over the two strongest baseline geometries persists across every replay-buffer size we test and under ER, DER++, and BiC; under EWC, all three geometries collapse alike.
authors: Berk Sezer, \"Ozg\"ur Soysal
bullets: Addresses the underexplored combination of device capacity heterogeneity and drifting client data.
Extends FjORD’s Ordered Dropout with two independent sub-model reduction axes: shortcut ratio and branch ratio.
Evaluated with ResNet-18 models trained from scratch on Split-CIFAR-100 across 10 class-incremental tasks.
Outperforms the two strongest baseline geometries across tested replay-buffer sizes under ER, DER++, and BiC.
Under EWC, DROD and the comparison geometries perform similarly, indicating a scope limitation.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual learning of models on drifting data streams under federated heterogeneous-device settings.
papers.title: DROD: Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout for Federated Continual Learning on Heterogeneous Devices
papers.tldr: DROD enables federated continual learning with differently sized client models and achieves the best mean accuracy among compared heterogeneous-model strategies in the studied setting.

papers.abstract: We empirically analyze two recently proposed encoder-free multimodal LLMs, Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small. Unlike previous multimodal LLMs, these models do not use modality-specific encoders to extract tokenized embeddings representing audio and image input; instead, they directly feed windows of samples, pixels, or spectral features to the Transformer language model. We analyze whether the early layers of these models learn to function similarly to dedicated audio and visual encoders. We find that these early layers do in fact act as ``implicit encoders,'' encoding audio and visual inputs in a way that is largely invariant to their cross-modal context. Furthermore, when performing multimodal reasoning tasks, we show that independently encoding the modalities throughout these early model layers achieves the same accuracy as jointly encoding them from the first layer onwards. Finally, we use layer-wise probing to analyze the salient information captured by the implicit encoders and find their behavior to be similar to several popular encoder models.
authors: David Harwath, Desh Raj, Xavier Velez, Sandra Arcos-Holzinger, Willie Jeng, Karen Livescu, Leibny Paola Garcia-Perera, Sanjeev Khudanpur
bullets: Analyzes Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small, which process raw audio and image features without dedicated modality-specific encoders.
Finds that early layers encode audio and visual inputs in ways that are largely invariant to cross-modal context.
Shows that independently encoding modalities through early layers matches the accuracy of jointly encoding them from the first layer.
Layer-wise probing indicates that the learned representations capture salient information similarly to several established encoder models.

papers.title: Encoder-Free Multimodal LLMs Learn Implicit Encoders
papers.tldr: Encoder-free multimodal LLMs appear to develop early Transformer layers that function as implicit, largely modality-independent audio and vision encoders.

papers.abstract: Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain-of-thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference-compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. Yet, it remains unclear what each iteration is actually computing, or whether the loop merely simulates a deeper untied stack. Here, we study directed permutation traversal, in which a model follows $H$ hops from a starting node and reports the node it reaches, so every intermediate hop has a known ground truth. We find that a minimum effective depth is necessary to solve the task, beyond which the degree of weight tying becomes the determining factor. For instance, a looped transformer with a four-layer block iterated eight times solves the task in every seed, while an identically-trained untied transformer of the same effective depth never does, succeeding only with a lower learning rate or supervision of its intermediate layers. Probing and intervening on the residual stream, we find that the looped model advances through the intermediate nodes gradually, forming a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, at that lower rate, exposes them only in its final layers. Taken together, our results recast looped transformers as iterative program learners, which allocate their iterations to successive steps of the algorithm and solve tasks that identically-trained untied models of the same effective depth do not. Code is available at https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop.
authors: Magnus Sesodia, Juil Sock, Philip Torr, Christian Schroeder de Witt
bullets: Studies directed permutation traversal, where each hop provides a known intermediate target.
Finds that sufficient effective depth is necessary, but weight tying strongly affects successful learning beyond that threshold.
A four-layer block looped for eight iterations solves the task across all seeds, while an equally deep untied model does not under identical training.
Residual-stream analysis shows looped models progressively represent intermediate nodes in an iteration-adaptive staircase.
Results support viewing looped transformers as iterative program learners rather than merely simulated deep stacks.
